en: [Page 1] Volume 18: The Saura Purāṇa composed by Vyāsa.
This book has been edited by Kāśīnātha Śāstrī, known by the surname Lele, and by those holding the title B.A.
(Bachelor of Arts).
It was printed by Vināyaka Gaṇeśa Āpaṭe at the Ānandāśrama Press in the city named Puṇya, using his own funds, and has been published.
This is the second edition. Śaka year 1846;
Christian year 1921.

Homage to that wielder of the Pināka bow, by whose command Virañci is the creator of the world, Hara is its protector, and he who is called Kālarudra is its destroyer. 1.
Naimiṣa forest is the most excellent of sacred fords, the supreme field among all fields, and the eternal refuge of sages. || 2 ||
The high-souled and most powerful devotees of Śiva, headed by Śaunaka,
were performing a long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra) there for the propitiation of Īśāna.
During that sacrificial session, by virtue of the great fortune of the sages,
the highly blessed Sūta, the best among those who know the Purāṇas, arrived to see the lord of sages.
Seeing him, those great-souled inhabitants of the Naimiṣa forest were delighted; intent on making inquiries, they questioned Romaharṣaṇa.
The sages said:
How was it previously [performed] by the Blessed One, the Sun, who is the very form of the Self?
The ancient Saura Purāṇa has been told; you ought to recount it to us here.
For you previously learned this directly from Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana;
O one of great austerity, there is no speaker of the Purāṇas superior to you.
There are many other disciples of that great-souled one as well;
nevertheless, out of affection for his disciples, you have been appointed to the Purāṇas.
O great sage, whatever other ancient texts have been spoken by you, they are sufficient; yet this [work] is endowed with devotion toward the beloved of Pārvatī.
We have heard that there is no liberation through sacrifices, nor through austerities, nor through gifts, nor by those other means; for without devotion to Śiva, there is no liberation. 10.
This divine Lord Bhānu is the eternal inner witness;
he speaks the truth of all things only after having known it, and not otherwise. (11)
[Page 11] "Indeed, therefore, there is great faith to hear the nectar from your mouth."
"O Sūta of firm vows, our Purāṇa, which causes the hair to stand on end, exists [within us].
Sūta said:
"Having bowed to the Sun, the supreme abode, who takes the form of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas..."
The triple truth, the source of the three worlds, the triple path, and the triple reality. || 13 ||
I shall fully proclaim this ancient Purāṇa dedicated to the Sun, which is based on the narratives of Śiva;
having heard it, a person shall quickly cast off the garment of sin.
Whether one recites both worlds or even just one world,
a person of faith— even if they have committed sinful deeds— shall go to the abode of the Sun.
Those twice-born who live by resorting to their ancient mode of livelihood, having pierced through that maṇḍala, attain union with Him (sāyujya). || 16 ||
Where the Sun himself is the speaker and his son Manu is the listener, O twice-born ones, the greatness is recounted by Śambhu; there is nothing superior to this.
This Purāṇa should be told to one who is righteous, free from malice, a twice-born man, devoted to his duty, and whose intellect is solely intent upon Śiva. 18.
There was Manu, the son of Sūrya, who was engaged in great austerity;
once that illustrious one went to the forest named Kāmika.
At the sacrifice of King Pratardana, which was accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
the great seers deliberated among themselves regarding the ultimate reality.
Those illustrious ones, Bhṛgu and the others, were unable to reach a definitive conclusion regarding the truth;
for while the Brahmins remained thus, their minds were deluded by Māyā.
To those whose minds were possessed by doubt, an incorporeal voice spoke:
"O best of Brahmins, perform penance; penance is the destroyer of ignorance. (22)
"They have heard the voice saying that everything is attained through austerity";
having heard this, all the sages, headed by Bhṛgu, had their sins burnt away.
Placing Mainu at their head, they went to the field of the twelve-fold Self, O learned ones;
it is renowned in the worlds as "Dvādaśāditya. (24)
And all these sages have had their sins burnt away by ascetic penance.
Behold me as the Supreme Deity, the all-pervading Lord who dwells within the heart of the universe.
Sūta said:
Having thus seen the Sun himself standing visibly before him,
Manu Vaivasvata then considered himself to have achieved his life's purpose.
Having established the Self within himself through his entire being,
that self-controlled Manu of noble vows, together with the sages, offered praise.
Manu said:
Salutations, salutations to the most excellent one, the giver of boons, who wears a garland of rays;
salutations to you, who consist of light, the infinite, the unconquered. 31.
Salutations to you, the eye of the three worlds, who are composed of the three qualities and are immortal;
salutations to Dharma, the swan, the cause of the birth of the universe.
Salutations to you who possess the bodies of both man and woman, who are perceived by the deluded,
who are beyond my knowledge, the Lord of all, the one with seven horses, and the triple-formed one.

Salutations to you who are the embodiment of the sacred utterances (vyāhṛtis), who possess three marks, who move swiftly, who have bay horses, and whose chariot is drawn by green steeds. Salutations to you! Salutations to the one whose vehicle is green! 34.
Salutations to you who possess one hundred thousand distinct marks, who possess many hundreds of thousands of marks, who wield the staff;
salutations to you who abide as one, who abide as two, and who abide as many.
To the one possessing the three powers, the white one, the sun, the supreme lord—
O God, you are Śiva, you are Hari, you are Brahmā, and you are the Lord of Heaven. || 36 ||
You alone are indeed the syllable *A*, the *Vaṣaṭ* call, *Svadhā*, and *Svāhā*;
apart from you, the Supreme Self, I do not perceive any other deity.
Having thus offered praise, the righteous Manu, together with the sages who longed for perfect insight, spoke to the Blessed One, who is composed of the three Vedas. (38)
But once that [object] is known, what is the nature of its cognition, and what is its essence? (41)
O Father, what was his conduct, and what sacred site (tīrtha) was presided over by him? O Lord, who were those residing at that tīrtha whom he favored? (42)
What is the definition of the Purāṇas and the sequence of religious observances?
And how is the rule for the conduct of the social classes and stages of life? (43)
"How is the śrāddha performed, and what is the procedure for expiation?
O Blessed One, you ought to explain all of this that has been asked here. (44)
O twice-born ones, having heard these words of Manu, the Blessed Lord Bhāskara began to explain in its entirety that which had been asked.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Praise of Naimiṣāraṇya and Other Matters," in the glorious Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 1 ||
Bhānu said:
Listen, my son, I shall proclaim the truth upon which [this work] is established—this Purāṇa, O highly fortunate one, which is a compendium of the meaning of all the Vedas. (1)
The Śruti declared: "That which is the true nature of the Blessed Lord, the Wielder of the Trident, by Him the entire universe is pervaded, and not by anything else. (2)
O lord of men, that very same self is the Lord Mahādeva together with Umā, the Blessed One whose form is consciousness, belonging to all living beings.
The one, absolute Śiva, the Great Lord, the God of gods, shines forth in many ways through his divine play in the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others.
Questioned by the gods, beginning with Brahmā, "Who are you, O god?", Śaṅkara replied, "I alone am [the one]; there is no other whatsoever," so says the Śruti.
At the beginning of creation, Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the two best of gods, emerged from Mahādeva, who is their very self and assumes forms for his divine play.
The knowers of that [reality] declare that one Supreme Self, the primordial creator and Lord, to be manifold; thus says the Śruti: "He is Indra, He is Mitra. (7)
There is nothing superior to him, nor is there anything even more minute;
by that great-souled Śaṅkara, this entire universe is filled.
Śiva alone, the stainless one, is to be meditated upon constantly by those seeking liberation;
having renounced everything else, he who is already liberated is truly released.
For that Great Lord, there is no action, nor any effect, nor bondage or liberation;
Maheśvara sports with Gaurī, whose nature is bliss. || 10 ||
The imperishable, supreme ether, the stainless light of Śiva—he who does not know that, what will he gain from the Vedas, even if he be a Brāhmaṇa? (11)
There is no other object to be known; Rudra alone is self-luminous and stainless.
When he is known, everything is known—so say the exponents of the Vedas. 12.
I, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śakra, and the other inhabitants of heaven, even today, long for the vision of Śambhu through various means. || 13 ||
O King, the Lord Śiva is known not by gifts, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice, but only through exclusive devotion. 14.
From which words turn back, unable to reach it along with the mind—from Bharga, the sustainer of the universe, the source of all, the Lord of Umā. (15)
His power consisting of knowledge is the imperishable Śivā, born of the mountain;
together with her, Mahādeva creates, protects, and destroys.
The ignorant declare a difference between those two, but not in the ultimate sense;
the non-difference of Śiva and Śivā is established, just like that of fire and its burning power. (17)
She is that supreme power, Māyā, the imperishable, unborn, and immutable daughter of the mountain;
she is Māyā who is the soul of the universe, O Rudra. Knowing her, one indeed becomes immortal. || 18 ||

In the manuscript designated as Chasaṃjñita, more than the verse beginning with "na tasya" is seen prior to it; specifically, the passage beginning with "dharmārthakāma" and ending with "vedasiddhānta" is additionally observed.
It is as follows:
Devotion to Śiva is truly the supreme cause for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; there is nothing else whatsoever on this earth that is so. (1)
He who desires happiness in the three worlds must always worship Sadāśiva;
for without devotion to Śiva, how can embodied beings attain bliss after death? (2)
Through devotion to Śiva, wealth, knowledge, fame, as well as the subjugation of enemies and victory—all this is attained; this is the truth, there is no doubt. (3)
Just as the word of the Veda declares, so too does a person obtain everything they desire for their mind— the destruction of disease as well as health.

If that is so, why do not all people practice devotion to Śiva? To this he replied: "When supreme happiness has been inscribed on the forehead by the Creator, then the intellect is awakened toward devotion to Śiva; it does not happen otherwise on this earth. (5)
The established doctrine of the Vedas is that when the attainment of bliss is inscribed upon the forehead, the mind becomes intent upon the service of Śiva.
15] One should [worship] the Lord, the Sovereign who pervades the universe, abiding within one's own self.
O King, by means of supreme devotion, one who knows this is liberated from the bonds.
Śaṅkara shines as his very manifestation alone and not by anything else;
for while he is shining, fire and the other elements do not shine at all.

When that Maheśvara is hidden, both knowledge and ignorance, the perishable and the imperishable, as well as the creator and the Lord of the world, do not appear as real entities; rather, the universe shines forth [as such] only from the perspective of appearance, not in reality. 21.
The entire universe is woven and interwoven within that Maheśvara; of this there is no doubt. When He is known, O lord of men, one is liberated from all fetters.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods, as well as the sages and the Manus—
all these are but playthings of that trident-bearing God of gods.
He alone is one, never manifold, and never of dual nature;
by His command the entire universe exists, governed by Him.
In the beginning of creation, the Lord Mahādeva, the Three-eyed One, sportively created Brahmā from his right limb for the purpose of creation. (25)
He gave the Vedas and Purāṇas to that foremost of the twice-born,
as well as [the knowledge of] Vāsudeva, the source of the universe, who is eternal and overflowing with the quality of goodness (sattva).
And for the sake of protection, Maheśvara created from his left side [the goddess],
and from his heart he created the one called Kālarudra, the cause of the world’s destruction.
The self-existent Śiva, who is devoid of qualities and the object of meditation for yogins, created [the universe];
indeed, the universe has arisen from him and abides within that Śaṅkara.
By his own divine play, he brings these three into dissolution right there;
he alone is the Self, Mahādeva, of all embodied beings. (29)
The Supreme Lord is to be known through knowledge joined with devotion;
I see no other deity superior to Mahādeva. (30)
The Vedas also declare that very same meaning during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara.
The Vedas said: He whom the wise yogis, whose latent impressions have been destroyed, perceive after restraining the aggregate of the senses—he alone is the Self, the Great Lord (Maheśvara). || 31 ||
That god whose servants are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Candra, and the others,
and by whose grace they live— that god is the Lord of Pārvatī.
Even now, we do not know that god who is the destroyer of Tripura, whose supreme nature even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, do not know.
May all the deities listen; this supreme word of ours is the truth:
there is no higher deity than Rudra Mahādeva. (34)
Just as there are no hairs on a tortoise, no horn on the head of a hare,
and no flower in the sky, so too there is nothing superior to Hara.
He who desires to attain happiness in this world without devotion to Śiva is like one who wishes to drink milk from the nipple on the neck of a goat.
The wise man should know Mahādeva as "I am this body.
What else remains to be known for the sake of liberation beyond this? (37)
Having worshipped the Great Goddess as Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, and Raudrī,
one should know that the state of Śaṅkara is that which the lords of yogins behold.
Having gradually moved through the circles and stationed oneself above the Śaṅkhinī,
that light which becomes manifest— one should know that to be the state of Śākara.
Having abandoned the path of the gods (devayāna) as well as the northern path of the ancestors (pitṛyāṇa), that subtle sound which arises from the sky is the designator of Śaṅkara. (40)
The omniscient Lord, the wielder of the trident, whose face is turned in every direction, the progenitor of all beings—he alone is Maheśvara. 42.
Those wise ones who behold the Lord, the consort of Umā, residing within the lotus of the heart even as small as the tip of a hair—verily, for them there is eternal peace. 42.
The All-pervading Lord dwells within the earth, yet the earth does not know Him at all;
salutations to that Self of the earth, whose form is the earth itself. (43)
He stands within the waters, yet they do not know the Supreme Lord who has transcended them;
salutations to Him, the soul of water, whose very form is water itself.
The immeasurable Self dwells within the body, yet one never truly knows Him;
salutations to that Fire-Self whose form is ever-present. || 45 ||
Salutation to that one whose self is wind, for whom wind is the very form, and who remains incessantly within the wind yet the wind does not perceive him as supreme. || 46 ||
He who eternally abides in the ether does not perceive that Hara as the ether;
salutations to Him whose very form is the ether, the Self of the ether. || 47 ||
The deity who abides in the sun does not perceive Śaṅkara as the sun;
salutation to that one whose very form is the sun, to the Sun-Self. || 48 ||
Salutation to that one whose nature is the moon, whom the omnipresent moon dwelling within the moon does not know as eternal, and whose very form is the moon. 49.
Salutations to that form which, while residing in the sacrificer, is never known by him;
salutations to the self of the sacrificer who is that very form. 50.
We have originated from you, and our dissolution is likewise in you alone;
by your grace, O Bull-bannered One, we have attained the status of authoritative means of knowledge.
Bhānu said:
O lord of men, having thus heard the praise of the Vedas, the Blessed Lord, the husband of Girijā, became manifest before those Vedas.
Resembling ten million suns, with a thousand eyes, a thousand feet,
and a thousand heads, that Puruṣa has the sun, moon, and fire as his eyes.
"Greater than the gross is the gross; subtler than the subtle is the Supreme," thus spoke the Blessed One, Maheśvara, the God of gods. (54)
Īśvara said: "O Vedas, by my grace you shall become honored by the world."
O best of Brahmins, they perform their rites depending upon you, and not otherwise.
Whatever action anyone performs by transgressing you,
that action shall become fruitless for them through your divine power.
This applies to daily rites, occasional rites, rites for specific desires, and whatever else is a means to liberation.
Thinking that "your word is not otherwise," the wise man does not grieve.
Those men who, disregarding you, compose treatises,
shall be tormented in hell for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras.
"For the sake of the highest good in the three worlds, there exists nothing superior to the Veda;
there is no doubt in this matter—this boon has been granted by me. (59)
Those twice-born ones who shall indeed recite this supreme hymn composed by you,
their study shall become meritorious through my grace.
Bhānu said:
"This divine splendor, which shines as the all-pervading absolute, [is that]."
Go for refuge to that very one, if you desire the supreme state. || 1 ||
That very same [reality], abiding in all beings, is pure consciousness alone, beyond darkness, imperishable, devoid of qualities, pure, blissful, supreme, and immutable. || 2 ||
To all beings, this is directly perceptible; for those lacking knowledge, it is the opposite.
[They do not see] the creator of the universal illusion, who possesses eighteen forms.
One should know Mahādeva, who is attainable through devotion, as abiding within the self—
that eternal Mahādeva, who is identical with the self and the object of meditation for yogis.
"Resorting to supreme devotion, attain the highest Nirvana;
various pilgrimages and diverse sacrifices have already been performed."
For those who, throughout thousands of births, develop devotion toward Śiva,
even a mere fragment of that devotion gives rise to the supreme, inexhaustible dharma.
"Therefore, there is no duty higher than that," so say the exponents of the Vedas;
yet, duty has been declared to be of many kinds by the sages who perceive the truth. (7)
In that regard, the supreme, eternal Śiva-dharma is inexhaustible;
whereas through sacrifice, pilgrimage, recitation, and charity, dharma may be achieved by many means.
The hardship of seeking spiritual accomplishments brings suffering upon the prosperity of others;
however, the Dharma of Śiva does not depend upon such accomplishments.
If even this form of sin, accumulated over thousands of births, were to be reduced to ashes by the power of Śambhu of immeasurable splendor, [it would be so]. (10)
Even if one has always committed sin, if one worships Śiva even once,
one is not tainted by that sin and goes to the state of Maheśvara.
"Even if they are devoted to sin, those who remember Mahādeva should be known as great-souled ones; this I speak as the truth. (12)
[It is] that which arose in the Padma-kalpa and was proclaimed by Brahmā. || 14 ||
"O King, listen with supreme faith as I speak;
having first bowed down to the Lord, the ruler of the world, I shall relate it to you. (15)
In the first age, the Kṛtayuga, there was a most righteous king known as Indradyumna, the sole sovereign over the seven islands.
His son was the highly fortunate one, renowned as Sudyumna;
he shone with all sovereign powers, just like the Lord of Śacī in heaven.
While that king was ruling the entire earth, staying there in the delightful city of Pratiṣṭhāna on the charming bank of the Gaṅgā.
Once, the Blessed One, the great sage Tṛṇabindu,
came there to see that Sudyumna, who was pleasing to behold.
Seeing that sage approaching, the mighty-armed king, who was intent upon the worship of Rudra, rose from his seat, stepped forward, and stood with palms joined in reverence.
Having saluted him appropriately, he then offered him an excellent seat;
he presented him with everything, including the honey-mixture (madhuparka) and other offerings, according to the prescribed rites.
"Today I am blessed and my purpose is fulfilled; my life has become fruitful, O best of sages, because the Blessed One has come to see me. (22)
"For what purpose have you come, O Brahmin? I have accomplished my purpose, O observer of noble vows.
Especially since you are a devotee of Śaṅkara, nothing here is difficult for you to obtain."
Bhānu said:
Having heard the words of Sudyumna, the high-minded sage spoke, being filled with the singular bliss of tasting the nectar of devotion to Śiva. (24)
Tṛṇabindu said:
"O King, what you have spoken is exactly so; there is no doubt.
Nevertheless, having heard of your conduct, I am filled with wonder. (25)
O King, you have arrived out of respect for your own birth;
O mighty-armed one, tell me, for I have a great curiosity to hear it. (26)
The Blessed One alone knows [this]; he is all-pervading and the Great Lord. || 32 ||
Even if this was performed without the thought "this is merit," whatever chanting of names such as "Bring! or "Strike! has been done— [33]
By that merit, his misdeeds are reduced to ashes;
it is my firm conviction that not even a trace of sin remains in him. (34)
Sudyumna said:
Having heard those words of the wise Citragupta, he duly honored Suvyāḍi according to the prescribed rites. (35)
In the meantime, there appeared a celestial chariot that fulfills all desires,
radiant as the sun's heat and resplendent with divine women.
O bull among sages, having ascended that which was brought by the divine messengers and having obtained the permission of Dharmarāja, I went to Amarāvatī.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there for ten thousand yugas,
I then went to the abode of Brahmā, where I was honored by Brahmā himself.
There, having enjoyed desired pleasures until the end of the kalpa, I shall then come here to this earth to experience the remainder of my karma. (39)
"O sage of noble vows, I am born in the lineage of the royal seer Indradyumna; by the grace of Śūlin, I remember my former birth. (40)
Sudden devotion has arisen in me toward Īśvara, who is worshipped by the thirty gods.
Who knows the majesty of Maheśa, the Supreme Self? (41)
Even from the mere utterance of his name, this fruit is obtained;
therefore, having understood this, one should chant the names of Śambhu, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
"The sages declared that liberation rests in the palm of his hand.
Bhānu said:
"Thus, this entire life-story of that wise one has been told in its entirety."
Having heard Suna's words, the sage was struck with wonder again and again.
Having embraced that high-souled bull among kings, he said, "I am going to my own hermitage," and departed. (44)
O King, this life-story of the high-souled Sudyumna has been told to you;
whoever reads it with devotion goes to the world of Brahmā.

151. Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Narrative of Sudyumna," in the *Śrīsaura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrībrahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Bhānu and Manu. || 3 ||
Manu said:
What did that sage do next after receiving [the message] from the presence of the king?
O Blessed One, O Lord, tell me the name of that hermitage.
Bhānu said:
On the bank of the Revā is a great holy place known as Jāleśvara, the hermitage of the sage Tṛṇabindu, frequented by perfected beings (siddhas). || 2 ||
Having gone there, that best of sages, endowed with devotion to Bhava,
installed a Śiva-liṅga and undertook a pilgrimage.
Manu said:
"O Blessed One, tell me truly which secret holy places (tīrthas) Śiva is present in, as well as others."
Bhānu said:
"The city named Vārāṇasī is the most excellent of holy places (tīrthas) and the most excellent of sacred fields (kṣetras); it is dear to the trident-bearing God."
In this place, the Lord Viśveśvara bestows upon all embodied beings here the supreme liberating knowledge that releases them from the cycle of worldly existence.
There, the Gaṅgā, consisting of Brahman, flows northward in embodied form;
she destroys all sins when seen, touched, or saluted.
"There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā, especially at Vārāṇasī.
Keeping in his mind the question, "What is that which brings the highest welfare? he departed. (11)
Where the blessed Sanatkumāra himself, the foremost of yogins and the disciple of Nandīśvara, took his rest upon that mountain of the Himavat.
It was crowded with hosts of gods, frequented by yakṣas and gandharvas,
and teeming with siddhas, cāraṇas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and apsarases.
There the Gaṅgā and Mandākinī shine, removing all suffering,
adorned with golden lotuses and other captivating flowers.
Having reached his hermitage, the great sage Pārāśarya,
having saluted him according to custom, sat down before him.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he spoke these words.
Vyāsa said:
The terrible Kali age has arrived, which excludes one from the path of merit,
is devoted to heretical conduct, and is crowded with people who follow the ways of barbarians.
In that age, there will be unrighteous beings, cruel, lacking in wealth and conduct, and small-minded; the Brahmins will become officiants for Śūdras.
In the Kali age, Brahmins indeed will not perform ritual bathing, worship of the gods, giving of gifts, fire-offerings, libations to the ancestors, or the private recitation of sacred texts.
The lowest of Brahmins will not study the Vedas for the sake of their own spiritual welfare;
rather, in the Kali age, they will study the Vedas solely for the purpose of receiving gifts.
Taking refuge in Puruṣottama, the twice-born will in the Kali age become devoted to reviling Śiva; Mādhava shall not be their protector.
This verse does not appear in the Saṃjñita manuscript.
23] Having abandoned their respective functions, they subsist upon the functions of others.
But when the Kali age has arrived, they will become Brahmins and the like.
Seeing these people devoted to sin, kings will become indiscriminate when the Kali age arrives, vainly conceited about their own caste.
Seeing Brāhmaṇas seated on high thrones at that time, the Śūdras of small intellect do not move away when the Kali age has arrived.
In the Kali age, there will be those wearing saffron robes, the Nirgranthas, the naked ones, the Kāpālikas, as well as Buddhists, Vaiśeṣikas, and Jains. (25)
But the lowest of the twice-born will become sellers of the fruits of penance and sacrifice;
and there will be ascetics by the hundreds and by the thousands.
In the Kali age, they revile Mahādeva, the supreme liberator from saṃsāra, as well as his high-souled devotees and the Brāhmaṇas. (27)
In the Kali age, wicked-souled royal servants beat Brahmins, yet the king does not restrain them even upon seeing it. (28)
"In such a terrible Kali age, O twice-born one, what is that which brings about the highest good?
Tell me, O Blessed One, that supreme means of liberation from the cycle of worldly existence. (29)

180. Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Kali Age and the Greatness of Vārāṇasī," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Bhānu and Manu.
Sanatkumāra said:
"Go to Vārāṇasī, O Vyāsa, where Śiva, the Lord of the Universe, resides;
there the law of the ages (yuga-dharma) does not exist, nor is the earth ever subject to the influence of time."
The *liṅga* of Viśveśvara is called the Jyotirliṅga;
upon seeing it, a living being shall not enter the cycle of worldly existence again for even a moment. (2)
Go and behold the supreme Liṅga there, O son of Satyavatī;
you shall attain the highest liberation, which is very difficult even for the gods to obtain.
Having bathed in the meritorious waters of the Gaṅgā, behold the Supreme Lord of the Universe;
He will grant you the supreme knowledge by which you shall become liberated.
As soon as you have seen the god Viśveśvara and remain [there] for that moment,
all those sages will come to see you.
"Speak on their behalf, according to my word: [explain] their supreme knowledge of Maheśvara."
Thus, the son of Satyavatī, the foremost among the devotees of Maheśvara, having heard that majesty in its entirety from his own guru Sanatkumāra, [proceeded].
Having prostrated with devotion before his guru Rudra, who is served by Brahmā and the other gods,
Vyāsa, together with his disciples, departed quickly toward Vārāṇasī.
Manu said:
O Blessed One, honored by the entire universe, tell me what Vyāsa did after going to Vārāṇasī, which is frequented by perfected beings, seers, and sages. 9.
Bhānu said:
Having reached Kāśī, the righteous-souled sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana bathed duly in the Jāhnavī and offered libations to the gods and the ancestors.
He went to see Viśveśvara, the stainless Jyotirliṅga; having worshipped him with his whole being, he prostrated himself like a staff.
Seated upon the southern form of the God, the great sage gazed at the Viśveśvara Liṅga while muttering the Śatarudriya;
in an instant, a stainless light beyond the Liṅga manifested.
Subtler than the subtle, the supreme bliss beyond darkness.
That light of Maheśvara, which is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and which possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns,
is established in the Vedāntas.
And from the sight of that wise sage, the son of Parāśara,
there arose the divine knowledge of Maheśvara, which is absolute and auspicious.
Then the sage, liberated while living, considered himself to have achieved his purpose, freed from the threefold suffering, non-dual, devoid of qualities, and tranquil.
"Aha! How is it that the Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe, is not served by anyone?
Upon seeing him, stainless knowledge has arisen within me in an instant.
Salutations to you, the Blessed One, the Lord of the Universe, the wielder of the trident!"
To the wielder of the Pināka bow, the creator of the world, who revolves the universal illusion.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Pārvatī, who is difficult to comprehend and immeasurable, whose form is supreme bliss, who is fond of devotion, and who is subtle.
Homage to the one who is the foundation of the world, the cause of the world's birth,
the destroyer, whose form consists of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and the impeller of them.
O Lord of All, a person such as I knows [Thee] in truth;
even the Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs and the sequence of the Upaniṣads, do not know [Thee]. || 21 ||
Bhānu said: Then, within that Great God, the supreme light, the consumer of the universe—
the trident-bearing one of immeasurable self, whose banner is the bull— manifested himself.
Then, out of compassion, he spoke these words to him with an auspicious voice: "Choose a boon that pleases your heart; I shall grant it to you. (23)
Vyāsa said:
"O Blessed One, O Śaṅkara, I have achieved my purpose through the sight of you;
knowledge concerning you has arisen, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. (24)
"O Lord of the gods of gods, grant me unswerving devotion toward you alone, the Supreme Lord; no other boon is desired by me. (25)
Bhānu said:
"So be it," and having granted this boon to Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor, the Lord of Gods vanished in an instant before that king of sages. || 26 ||
Therefore, no other devotee of Śiva was born in the world superior to Vyāsa—neither Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, nor the high-minded Arjuna. (27)
Thus, having obtained boons from Hara, the lordly sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana went there to behold those liṅgas which were present. || 28 || 208 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Granting of Boons by Mahādeva," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Bhānu and Gaṇu. || 5 ||
The sages said:
O Sūta, tell us which divine liṅgas the sage went to see, and describe their greatness in its entirety.
Sūta said:
O best of sages, I shall relate that very same account which was previously told by Bhānu to Manu; listen as I speak it.
To the southeast of Avimukta is a pond renowned throughout the three worlds,
where Śiva, the Lord of the Universe, is eternally present.
O best of the twice-born, that bath which is difficult even for the gods to obtain—
those by whom that water has been drunk with devotion are indeed Rudras upon this earth.
O you of excellent vows, three signs arise in their hearts:
that water is difficult to obtain, and it remains indeed sealed within them. (5)
There, the son of Satyavatī, having bathed according to the prescribed rites and beheld Avimukteśvara, then proceeded to Lāṅgalīśa.
There, the gods beginning with Brahmā serve the wielder of the trident;
by the mere sight of him, the Pāśupata knowledge arises.
That sage went afterwards to see the Lord of Tāraka,
where at the time of death the Blessed One bestows that supreme knowledge.
In that very place where he installed the supreme liṅga of the God,
by the mere sight of which one dispels even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having seen that supreme liṅga, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī,
went to see Śukreśvara, the bestower of all spiritual perfections.

It was there that the sage Śukra, possessed of immeasurable splendor, propitiated [the deity] and obtained the science of restoration to life (saṃjīvanī), which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
In the south-eastern quarter of the deity stands a beautiful well;
bathing there bestows the auspicious fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Having bathed in that well and beheld Śiva as Śukreśvara,
the sage went to see Brahmeśvara, where Brahmā himself resides in his cosmic form (Virāṭ).
Having performed most formidable austerities for the pleasure of the Lord of Pārvatī,
Brahmā attained the status of Brahman, as did other great sages who attained Yoga.
By the sight of that *liṅga*, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
then the Blessed One went again to the imperishable Oṃkāreśvara.
O twice-born ones, by remembering that Linga, one is liberated from all sins; there, indeed, the subtle Śiva eternally resides in person.
For the sake of favoring the worlds, he is the liberator from the bonds of Paśu;
there, the perfected ones of the Pāśupata tradition [worship] the Lord Oṃkāreśvara.
Having worshipped [it], those best of the twice-born attained supreme perfection;
one who has fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight at that liṅga—
This verse is not present in the manuscripts designated as Gha, Ṅa, Cha, and Sa.
27] If one should remain awake, one shall attain supreme accomplishment.
Then the son of Satyavatī went to Kṛttivāseśvara.
There, where the gods headed by Brahmā, as well as sages of purified souls devoted to the recitation of the Rudra-mantras, worship Mahādeva.
At Kṛttivāseśvara is the Liṅga; there are many Brahmins who perform divine sports (līlās).
To the eastern quarter of the deity is the great lake known as Haṃsatīrtha.
Those great-souled ones who, having bathed there, behold the auspicious Mahādeva Kṛttivāseśvara, are indeed honored by Brahmā and the other gods. || 22 ||
He who beholds with devotion even once the omnipresent Lord Kṛttivāseśvara does not fall into saṃsāra again; he is indeed Rudra himself—of this there is no doubt. (23)
Having bathed at Haṃsatīrtha and having worshipped with supreme devotion the omnipresent Lord Kṛttivāseśvara, Śiva, who is clothed in animal hide; || 24 ||
He does not fall into saṃsāra at all; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
He went to see Ratneśvara, where liberation is firmly established.
The fruit of merely seeing that linga cannot be described;
this yoga, which is superior to all else, is practiced by those who know the Vedas.
O twice-born ones, this Pāśupata yoga, which liberates from the bonds of the individual soul (paśu), is fully accomplished in twelve years once the Pāśupata [observance] has been correctly performed.
Then, upon seeing the light at Ratneśvara, that best of men,
the great sage Pārāśarya, worshipped Ratneśvara.
To behold the Lord of the God of Gods, Vṛddhakāleśvara, he went there;
in that liṅga, Mahādeva always resides through his divine play. (29)
O twice-born ones, for the sake of favoring the worlds, Viśvabhuj, together with me, [established] all those divine lingas that exist upon the earth.
When Vṛddhakāleśvara is seen, it is as if all [the other shrines] have been seen; of this there is no doubt.
To the east of the deity is a well frequented by sages.
It was filled with waters of merit by Śambhu, the God of gods;
those ordinary people who drank even three handfuls of its water [attained liberation].
Nature is liberated from them, and they become beings with liberated souls.
There, O brahmins, Dvaipāyana, having performed his ablutions with a concentrated mind, [33]
Having fully worshipped the Buddha-kāleśvara-liṅga, he then departed for the delightful bank of the Mandākinī, which is frequented by sages and perfected beings.
There is the unsurpassed Mokṣaliṅga named Madhyameśvara,
where the gods beginning with Brahmā and the sages beginning with Sanaka reside.
Desiring the vision of Śiva, they worship the supreme liṅga;
having bathed in the Mandākinī and beheld Madhyameśvara, the sage indeed [attains his goal]. (36)
Having bathed at Ghaṇṭākarṇa and installed that pure, auspicious Liṅga,
the best of sages attained supreme knowledge.
Having seen Vyāseśvara Śiva there at Terest,
wherever one may die, one shall be as if dead in Vārāṇasī.
Then the son of Satyavatī went to behold the Lord Kapardīśvara, that supreme Liṅga of the Supreme Lord, like a lordly elephant;
there is an unsurpassed sacred bathing place (tīrtha) there named Piśācamocana.
"The great sage has said that it is a staircase to the world of Rudra. || 40 ||
Those who shall behold Kapardīśa have achieved their purpose; there is no doubt that, having assumed human bodies, they are indeed Rudras—of this there is no doubt. (41)
Having bathed at that sacred ford and offered libations to the gods and ancestors,
the sage worshipped the Lord Kapardīśvara and departed.

250 || Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Vārāṇasī, Liṅgas, and the Himavat," in the glorious Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 6 ||
Sūta said:
The blessed Lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana went once again to the god Dakṣeśvara, who bestows success upon his devotees.
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of liberation from that sin which arose in Dakṣa Prajāpati due to his contempt for Śiva, [he performed penance] at that liṅga.
Having propitiated the Lord of the gods for many hundreds of years,
the Blessed One, the God of gods, together with Umā, became pleased with him.
[29] Having harbored enmity toward Śambhu in his mind, O you of excellent vows,
Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, performed a sacrifice on the bank of the Ganges.
To that sacrifice were invited the hosts of deities headed by Indra,
as well as sages, seers, perfected beings (siddhas), and kings of celebrated prowess.
And Brahmā, born from the lotus, was summoned along with Viṣṇu by that wise one; and all the gods were summoned for the sake of their sacrificial portions.
Seeing them deprived of Śiva, he spoke thus to Dakṣa.
Brahmā said:
"Alas, O Dakṣa! Great fool, evil-minded one, what have you done?"
"How is it that all the gods have been summoned together, yet Śaṅkara is not? (13)
That Śaṅkara, the Lord of the Universe, is the inner witness of all embodied beings;
in the ultimate sense, he alone is the enjoyer of all sacrifices. 14.
And all these sages are your assistants;
they do not know the supreme nature of Mahādeva, the wielder of the trident.
And these gods, Śakra and the others, have come as partakers of the sacrifice;
deluded by his māyā, they all do not recognize the wielder of the Pināka bow.
By the touch of the dust of whose feet I attained the state of Brahman, as well as the established order of dharma and adharma, and the system of castes and stages of life. [p. 30] 19.
They abide by the command of that god of gods, the wielder of the trident;
and she is the supreme power, Gaurī, who moves about assuming forms according to her own will.
"O evil-minded one, shrouded in darkness, you think, 'She is your daughter.
Who knows her to be the Sovereign of the Universe, who forms half the body of the Lord? (21)

Even now I do not know [the extent of] the Discus-wielder; what then can be said of Śakra? [I do not know him] even when the Wielder of the Pināka is with Gaurī, who assumes whatever form she desires by her own will.
It is true, without a doubt, that he causes the entire universe to revolve;
that very Maheśvara binds us and others who are like cattle. (23)
"He alone is the God who liberates the bound souls (paśus); such is the Vedic revelation. By the mere chanting of His names, the cage of sin is shattered.
O evil-minded Dakṣa, why is that God not worshipped by you?"
Where there is contempt for Śambhu, the wise should certainly not remain. || 25 ||
Having spoken thus, Brahmā departed while being praised by the great seers.
Sūta said:
When the four-faced god, the grandfather of all the worlds, had departed,
Dadhīci himself, the foremost of sages, spoke to Dakṣa.
Dadhīci said:
"O Dakṣa, why is Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe, the eternal witness of all actions, and the God of gods, not worshipped by you? (28)
How can one know the wielder of the trident, whose very embodiment is knowledge, without the grace of Him for whom the syllable Om is the expressive designation? (29)
Rudra, who is sung of as the one and only in all the Vedas— by even a mere fragment of his grace, liberation becomes a handmaid.
Whether out of incidental circumstance, curiosity, greed, fear, or even ignorance,
a mortal who utters the name "Hara" is liberated from all sins.
"Alas, O Dakṣa, your ignorance is the cause of your own destruction!
Having heard these words of Dadhīci, the discerning Dakṣa—
O Brahmins, he spoke to Dadhīci in the presence of Śakra and the other gods.
Dakṣa said:
"O best of the twice-born, I do not perceive anyone other than the divine Nārāyaṇa as the cause of all things; that there is no such [other cause] is indeed firmly established. (34)
Dadhīci said:
"That deity who, together with Umā, is called Soma by the wise—he alone is the cause and none other; for indeed, such is the Vedic revelation even regarding Viṣṇu. (35)
Therefore, O Dakṣa, why is he who is superior to all the gods, the moon-crested Lord, not worshipped in all sacrifices? 36.
"That which you have determined—that Viṣṇu is the protector of the sacrifice—will quickly turn out otherwise, even as the Lord of Kamalā looks on. (37)
And all these Brāhmaṇas who hate Maheśvara shall become speakers of the Vedas with their minds afflicted by darkness. 38.
All those devoted to the practices of heretics go to hell;
indeed, when the Kali age has arrived, they become impoverished priests for Śūdras.
Rudra is superior to all, the liberator from the bonds of the bound;
may you never have a fate that turns away from him and leads to the performance of sacrifices for others.
Thus did the eminent sage Dadhīci depart for his own hermitage,
Oṃkāra, frequented by sages, on the bank of the Narmadā.
In the meantime, Gaurī, who is Śivā and whose nature is the supreme ether,
heard the account of Dakṣa’s sacrifice from the mouth of the divine sage.
Beholding Rudra, who is superior to all, the shatterer of the afflictions of those who bow to him, whose singular form is supreme bliss, the Queen of the Gods gazed upon him. (43)
The Goddess said: "This Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, who was my father in a previous birth—how is it that he proceeded to perform a sacrifice while disregarding us both? (44)
O Śaṅkara, all the gods were summoned together with Viṣṇu—the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts. || 45 ||
The ṛṣis, the munis, the siddhas, the daityas, and those who are dānavas;
the highly fortunate kings, as well as the gandharvas and the kinnaras. (46)
"O you who are compassionate toward your devotees, quickly destroy the sacrifice of that scorner; by that, joy arises within me. (47)
Having thus heard the words of the Goddess, Śambhu, the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
instantly created the exceedingly powerful Vīrabhadra.
He had a thousand lion-faces, possessed a radiance equal to the fire of universal destruction, had a thousand arms, wore matted hair, and was terrifying to the wicked. 49.
The God who grants boons to his devotees, whose eyes are the sun, moon, and fire;
and the goddess Bhadrakālī, the terrifying one, who arose from the wrath of Umā. (50)
And hundreds of other goddesses and Rudras were born from his pores;
then the mighty Vīrabhadra appeared together with Bhadrakālī.
Dispatched by the God of gods with the intent to destroy Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
he went to Dakṣa’s sacrifice and reduced it to ashes, O twice-born ones.
Then Dakṣa, having seen that miraculous deed and being overwhelmed with fear,
quickly went for refuge to the trident-bearing Vīrabhadra.
O twice-born ones, Vīrabhadra, an ocean of the nectar of compassion, spoke to that Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, for the sake of his liberation from sin.
Vīrabhadra said:
"Go, O Dakṣa, to Vārāṇasī, which destroys all sins, where Śaṅkara resides for the sake of showing grace to the worlds. (55)
"By the grace of the Blessed One, the God of gods, the wielder of the trident,
you shall attain liberation in this very body."
Sūta said:
Having heard the words of Vīrabhadra, the highly intelligent Dakṣa,
having abandoned all attachments, went quickly to Vārāṇasī.
Having installed the great liṅga on the delightful bank of the Gaṅgā and having worshipped it with supreme devotion, he attained dissolution into that very liṅga.
O best of sages, the majesty of Dakṣeśvara has been told;
now the majesty of Trilocana is being described by me.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Dakṣeśvara and Other Matters," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
Sūta said:
No liṅga superior to Trilocana is seen in Vārāṇasī.
O best of the twice-born, whatever lingas are established in Vārāṇasī become as if already seen when the three-eyed Liṅga has been beheld.
The three-eyed God of gods thus destroys even countless sins, whether committed knowingly or unknowingly. (3)
The three-eyed God of gods grants supreme liberation even to all living beings who are bound by the noose of Māyā.
The Liṅga faces west and is adorned with a serpent-girdle;
by the mere sight of it, one obtains the fruit of worshipping ten million Liṅgas.
Having thoroughly worshipped Trilocana, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana went to see Kāmeśvara, the unsurpassed Siddha-liṅga.
There, the Great Lord Maheśvara, the God of gods, being pleased, bestowed upon Durvāsas various supernatural powers (siddhis) that are difficult for anyone else to attain.
Furthermore, another boon was granted by the trident-bearing God of gods:
that [merit] shall belong to all austerities performed as well as those being performed.
O Sage, anger is said to be the cause of destruction; may it not befall you in any other way. To its south lies what is known as Kāmakuṇḍa.
Having bathed there with devotion and beheld Śiva as Kāmeśvara,
a person is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and attains the supreme goal.
Moreover, even the four-faced god Brahmā does not know the number of other lingas situated in Vārāṇasī.
Who indeed can describe his majesty, except for the gods and Maheśvara himself?
Or perhaps Nandīśvara knows it, by the grace of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Then, O best of the twice-born, the large-eyed lady went to see the supreme goddess Śivā, where that auspicious goddess was present.
Having seen her and worshipped her according to the rules with devotion, that great sage composed a hymn of praise for Gaurī, who is the very embodiment of supreme bliss.
Vyāsa said:
O large-eyed one, salutations to you, O Śivā, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman!
You alone are the mother of all the celestial dwellers, beginning with Brahmā.
Straight, coiled, and subtle, it bestows the accomplishment of yoga. || 16 ||
Svāhā, Svadhā, Mahāvidyā, Medhā, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Satī, Dākṣāyaṇī, Vidyā, and Śivā, who consists of all powers. (17)
Aparṇā, Ekaparṇā, and likewise Ekaikapāṭalā. || 18 ||
Umā, Haimavatī, Kalyāṇī, and Caitramātṛkā as well.
Khyāti is the highly fortunate Prajñā, renowned in the world as Gaurī;
she is the Mother of the Gaṇas, the Great Goddess, Nandinī, and Jātavedasī. ||19||
Sāvitrī, Varadā, Puṇyā, Pāvanī, the world-renowned Lokaviśrutā, Āryatī, Niyatī, Raudrī, Durgā, Bhadrā, and Pramāthinī. (20)
Kālarātrī, Mahāmāyā, Revatī, Bhūtanāyikā, Gautamī, Kauśikī, Ārthā, Caṇḍī, Kātyāyanī, and Satī. || 21 ||
She who has the bull as her emblem, the wielder of the trident, the supreme practitioner of celibacy, the mother of Mahendra and Upendra, Pārvatī, whose vehicle is the lion. || 22 ||
Having thus praised him with those divine and auspicious names,
O best of the twice-born, Vyāsa felt his purpose fulfilled in Vārāṇasī.
In Vārāṇasī there is Viśālākṣī, the Gaṅgā, and Śiva as Viśveśvara; devotion to Paśupati is also there—indeed, this quartet is difficult to find. (24)
O twice-born ones, he who beholds Viśālākṣī after bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā obtains the unsurpassed fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. Thus,
a portion of the majesty of Vārāṇasī has been recounted by me.
Whoever recites or even hears this attains the state of Maheśvara.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Trilocana and Other Matters," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
The sages said: What is the defining characteristic of the Purāṇas, and what is the fruit obtained by giving them?
Also, [tell us] specifically regarding other gifts and religious observances.
[Please explain] the characteristics of those castes and stages of life exactly as they are,
as well as the rules for ancestral rites (śrāddha) and how expiation (prāyaścitta) should be performed.
O Sūta, you ought to tell us all of this in its entirety:
the Mātsya, the Gāruḍa, and after that, the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa. (11)
Two parts are declared to be the one known as the Brahmāṇḍa;
the remaining portions are the Upapurāṇas, which have been mentioned by the learned.
This is the unsurpassed Saura Khila of the Brahma Purāṇa, joined with two Saṃhitās, meritorious, and based upon the narratives of Śiva. (13)
The first was spoken by Sanatkumāra, and the second was uttered by Sūrya;
this most meritorious compendium is renowned as the destroyer of sins.
O twice-born ones, this ancient Purāṇa was formerly narrated by the Sun to Vaivasvata Manu; it is the best among all gifts. (15)
O best of the twice-born, whatever gifts are renowned in the worlds, he who gives them to a Brahmin devoted to Śiva and rich in asceticism [obtains their full merit]. 16.
On the fourteenth day, one endowed with faith who gives the first Purāṇa, the Brāhma, obtains the fruit of all of them; of this there is no doubt. (17)
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā,
who gives a gift on the day of his preceptor dedicated to Brahmā.

On the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), being self-restrained and pure, one who offers [this] to a Vaiṣṇava Brahmin learned in the Vedas shall obtain the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, dedicated to Viṣṇu.
O twice-born ones, he who gives [this] to one learned in the Vedas shall attain the station of Viṣṇu;
and he who gives the Bhāgavata to a devotee of the Sun, O brahmins, [attains the same].
Freed from all sins and devoid of all diseases,
he shall live for more than a hundred years and, at the end, attain the state of Vaivasvata.
The third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha is known as Akṣayā;
on that lunar day, one who has restrained the self [should give] to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires.
One who, endowed with faith, gives the Purāṇa known as the Bhaviṣya, obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. (23)
But he who, with a restrained mind, gives [an image of] Mārkaṇḍeya on the seventh lunar day,
being freed from all sins, attains the world of the Sun.
One should indeed offer the Āgneya [oblation] to one who has maintained the sacred fires;
he obtains the eternal fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. || 25 ||
He who, with a concentrated mind, gives the Nāradīya [Purāṇa] to a twice-born devotee of Śiva on the fourteenth day, is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 26 ||
He who, being composed, gives this *Brahmavaivarta* to a Vaiṣṇava,
attains the world of Brahmā, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
one should indeed give a Liṅga made of excellent materials to a preeminent Brahmin who is devoted to the worship of Śiva.
Freed from all sins and endowed with all sovereign powers, he goes to the abode of Maheśvara, which stands above all worlds. || 29 ||
He who, having become self-restrained on the twelfth lunar day, gives a boar to an ascetic Brahmin, goes indeed to the world of Viṣṇu.
O best of Brahmins, by giving the Skanda [Purāṇa] on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight dedicated to Śiva,
one becomes a possessor of knowledge through the grace of Mahādeva.
On the twelfth or the fourteenth day, one should give an excellent dwarf image;
he attains that supreme, imperishable world of the deity. || 32 ||
On the fourteenth day, one should give alms to a self-restrained yogi;
[one thereby obtains] whatever merit comes from all forms of giving and whatever fruit comes from all sacrifices.
The wise man attains that fruit and, in the end, the supreme state of Śiva;
he should give a fish to a preeminent Brahmin during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa).
Liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
O twice-born ones, one should offer a gift related to Garuḍa on the day of Śivacaturdaśī for the sake of Śiva.
One obtains the unsurpassed fruit of a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices by giving that which is known as the Brahmāṇḍa to a devotee of Śiva. || 36 ||
O you of excellent vows, when the sun’s southern course has begun, or during an eclipse of the moon or even the sun, one should do so with devotion before Śiva.
One attains the leadership of the Gaṇas of the trident-bearing God of gods.
Thus has been described the sequence of the Purāṇas and the fruit that results from giving them as a gift.
O Brahmins, that which Sūrya himself spoke has been declared in brief.
Whoever should recite this chapter in the presence of Mahādeva, [attains the highest state]. (39)
Completely liberated from all sins, one shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. || 40 ||

375 || Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Fruits of Giving the Purāṇas in Sequence, Beginning with the Brāhma," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 9 ||
Sūta said:
Charity is of four kinds—daily, occasional, for a specific desire, and pure;
it should be bestowed upon a worthy recipient, not even in the slightest degree upon an unworthy one.
O best of sages, listen as I proclaim those who are worthy vessels,
who were told by the Sun, the God of gods, to Manu.
There is nothing superior to generosity in the three worlds;
through generosity heaven is attained, and through generosity alone prosperity is obtained. (3)
Through giving one may obtain happiness, beauty, splendor, fame, and strength;
through giving one attains victory, and through giving liberation is attained.
"By means of giving one conquers enemies; by means of giving disease is destroyed.
There is nothing else at all but giving—thus the divine Ravi has declared. (6)
Therefore, having carefully examined a worthy recipient, one should give with diligence;
otherwise, everything becomes like an oblation poured onto ashes. (7)
They were knowers of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, peaceful, and masters of their senses;
they were devoted to the performance of rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, steadfast in truth, and maintained households.
They were ascetics who frequented sacred fords, grateful, and moderate in speech;
they were devoted to the service of their gurus and were constantly habituated to the private recitation of the Vedas.
Those who are devoted to the worship of Mahādeva, adorned with the ashes of the Śiva-scriptures,
or those Vaiṣṇavas who are devotees of the Sun— these best of the twice-born are worthy recipients.
If one desires the fruit of lordship, it should be given only to these;
it is certain that even in times of distress, it must not be given to others. (11)
But that Brahmin who is a devotee of Maheśvara, even if he possesses only his birth [as a caste], is the most excellent of all recipients; what is given to him becomes inexhaustible.
Whatever is given to another after bypassing a devotee of Śiva, that gift becomes fruitless, and one falls into hell. || 13 ||
Therefore, recognizing him as a most excellent recipient—a sinless devotee of Śiva—one who desires imperishable fruit should give everything to him. (14)
That gift which is always bestowed without aiming for any fruit is called "eternal" (nitya) by Bhānu, the God of gods. 15.
That gift which is bestowed with faith for the sake of purifying evil is declared by the seers who proclaim the Vedas to be an occasional gift (naimittika-dāna). || 16 ||
Whatever gift is given with devotion for the sake of a son, for the sake of wealth, for the sake of heaven, or for any other purpose, it is designated as "kāmya" (motivated by desire). || 17 ||
That gift which is given to a devotee of Śiva for the sake of pleasing Hara is declared to be pure; it is the sole means for attaining liberation. (18)
Whatever gift is given, especially to one who is poor—
even he who, endowed with faith, gives away but a small piece of land— [attains great merit].
He goes to the abode of Brahmā, where the Lord Virāṭ himself resides.
He who gives land, together with sugarcane, wheat, peas, and barley,
to a poor person goes to the abode of the Sun.
Even he who, endowed with faith, gives a plot of land the size of a cow-hide to a peaceful devotee of Śiva, is liberated from all sins. (22)
There is no gift superior to the gift of land here upon this earth;
for that which is given by you to the poor becomes inexhaustible. (23)
A gift of land, especially, must never be given to one who is wealthy;
he who gives it out of fear or affection shall go to an inexhaustible hell.
Those sinful kings, blinded by greed, who collect taxes from those most righteous men by whom villages were granted to the Brahmins. (25)
They are cooked in the hells for as long as thirty thousand kalpas;
at the end of that time, they become flies, lice, bedbugs, and mosquitoes.
Worms, web-footed birds, pigs, and likewise birds;
dogs, iguanas, hares, porcupines, donkeys, horses, and ants [are born there]. (27)
Mice, chameleons, trees, shrubs, and the like exist for a thousand yugas; at the end of that period, they become the Mleccha tribes.
No atonement for them is seen even through hundreds of penances;
O best of sages, the killer of a Brahmin attains purity only after a long time. (29)
One who collects taxes from a village of Brahmins shall never attain purity;
therefore, a wise man should diligently avoid collecting taxes there.
There is no sin greater than the taking of taxes from those who do not give;
the wise know that among all gifts, the gift of knowledge is the supreme gift. (31)
And that gift [should be given] to one who is disciplined, devoted to his caste and stage of life, a Brahmin indeed, peaceful, and intent on service. || 32 ||
That which is given for the sake of the world of Brahmā is called the gift of knowledge;
the wise who proclaim the Vedas praise the gift of food.
Since food itself is life, it is indeed equal to the gift of life;
therefore, wise men should give food every single day. (34)
"Without even examining [the merits], [the gift] is for all," according to the ordinance of Svāyambhu;
by this, Virañci was pleased, and the Lord of Kamalā was likewise pleased. (35)
And by this very [act], the Blessed Lord Śacīpati was gratified;
therefore, those wise ones who know the Vedas declare that this gift is most distinguished. (36)
"Raw food should never be given to a householder, nor to a traveler;
that is forbidden," so the divine Ravi declared. (37)
The gift of water is indeed said to be equal to the gift of food;
for water alone, O best of the twice-born, is the life of all living beings. (38)
The giver of sesame seeds obtains a son; the giver of clothing, supreme beauty;
the giver of a lamp, clear vision; and the giver of a vehicle, supreme prosperity. (39)
Likewise, the giver of a bed and the giver of grain attain supreme happiness;
the giver of a horse attains the world of the Aśvins and great beauty.
Those who know the Vedas understand that the gift of the Veda is a great gift;
by that great gift, union with Brahman is traditionally taught.
That fool who, having accepted a fee, teaches the Veda, or he who studies it after being paid—both of them are remembered as sinners. (42)
The Vedas that have passed through the mouths of those two are censured in all ritual acts,
just as water contained in a vessel for liquor becomes censured.
By giving mouthfuls of grass to cows, one is liberated from all sins;
as are those who offer various kinds of edible roots and fruits. (44)
By giving vegetables to Brahmins, one shall become exceedingly happy;
by the gift of fuel, the digestive fire is kindled. (45)
The gift of an umbrella brings happiness to those who have gone to the other world;
and he who bestows medicine upon the sick for the sake of curing their disease, [attains merit]. (46)
He who gives a cow, adorned and accompanied by her calf and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), becomes free from disease, long-lived, and always happy. || 47 ||
The sixteen seasons and whatever gift is prescribed for sacred bathing places (tīrthas); || 50 ||
That gift becomes inexhaustible, especially when given to a yogin during the solstices, the equinoxes, and during lunar or solar eclipses. (51)
That which is given on occasions such as the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti) becomes inexhaustible;
whatever is given with Śiva in mind, whether it be small or great.
What is given especially at a temple of Śiva becomes inexhaustible.
When the full moon of Vaiśākha is conjoined with the Viśākhā asterism, it is so. (53)
On that lunar day, having worshipped seven or five Brahmins with black sesame seeds or honey, the wise man, having fasted, [should perform the rite].
Thinking, "May Yama, the King of Dharma himself, be present," one should give according to one's ability to a knower of the meaning of the Vedas or to a yogin of Śiva. || 55 ||
By the grace of the King of Dharma, one is liberated at that very moment from all sins committed throughout one's life, whether physical or mental. (56)
He who places sesame seeds, gold, honey, and clarified butter upon a black antelope skin and gives them to a Brahmin is liberated from all sins.
He who bestows a cow, food, and a water-pot on the full moon day of Vaiśākha for the sake of Yama, the King of Dharma, is liberated from all sins. || 58 ||
On that well-known lunar day of Śiva, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha, a person, with devotion, having in mind the Lord Śaṅkara—
Whether it be gold, clothing, fruit, or even grain—whatever is given to one who knows the Vedas becomes inexhaustible. (60)
The gift of fearlessness toward all beings is remembered as the supreme gift;
there exists no gift superior to that, even without the use of wealth. (61)
Whoever recites or even hears this shall obtain the fruit of giving a cow.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gift of Horses and Other [Vehicles]," in the *Śrī Brahmāpurāṇopapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka at Śrī Sora.
Sūta said:
O you of excellent limbs, listen; I shall describe another vow, which was spoken directly by Śiva himself to Skanda when he questioned him.
Skanda said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, whose crest is adorned with the moon;
O Bharga, Lord of the lords of the universe, ocean of the nectar of compassion! (2)
With whom are you quickly pleased, or by what means are you known? What is the yoga that has you as its object, and what is the knowledge that has you as its object? (3)
O Mahādeva, out of affection for your son, tell all of this to me.
Īśvara said:
O Skanda, my devotee is always dear to me, regardless of whether he possesses superior qualities;
even if he eats all things, consumes all things, or violates all rules of conduct. || 5 ||
One who regards me as supreme is indeed liberated from mind, speech, and body; of this there is no doubt.
I am not pleased by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice.

"Delighted by even a fraction of devotion, I shall swiftly bestow the supreme state upon one who constantly wears the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), is peaceful, and has a rosary of rudrākṣa beads as a bracelet. || 7 ||
Free from deceit and possessing true resolve, such a devotee would be my most excellent;
indeed, the supreme Vaiṣṇava is the highest among the devotees of the Sun, Fire, and Moon.
A devotee of Śiva is superior to thousands of Vaiṣṇavas,
even if he is devoted to sin, cruel, and devoid of the conduct prescribed for his own stage of life.
O Saṃ,
if he should be my devotee, he alone is indeed worthy of worship and honor.
Those who, relying on deceit, subsist upon their devotees; || 10 ||
Even they are liberated from saṃsāra, how much more so those people who are devoted to me! And who can truly know the majesty of my devotees? || 11 ||
"I know, you know, and Nandin or Guha knows—whether one is on the right path or off the path, whether a fool or even a wise man. (12)
The eleventh chapter found in the six abbreviated manuscripts is the fifteenth in the Karve-Sarsikar manuscripts;
in those manuscripts, the eleventh chapter is entirely different.
It has been included in this manuscript in place of the fourteenth chapter.
The first verse beginning with "mitram" does not exist.
And yet, O Six-faced One, only a single entity has been imagined by me within myself.
The wise, however, perceive this world as the one form of the Self— the non-dual, singular, supreme Self, whose very nature is knowledge. (29)
I am the Self, all-pervading, pure, resembling a crystal stone;
free from limiting adjuncts, peaceful, self-luminous, and the illuminator. || 30 ||
Just as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell appears within the shell itself, so too does everything appear within the Self;
through the thorough knowledge of the reality of the shell, that [illusory silver] is destroyed, and likewise [the world] is destroyed within the Self.
The self never possesses either agency or enjoyership;
it is determined that agency arises solely through the non-discrimination of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
The proponents of the Veda say that for the self—which is eternally liberated, indivisible, and six-faced—there is nothing whatsoever that remains to be done. (33)
In reality, agency belongs only to the instrument and not to the Self;
for that reason, the Self is not tainted by karma known as merit and demerit.
All qualities such as intellect (buddhi) and the rest arise from the Great Intellect (mahat);
and from the ego (ahaṃkāra) arise the subtle elements (tanmātras) and the sense organs.
From the subtle [tanmātras] come the five gross elements; from them, this gross world arises.
The unmanifest consists of twenty-four principles, while the Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth.
Neither an effect, nor an instrument, nor an action exists for it;
all this has been declared to be within the Self alone due to one's own ignorance—so says the Śruti. (37)
Thus, O dear son, this knowledge concerning me has been told to you.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Śiva’s Devotees," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 11 ||
Īśvara said: It was previously established that yoga is one-pointedness of mind directed toward Me;
now listen as I shall describe its eightfold means.
O Six-faced One, the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas), as well as the postures (āsanas), have been described;
thereafter, breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and concentration (dhāraṇā) are proclaimed.
Meditation as well as concentration are declared to be the limbs of yoga; these have been briefly explained. Now listen, my son, to the observances.
Study of the scriptures, contentment, purity, and worship of the Lord. || 4 ||
O child, these have been described as bestowing the perfection of yoga;
for they produce no distress whatsoever for any living beings.
Non-violence has been declared by the virtuous to be the bestower of yoga-perfection;
now hear the explanation of truth and non-stealing. (6)
The taking of another's property by means of valor or even by force—this is what is called "theft" by the virtuous; its avoidance is non-stealing.

In other contexts, celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is said to be the renunciation of sexual intercourse; here, however, it is defined as the non-acceptance of gifts from the four [classes], even in times of distress and according to one's desire.
Non-possessiveness is said to be the means for the accomplishment of yoga;
it consists of the emaciation of the body through practices such as the Vāndrāyaṇa vow.
O son, austerity has been described; now listen to the study of the Vedas (svādhyāya):
the Ṛṇavas, the Śatarudrīya, as well as the Atharvaśiras and the Śikhā.
O son, the recitation of these is proclaimed as "svādhyāya" (self-study);
being content with whatever is obtained by chance is recited as "saṃtoṣa" (contentment). || 11 ||
Purity and cleanliness are prescribed both externally and internally through the acts of speech, mind, and body, by means of praise, recollection, and worship. (12)
"O son, firm devotion to me is this worship of the Lord;
and the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) have been declared in brief, but not in detail. (13)
The yogi who is endowed with restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) is praised for liberation;
being firm in intellect and undeluded, he should first practice the posture (āsana). 14.
The lotus-seat, the svastika-seat, the lion-seat, the cock-seat, the tortoise-seat, the vajrāsana, the tiger-seat, and the half-moon-seat. (15)
—The staff, the Tākṣya-posture, the trident, the sword, and the mallet;
the crocodile, the triple-path, the wooden post, the pillar, or the elephant-ear. || 16 ||
Also the Bhīma, the Vīrāsana, the Vārāha, the Mṛgavaiṇika,
the Anālika, and likewise the Sarvatobhadra. || 17 ||
Thus, these seats here are twenty-seven in number.
That which is called prāṇāyāma is declared to be of two kinds, and it is described as follows.

"The *agarbha* and the *sagarbha*: of these two, the first is remembered as the unconquerable (*ajaya*), while the second is declared to be conquerable (*sajaya*) by the mothers through the recitation of the *vyāhṛtis*. (21)"
Exhalation (recaka), the void (śūnyaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka)—
thus is the fourfold division of prāṇāyāma described here by the wise.

The channels of the vital breaths are said to be the locus of the movement and cessation of coming and going; the exhaling breath is called *recaka*, while the neutral state is called *śūnyaka* as it remains in its natural condition.
Pūraka [is so called] because of the filling of the air, and kumbhaka because of its retention;
on the right side of the embodied being is the immortal channel, Piṅgalā. (24)
It is known as Pitṛyoni, and the Sun is its presiding deity;
and that channel which flows toward the left is remembered as Iḍā. (25)
It is known as Devayoni; the Moon is its presiding deity. Between these two is the renowned channel named Suṣumnā. (26)
The channel resembling the urine of a lotus is called Kāryā, with Brahmā as its presiding deity;
from there, one should join oneself to the void, the supportless state, in the center within one's own self.
One should designate the state of emptiness from the awakening of the wind situated outside;
then, through the lunar deity, one should again drink the supreme nectar.
By that, there shall be nourishment as well as the washing away of impurity;
having filled [the breath] residing in the abdomen, one should restrain the upward-moving wind (uccairvāyu). || 29 ||
Retention (*kumbhaka*) is like a water-jar (*kumbha*); exhalation (*recaka*) is that which has been turned out.
Having drawn up the breath with self-restraint, one should lead it to the deity of the navel.
Starting from the tip of the thumb, one should release [the breath] through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
having contracted the wheel of the kucikā and led it upward by three finger-breadths.
Having thoroughly agitated the Śaṅkhinī, the sage should then lead it into the Brahma-cave;
by this means, he should purify the stainless path of Īśvara.
O child, for those desiring liberation, the limbs of yoga are always [necessary] for the attainment of yoga. (33)
Having abandoned the path of fire, one should very slowly draw the breath upward with the finger; having drawn it into the navel, one should hold it there with a gentle mind.
Maintaining control over his vital breaths and endowed with the sovereign power of yoga, the yogi is born at the beginning of the year free from old age and death. || 35 ||
One should draw in the external air with the left [nostril] and fill the abdomen; meditating on the space between the navel and the nose, one will certainly conquer the vital breaths three times.
O child, steadiness of mind arises from fixing [the breath] in three places;
the yogi who has mastered his posture should fix the vital air at the big toe, the navel, and the tip of the nose. (37)
One should indeed direct the apāna wind toward the region of the hips and the back;
one should practice concentration right there—this is the method for conquering the vital air (vāyu). || 38 ||
Exhalation, inhalation, and even retention do not exist [in this state]; by fixing the mind on the supportless, one becomes a conqueror of the vital breaths in an instant. (39)
The restraint of the senses as they naturally roam among their objects is called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal). || 40 ||
Whatever one perceives, one should perceive all that as being like the Self within the Self;
this is indeed declared to be withdrawal (pratyāhāra), the supreme means for accomplishing yoga.
When the five sense organs of action produce their respective effects through the other four [elements], if the world remains steady therein, then the mind enters the ālaya. (42)
The wise man should perform fifteen *dhāraṇās* of the rising breaths;
having restrained the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*), he should cast the mind within the sun. (43)
Through the practice of yoga for six months, one beholds the gods, the Siddhas, the Gandharvas, the Cāraṇas, and the hosts of sky-dwellers, as well as the subtle light.
When [the truth] is seen, there is neither old age nor death, and one becomes omniscient.
The channel named Sphoṭa is proclaimed [to be there], and within it lies the world of Kūrma.
Having uttered the principle of the Bindu, one should then meditate upon its qualities at its end:
the past, the present, the future, and that which is far away. (46)
One should certainly practice that knowledge which is called *sphoṭa*;
one should constantly meditate upon Sadāśiva on the forehead, at the crown of the head, and in the heart. (47)
Having five faces and ten arms, with a serpent as his sacred thread.
Having thus meditated upon the All-pervading Lord within oneself, the wise know that to be true meditation; therein arises the state of *unmanī*, wherein one neither hears nor sees.
One does not smell, nor touch, nor perceive anything at all; one should contemplate the breath in the nose while it resides in the secret places such as the abdomen.
Thinking "I am the Lord," the lord of yogis, whose singular form is supreme bliss, liberated from old age and death, the sage shall become Śiva himself. (51)
That which is devoid of coming and going, truly abandoned of sense objects, and characterized by the state of the transcendent (unmanī) alone, is designated as samādhi. || 52 ||
There is no thought of a gross object, nor even the contemplation of the subtle;
neither external nor internal, O son, is there the piercing of the knot of Brahman.
Neither thick nor thin, neither short nor missing;
neither white nor yellow, neither black nor variegated. (54)
Having placed within the abode of the heart-lotus the Self— known as the Universe, the source of the universe, which stands beyond the darkness of all beings.
The support of all is the unmanifest, blissful, and imperishable light;
it transcends both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, being the subtle, auspicious void.
Within that, one should meditate upon the Lord, whose form is Brahman, who exists within all beings,
who is without beginning, middle, or end, and who is the abode of qualities such as bliss.
Having established the Great Puruṣa, Brahman, Brahmā, and the imperishable Brahman, as well as the Self within the Supreme Self at the conclusion of the syllable Om; 58.
One should meditate upon the Lord Īśāna in the sky, situated in the midst of space, the cause of all existents and the refuge of the single essence of bliss. (59)
One should meditate upon Śambhu, the ancient Puruṣa; thus one may be released from bondage.
But he who desires to cross the ocean of saṃsāra without devotion to Śiva [is lost]. (60)
Just as a fool desires to cross the ocean with the help of dogs and their tails, so too, without service to Śambhu, there is indeed no crossing over the cycle of worldly existence. 61.
The bliss of Brahman, which is subtle, that those seeking liberation behold. || 64 ||
In the midst of that, the absolute Brahman, characterized by pure knowledge, remains as if to drink [that essence]; he who is protected by Maheśvara attains the divine yoga. || 65 ||

Whether it lasts for one hundred thousand moments, two hundred thousand, or three hundred thousand, that which is not composed of the elements and is entirely free from all limiting adjuncts is designated as *samādhi*.
O son, wherever one directs the mind— whether externally or internally—
the form of the Self is experienced as bliss in each of those places.
Having established the self within me, the supreme light devoid of qualities,
