one who remains for even a moment shall have direct experience of that [Self].
"O destroyer of Krauñca, by my grace alone shall a yogi become omniscient, perfected, and free from old age and death; it cannot be otherwise.
Therefore, having completely renounced all the multitude of difficult-to-perform actions,"
"Let him come to me alone for refuge; I shall destroy his ignorance. (70)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others of mixed castes—
whoever is purified by the disposition of devotion to me— go to my supreme abode.
When the dissolution of the universe has arrived and even the lotus-born Brahmā has perished,
my devotees do not perish at all, for they assume forms according to their own will.
For yogins, for those who perform ritual actions, and for ascetics of restrained self, I alone am their goal; there is no other—this is the certainty. 73. 548.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Restraints, Observances, Breath-Control, and so forth," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Śiva and Rukandā. || 12 ||
Skanda said:
"O Lord, this body, which is composed of the elements, is the supreme vessel for calamities and diseases;
its object [the self] is always afflicted by states consisting of pleasure and pain."
When the yogin is overwhelmed by sufferings arising from within himself, and likewise by those pertaining to the physical elements, what then is his remedy?
Tell me, O Yogin, about the afflictions of torments and the blessings [that arise]. (3)
The Lord said:
"In this world, the obstacles for yogins— whether they be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)—
all become creators of yoga even for you."
Intuition, hearing, news, sight, taste, and touch—these six indeed are the sattvic secondary afflictions (upasargas). (5)
"I am poor and I am wealthy; likewise, I am brave and I am weak;
I am a fool and I am very learned; I am handsome and I am ugly. (6)
I am a giver and I am a miser; I am happy and I am the one who enjoys pleasures; I am of low birth and I am of noble birth; I am a thorn and I am free from thorns.
All this prattling such as "all this is indeed my property," which consists of egoism, is entirely of the nature of *rajas*. (8)
Blindness, deafness, lameness, and the affliction of malignant diseases;
headache, fever, colic, consumption, fainting, vertigo, and so forth. (9)
All those diseases, whether of the nature of rajas or tamas, joined with the ego-sense of tamas, afflict the embodied being here in this world through their mixed states.
Merely through the state of dullness, there arise delusion, infatuation, ignorance, muteness, and so forth; these are known as the qualities of tamas. (11)
The Guhyakas, Yātudhānas, Kiṃnaras, Uragas, Rākṣasas, the fierce Devadānavas, Daityas, Mātṛs, and the Gaṇas; || 12 ||

But the tamasic planets and spirits, having become like the wind, constantly afflict a man here in this world— those obstacles which, by means of the planets, harass one devoted to the practice of yoga.
And for the sake of warding off such obstacles as these, O child, I shall describe various forms of concentration (dhāraṇā) for the purpose of attaining success by yogins.
One should contemplate the *praṇava* together with its seed-syllable, kindled by fire, as unified with the seven constituents beginning with the skin, at the throat and the tip of the nose. (15)
And among all the obstacles related to Varuṇa, the knower of Yoga should always practice this very [method];
thus the obstacles and the like will pass away.
Or, if a yogi devoted to yoga is overcome by a disease of bile,
he should contemplate there the well-formed syllable of the Lord of Cods (Indra).
One should meditate on the moon, the source of nectar, upon one's own head as desired.
Having entered [the body] in the form of Brahman, one should contemplate the arising of Nirvāṇa from the body;
and by that same [Brahman], which is cool and fragrant, the element of fire (hṛttattva) is also [purified].
Just as darkness is dispelled by the sun, bile-related ailments and other afflictions—
such as poison, fever, and old age— are certainly destroyed through constant practice.
The yogi destroys blindness and divine vision arises;
he should drink another [substance] being thrown [into the mouth] with the mantra dedicated to the deity Candra. || 21 ||
Having drunk [the essence] from the earthly horse, one should destroy the pillar of wind;
for him there is indeed incomparable nourishment, stability, and freedom from disease.
And remembering the heart-principle as having the luster of a well-drunk [liquid], one likewise attains immortality.
In this regard, one should contemplate the oneness of the auditory faculty with space and wind. || 23 ||
One should release this wind again, which destroys deafness;
one hears everything from afar and shall always possess a retentive memory. (24)
Then, through the yoga of constant practice, one becomes composed of wind and mobile;
and within the lotus of the tongue, one perceives that [lotus] together with its pericarp and the observer thereof.
Having recollected her, one should again meditate upon Sarasvatī of white complexion in the center;
she destroys diseases of the head and diseases of the mouth. (26)
In this way, one attains wisdom, mindfulness, intelligence, poetic skill, and supreme intellect;
one always effects the immobilization of the wicked and conquers all the bodily winds.
The god situated in the heart-lotus, endowed with eighteen arms, dark-blue and reddish-brown in color, of great form, and wearing the matted locks of Śiva; (28)
He was formidable, clad in a lion’s skin, adorned with all ornaments,
wearing necklaces and decorations of serpents, and equipped with every kind of armlet and anklet.
It was seen filled with garlands of flames, illuminating the faces of the quarters;
it was impenetrable, victorious, fierce, invincible, and the lord of the thirty gods.
This meaning of the verse is seen in hundreds of manuscripts prior to the verse beginning with "nāśayedandhatām" (he would destroy blindness). It is as follows:
"But when that mantra has been recited, one should raise [the victim] up in an instant by means of this [mantra]."
O Six-faced One, having established the characteristic mark (*lakṣa*) right there, one should apply it to Māyā;
just as ghee, when applied to ghees themselves, attains a state of non-distinction through oneness.
In that very same way, he should not become absorbed again; rather, by this method, he should proceed toward the supreme fourth state.

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Sāttvika, Rājasa, Vighna, and Other Obstacles," in the dialogue between Śiva and Skanda within the glorious Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa. 13.
Sūta said:
O best of sages, listen as I shall fully declare the lunar days (*tithis*);
among them, the eighth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇāṣṭamī*) is meritorious and the destroyer of all sins.
That which is the eleventh chapter in the *Kāmasaśita* manuscript has been compiled here.
There is no other vow than the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow that bestows such great prosperity;
by performing the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow, Brahmā attained the status of Brahmā.
Viṣṇu attained the state of Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Gods (Śacīpati) attained the lordship of the gods,
Kubera attained the sovereignty of the Yakṣas, and Yama himself attained the office of the restrainer.
Candra attained the state of the Moon, Gaṇādhipa attained the state of Gaṇeśa,
Skanda attained the position of Senāpati, and likewise did the other lords of the Gaṇas.
Having performed it, they attained sovereignty, good fortune, and became beloved of the gods;
by the power of this vow, Hari became the husband of Lakṣmī.
Yayāti attained sovereignty over the whole earth, as did other excellent kings;
likewise, there were sages, ascetics, perfected beings, and the daughters of the Gandharvas.

Having performed this very rite, the preeminent sages attained supreme perfection. This excellent Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow, which grants the fruit of all desires, was proclaimed by Nandīśvara to the high-souled Nārada.
It concerns the southern peak of Mount Meru, which is saluted by gods and demons alike.
There, having seen Nandīśvara— the omniscient one, beloved of Śambhu,
being attended by sages and praised by the hosts of Maruts— || 9 ||
Having praised the benefactor of all with various hymns,
the sage Nārada then prostrated himself like a staff and spoke.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, knower of all principles, bestower of fearlessness upon all!
By the performance of what [practice] does the state of one whose livelihood is penance arise? (11)
Fortune, splendor, sovereignty, offspring, and likewise fame;
and at the end, eternal liberation which releases one from the bonds of Paśu.
"O Blessed One, O Śaṅkara, out of compassion, tell me of that vow.
Nandikeśvara said:
"O divine sage Nārada, listen; there is a most excellent vow called Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, by the performance of which I attained the status of Gaṇeśa."
When the month of Mārgaśīrṣa has arrived, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one who has conquered his senses should perform the cleansing of the teeth using an *aśvattha* twig as a toothbrush.
O Nārada, having performed the ritual bath and the libations according to the rules,
one should then return home and worship the Lord Śaṅkara.
Having consumed cow urine according to the rule, one should fast during the night;
the fruit of this shall be eightfold that of the Atirātra sacrifice.
One should worship the Blessed One Maheśvara, whose name is Śambhu. || 17 ||
Endowed with faith, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
in the month of Māgha, the consumption of cow’s milk at the banyan tree is prescribed. (18)
Having properly worshipped Māheśvara, one obtains the fruit of eight Gomedha sacrifices;
that same [rite] is prescribed for the month of Phālguna, and that very same consumption [of the substance] should indeed be performed.
One should worship Mahādeva; the fruit is that of eight Rājasūya sacrifices.
In the month of Caitra, people should avoid consuming wood from the *audumbara* tree. Thus one should worship the one named Sthāṇu; one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having worshipped Śiva in Vaiśākha and having drunk water infused with *kuśa* grass, [one attains the same].
O Nārada, one indeed obtains the eightfold fruit of a human sacrifice; in the month of Jyeṣṭha, wood from the Lakṣa tree should be used, and the all-pervading Lord Paśupati is to be worshipped.
Having consumed water from the horns of cows, one should sleep in the presence of the Lord;
he shall obtain that merit which comes from the gift of ten million cows.
And in the month of Āṣāḍha, having worshipped the one named Ugra and having consumed cow-dung,
the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice shall be eightfold.
O Nārada, it is said that in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship a hundred Palāśa leaves;
having consumed them, one shall dwell in the city of Śiva for a kalpa.
On the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship Tryambaka;
by subsisting on bilva leaves, the fruit of all initiations shall be attained.
In the month of Āśvina, the tooth-stick of the jambu tree is prescribed.
One should worship Īśvara with devotion and consume rice-water.
One shall obtain eightfold the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
On the eighth day of the month of Kārttika, one should worship the deity named Īśāna.
Having drunk the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) once, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
at the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins who are devoted to Śiva. (29)
One should devotedly offer them milk-rice mixed with honey and well-saturated with ghee, along with gold and garments according to one's ability. (30)
O Nārada, one should give to the god cooked rice, a canopy, a banner, and a chowrie; and having adorned a cow, one should give her along with a copper vessel containing jewels.
And [he should give] ornaments, clothing, and a sacrificial fee according to his own ability. || 32 ||
"For a full hundred million kalpas he is honored in the world of Śiva;
O divine sage, this Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow has been properly performed by me. (33)
This was spoken of old by the God of gods, the creator of the universe, to the Goddess.
Sūta said: O best of sages, having thus heard from Nandīśvara about the meritorious Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow, Nārada went to Badarikāśrama.
Whoever recites or even hears of the power of this vow obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the great sacrificial session (atisatra). || 36 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Vow of Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 14 ||
Sūta said:
There is another vow of the Discus-wielder, the God of gods, which removes all sins;
it is that which was formerly spoken by Bhānu to the yogi Yājñavalkya.
Yājñavalkya said:
What are the fruits and what is the ultimate goal of Jayā and Vijayā?
O son of Kaśyapa, tell me of that distinguished merit which resides therein.
Sūrya said:
The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is the beloved of Viṣṇu; it is indeed the Vaiṣṇava tithi. If it should ever be obtained conjoined with the Śravaṇa nakṣatra, [it is most auspicious]. || 3 ||
O best of the twice-born, that day in the bright fortnight is proclaimed as Vijayā;
it should be observed with diligent effort, for it destroys all sins.
That twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna which is conjoined with the Puṣya asterism is indeed named Jayā; it brings about the destruction of all sins.
O best of the twice-born, by fasting on that day, a mortal becomes one who has accomplished his purpose;
having bathed on it, he is always considered to have bathed—of this there is no doubt.
Having worshipped it with garments, flowers, and other offerings, one obtains the fruit in the evening;
indeed, by reciting [the mantra] once at dawn, one attains the fruit of a thousand recitations.
Indeed, giving gifts, feeding Brahmins,
performing fire-sacrifices, and observing fasts yield a thousandfold merit for each.
Whatever learned brahmin, endowed with faith, recites even a single Ṛk verse,
he always obtains the fruit of the entire Ṛgveda.
Whatever sin has been committed over seven lifetimes, whether it be small or great,
one destroys it by diligently worshipping Govindarāja with a garland. 10.
O best of the twice-born, he who performs a fast after bathing on that day is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
The devoted man who, having performed this Dvādaśī,
passes the night, is honored in heaven for as long as a day of Brahmā lasts.
When that day has arrived, I shall tell you what must be done:
fasting on the eleventh day, one should worship Viṣṇu on the twelfth day.
With various offerings of perfumes and flowers, a person should worship according to the prescribed rite:
first the feet for Matsya, and likewise the hips for Kūrma.

One should worship the belly with "To Varāha," the chest with "To Narasiṃha," the throat with "To Vāmana," and the two arms with "To Rāma. One should worship the face with "To Rāma" and the nose with "To Pradyumna."
The two eyes are by the name of Kṛṣṇa, and likewise the head is by the name of Buddha. || 16 ||
And having propitiated Govinda and likewise Gopāla with devotion at night, one should recite "Aferal art haānvāmana" on all sides.
Then, the wise man should place a pure black antelope skin before him;
upon that, he should place an āḍhaka measure of black sesame seeds.
One *prastha* for the middle [class], and likewise one *kuḍava* for the poor;
if sesame is unavailable, barley should be used, and if that is unavailable, wheat.
O Brahmā, a human being obtains a happy fruit there by means of sesame seeds;
he should prepare a vessel of gold, silver, or copper according to his own capacity. || 20 ||
Having covered the vessel with unwashed, well-examined cloths, and having fashioned a golden dwarf (Vāmana) along with a rosary and a water-pot; 21.
Having fashioned an image of Hari according to one's ability, wearing a sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*),
and having thus made Vāmana in such a form, a devoted man— || 22 ||
Having fasted properly, one should devoutly place [the image] situated within the vessel of thread;
one should worship Hari with flowers, perfumes, fruits, and incense appropriate for the time.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, and then the Dwarf; || 24 ||
Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki—these are the ten;
one should worship the Lord with these names as mantras and with food offerings.
For a devotee here, the fruit is especially increased ten millionfold.
Therefore, one should place curd-rice in a jar near him.
A water-pot filled with water and mixed with fragrant substances, as well as an umbrella, a rosary, sandals, and likewise a pill. || 27 ||
Having thus worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, according to the prescribed rite,
one should keep a vigil there accompanied by the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
Thus, at the end of every night when the dawn has become clear,
it should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the scriptures, who maintains a family,
who is a devotee of Viṣṇu, and who is peaceful; indeed, it is especially given to such a one.
And when a guru exists, it is certain that [the teaching] must not be given to anyone else. || 30 ||
A gift given to one who studies the Vedas is equal [in merit]; to one who knows them, it is likewise twofold;
and a gift given to a teacher (ācārya) is multiplied a thousandfold.
If a guru is present, whoever offers the vow to anyone else falls into a miserable state; that which has been given becomes fruitless.
Whether ignorant or possessed of knowledge, the Guru alone is Janārdana;
whether established on the right path or on a wrong path, the Guru alone is always one's refuge.
That lowest of men who, out of delusion, opposes a teacher who has set out on the right path, shall be cooked in hell for ten million births.
Having thus given according to the prescribed rite with devotion to a Brāhmaṇa, it should be presented with this mantra recited from the Purāṇas. || 35 ||
The Brāhmaṇa, the best of the twice-born, should accept it with a mantra;
Vāmana is the giver who bestows intelligence, and Vāmana himself resides within the object given.
"Vāmana is indeed his giver; salutations again and again to Vāmana. This is the mantra for giving.
"Vāmana receives, and Vāmana indeed gives;
Vāmana is the savior of both; salutations again and again to Vāmana. (37)
Thus ends the mantra for receiving [the gift].
Food is Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, the Moon, and the Sun.
May Anila, Yama, and likewise [the others], always take away my sin. || 38 ||
Thus ends the mantra for the gift of food:
"May Parjanya, Varuṇa, Sūrya, Salila, Keśava, Śiva, Tvaṣṭṛ, Yama, and Vaiśravaṇa always remove my sin. (39)
Thus ends another [account] regarding the offering of water.
Having given food to the Brahmins and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to his capacity,
and having consumed the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), he should afterwards eat while remaining silent.
Furthermore, this same procedure is prescribed for every part of the night according to one's desire;
now hear, O Brahmā, what the fruit is when that vow has been completed. || 41 ||
Until the dissolution of Brahmā, he is honored in heaven,
having enjoyed manifold pleasures in the worlds beginning with the world of Brahmā.
Furthermore, having returned from heaven to earth, he is born into a family of great men;
he shall obtain sovereignty over the seven continents—of this there is no doubt. (43)
One obtains all desires and thereafter attains liberation;
he is the god who is the younger brother of Indra and the delighter of the heart of Ramā.
"O Lord Vāmana, Bali has been bound by you; please accept this arghya. This is the mantra for the arghya offering.
One who constantly hears or recites this unsurpassed hymn shall be liberated from all sins through the fruit of Śravaṇa-dvādaśī. (45)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī Vow," in the glorious Saura Upapurāṇa of the Brahma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Yājñavalkya. 15.
Sūta said:
O best of sages, listen as I describe another vow,
which increases good fortune, is meritorious, and destroys even the greatest sins.
It pacifies all evils, bestows the pride of all sovereignty, and is auspicious;
whatever desire a person may long for, that very thing he attains. || 2 ||
In ancient times, the god Rudra burnt the unassailable Kāma;
therefore, that lunar day was observed as a fast by him, and thus it is called Anaṅga-trayodaśī.
O twice-born ones, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
having bathed according to the prescribed rite, one should remain fasting and with senses subdued.
With unswerving devotion, one should worship the Moon-crested God with various kinds of flowers, incenses, food offerings, and likewise with fruits.
One should perform a hundred and eight oblations with sesame seeds while reciting the name of Śambhu;
having worshipped [the deity] by the name Anaṅga and consumed honey, one should sleep at night.
A person obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices by properly worshipping the Lord of Yoga and applying sandalwood paste in the month of Pauṣa.
A person who,
having conquered the senses, thoroughly worships Nāṭeśvara during the month of Māgha, obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
O best of Brahmins, having consumed a pearl, I shall declare its fruit:
it becomes a hundredfold the fruit of a sacrifice involving much gold.
Having worshipped Vīra in the month of Phālguna, a woman who consumes kaḍūnela obtains the fruit of a Gomedha sacrifice and rejoices like the king of the gods.
On the Caitra [full moon], one should consume camphor known as Surūpa, fashioned from various jewels; by doing so at night, one obtains the fruit of a human sacrifice (naramedha). || 11 ||
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship the Lord of Gods in His great form;
by consuming a nutmeg, one obtains the fruit of donating a thousand cows.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should cause the person named Pradyumna to consume cloves at night;
[this yields] eight times the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
One should worship the deity named Umābharta in the month of Āṣāḍha;
by consuming water mixed with sesame seeds, one obtains the fruit of a white lotus.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the Supreme Lord, the wielder of the trident;
by drinking fragrant water, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
In the month of Bhādrapada, O sages, one should worship Sadyojāta;
having consumed agarwood, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices. || 16 ||
When the month of Āśvayuja has arrived, one should worship the Lord of the Thirty-three;
by consuming golden water, one obtains the fruit of ten million gold pieces.
And on the full moon day of Kārttika, one should worship Viśveśvara with devotion;
having consumed the fruit of Madanāraka, one becomes possessed of splendor like that of Kāma. (18)
O twice-born ones, I shall indeed declare the tooth-sticks month by month:
those made of Mallikā, Khadira, Lakṣā, and likewise of Apāmārga.
The *jambū*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and likewise that which is born from the *vaṭa* tree;
first, that of the *mālatī*, and then likewise that of the *marutraka*. [p. 60] 21.
O you of excellent vows, [he offered] karavīra, as well as kunda, and arka leaves;
then mandāra flowers and mallikā blossoms.
Kādamba flowers, yūthikā blossoms, dhattūra, śatapatra,
and sprouts of durvā grass should be offered as food offerings (naivedya) in their respective order.
There should be boiled rice, rice mixed with sesame, sugar-candies, and likewise sweetmeats; there should be *kaṃsāra*, barley-gruel, and then *sauhālika*.
The five kinds of solid food are declared to be supreme, followed by *ghṛtapūra*;
thereafter, the food offering (*naivedya*) should consist of *śāli* rice mixed with sugar. (25)
One should arrange various kinds of food offerings on the full moon day of Kārttika;
O best of sages, listen as I declare the names of these worship services.
One should worship the feet with "Salutation to Śaṃkara" and the ankles with "To Gauī and Śiva";
one should worship the knees with "To Śivā and Śambhu" and "To Udbhava."

Having worshipped the waist for the destruction of Manmatha with "Salutation to Madanā," the navel for Bhava with "Salutation to Bhavānī," and Umā with "Salutation," [he worshipped] the Lord of the Suras. (28)
Salutation to the chest for the God of gods; salutation to Śivā for Aparṇā. Salutation again and again to the two breasts for Viśveśvara; salutation to Surakānti. || 29 ||
Salutation to the neck of the one of terrible and fierce form; salutation to Śivā, the daughter of the mountain.
Salutation to the shoulders of the one worshipped by the thirty gods; salutation to Śivā, the wielder of the trident. || 35 ||
Having said "O Dhūrjaṭi, [protect] my arms," [he worships] the auspicious one with "Salutation to Dhūsarā";
having said "O Śūladhara, [protect] my hands," [he worships] Umā with "Salutation to Śūlinī."
Having worshipped the face of the God with the mantra "Vāmadeva," and having said "Salutation to Vāmā," one should worship the nose with "Salutation to Kapālī."
Having said "Salutation to Mṛḍānī," [he should touch] the forehead; [then] "Salutation to Indudhārī," and afterwards "Salutation to Alakā" and likewise "Salutation to Trinetra."
One should worship the Goddess for Tryakṣa, and for the head, "Salutation to Gaṅgādhara"; then, having worshipped Kātyāyanī, [one should offer] salutation indeed to Vyomakeśa.
Having worshipped the hair according to the prescribed rite, saying "Salutations, salutations to Keśinī," one should place it upon a mango leaf and set it down atop the water jar.
Having covered it with a white cloth and having worshipped it according to the rules, O twice-born ones. || 36 ||
Then, free from stinginess regarding his wealth, he should give that to the preceptor;
water-pots filled with water, along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), should be given to the Brahmins.
O Brahmins, he who thus observes the Anaṅga-trayodaśī with devotion should feed Brahmins who are solely devoted to Śiva.
He attains sovereignty, good fortune, and long-lived sons;
and having reached the world of Śiva, he shall become most dear to Śambhu. (39)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Anaṅga-Trayodaśī Vow," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 16 ||
The sages said:
O Sūta, that which has been spoken by you is the supreme, partless knowledge (*naiṣkala-jñāna*).
We have heard it all, and our minds are filled with joy.
Indeed, eternal devotion has arisen within us toward the eternal Śambhu;
now, please explain in truth the rules for the conduct of the castes and stages of life.
Sūta said:
O you of excellent vows, I shall declare the rule for all four castes,
which was formerly spoken by Bhānu to Manu, the Parameṣṭhin.
"By those who are ever devoted to the yoga of action, Viśveśvara Śambhu is worshipped, and by no other"— such is the Vedic revelation.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the fourth is said to be the Śūdra.
These are indeed the four castes; the first three are traditionally known as the twice-born (dvija).
The householder, the student, the forest-dweller, and likewise the ascetic—these are the four stages of life; a fifth does not exist among them.
The wielding of the rod of punishment is ordained for all stages of life;
indeed, no one is called an "āśramin" (one belonging to a stage of life) without the rod of punishment.
He should be a celibate student (brahmacārī), carrying a staff, wearing a black antelope skin, and likewise girded with a belt; he may be shaven-headed, or have a top-knot, or have matted hair.
O you of excellent vows, his subsistence should always be by means of alms;
likewise, he should perform the fire-ritual in the evening and in the morning according to the prescribed rule.
One who abandons what has been offered as alms is fallen from all ritual acts;
having bathed and satiated the gods and others, he should thereafter perform the worship of the deities.
One should be habituated to saluting the elders in their proper order;
however, once a salutation has been performed, one should not offer a return salutation.
He who does so is not worthy of being saluted; he is exactly like a Śūdra.
Whether it be internal, Vedic, or likewise even worldly.
Since one receives [instruction] from a teacher, one should salute him first;
however, upon rising, one should say "I am so-and-so" to those who are younger.
A Brahmin should never, under any circumstances, offer salutations to Kṣatriyas and others;
rather, being firm in his vows, he should always collect alms from the houses of the learned.
Having offered it to the guru, he should eat while restraining his speech with the guru’s permission;
his subsistence should always be by means of alms, and the observer of the vow should not eat the food of a single person.
For celibate students (brahmacārins), begging for alms is said to be equal to fasting;
excessive eating, however, is detrimental to health, longevity, and the attainment of heaven.
It is demeritorious and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.
One should eat food and other items facing either the east or directly toward the sun.
One should never face the east; this is the eternal rule.
Having washed his feet according to the injunctions and sipped water (ācamana), the twice-born man, being self-restrained, [should proceed]. 18.
One should eat while observing silence and constantly remember Lord Sadāśiva; a wise person should not sip water while wearing shoes, standing in water, or without a turban.
A twice-born Brāhmaṇa, being self-restrained, should not first sip water while raindrops are falling, nor while standing, nor while talking; rather, he should first sip the three sips of water. 20.
Having rinsed the mouth with the root [of the thumb], one should likewise touch the face;
and with the thumb and the ring finger, one should touch both eyes. (21)
With the thumb and forefinger, he should touch the two nostrils;
with the little finger and thumb joined, the twice-born man should touch the pair of ears.
One should touch the heart with all the fingers or with the palm;
likewise, one should touch the head with the thumb, or else both [the heart and the head] with the thumb.
Having placed the *brahmasūtra* on his right ear, facing north during the day for urination and defecation, and facing south at night. [24]
O best of Brahmins, having covered the ground with leaves or grass and remaining observant of silence, one should keep the head lowered; never otherwise.
Not on a path, nor in a cow-pen, nor on a riverbank, nor in the shade, nor near a well;
not on husks, charcoal, or potsherds, nor in a field, nor at a crossroads. (26)
One should not study in a garden, nor in a cremation ground, nor while looking at the stars and such,
nor indeed while facing women, teachers, Brahmins, or cows.
Thereafter, one should perform external purification until the odor and residue are removed; O Brahmins, internal purification is that whereby the purity of the mind is attained. (28)
One should always be self-controlled, with a mind under restraint, free from anger, and pure;
one should always employ speech that is sweet and speaks what is beneficial. (29)
Harming others, backbiting, as well as lust and greed;
gambling, slandering people, and likewise sexual dalliance with women. || 30 ||
One should avoid perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, umbrellas, and the cleaning of teeth; likewise, all stale food, colored substances, and prepared salt should be avoided.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should constantly avoid bathing for the removal of dirt, conversing with Śūdras and others, and showing disrespect toward his guru. (32)
He should daily bring for his teacher a water-pot, flowers, cow-dung, earth, and *kuśa* grass; and he should go out for alms every day.
Having sipped water and being self-restrained, he should always study facing the north, having clasped the teacher's feet and gazing at the teacher's face. (34)
"The Veda is the eternal eye for all beings;
the Veda alone, and nothing else, brings about the highest good for men"—thus spoke the Sun. (35)
That twice-born Brāhmaṇa who, without having studied even very many scriptures, listens [to them], does not fall into hells. (36)
This verse does not appear in the manuscript designated as *x*.
64] A Brahmin who has not studied the sciences but nevertheless engages in ritual practices...
He does not obtain the fruit of the rite; he is exactly like a Śūdra.
The daily rites, the occasional rites, those performed for specific desires, and whatever other Vedic ritual there may be—all these become fruitless for a Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas. (38)
The son of a Brahmin who has not studied [the Vedas], even if he is endowed with learning, should be known as a Śūdra’s son; he does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda. (39)
Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or even four Vedas along with their auxiliary branches, O twice-born ones,
and having given the teacher his fee, one may become a householder.
Then he should marry a maiden endowed with auspicious physical marks, who is not born of his mother’s lineage and who does not belong to the same ṛṣi-lineage or gotra as his own. (41)
Beyond the fifth generation on the mother’s side and likewise beyond the seventh on the father’s side, she should be born of a noble family and lineage, free from disease, and beautiful in form. (42)
He who marries a girl from within five generations on the mother’s side or seven generations on the father’s side becomes one who has violated the preceptor’s bed.
Some desire that [the marriage] be performed according to the Brāhma rite or likewise the Daiva rite;
others prefer the Ārṣa rite, though it is censured in matters of religious duty.
He should carry a bamboo staff, an inner garment, and likewise an upper garment;
two sacred threads, and a water-pot containing water.
He should always carry an umbrella, a pure turban, sandals or shoes, and golden earrings; he should keep his hair and nails clipped and remain pure.
He should always wear white garments, be fragrant, and be pleasant to behold; indeed, when he has the means, he should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes. (47)
A Brahmin should approach his wife during her fertile season, avoiding prohibited lunar days:
the sixth, the eighth, the fifteenth, the new moon, and the fourteenth. (48)
One should always remain a celibate student, especially during one's lifetime;
one should take up the domestic fire (āvasathya) and offer oblations into the sacrificial fire (jātavedas).
One should perform daily the work prescribed by the Veda without sloth;
failing to do so, one quickly falls into most terrifying hells. (50)
One should perform the rites pertaining to Brahman and likewise the twilight devotions;
the wise man should not take on sin, nor should he proclaim his own merit to anyone.
Of one's age, occupation, wealth, learning, and noble lineage. || 52 ||
One should always conduct oneself in a manner consistent with the wisdom of Viṣṇu,
acting in full accordance with what is declared in the Śruti and Smṛti, and following that which is practiced by the virtuous.
One should practice that conduct; I shall now describe the virtuous ones.
The region between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa.
Those twice-born who have been born there are indeed proclaimed as virtuous;
the dharma practiced by them is in accordance with the Śruti and Smṛti.
This indeed was declared as right conduct by Śambhu, the God of gods:
[the people] from Kurukṣetra, the Matsyas, the Pāñcālas, and those born in Śūrasena. (56)
These regions are meritorious lands, while all others are censured;
in these excellent regions, Brahmins who desire righteousness should dwell.
"Right here Dharma is seen, and not elsewhere," so said Ravi; [he likewise mentioned] Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Saurāṣṭra, and Gurjara. (58)
One should avoid these regions: Ābhīra, Kauḍūṇa, Drāviḍa in the southern path, Andhra, and Māgadha. (59)
One should be constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas and dedicated to the five great sacrifices;
being peaceful, self-controlled, having conquered anger, and free from greed and delusion. (60)
Devoted to the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra, dedicated to devotion for Śiva, performing ancestral rites (śrāddha), intent on giving gifts, endowed with forgiveness, and compassionate. || 61 ||
A householder is truly defined by his state, not merely by his dwelling in a house;
for the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain is not worshipped as a deity apart from his own body.
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic,
one who performs actions imbued with devotion to Śiva shall be liberated from bondage.

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for Conduct according to the Castes and Stages of Life," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 17 ||
Sūta said:
One should speak only such words as are not false and do not pierce the vitals;
one should not harm any living beings, nor should one revile the Vedas.
Indeed, no purity whatsoever is seen in those who revile Maheśvara. || 3 ||
Whether it be water, grass, vegetables, earth, or even wood,
a living being who steals these from another falls into hell.
One should not be a constant beggar, nor should one ever beg for what has already been requested;
for such a foolish beggar takes away the very life-breaths of that person.
Flowers should be gathered by the twice-born for the ritual of worshipping the gods,
but not from a single source alone, unless permission has been granted.
A wise man should indeed take grass, wood, fruit, flowers, or light for the sake of dharma; otherwise, he would become fallen. || 7 ||

If a handful of sesame, beans, barley, and so forth is offered by Brahmins who are afflicted by hunger and established in their vows, it is not otherwise; such is the settled rule for those who know the Dharma. (8)
Through falsehood, adultery, as well as the eating of forbidden food,
and by practicing conduct contrary to the revealed Dharma, a family indeed perishes quickly.
There are three types of elders: one advanced in knowledge, one advanced in austerity, and one advanced in age.
Each preceding one among these should be saluted; in the absence of the preceding one, each succeeding one should be saluted.
A Brāhmaṇa should constantly wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) during all ritual acts, using ash produced from the Śiva-fire or from the Agnihotra fire. || 11 ||
One should never dwell with fools, nor with those who have fallen from their status,
nor with those devoted to reviling the Vedas, nor even with those who revile the Lord.
One should always avoid backbiting, groundless enmities, and disputes; nor should one point out to anyone a cow suckling her calf in another's field. (13)
One should not engage in conflict with many people, nor likewise with those who are skillful;
one should not speak of the lunar day of the fortnight, nor should one point out the constellations.
One should not speak of evil to the wicked, nor of non-evil to those who are not wicked;
by speaking the truth one becomes equal in fault to them, but by speaking untruth one incurs double the fault.
The tears that fall from the weeping of those who have been falsely accused destroy the sons and livestock of those false accusers. (16)
"Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, violating the teacher's bed, and opposition to the elders—none of these are seen in one who utters false accusations. (17)
One should completely abandon pride, intoxication, grief, and hatred;
on Sundays, one should not consume fried *bhairava* cakes.
A person desiring wealth should speak the truth; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
However, on Sundays, one must avoid salt in one's eating vessel. (19)
Likewise, when crushing sesame seeds on the ground out of a desire for wealth, one should not cause pain to anyone; yet one may strike one's son or disciple. (20)
One should not speak of a river as a river among rivers, nor of a mountain as a mountain among mountains;
furthermore, one should not abandon a traveling companion during a journey or at a meal.
One should not smear the body with oil remaining after anointing the head;
one should not play with snakes or weapons, nor touch one's own bodily apertures.
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor should one gratify the gods with worldly offerings, even if they are derived from external sources.
One should not clip one's teeth, nails, or hair, nor should one wake a sleeping person.
One should not expose oneself to the morning sun and should avoid darkness. || 24 ||
One who is impure should not worship the gods or the sages through service;
nor should one offer water with the left hand to a guest, to a father, or to the ancestors.
The water that was drunk from a single hand was like wine;
[he drank it] before Viśveśvara, the beloved of Umā, the all-pervading Lord who dwells within the universe. 26.
One should not say that Śambhu is equal to Brahmā and the others, nor to the Śaktis, nor even to Pārvatī;
yet one may say he is equal to the gods such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Whoever is possessed by darkness shall never touch him;
one should speak of the Lord Umāpati as superior to all. 28.
Likewise, the twice-born who seek their own welfare should always address the goddess Girijā;
they should not speak with another's wife, nor should the twice-born perform sacrifices for those unworthy of sacrificing.
One should not revile yogins, those who have attained perfection, or those who observe vows, for such is the way.
He should not step on the shadow of his guru, nor should he ever disregard the guru’s command;
with a concentrated mind, he should perform his bath according to the procedure to be described.
Having touched the ground with the *vyāhṛtis* while digging with the hope for stability,
one should take up the earth with the mantra "Thou art raised" (*uddhṛtāsi*) and the cow dung with "Gandhadvārā" (*gandhadvārā*).
Having taken Apāmārga and Dūrvā grass with the mantra "apāgham," and having reached the bank of a body of water, he should remain composed in a pure place while holding the Dūrvā.
Having sprinkled the bank of the sacred ford with the mantra "ādityāḥ," the one of excellent vows,
having established it in a pure place, should then sprinkle it with the Gāyatrī.
He should then divide that [mud] into two portions; he should cast one portion in the directions with the four mantras beginning with Indra, in due order.
Having immersed oneself in the water and subsequently seated on the bank,
one should apply the remaining portion [of the clay] with mantras in the proper sequence.
With the mantra beginning with "akṣībhyām," the wise man should smear his face;
with "grīvābhyām," his neck; and likewise his arms with the mantra beginning with "tallina."
Having declared the body to be the sacrifice, one should then smear the heart;
with the mantra "Nābhi mānanda nanda," one should place the remainder upon the head.

With the mantra beginning "mūrdhānam," the wise man should offer sesame seeds, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and so forth; then, having recited "hiraṇyaśṛṅgam" and requested the holy water (tīrtha), he, being pure in mind, should afterwards recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
One should recite the two-footed verse of the Goddess, which destroys all sins.
This is the Varuṇa bath; now the mantra-bath is described.
Next, one should perform the Āgneya bath with ashes, the Vāyavya bath with dust, and the Divya bath with heat and rain. 41.
Furthermore, there is another mental bath consisting of meditating upon Śiva with a moist garment;
indeed, for all one's own kinsmen, this mental bath is the most excellent.
*x Here, it appears that "having dug with a probe" is required;
then, having said "the heart," and so forth.
Then, seated upon a seat of darbha grass, the twice-born man should mutter the Gāyatrī mantra.
For all members of the three twice-born classes, the Gāyatrī is the supreme goal;
that which is the ultimate reality of the Gāyatrī is Maheśvara, the God of gods.
Knowing this, the wise man should recite [the Gāyatrī] and enjoys its fruit;
for he who otherwise considers the Gāyatrī to be of the nature of Śiva [is mistaken]. (46)
He is cooked for a duration of many kalpas in that most terrible hell;
the four feet of the Gāyatrī are indeed the four Vedas. || 47 ||
The deities of the feet [of the Gāyatrī] are, in order, Virāṭ, Agni, Viṣṇu, and Soma.

Having understood this according to the prescribed rule, one should mutter the Gāyatrī, the mother of the Vedas; thus, the light of Maheśvara shines forth eternally. Then, one should worship the Sun, who is the imperishable form of Rudra.
With devotional hymns and mantras derived from the Vedas and Itihāsas, as well as the Pāvamāna hymns, for the successful accomplishment of the Brahma-yajña; 50.
Having become composed, he should mutter the Rudra hymns with particular care;
then, returning home in silence, he should worship the imperishable Śiva.
With the six-syllabled mantra and likewise with the Mānastokī hymn;
indeed, there is no mantra superior to the six syllables even among the four Vedas.
The Blessed One, the Sun himself, the god of gods, declared: "It is not so;
[the goal is attained] even by leaves, flowers, fruits, or even by dūrvā grass and water. (53)
A Brahmin should never eat without having first worshipped Mahādeva;
this applies to Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, as well as to those engaged in ritual action and to yogins.
"The Lord Viśveśvara, Bhava, is the sole refuge and there is no other"—such is the sacred revelation (Śruti).
Endowed with faith, the householder should perform the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña). || 55 ||
By abandoning the five sacrifices, one falls away from the stage of life (āśrama).
These are: the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to all beings, the sacrifice to the ancestors, and likewise another— 56.
The human sacrifice and the Brahma-sacrifice are proclaimed as the five sacrifices. They know the sacrifice to the beings (bhūtayajña) to be the offering of food with the remnants of the oblation.
One should diligently feed even a single Brahmin with the ancestors in mind.
They declare that the daily śrāddha is for the prosperity of the ancestors;
having set aside food according to one's ability, one should indeed give it to a brāhmaṇa.
One should honor the guest with devotion, endowed with a disposition toward Śiva;
that guest is a stairway to heaven—thus spoke the divine Sun.
One should give a gift, perform a vow, or offer alms with a sense of devotion toward worldly existence;
they say that the fruit of such an act is inexhaustible, for a state of devotion toward worldly existence is indeed difficult to find.
One should be constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas and intent upon their investigation;
this is declared to be the Brahma-sacrifice, which bestows the fruit of the world of Brahman.
Having performed these [rites] constantly, one should eat according to the duties of one's stage of life (āśrama-dharma);
for he who eats food otherwise shall, after death, become a pig.
If there is but one steady devotion toward Sthāṇu, the Lord of the Universe, what need is there for those five great sacrifices or for various other rituals? (64)

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Duties of the Twice-born," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 18 ||
Sūta said:
A Śrāddha ceremony should be performed on the new moon day, during the Aṣṭakās, at the two solstices, during the equinoxes, at the Vyatīpāta yoga, and especially at sacred fords (tīrthas). || 1 ||
Having properly examined the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas—
especially those who are devotees of Śiva and devoted to the recitation of the Rudra-mantra.
In the absence of devotees of Śiva, one who is composed should, with faith and the thought that they are Śiva himself, feed brahmins devoted to virtuous conduct during the śrāddha rite.
Devoted to vows and fasting, drinkers of Soma, with their senses restrained,
they were intent on the Agnihotra sacrifice, peaceful, eloquent, and worshippers of their gurus.

The disciples were those who had thrice kindled the Nāciketa fire, those who knew the Trimadhu and Trisuparṇa hymns, those who understood the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, and reciters of the Purāṇas and Smṛtis. || 5 ||
One should feed even a single Brahmin who is devoted to the inner sciences, who purifies the assembly, and who is solely intent upon devotion to Śiva.
By that [gift], all those who defile the row of guests become purified—
those who live by killing or imprisonment, the base man, and those who employ Śūdras.
Those who sell the Vedas, as well as those who sell the sacred revelation (Śruti),
others who trade in the Vedas, thieves, and the Kuṇḍa and Golaka castes. (8)
Those who serve as scribes, those with long ears, those who constantly attend upon kings, those who announce the lunar mansions and dates, and those who subsist on the science of medicine; || 9 ||
Those who suffer from disease, authors of poetry, singers, those of the same lineage, those devoted to reviling the Vedas, the ungrateful, and likewise the malicious; || 10 ||
Those with deficient or redundant limbs should be carefully avoided at a śrāddha;
if one should have sexual intercourse with a woman [during the rite], he incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin.
One who eats at a śrāddha feast should indeed avoid traveling on a journey, quarreling, anger, and beating one's son, wife, or others on that day. 12.
Then, one should wash the feet upon an auspicious mandala that has been honored;
for a Brāhmaṇa it is square, and for a Kṣatriya it is triangular.
The circle [of water] is for the Vaiśya, while sprinkling with water is prescribed for the Śūdra.
Then, having seated the Brahmins and provided them with seats of Kuśa grass... (14)
Thereafter, for the protection of the śrāddha, one should scatter sesame seeds;
then, having invoked the Viśvedevas with the verse "viśvedevāsaḥ," [one should proceed]. (15)
Having poured water with the *śaṃ no devī* mantra into a vessel containing a *pavitra*,
one should likewise place barley and flowers while reciting the mantra *yavo 'si*.
With the mantra "yā divyā," one should pour the arghya water into the hand;
then, according to one's ability, one should offer perfumes, garlands, incense, and garments. (17)
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), one should thereafter invoke the ancestors;
having invoked them with the verse beginning "uśantas tvā," and with their permission, [one proceeds].
With a concentrated mind, he should recite the verse "āyantu naḥ" and likewise the mantra "tilo 'si" over black sesame seeds;
then, as before, he should cast them into the hand of the patient.
One should pour the remnants into the vessel so that it becomes overturned, saying, "Thou art the seat for the ancestors. Thereafter, the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa) is prescribed;
having said, "I shall offer into the fire," one proceeds with the permission, "Do so."
One should offer food soaked in ghee into the fire, as in the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña).
In front of Mahādeva, or in a cow-pen, one endowed with faith [should perform this]. || 22 ||
Having performed the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa), one should feed the Brahmins;
some desire it in this manner, O twice-born ones, but this is certainly not the opinion of Bhānu.
One should offer various kinds of milk-rice (pāyasa) and even very many edible foods, as well as things to be licked and sucked; likewise, the Kāmapuṣpa fruit, excluding other fruits.
Even if various kinds of meat are offered with a desire to please the ancestors,
if they are prohibited [meats], the śrāddha will certainly not become inexhaustible.
The twice-born man who does not eat meat when appointed to a rite for the ancestors goes to hell after death and attains the state of a beast.
Then, he should cause the Brahmins to hear the Dharmaśāstra, the Purāṇas, as well as the Atharvaśiras, the Rudras, and the Pauruṣa Sūkta.
All the Brāhmaṇas, restrained in speech and consuming their food with ghee, should eat;
afterwards, one should scatter the *vikira* (scattered grains) and then speak regarding the remaining food.
Having given water for washing the hands, one should indeed perform the recitation of the *svasti* blessing;
having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability, one should utter the word *svadhā*.
Having recited the verse beginning with "May our donors prosper,
O Vāja," and having praised and paid obeisance to the Brāhmaṇas, he should dismiss them.
One who performs the Śrāddha should eat on that night, but must abstain from sexual intercourse;
likewise, one should diligently avoid Vedic study and traveling on the road. || 31 ||
A traveler, one in distress, and especially one who maintains no sacred fire, as well as one who is weak, should always perform the *āmaśrāddha* (the rite with uncooked food). || 32 ||
Even if he is destitute, one should perform a śrāddha with fruits or roots;
or, having bathed, one should satisfy the ancestors with faith by offering water mixed with sesame seeds.
When a Śrāddha is performed with faith, the Lord Nīlalohita— the soul of the universe, the Lord of all, and the consumer of sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors— becomes pleased.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Śrāddha Rite," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between the deceased Śaunaka. 870 || 19 ||
Sūta said:
Now, O twice-born ones, listen as the dharma of those dwelling in the forest is being declared,
by which that Blessed One, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, may be pleased.
Having observed that his own body is afflicted by gray hair and other signs of decay,
the best of the twice-born should entrust his wife to his sons and go to the forest. || 2 ||
Constantly subsisting on fruits and roots and devoted to the five great sacrifices, one should honor the guest with devotion, considering him to be Śiva; such is the sacred revelation.
He should eat only eight mouthfuls, wear rags, and have matted hair;
he should bathe three times a day and be constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas.
One should practice compassion toward all living beings and not eat at night;
one should avoid flowers and fruits grown in villages.
If he should go [to the forest] accompanied by his wife, he must always remain a celibate student;
if a twice-born man who has entered the forest life should go with his wife, he would be liable for penance.
He would be her first-born son, yet he would be equal to a caṇḍāla;
he would be compassionate toward all beings and always delight in sharing with others.
One should avoid slander, false speech, sleep, and laziness;
one should either subsist on withered leaves or always live according to the kṛcchra penance.
Constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva and intent upon meditation on Śiva—
such is the twice-born who always conducts himself in this manner while in the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
When detachment toward all things arises in the mind, one attains the supreme goal, the eternal state, at the end of the body. (10)
Then the wise man should renounce; otherwise, he would become fallen.
Devoted to the study of the Vedāntas, self-controlled, tranquil, and having conquered his senses— || 11 ||
Always free from the sense of "mine," fearless, beyond dualities, and without possessions,
he should wear a worn-out loincloth, or be shaven-headed, or even naked.
"Or the wise man may become a triple-staffed ascetic (tridaṇḍin); such is the Vedic revelation.
He should be equal toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor. (13)
He should always subsist on alms and never eat the food of a single person. If an ascetic should ever become a consumer of food from a single source, he is a glutton.
There is no atonement for him whatsoever in the treatises on Dharma; he shall always be one who bathes at the three sessions of the day, with his body smeared with ashes. 15.
One who contemplates the scripture of liberation should constantly recite the Praṇava,
[meditating upon] the infinite, qualityless, peaceful Puruṣa who is beyond Prakṛti. 17.
I bow to Śaṅkara, the cause and support of all worlds, whose face is turned everywhere; he is the embodiment of consciousness, the immovable pillar, blissful, undecaying, and all-pervading.
The one Great Lord, Brahman, who impels all beings.
It is immeasurable, without beginning or end, self-luminous, and eternal. || 19 ||
Abiding therein, becoming absorbed in that, and disciplined in yoga, the great sage attains the supreme Brahman in a very short time. || 20 ||
11. By the very act of renunciation, that twice-born one is completely liberated from sins;
the man of knowledge, devoted to the sacrifice of the Virāṭ-pada, attains liberation.
Thus has the entire system of the four stages of life been declared without exception;
Śambhu is pleased with him who practices it with diligence.

Here ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Duties of Forest-Dwellers and Others," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 20 ||
The sages said:
O Sūta, how was the creation described by the Blessed Vivasvat? And likewise, what were the Manvantaras and their respective deeds?
Furthermore, the process of re-creation occurs in its entirety exactly as before.
"O Sūta, tell us everything exactly as it was heard by you from Nyāsa. Sūta said:
"Listen, all you sages, to the spontaneous play of the Great Lord;
everything that moves and is immobile consists of the essence of Mahādeva."
...by him this entire universe is agitated; therefore, the Blessed Lord Śiva is the agitator. He is established in the state of primordial matter (pradhāna) through contraction and expansion. || 4 ||
O twice-born ones, from Pradhāna when it was being agitated by the Puruṣa,
there appeared this expanded seed which consists of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
That which is called the principle of Mahat is said to be the principle of Buddhi (intellect).
By the will of the Lord, the principles beginning with Buddhi and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa) arise from the Unmanifest (avyakta).
From that very Puruṣa presiding over it, the foremost of sages were born;
from that, O twice-born ones, the ego (ahaṃkāra) was born, and from that, the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi).
[75] Thereafter, the elements were born and impelled by the will of Śiva;
they say that the mind is born from the unmanifest (avyakta), and it is declared to be of a dual nature.
From the *vaikārika* ego (ahamkāra) arises the *vaikārika* creation;
they say the organs are *taijasa*, while the ten deities are *vaikārika*.
The Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi which is Tāmasa—this threefold ego (ahaṃkāra) is described by those who contemplate the principles (tattva). || 10 ||
From the Bhūtādi [tattva] arose the creation known as the gross elements and their subtle counterparts (tanmātras).
The elemental ether (*bhūtādi*), undergoing transformation, indeed produced the subtle element of sound (*śabdamātra*). From that, space (*ākāśa*) is born; sound is considered its quality.
And space itself, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of touch (*sparśamātra*). From that, wind (*vāyu*) arises; touch becomes its quality.
And the wind, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of form (*rūpamātra*). 13.
From that, fire (tejas) was produced; they know form (rūpa) to be its quality.
Then, fire itself, undergoing transformation, became the subtle element of taste (rasa-mātra). || 14 ||
From that, water was produced; taste is considered its quality.
Then, undergoing transformation, the waters created the subtle element of smell.

From fragrance, the earth was born, and fragrance is indeed its quality. When space, which consists of the subtle element of sound, absorbed the subtle element of touch, it became twofold; thus wind is said to possess two qualities, being known as consisting of sound and touch.
In the same way, form belongs to space, while both sound and touch are its qualities.

From that, fire (tejas) arose, possessing the three qualities and endowed with sound, touch, and form; all the [remaining] qualities entered into it, while the first three qualities remained present. (18)
The waters, possessing four qualities, entered into smell alone;
therefore, earth is said to be the most powerful among the elements, possessing five qualities. (19)
And because they are presided over by the Puruṣa and through the favor of the Unmanifest,
they produce the cosmic egg, beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements.
In that [egg], the effect and the instrument of the Supreme Lord were fully accomplished;
within the elemental egg was Virañci, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) known as Brahmā.
Therefore, the passage from "from that he was born" up to "then there was only taste" does not exist in the manuscripts written in the Vahva and Cachasa scripts.
[p. 76] He was the first creator of beings; Brahmā appeared in the beginning. (22)
The spinal cord of that Supreme Lord became Meru, and the mountains became his placenta;
the oceans were the amniotic fluid of that Parameṣṭhin.
O brahmins, everything there—the gods, asuras, and humans—came into being;
and by waters ten times greater than that, the egg was encompassed on the outside.
The waters are surrounded on the outside by fire ten times their extent;
and fire is surrounded on the outside by air ten times its extent. (25)
The wind is enveloped by space, but space is enveloped by the source of the elements (bhūtādi);
and the source of the elements is enveloped by the Great One (mahat), while the Great One is enveloped by the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Enveloped by these seven primordial coverings, the entire egg—
whose origin is the Unmanifest (avyakta)— dissolves in the natural order of succession.
The qualities (guṇas) become unbalanced or balanced solely by the power of time;
when there is equilibrium of the qualities, it should be known as dissolution (laya), and in their imbalance, it is called creation (sṛṣṭi).
O best of Brahmins, the cosmic egg itself is called the field (kṣetra) of Brahmā;
he alone is declared to be the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), as well as Virañci and Prajāpati.
There are thousands of millions of cosmic eggs extending horizontally and upwards;
Brahmās, Haris, and Rudras are established here and there within them.
By the command of Mahādeva, the trident-bearing God of gods,
[he presides over] the innumerable cosmic eggs whose nature consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
The Śruti declares that Mahādeva is the cause of manifestation and dissolution;
the Blessed One possesses infinite power and is the abode of infinite majesty.
O twice-born ones, Mahādeva, the lord of Ambikā, is endowed with infinite sovereignty; for him, there exists neither instrument, nor object, nor action.
The Lord Īśa sports according to his own will with Avijayā;
thus, O best of sages, the elemental creation has been described in brief.
But this creation of Brahmā is now described as being devoid of prior conscious intent.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Primary Creation," in the *Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa* of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 21 ||
As he was reflecting further, the creation of beings (bhūtasarga) arose;
they were known as those who delight in sharing, yet are cruel and possessive.
These five creations have been fully described by the divine Sun;
O twice-born ones, the first creation of the Great One (Mahat) belonging to Brahmā is to be understood.
The second creation is said to be that of the subtle elements (tanmātras);
the third, O twice-born ones, is called the creation of the senses, which is the transformational (vaikārika).
Thus this primary creation (prākṛta-sarga) has arisen preceded by intelligence;
the fourth is the principal creation (mukhya-sarga), for the immobile beings are indeed known as the principal ones.
That which is called the animal womb is indeed the fifth;
likewise, the sixth is known as the divine creation, consisting of those who move upwards. || 33 ||
Then follows the seventh creation, that of those with downward-flowing currents, which is the human creation.

O best of the twice-born, the eighth is the elemental (bhautika) creation of the elements and so forth. And the ninth is the Kaumāra creation; these [last three] are both primary (prākṛta) and modified (vaikṛta).

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Primary Creation and Other Beginnings in the Vārāha Kalpa," in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka within the *Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa* of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*. || 22 ||
Sūta said:
Then that Blessed Lord created from himself his sons:
Sanātana, Sanaka, and also Sanandana.
Padmasambhava did not set his mind upon creating these five— Śambhu, Sanatkumāra, and the others— for they were solely intent on meditating upon Śiva.
When they were thus indifferent toward creation, Prajāpati, overcome by delusion,
performed supreme ascetic penance, yet he attained nothing at all.
After a long time had passed,
Hara, who is the very essence of life, arose from the forehead of Brahmā, overcome with anger.
For some reason, O gods, he who possessed a splendor equal to ten million suns emerged from there,
having pierced the forehead of the Blessed Lord Brahmā.
Because he caused the Lotus-born One (Brahmā) to weep, he is remembered as Rudra;
O best of sages, listen now to his other seven names.
Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Paśupati, Bhīma, Ugra, and Mahādeva— these, O best of beings, are his names. (44)
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, the sun, and the moon—
the eighth is the initiated one; these are the forms of the Trident-bearing Lord therein.
By these [powers] this entire universe is pervaded; because he consists of this whole world, Śiva is remembered by the name "the Lord of the Universe" (Viśveśvara). || 9 ||
Commanded by Viriñci to "create progeny," the moon-crested Maheśvara created through his mind the Rudras, who were equal to himself.
They had blue throats and three eyes, were adorned with crowns of matted hair,
bore the bull as their emblem, were free from passion, and were exempt from old age and death.
Having seen all those hundreds of millions of supreme Rudras, who are omniscient and bestow grace upon all, Virañci spoke to Śaṅkara.
O Lord of the Gods, do not create such offspring who are free from old age and death; create instead other offspring who are accompanied by mortality.
Śambhu said to Brahmā, "I have no such offspring.
From that time forward, the Soul of the Universe did not procreate auspicious progeny.
Then he became engaged in play with the Rudras born from his own self;
because he remained as motionless as a pillar (sthāṇu), he is remembered as Sthāṇu. || 15 ||
Knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, austerity, truth, forgiveness, fortitude,
the state of being a seer, self-awakening, and supreme lordship—
these ten imperishable qualities abide eternally in Śaṅkara.
He alone is the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, the Lord of the Universe, Nīlalohita.
Then the Blessed Lord Brahmā, having gazed upon Śaṅkara, said to him:
"Just as you have favored me by granting me the boon of sonship," || 18 ||
"Whatever was desired has become half-successful through that which was contemplated.
Having thus addressed Śambhu, the Lord of the Universe, the four-faced one [spoke].
Placing his joined palms upon his head, he praised him with this hymn.
Brahmā said: Salutations be unto you, O Mahādeva; salutations to you, O Supreme Lord.
Salutations to the auspicious God; salutations to you who have the form of Brahman.
The power of Maheśvara belongs to you; homage to him whose nature is wind. || 38 ||
Salutation to Him whose nature is the four-faced one, who, remaining established within His own self, creates this entire universe in accordance with its own past actions.
Salutation to that Soul of the Universe, who, pervading the entire world through his power of illusion (māyā), reclines upon the couch of Śeṣa by means of the yoga of self-realization.
Salutations to that Śeṣa, the support of all, who constantly bears upon his head the cosmic egg consisting of the fourteen worlds. || 41 ||
Salutation to that one whose self is Rudra, who, having drunk the supreme bliss at the limit of the beyond, the divine sole witness, dances with infinite majesty. 42.
Salutations to You, the Supreme Self, the Lord who dwells within as the controller of all beings, the divine witness of all. 43.
Salutation to Him whose hair consists of clouds, whose every limb and joint consists of rivers, and whose belly consists of the four oceans— to Him, the embodiment of space.
Salutation to that one whose nature is Yoga, whom those who practice yoga perceive as light—being sleepless, with controlled breath, contented, and possessing equal vision. (45)
That by whose light this world shines—that Supreme Lord’s reality, which is eternally formless and of the nature of consciousness—I am that which is beyond darkness. (46)
Salutation to that Self of Knowledge, by whom the yogi, with his impurities completely destroyed, crosses over the illusion that is without end or limit. 47.
There is no verse suitable for the book named after the elephant.
80] Salutation to Him who is established within His own self, whose nature is the four-faced one. 39.
Salutations to that Soul of the Universe, who, having pervaded the entire world through his illusory power (māyā), reclines upon the couch of Śeṣa by means of the yoga of self-realization. 40.
Salutations to that Śeṣa-soul, who constantly bears upon his head the entire cosmic egg consisting of the fourteen worlds, the support of everything. 41.
Salutation to that one whose essence is Rudra, who, having drunk the supreme bliss at the ultimate limit, dances as the sole divine witness, possessing infinite majesty.
Salutations to You, the Supreme Self, the Lord who dwells within as the controller of all beings, the God who is the witness of all. 43.
Salutation to Him whose hair consists of clouds, whose every limb and joint consists of rivers, and whose belly consists of the four oceans— to Him, the embodiment of space.
Salutation to that Self of Yoga, whom those who practice yoga—sleepless, with controlled breath, contented, and possessing equal vision—behold as the light. 45.
That by whose light this world shines, I am that which is beyond darkness—
the reality that is eternally formless, the supreme Lord in the nature of consciousness. (46) By means of which the yogi, with his impurities completely destroyed, crosses over Māyā.
Salutation to that Self of Knowledge, who is without end and without limit in the future. || 47 ||
I take refuge in you, the Supreme Self, the Supreme Lord— eternal bliss, without support, partless, and the highest Śiva. 48.
Having thus praised Mahādeva, Brahmā, permeated by his being,
stood with palms joined in reverence, bowing down while reciting the eternal Brahman.
Then Hara, the Great God, bestowed upon him supreme eternal union, sovereignty, the true nature of Brahman, and dispassion.
Having touched [the water] with his two very beautiful hands, Maheśvara,
that Great God, spoke while bestowing grace upon the Grandfather (Brahmā).
"O Brahmin, that which you requested—that I become your son—has been done by me.
Now, at my command, do you create various kinds of progeny. (52)

O Brahman, though I am divided threefold under the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, I am devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) through the qualities of creation, preservation, and dissolution; of this there is no doubt.
You, my son, were created before me for the sake of creation; you are the Supreme Person, fashioned from my right side as Dakṣa and from my left side as Bhava.
From my very heart, Rudra was born, assuming a form at will;
he who is the Supreme Lord, beyond those known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara.
"The wise know that great one as Mahādeva, O Brahmā.
Having thus addressed Brahmā and having granted various boons, [he departed]. (56)
Mahādeva vanished from the sight of the lotus-born Brahmā;
through his grace, thereupon the arising of knowledge occurred for him. || 57 ||
And from that, there is the severing of the bonds, and he shall become Śiva himself;
his diseases, such as goiter, seizures, and the like, perish.
He attains success in this world as well as long life;
liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Origin of Hara and Other Matters," in the *Śrīsaura*, a subsidiary (*upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrībrahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 23 ||
The sages said: How did that Blessed One, though the all-pervading Lord and the primordial source of everything, become the son of the Four-faced One? For what reason did this occur?
"How is it that Viriñci has that lotus-womb? Tell us, O speaker! [82]
Sūta said:
When the world, including all moving and non-moving beings, had perished in a terrible ocean of one vast expanse,
there remained neither gods nor Dānavas, nor sages, nor Manus.
Then, when that reabsorption has occurred, they become weary of it;
the great yogi Nārāyaṇa rests within that darkness.
O twice-born ones, having entered into yogic sleep upon the couch of the serpent Śeṣa,
a lotus emerged from the navel of the blessed Lord Hari.
Endowed with divine fragrance and extending for a hundred yojanas,
it is considered to remain as a celestial bed for him for a hundred divine years.
Brahmā went to that place where Puruṣottama was;
and having raised up Madhusūdana with his hand, Brahmā spoke to the Lord of the Gods, who had been deluded by Māyā.
"In this terrible single ocean, who is it that lies here?
Ah! Tell me. When thus addressed, Viṣṇu, the treasury of splendors, spoke to Brahmā.
"How is it that you do not know me, O fool?
Know me to be the all-pervading Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), the source of everything, the foremost of the gods," thus spoke the Lord.
Having spoken thus, the Discus-wielder (Viṣṇu), though knowing the Grandfather (Brahmā), asked him, "Who are you? Then Brahmā spoke to Hari.
"I am indeed the first of all beings, the Lord of the entire world;
know me, O bull among men, to be Brahmā, the supreme deity. (11)
The entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, always abides within me; at the end of dissolution, it likewise merges into me alone—of this there is no doubt.
Thus addressed by the Grandfather, the Blessed Lord, the Consort of Kamalā,
entered the body of Brahmā and beheld the worlds therein.
Filled with wonder, the Lord of Kamalā emerged from the mouth of Brahmā;
the thousand-headed Puruṣa then spoke again to Brahmā.
O Brahmā, you too, having quickly entered my mouth,
observe the worlds consisting of the moving and the unmoving, including gods, asuras, and humans.
Then the blessed Lord Viriñci, having entered the belly of the Lord of Kamalā and beheld all the worlds, was struck with wonder.
Not seeing an exit door, as it was closed by the wielder of the discus,
he could not find the path of the stalk of the navel-lotus.
Having emerged by that path, Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman, shone forth—
the Grandfather, the God of gods, seated in the midst of a lotus.
The wielder of the mace, of immeasurable splendor, said to Brahmā:
"O Grandfather, all this was done by me for the sake of sport."
O best of gods, the closing of the door was not done by me out of stinginess;
you alone are the one honored by the world, the primordial Grandfather of all. (20)
I entreat you to become my son; O Lotus-seated One, grant this to me.
For the sake of my pleasure, you shall attain the renown as "Padmayoni" (Lotus-born).
Then the Self-Existent One, the all-pervading Lord who is the soul of all beings, having granted this supreme boon to the Creator of the Universe, attained great joy.
Then he said to Viṣṇu: "Nothing superior exists for the two of us; everything consists of you and me, a single form existing in two ways. (23)
Thus addressed by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, Viṣṇu said:
"O Virañci, this promise of yours shall indeed be fruitless."
Do you not see the Lord of the Universe, the self-luminous, eternal, the soul of all, the beloved of Umā, the supreme one who is without beginning or end? 25.
"O Creator, go and seek refuge in that supreme deity who is superior even to us.
Having heard these words spoken by Hari, Brahmā said to him:
"O Hari, you speak in vain, saying that there is someone superior to the two of us;
you have been overcome by sleep—abandon this delusion, O high-minded one! (27)
5 E Viṣṇu said:
"Do not speak thus, O Lotus-seated One; for without knowing the supreme state in Maheśvara, I tell you that 'He exists'—and not otherwise. (28)
His soul is deluded by the Māyā of the Supreme Lord; there is no doubt of this.
Rudra is the wielder of Māyā and the soul of the universe, while the power of Māyā belongs to Śaṅkara.
In the manuscripts designated as Kakhamavaḍaca, the words "Viṣṇu said" do not appear.
He who is the one Blessed One, the Lord, there is no second whatsoever.

Although he is ever seated within the hearts of all people, he remains unperceived by others; yet, perceiving the entire universe, he presides over it at all times. (35) The Lord, whose power is infinite and who is the singular Self, presides over even those causes that are joined with Time and the Soul, as if in sport. (36)
That Śambhu’s supreme power is accessible through meditative absorption, captivating, devoid of qualities, yet concealed by its own attributes; it is partless and auspicious. (37)
This god, Mahādeva, is to be known at all times by people;
no state whatsoever superior to him is attained. (38)
This [Self] is beginningless and endless, pure by its very nature; it is infinite, perfectly complete, and the cause of all that moves and is immobile, dependent solely upon its own will. (39)
He is the highest among all successively higher beings, and he is unsurpassed;
his majesty is infinite, and his power is unbounded.
By this act of painting, the world is first created;
and at the time of its end, it shall again undergo dissolution within this very same [canvas]. (41)
O fool, he is visible even to fallen, wicked, and contemptible people;
yet he is to be worshipped and honored both internally and externally by those who possess devotion. 42.
His form is threefold: gross, subtle, and beyond that.
The gross is visible to gods such as ourselves, while the subtle is seen by yogis.
But beyond that, that which is eternal, consciousness, bliss, and imperishable, is perceived by devotees who are devoted to it, intent upon it, and established in their vows. (44)
