O Brahmin, what is the use of saying more here? One should always cultivate devotion alone toward Śiva, the Lord of all, by which one who is endowed with it is liberated.
That devotion arises from grace alone, and grace is born of devotion;
just as here a seed comes from a sprout, or as a sprout comes from a seed.
By even a fragment of his grace, the fetters of the bound soul (paśu) are completely destroyed;
therefore, Śambhu is Paśupati, while we and others are the bound souls (paśus). || 47 ||
Śambhu bestows liberation upon all according to their inner disposition;
one is liberated while still in the womb, and another likewise while being born.
Whether a child, a youth, or even an elder, another is liberated;
some who have entered the womb of animals, or another who is a denizen of hell, is liberated. (49)
But another, having reached the belly, is released by falling back into his own side;
some, having become one whose merit is exhausted, returns once more and is then released. (50)
Someone, having ascended to that [higher state], remains there for a time and is then liberated;
therefore, liberation for human beings is not held to be of a single uniform kind. || 51 ||
Nirvāṇa is attained through serenity alone that accords with the state of one's knowledge;
O Blessed One, you are the one form, while the other is the supreme Nārāyaṇī.
Raudrī is declared to be the third, the one who effects the destruction of the world.
O Four-faced One, Śambhu is the impeller of these [goddesses] in their respective tasks.
O Brahmā, how is it that you do not behold that Lord Mahādeva, who, though devoid of qualities, is the presiding overseer of the qualities and whose form is independent sovereignty?
"I grant you divine vision by which you shall behold that Śiva.
Having obtained divine vision from the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, Brahmā indeed beheld him.
Brahmā beheld Mahādeva standing visibly before him, having attained the supreme, attributeless, and transcendent divine knowledge.
Having gone to him alone for refuge and having praised him with various hymns, Mahādeva, becoming pleased, then spoke to the four-faced one: || 57 ||
I desire you alone as my son, or a son who is equal to you.
Deluded by your māyā, O Śambhu, I did not know you as the supreme Śiva;
I bow to your lotus feet, the medicine for the existence of yogis. 62.
Having heard their loud words, the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
looked toward his son, the wielder of the discus, and then spoke to Brahmā.
"O Brahmin, O dear son, I shall fulfill that which has been requested by you.
I, O grandson, shall become present among your sons through a portion of myself. (64)
O sinless one, knowledge concerning me will swiftly arise within you;
by my grace, create this world of moving and non-moving beings.
O sinless Brahmin, this lord of yogis, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, is undoubtedly a portion of myself; at my command, O faultless one, he shall provide you assistance.
O best of the twice-born, having thus granted the boon to Brahmā,
Śambhu then spoke to Hṛṣīkeśa, who stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
"Choose a boon, O imperishable Nārāyaṇa; I shall grant it to you. There exists no difference between us two; you are my own power (śakti), of this there is no doubt. (68)
All this, consisting of the unmanifest and the nature of the Puruṣa, composed of knowledge and the object of knowledge, is pervaded by you and pervaded by me, O Hari. (69)
I am the knower, you are the form of knowledge; I am the thinker, you are the intellect.
You are primordial nature (prakṛti), O best of gods, and I am the spirit (puruṣa); of this there is no doubt.
You are the moon and I am the sun; you are the night and I am the day.
You alone are the illusion of the universe, and I am the illusion, O Supreme Lord. (71)
*Brahmā said:* [The reading *ini 6ṅacaṅasajñi* does not exist in the manuscripts.
Having thus heard the words of Śambhu, Vāsudeva, the stainless one, [acted accordingly].
O best of the twice-born, he spoke to Mahādeva, the Supreme Self.
Viṣṇu said:
"O Lord worshipped by the gods, let my devotion to you be unwavering and unswerving; what need have I for other boons? What shall I do? (73)
Having addressed the wielder of the Śārṅga bow with the words "So be it," and having embraced him,
Hara said, "Protect this by my command," and then vanished.
O best of sages, just as the three-eyed god became the son of Brahmā, so has everything been told to you in its entirety and without omission.

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of Brahmā’s Origin from the Lotus and Other Matters," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 24 ||
"How is it that the Blessed Gaurī, who forms half the body of Śaṅkara, is eternal, consisting of the Supreme Brahman, and situated in the midst of the supreme ether? The sages said: [1]
She consists of all powers, is peaceful, devoid of qualities, free from affliction,
without beginning, middle, or end, and liberated from all limiting adjuncts.
The Sovereign of the Gods, illuminating this entire universe with her own radiance,
is eternal bliss, free from fear, indivisible, and stainless.
How did that Supreme Goddess create a separate body?
We wish to hear that; O Sūta, you ought to tell it here.
Sūta said:
Having obtained a boon from Mahādeva, the Lord of the Universe, the blessed Grandfather (Brahmā) created progeny;
yet those progeny did not multiply.
Then Brahmā became distressed upon seeing his subjects so weak;
he considered himself to have failed in his purpose, and thereupon Hara manifested himself.
Śambhu said to Brahmā: "O sinless one, the cause of your sorrow has been understood; that which will bring you peace in every respect shall come to pass."
Saying "So be it," Śiva himself, the Lord of the Universe and the God who is half-female (Ardhanārīśvara), began to perform the act.
From his own portions, Mahādeva created separately the Sovereign Lady,
the supreme Śakti whose essence is Brahman, resplendent like ten million rising suns.
She is the abode of the power of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), situated in the midst of the supreme space.
I bow to Sāvitrī, the mother of the Vedas, who is saluted by Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu; she who possesses eight forms, who is unborn, who transcends both Pradhāna and Puruṣa,
who is the abode of the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāma, and who is the supreme Kuṇḍalinī in her upright form.
The sovereign of all, consisting of the universe, and devoted to the Lord of the Universe.

She who effects the dissolution of the universe, who sets in motion the universal illusion (māyā), who brings about creation, preservation, and destruction, and whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest. || 17 ||
Protect me, O Lord of the gods of gods, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge;
I know of no other resort for me, O you who are worshipped by the three worlds. (18)
"O auspicious one, you are my mother and my father is Śiva, the Lord of All.
O beloved of Śaṅkara, I have been created by the Destroyer of Tripura for the sake of creation.
Various kinds of progeny have been created, yet they do not attain growth."
After that, it is said, all creatures were born from sexual union.
"I wish to create after having first brought about this creation; indeed, the emanation of all powers proceeds from you. (21)
O Śivā, that lineage of powers which you did not previously create—O Goddess, you are the bestower of all powers upon all embodied beings. (22)
There is no doubt that you alone are she; therefore, O Eternal One, become the bestower of boons by means of one portion of yourself for the sake of the expansion of my creation. (23)
"O lady of pure smiles, become the daughter of my son Dakṣa";
thus was the goddess entreated by Brahmā at that time, O best of sages.

[89] Hara, the Lord of the Universe, smilingly beheld that goddess who had been created from the middle of his eyebrows, possessing a radiance equal to his own, and emitted a single power (Śakti) from between his brows that was equal in splendor to himself. 25.
"O Goddess, at the word of Brahmā, carry out his desire as you wish.
Having received the command of Śambhu upon her head, that supreme sovereign lady [did so].
By her own will, she became the daughter of Dakṣa, possessing the form of Brahmā;
then again, the primordial supreme Śakti entered the body of Śambhu.
"For it is our sacred tradition that the Lord shines as Ardhanārīśvara;
from that time forth, O best of Brahmins, progeny have arisen from sexual union. (28)
Thus, O sages, the supreme origin of the Goddess has been told to you;
whoever reads or even hears this, their lineage shall increase. (29)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of Gaurī’s Identity with Pṛthā’s Body and Other Matters," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. 25.
Sūta said:
Having obtained an incomparable boon from Śiva and Śivā, the blessed Lord Brahmā, Hiraṇyagarbha,
created Marīci and other stainless sages.
The omnipresent Lord created Marīci, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Dakṣa, Atri, and Vasiṣṭha by means of his mind.
The Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) created in due order all the gods, asuras, humans, and even the ancestors, as well as the rākṣasas in the darkness.
From his anus he created Gandharvas and Nāgas by the thousands,
and from his arms he created Viśas and Kṣatriyas.
From his two thighs he created the Vaiśyas, and from his feet the Śūdras;
thereafter, he produced the Vedic meters, the Vedas, the sacrifices, and the Kalpasūtras.
Then, having created the auxiliary sciences of the Vedas (vedāṅgas), the Grandfather, the God of gods, set his mind upon creating through sexual union.
He himself became a woman by one half and a man by the other half;
from that half which was a woman, Śatarūpā was born.
Brahmā created Svāyambhuva Manu with half of his own body;
and as for the goddess Śatarūpā, she performed most difficult austerities.
And there are four daughters, O best of the twice-born, who are faith and the other virtues. (19)
Kṣamā bore Kardama and Ambarīṣa from Pulaha,
as well as Durvāsas, Soma, and the yogi Dattātreya.
Anasūyā, however, gave birth to faultless sons for Atri,
as well as Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumati.
Smṛti gave birth to daughters endowed with auspicious marks who were the wives of Aṅgiras;
from Pulastya, Maitrī gave birth to a son named Datta, who was free from pride.
He who was known as Agastya in a previous birth during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara begot a progeny of sixty thousand sons through his sacrifice.
In their lineage, forty-five [kings] came into being. || 28 ||
These thirty-nine, beginning with Pāvaka, as well as all those who possess shares in the sacrifices and all ascetics [are likewise entitled]. (29)

All the ancestors, the sons of Brahmā— both those who have performed sacrifices and those who have not— are devoted to the worship of Rudra, with their foreheads marked by the triple line (tripuṇḍra).
The Agniṣvāttas and the Barhiṣadas—thus was their twofold division established.
From them, Svadhā gave birth to two daughters renowned throughout the world.
Both Menā and Dhāriṇī there were devoted to the path of yoga;
Menā gave birth to Maināka and Krauñca, the sons of Himavat.
Then he begot two daughters, Gaurī and Gaṅgā, who are the mothers of the world; and Dhāriṇī bore Mandara, which possesses beautiful caves.
Dhāriṇī gave birth to Velā, who was most beloved by Mahādeva, adorned with various minerals, as well as Niyati and Āyati.
The shoreline (Velā) gave birth to Sāmudrī by name from the ocean;
and she, in turn, bore ten sons to Prācīnavarhis.
All those known as the Prācetasas existed during the Svāyambhuva Manvantara; it was through their curse that Dakṣa, the Prajāpati, became their son.
[92] Now, therefore, I shall relate to you the lineage of Manu’s sons. || 37 ||

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Lineage of the Daughters of Dakṣa and the Creation of Marīci and Others," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahma Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 26 ||
Sūta said:
The son of Uttānapāda was the high-minded Dhruva;
having propitiated the supreme deity Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all ailment, [he attained his goal]. (1)
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, established in them and devoted to them,
he attained the supreme state through the grace of that God.
Dhruva had four sons: Sṛṣṭi, Dhanya, and another, Harya, and Śambhu;
they were high-souled devotees of Viṣṇu of celebrated power.
Chāyā gave birth to five sons who were devoted to the dharma of creation:
Ripu, Ripuñjaya, Vipra, Śala, and Kṛtejas.
Bṛhatī, the wife of Ripu, gave birth to a son named Cakṣuṣa;
Puṣkariṇī bore a son, Cakṣuṣa Manu.
Born of that lineage were the innumerable Aṅgas, Tuṣas, Śivas, and others.
From Aṅga came Vena; from Vena came the son of Vena (Vainya), who is remembered as Pṛthu.
That protector of the earth was renowned by whom the earth was milked;
no king equal to him exists upon the surface of the earth.
Devoted to the worship of Vāsudeva and dedicated to Vāsudeva,
he propitiated Govinda through austerity on the auspicious slopes of Govardhana.
O best of sages, Viṣṇu spoke to Pṛthu from within him:
"O royal sage, by my grace there shall be two sons for you—
great-souled universal emperors, devoted to me and dedicated to their father."
Thus the king obtained his boon from Puruṣottama, the Lord of Gods.
Having established supreme devotion and taking refuge in the word of the Blessed One,
the highly fortunate wife of Pṛthu gave birth to two sons in due time.
Śikhaṇḍin was Havirdhāna, and Suśīla was the son of Śikhaṇḍin;
he was named Śvetāśvatara and was solely intent on meditation upon Śiva.
[93] Having worshipped, Suśīla attained the supreme yoga of the Lord.
The sages said: "How was this unsurpassed knowledge obtained by King Suśīla? (43)
We wish to hear that; speak it, O high-minded Sūta!
Sūta said: That son of Śikhaṇḍin, who was devoted to the stage of student life (brahmacarya), having studied the Vedas according to the rules, attained supreme detachment. || 15 ||
O twice-born ones, a reflection for his ultimate welfare once occurred to him:
"Since there are various types of karma considered to be both active (*pravṛtta*) and withdrawn (*nivṛtta*), there will be no final liberation for me from these two.
Having reflected thus in his mind, he went to the region of the Himalayas.
There he beheld the forest named Dharmavana, frequented by sages and perfected beings, inhabited by yogins, and containing the abode built by Mahādeva.
Where the great-souled perfected ones, the great seers beginning with Marīci, as well as the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa and other gods and demons [attain success]. (19)
Having propitiated Mahādeva, many indeed attained perfection in that place where the Mandākinī Gaṅgā shines, the remover of sins.
He saw her hermitage on its bank, frequented by the lords of yogis;
having bathed there in the waters of the Mandākinī and having worshipped Maheśvara, [he stayed]. (21)
Engaged in the discourse of Mahādeva and having praised him with various hymns,
he remained there for a moment meditating upon Śiva, the Lord of the Universe.
Then they beheld the great sage named Śvetāśvatara,
a peaceful follower of the Mahāpāśupata sect, wearing a worn-out loincloth.

Having saluted the feet of the sage with his head while joining his palms in reverence, the king— whose entire body was smeared with ashes and marked with the triple-line forehead mark (tripuṇḍra)— paid homage.
He spoke to that best of sages, who is compassionate toward all beings:
"Today I am blessed and my purpose is fulfilled; my life has become fruitful. (25)
My ascetic practices have indeed become fruitful through the sight of you;
I shall be your disciple there—protect me from the fear born of saṃsāra. (26)
"If I possess the fitness to become your disciple...
Then those bulls among sages addressed the king.
That which is called the "foot-fall" (pādapata) is the stage of yoga-asceticism, according to the Śruti.
He was established among all the gods as a Guru by those who know the Vedas;
yet, through the grace of that sage, he also became free from sin.
Devoted to the study of the Vedas, peaceful, intent on overcoming fear, and having conquered his senses,
one who possesses good character shall attain liberation by resorting to the rule of renunciation.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Lineage of Uttānapāda and Others," in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka within the *Śrī Saura*, a minor Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*.
Sūta said:
In former times, the patriarch Dakṣa was impelled by the Self-born One (Brahmā) to create progeny;
he then created the gods and the asuras. || 1 ||
The daughter of Prajāpati Viraṇa was Ariṣṭā;
indeed, the Prajāpati Dakṣa begot sixty daughters by her.
And he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
twenty-seven to Soma, and four to Ariṣṭanemi.
Prajāpati Dakṣa gave two daughters to Bahuputra, two to the wise Kṛśāśva, and likewise two to Aṅgiras.
Sādhyā, Viśvā, Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtī, Arundhatī, Marutvatī, Vasu, Bhānu, Lambā, and Jāmī—these are the ten. || 5 ||
Dharma’s wives were Tāra and the others; their progeny is now described: from Sādhyā were born the Sādhyas, and from Viśvā the Viśvedevas.
From Saṃkalpā was born Saṃkalpa; from Gūti were born the Muhūrtas;
from Arundhatī was born Arundhatī; and from Marutvatī was born Marutvān.
Those of Vasu are declared as the Vasus, and those of Bhānu are remembered as the Bhānus;
those of Lambā are named Ghoṣas, while those born of Jāmī are the Nāgavīthis.
The three radiant gods are all-pervasive in every direction; they are known as the Vasus, and they desire the welfare of all beings. || 9 ||
Āpa, Nala, Soma, Vānila, Anala, Mātyūpa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. || 10 ||
Having worshipped him, Suśīla attained the sovereign yoga.
The sages said: "How was this unsurpassed knowledge obtained by King Suśīla? (43)
We wish to hear that; speak it, O high-minded Sūta!
Sūta said:
He who was Śikhaṇḍin’s son, devoted to the stage of studenthood (brahmacarya), having studied the Vedas according to the rules, attained supreme detachment. || 15 ||
O twice-born ones, a reflection for his ultimate welfare once arose in him regarding the various types of action considered to be both engaged (pravṛtta) and withdrawn (niṣṭatta).
Thinking to himself, "There will be no ultimate liberation for me from these two," he went to the slopes of the Himalayas.
There he beheld the forest named Dharmavana, frequented by sages and perfected beings, inhabited by yogins, and containing the abode built by Mahādeva.
Where the great-souled perfected ones, the great seers beginning with Marīci, as well as the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa and other gods and demons [attained their goals]. (19)
Having propitiated Mahādeva, many indeed have attained perfection in that place where the Mandākinī Gaṅgā shines, the remover of sins.
He beheld her hermitage on its bank, frequented by the lords of yogis;
having bathed there in the waters of the Mandākinī and having worshipped Maheśvara, [he remained].
Having praised him with various hymns joined with the stories of Mahādeva,
he remained there for a moment meditating upon Śiva, the Lord of the Universe.
Then he beheld the great sage named Śvetāśvatara,
a peaceful follower of the Mahāpāśupata sect, wearing a worn-out loincloth,
with his entire body smeared with ashes and marked with the triple-line sectarian tilaka.
Having saluted the feet of the Sage with his head, the king stood with palms joined in reverence.
He spoke to that best of sages, who is compassionate toward all beings:
"Today I am blessed and my purpose is fulfilled; my life has become fruitful. (25)
My ascetic practices have indeed become fruitful through the sight of you;
I am your disciple—protect me from the fear born of saṃsāra. (26)
"If I possess the fitness to become your disciple,
may that sage [then] attend upon the king.
Yoga
"That which is called 'the yoga of sin' or 'another stage of life' is what the Śruti declares. (68)
The house was built by those learned in the Vedas and the science of architecture;
through the grace of that sage, he too became a protector of the earth.

Devoted to the study of the Vedas, peaceful, intent on overcoming fear, and having conquered his senses, one who is well-disciplined shall attain liberation by resorting to the rule of renunciation. (30) 1191)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Lineage of Uttānapāda and Others," in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka within the *Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*, the *Śrī Saura*.
Sūta said:
In the beginning, the Prajāpati Dakṣa was commissioned by the Self-born One (Brahmā) with the command,
"Create progeny," and he then produced the gods and the asuras.
The daughter of Prajāpati Aṇu was Ariṣṭā;
Dakṣa, the lord of progeny, begot sixty daughters by her who were indeed free from disease.
And he gave ten to Dharma, thirteen to Kaśyapa,
twenty-seven to Soma, and four to Ariṣṭanemi.
Prajāpati Dakṣa gave two daughters to Bahuputra, two to the wise Kṛśāśva, and likewise two to Aṅgiras.
Sādhyā, Viśvā, Saṃkalpā, Muhūrtā, Arundhatī,
Marutvatī, Vasu, Bhānu, Lambā, and Jāmī— these are the ten.
The wives of Dharma were indeed the Āratīs; their progeny is thus described. From Sādhyā were born the Sādhyas, and from Viśvā were born the Viśvedevas.
From Saṃkalpa was born Saṃkalpa; from Mūrti were born the Mūrtajas; from Arundhatī was born Arundhatī; and from Marutvatī was born Marutvat.
Those born of Vasu are called Vasavas; those of Bhānu are known as Bhānus.
Those born of Lambā are named Ghoṣas, while those born of Jāmī are the Nāgavīthis.
The three luminous deities are all-pervading in every direction; they are designated as the Vasus.
Āpa, Nala, Soma, Dhruva, Anila, Anala,
Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus.
Dhruva’s son was Kāla, who inspired fear in all the worlds; Viśvakarman was the son of Prabhāsa. This, indeed, is the lineage of Dharma.

Aditi, Diti, and likewise Danu are considered another; Ariṣṭā is called Surasā, as well as Svadhā and Surabhi. Vinatā, Tāmrā, Kadrū, Krodhavaśā, and Virā—O best of the twice-born, these are the wives of Kaśyapa, the sage. (12–13)
Aṃśu, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Vivasvat, Savitṛ, Pūṣan, Aṃśumān, and Viṣṇu. || 14 ||
In the previous interval of Manu Cākṣuṣa, they were known as the Tuṣitas;
in the Vaivasvata interval, they are declared to be the Ādityas, the sons of Aditi.
Diti bore two sons from Kaśyapa, the bull among sages:
first Hiraṇyakaśipu, and immediately after him, Hiraṇyākṣa.
That Hiraṇyakaśipu, who was arrogant due to the boons granted by Brahmā,
oppressed all the deities, beginning with Śakra.
Having gone for refuge to Brahmā, the gods spoke with palms joined in reverence.
The gods said: "O God of gods, Lord of the world, Four-faced One, Supreme among deities! (18)
We have been destroyed by the Daitya Hiraṇyaka with various weapons and missiles;
his wife has been carried off by him, as have the thunderbolt and other armaments.

"Protect us who are terrified by fear; for us, there is no other refuge. Having heard what was thus spoken by the gods, the Grandfather (Brahmā) went quickly with the deities to where the imperishable Viṣṇu resides, and after praising him with various hymns, the lotus-seated one spoke.
Brahmā said: O Lord, Hiraṇyakaśipu, rendered exceedingly arrogant by my boon,
oppresses all the gods and the sages who have shaken off all taint.
O Mādhava, I do not see anyone who will quickly slay him;
considering that he himself will be his own destroyer, we have come here. (23)
"You ought to slay him quickly for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
Having heard these words spoken by the inhabitants of heaven, Nārāyaṇa—
Having made half of his body human and half of his body likewise that of a lion,
the Blessed One, in the form of Nṛsiṃha, [appeared] in the city of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
The Lord, the divine and powerful Nārāyaṇa, appeared,
emitting a most terrible roar that struck fear into the asuras.
Seeing the extremely terrifying Nṛsiṃha, Hiraṇyakaśipu dispatched the great asuras, headed by Prahlāda, for the purpose of slaying him.
Mahāvīrya,
Aca, Saṃhrāda, and Hrāda— these were the four sons of Hiraṇyakaśipu, renowned for their prowess.
Then the Dānavas fought with Narasiṃha;
Prahlāda hurled the Brahma-missile at that man-lion.
Anuhrāda sent the Vaiṣṇava weapon, and another, Vātāpi, sent the Kaumāra; likewise, Āgneya sent the Vāruṇa weapon, and other great asuras did the same.
Having encountered the Blessed One, that lion among men, those four [arrows] were shattered like a tree struck by a thunderbolt. (31)
Seizing his four sons with both hands, the Man-lion threw them from the sky to the ground, and did so again and again.
Seeing them thus distressed, Hiraṇyakaśipu himself,
blazing with anger, went to where the Man-Lion was.

Then Prahlāda, the king of the Daityas, having turned away from the battle with his horses and having recognized the divine nature of the Lord of immeasurable splendor in the form of Nṛsiṃha, meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa and restrained the Dānavas.
"This Nārāyaṇa is a yogī, the eternal Supreme Self;
he is to be meditated upon by you, not to be fought—this is certain. (35)
Disregarding the words spoken by his son, Hiraṇyakaśipu fought with Hari once again for three hundred years.
Then Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
tore Hiraṇyakaśipu apart with his claws.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Creation of Gods and Asuras and Other Matters," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. 28.
Sūta said: After Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain, Prahlāda, the best of the Daityas, [ascended the throne].
He installed the mighty-armed Hiraṇyākṣa upon the throne. (3) || 1 ||
Having defeated even the gods in battle, they indeed fled for refuge to their own kin;
and Hiraṇyākṣa, having propitiated Mahādeva, the Ender, through ascetic penance.
He obtained a mighty-armed son who was the destroyer of all the immortals;
out of fear of Hiraṇyākṣa, the gods went for refuge to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Then, having seen the gods, the Blessed One assumed the form of a boar for the sake of slaying Hiraṇyākṣa, and Hiraṇyākṣa was destroyed.
When Hiraṇyākṣa was gone, Prahlāda, the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas,
abandoned his tamasic disposition and took possession of his own kingdom.
Then, on one occasion, he was deluded by the illusion of the gods;
having seen a certain Brahmin with a lean body who had come to his house.
The Daitya showed contempt for him, and he was cursed by that Brahmin:
"O Daitya, relying upon whose strength you hold me in contempt... (7)
"May your devotion toward the Lord Janārdana perish quickly!
Having thus cursed him, O best of sages, the brahmin departed for his own hermitage.
Then the lord of the Daityas waged war with Viṣṇu;
remembering the slaughter of his father, he also conquered the other gods.
By the grace of the Blessed One from before, the king of the Daityas once again abandoned all that was illusory and went for refuge to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Having consecrated Andhaka in the kingdom, he himself became absorbed in yoga;
then the god Mahādeva, the refuge of all embodied beings, [remained there]. 11.
For some reason, the Lord of the Mountain-Daughter (Śiva), having established the Goddess Girijā upon Mount Mandara, went out for alms together with the Brahmins.
Śiva made the gods, along with Nārāyaṇa, attendants at his side;
then the gods, assuming female forms, served Pārvatī.
Having stationed the countless lords of the Gaṇas, headed by Nandin, and having commanded Mairava and Nandin to remain at the gateway; || 14 ||
Then that Bhairava, having carried out the command of Śambhu, the Auspicious One, [departed]. || 25 ||
Suddenly seizing his trident, he went into battle with the Daitya;
having pierced him through with the tip of the trident, he danced with the playful ease of his own nature.
When the Daitya was placed upon the tip of the trident, Brahmā and the other sages then praised him with various hymns; at that time, the world became filled with joy.
Andhaka said:
With a concentrated mind, I bow my head to the one Blessed One whom they know as the principle of the Lord (Īśatattva)—
the ancient, meritorious, and infinite-formed Time, the Seer, the cause of both union and separation through yoga.
* Here, in all the manuscript copies, the word ending in "śaktayaḥ" occurs.
In that case, the nominative case is to be understood in the sense of the accusative;
this is due to its being archaic (ārṣatvāt).
Homage be to the one who has the moon as his ornament and stands in the midst; homage be to the god with golden arms. ||39||
Salutation to the one who is exceedingly secret, who dwells within the cave of the heart, who is ascertained through the wisdom of the Vedānta;
salutation to Maheśa, the abode of the stainless splendor of the three times; salutation to Śiva. 40.
Then the Blessed One Bhairava, having become pleased by this hymn,
descended from the tip of the trident and spoke, O Supreme Lord.
O best of Daityas, I have been gratified by you with this excellent hymn of praise;
I am pleased and shall indeed grant you the rare status of a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya).
"O child, become a Gaṇa named Bhṛṅgin, equal to Nandīśvara.
Having thus obtained the boon, the Daitya became as radiant as ten million suns.
Blue-throated, with a single eye, bull-bannered, and wearing matted locks—
seeing him, all the deities were their minds filled with overflowing joy. (44)
They praised that lord of the Gaṇas who was in the presence of Bhairava,
and then [they praised] the goddess Śivā, the sovereign of the universe, who stood near Śambhu.
Having praised her with his whole being, Śivā, who is compassionate toward those who have come for refuge,
accepted the Daitya as her son with a joyful mind.
Then, having obtained the permission of Maheśa, that Kālabhairava,
the soul of the universe, went to his own city in Pātāla together with the Mothers.
Therein resided the supreme, dark (tāmasī) form of the Blessed Viṣṇu;
then Bhairava, beholding her, joyfully embraced her. 48.
The forms of Bhairava and Viṣṇu became one and the same;
he who was Kālābhairava was himself Nṛhari.
That very Bhagavān who is Nṛhari is indeed Bhairava;
by the worship of Nṛhari, Bhairava certainly becomes pleased. (50)
The worship of Bhairava alone is the worship of Nṛhari;
those people who perceive a difference between the two are deluded by Māyā. (51)
They are cooked in hell until the dissolution of all beings.
Therefore, the forms consisting of Rudra and Nārāyaṇa should always be worshipped;
when the Blessed Lady is pleased, she becomes the remover of ignorance.
Thus, O twice-born ones, the slaying of Andhaka has been briefly recounted by me,
as well as the manifestation of Bhairava and his heroic prowess.
Whoever recites this chapter in the presence of Mahādeva shall be liberated from all sins and become an attendant of Śiva. || 55 ||

1283 || Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Account of the Slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa and Other Deeds," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 29 ||
Sūta said:
Mahāda, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu and the best of the Daityas,
remained himself established in that kingdom when the Daitya Andhaka had been slain.
Having ruled the kingdom for a very long time,
that most righteous and wise king, endowed with qualities such as tranquility, became dispassionate toward sovereignty.
Having consecrated Virocana as the best among the wise in the kingdom,
he then departed for the forest of asceticism, being wholly devoted to Vāsudeva.
And Virocana was slain by the Discus-wielder, the God of gods;
Bali became his son, a Daitya devoted to righteousness.
Having been bound, that Bāṇāsura was led to Pātāla by the Discus-wielder, the God of gods;
his son was a devotee of Śiva, the Lord of the Universe.
The Blessed One bestowed upon him the unsurpassed leadership of the Gaṇas;
likewise, Tāra, Śambara, Kapila, and Śaṅkara [were given].
O twice-born ones, Svarbhānu and Ṛṣaparvan were these two sons of Bāṇa;
O best of sages, Surasā bore to Kaśyapa the sky-dwellers.
Anantā and the others, the powerful sons of Kadrū who were even more mighty,
as well as the Gandharvas, Ariṣṭā likewise gave birth to from Kaśyapa.
Vinatā gave birth to the renowned Garuḍa and Aruṇa;
likewise, the twice-born [sages] procreated others, ranging from animals down to stationary beings.
Having brought forth both the stationary and the moving beings, Kaśyapa then performed supreme austerity once more for the sake of increasing his progeny.
Through the power of his asceticism, two sons were born to Vatsara:
Naidhruva was born from Vatsara, and the high-minded Raibhya was likewise born.
Sumedhā gave birth to sons who were drinkers from the sacrificial ladle (Naiṛvāṇakuṇḍapāyins).
From Asitā, the wife of Ekaparṇa, the sage Devala was born.
Having propitiated Śambhu, Devala attained supreme perfection.
Śāṇḍilya was born from Devala; these are the descendants of Kaśyapa.
The royal sage Tṛṇabindu gave his daughter named Ilavilā to Pulastya; from her was born Viśravas. [14] Likewise, Puṣpotkaṭā, Vākā, Kaikasī, and Devavarṇinī—
That high-souled descendant of Pulastya had four wives.
Kubera was born of Kaikasi, as was Rāvaṇa;
likewise Kumbhakarṇa, Śūrpaṇakhā, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
From Puṣpotkaṭā there were three sons and daughters.
Beings, wild animals, piśācas, and all those with fangs likewise. || 19 ||
All those were known as the Paulastyas; Kaśyapa was the son of Marīci, and from Bhṛgu was born Śukra, the great preceptor of the Daityas.
The wise Śukra,
having propitiated Mahādeva in the past at Badarikāśrama, obtained the Saṃjīvinī lore;
that great sage became free from old age and death, possessing a body of adamant.
He became renowned as a Yogācārya through the grace of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain (Śiva). || 22 ||
O twice-born ones, Anasūyā gave birth in due order to three sons:
Dattātreya, Candramas, and the sage Durvāsas.
They became known as the Ātreyas, while Ṛtu likewise remained childless;
O best of sages, Nārada gave his daughter to Vasiṣṭha.
From Arundhatī and Arundhatī was born one named Śakti;
from Śakti came Parāśara, who was the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.
From Dvaipāyana, Śuka was born; these were the five sons of Śuka:
Bhūriśravas, Prabhu, Śambhu, Kṛṣṇa, and Gaura as the fifth.
The maiden named Kīrtimatī—these are the lineages that have been proclaimed.
From Kaśyapa, Aditi obtained Bhāskara, who was superior in splendor.
Saṃjñā, Prabhā, and Chāyā are recorded as these wives of the Sun. Saṃjñā gave birth to Sūrya and Manu, in whose lineage kings arose;
she also bore Yama, Yamunā, and King Revanta.
Radiance comes from the sun at dawn, and shadow from Sāvarṇi.
Śani, Tapatī, and Viṣṭi followed in due order;
then Ikṣvāku, Bhaga, Dhṛṣṭa, and Śaryāti. || 30 ||
Nariṣyanta, Nābhāga, Ariṣṭa, Karūṣa, and the highly resplendent Vṛṣadhvaja—these nine were the sons of Vaivasvata. || 31 ||
Ilā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Variṣṭhā—these three are remembered as his daughters. And from Ikṣvāku there was born a son renowned as Vikukṣi. (32)
O Kakutstha, he indeed had a hundred sons, of whom Kakutstha was declared to be the eldest.
From him Suyodhana was born, and Pṛthu became his son. || 33 ||
Viśvaka was his son, and Damaka was indeed his son;
from him Śaryāti was born, and Yuvanāśva was his son.
Śrāvasti was his son, by whom Śrāvastī was built; from him came the famous Kuvalaya, and from him Dhundhumāra was born.
Dhundhumāra had three sons of great prowess, headed by Dṛḍhāśva;
and the heir of Dṛḍhāśva was Hariścandra.
Rohita was his son, and Rohita’s son was also [named] Rohita;
from him was born a son named Dhundhu, and Dhundhu had two sons. (37)
Sudeva and Vijaya were born, and Kuruka is remembered as having been born from Vijaya.
Then Ko was born from Kuruka, and from him Bāhu became the son.
Sagara was his son, and Aṃśumat is remembered as his grandson;
Dilīpa was his son, and from him Bhagīratha was born. (39)
Pleased by his asceticism, Śambhu granted him an unsurpassed boon;
Hara, desiring the protection of the worlds, bore Gaṅgā upon his head.
Having obtained a boon from Mahādeva, Bhagīratha ruled the kingdom for twelve thousand two hundred years, ten times ten thousand. (41)
Detached from the enjoyments of sovereignty and regarding the entire universe as a magical illusion,
he approached Jābāli and attained that knowledge which has Śiva as its essence.
Having received the favor of the Sage, the king attained supreme perfection.
Śruta was his son, and Nābhāga was his son.
From him was born Sindhudvīpa; from him came Ayutāyu;
Ṛtuparṇa was his son, and Sudhāmā was his son.
To whomsoever the Blessed One granted unsurpassed lordship over the Gaṇas, his son was Kalmāṣapāda; his son, born of his wife, was Aśmaka.
From the sage Vasiṣṭha, the best of brahmins, Nakula was born as his son;
Nakula’s son was the king named Śataratha.
From him was born Ilaghila, and from him Vṛddhaśarman was born.
Therefore, his son was Khaṭvā, who was named Viśvasaha.
From him Dīrghabāhu was born, and Raghu was his son;
from Raghu was born the famous Aja, and from him King Daśaratha.
He had four sons, knowers of dharma and renowned throughout the world:
Rāma, Bharata, and the third was known as Lakṣmaṇa. (49)
And the fourth was Śatrughna; Rāma himself was Nārāyaṇa, whose resolve is truth, who is Dharma itself, and who is devoted solely to Mahādeva.
Sītā became his wife, for she was born from a portion of Pārvatī;
since in former times Gaurī had been propitiated by Janaka through ascetic penance. (51)
Śambhu, being pleased, gave that unsurpassed bow to Janaka;
[Rāma] then broke that bow which was situated in Janaka’s house.
Having witnessed the prowess of that virtuous Rāma,
Janaka, the best among the knowers of Brahman, gave Sītā to him.
When Rāma was about to be consecrated in the kingdom by his father,
Kaikeyī, the king’s beloved daughter-in-law, then restrained him.
"O Lord, since you have already granted a boon in the past, you ought therefore to appoint my son Bharata as king. (55)
Having heard these words of hers, he consecrated him in the kingdom and sent that Rāma, along with Lakṣmaṇa, away to the forest.
Then, having gone to the forest and seen his wife while he was living there,
the Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, a descendant of Pulastya, took her and returned again to Laṅkā.
O twice-born ones, not finding Sītā there, the two sons of Daśaratha, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, became sorrowful; they then entered into friendship with the king of the monkeys.
The heroic monkey named Hanumān, a friend of Sugrīva,
went to the city of Rāvaṇa and beheld the daughter of Janaka.
To inspire confidence in Sītā, whose eyes were filled with tears and whose face resembled a blue lotus, he gave her Rāma’s very own ring.
Upon seeing the ring, Sītā then became greatly delighted;
having comforted her, he then departed for the presence of Rāghava.
[107] Seeing him arrive, Rāma’s eyes blossomed with great joy;
having heard the account from his words, he resolved to go to war.
Then, having built a bridge and fought with the Rākṣasas, the high-minded Rāma,
firm in his vows, slew Rāvaṇa along with his brothers.
He brought that Sītā who was staying in the midst of the Aśoka grove;
then Rāghava, having installed Mahādeva in the middle of the bridge, [proceeded].
Śiva, whose prowess is auspicious, attained supreme devotion toward Śiva;
he is the great god Mahādeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, renowned as Rāmeśvara.
Merely by the sight of him, one is cleansed of the sin of killing a Brahmin;
thereafter, the lotus-eyed Rāma was consecrated in the kingdom.
Protecting the entire earth through righteousness, O best of sages,
he worshipped Śaṅkara, the Lord of the gods of gods, with the horse-sacrifice.
Then, by his grace, Rāghava attained his own station;
thus has the life of Rāma been recounted by me in brief.
O Brahmins, this has been recounted in detail once more by Vālmīki;
Kuśa and Lava were the other two sons of Rāma, both of whom were firm in their vows.
From Kuśa was born Atithi, who was true to his word, possessed of great vows, and devoted to Mahādeva; Niṣadha was his son, Nala was his son, and Nabhas was his son.
From him was born Candrāvaloka, and from him Tārāpīḍa arose;
from him came the one named Candragiri, and his son was Bhānujit.
All these kings who have been described are born of the Ikṣvāku lineage;
they were righteous-souled, possessed of great strength, illustrious, and firm in their vows.
Whoever constantly recites this supreme *Īśvarakośa* is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of the Sun. (73)

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Lineage of Kings Born in the Ikṣvāku Family, Beginning with the Coronation of King Prahāda," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 30 ||
Sūta said:
King Purūravas, the son of Ilā, was supremely righteous;
through Urvaśī, he begot six sons of refined vigor.
But the wise Jayadhvaja was devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa. || 12 ||
The heirs of Jayadhvaja are known as the Tālajaṅghas;
their eldest was Vītihotra, and all of them are remembered as Yādavas. || 13 ||
[The text provided consists of two vertical bars (||) and contains no prose to translate.]
His heir was Viśruta, and his wife was a devoted spouse;
once, while sporting with her on the bank of the Yamunā, the king—
There he saw Urvaśī, intent upon playing the lute;
afflicted by the arrows of the god of love, the king spoke to Urvaśī.
Having received permission, the king then departed toward his own city.
Seeing his wife devoted to her husband, he became overwhelmed with fear;
but that beautiful woman, through her own spiritual power, perceived his intention.
"Do not fear," said that devoted wife to her husband.
"There is no fault in you, O Indra among kings; all this is the working of Desire. (22)
Through desire one attains heaven; through desire one then goes to hell.
Desire, when pursued according to the prescribed rule, bestows heaven; otherwise, it leads to the abyss.
Therefore, O Lord of Men, you have practiced that [asceticism] by abandoning the prescribed rule;
consequently, a great sin has arisen. Perform the purification of that sin.
Having heard what was spoken by his wife, he went toward Kaṇva’s hermitage;
having learned of her purity from her words, he proceeded to the Himalaya mountain.
On the way, he beheld the Gandharva Viśvāvasu, the subduer of enemies.
He was sporting with his beloved, adorned with a divine garland.
Having seen that garland together with the Apsaras, that lord of kings then thought:
"This garland is worthy of Urvaśī alone; it does not belong to anyone else. (27)
Having reflected thus in his mind, the best of kings prepared to fetch the garland; then a great battle ensued between him and the Gandharva. (28)
Having fashioned and taken that garland, he went toward the Apsaras;
searching for her, he wandered over the entire earth.
Having gone forth for the sake of Virasce’s task, he has returned here once again. || 36 ||
"I shall go again to that place where the Lord of Satyaloka resides.
Having heard these words of the sage, the king took leave of Nārada.
Having gone quickly to that place, he saw Urvaśī there;
he presented the garland to her, and she became adorned with it.
O best of sages, while he was sporting with her, another hundred years passed;
then one day, she questioned the king.
"O mighty-armed King, tell me, if I am dear to you, what did you do after going to your own city? (40)
Thus questioned by her, the king then related everything;
having heard what she had said, he then addressed the king in reply.
"O you of excellent vows, you must not stay with me from this point forward;
otherwise, O sinless one, Kaṇva will cast a curse upon you, for my wife is yours."
Although addressed thus by that slender-limbed woman, he did not abandon Urvaśī;
then, perceiving his persistence, she assumed her own physical form.
"I desire to sport with you; you ought to sport with me here.
Having heard the king's words and seeing him who resembled the God of Love, she— [16]
Then Urvaśī sported with him for a long time;
but when a thousand years had passed, he became detached from the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.
"I shall go to my own city, the famous Urvaśī," he said;
she replied to him again, "It is not enough with such enjoyment alone. (18)
"O King, you must not go; you must remain for my pleasure.
Then the king spoke to that illustrious lady after she had gone to the city.
"I shall come quickly to your presence.
Having thus received permission, the king then departed for his own city.
Seeing his wife, devoted to her husband, he became overwhelmed with fear;
but that beautiful woman, through her own power, perceived his intent.
"Do not fear," said that devoted wife to her husband;
"there is no fault in you, O Indra among kings; all this is the work of Kāma. (22)
Through desire one attains heaven, and through desire one then goes to hell;
when desire is pursued according to the prescribed rule, it bestows heaven, but otherwise it leads to a pit.
Therefore, O lord of men, because you practiced that [asceticism] while abandoning the prescribed rule, a great sin has arisen; perform the purification of that sin.
Having heard what was spoken by his wife, he went toward Kaṇva’s hermitage;
and having learned of her purity from her words, he proceeded to the Himalaya mountain.
On the way, he saw the Gandharva Viśvāvasu, the subduer of enemies,
sporting with his beloved and adorned with a divine garland.
Then, seeing that garland together with the Apsaras, that lord of kings said:
"This garland is worthy of Urvaśī alone; it is not for anyone else. (27)
Having reflected thus in his mind, the best of kings prepared to fetch the garland; then a great battle ensued between him and the Gandharva. (28)
Having made and taken that garland, he went toward the Apsaras;
searching for her, he wandered over the entire earth. (29)
She offered a garland, and by it she became adorned.
O best of sages, as they continued to take delight together, another hundred years passed; then, on one occasion, she questioned the king.
"O mighty-armed King, tell us what you did after going to your own city, where your beloved resides. (40)
Thus questioned by her, the king then related everything to her;
having heard what he had said, she then addressed the king in reply.
"O you of noble vows, you must certainly not stay with me from this point forward;
otherwise, O sinless one, Kaṇva will cast a curse upon you, for my wife is there."
Although addressed by that slender-limbed woman, he did not indeed abandon Urvaśī;
then, perceiving his persistence, she assumed her own physical form.
[113] Seeing her covered with grey hair, that best of kings immediately abandoned Urvaśī and resolved to practice asceticism.
For twelve days the king subsisted on bulbs, roots, and fruits;
for that same duration he lived on air alone, and thereafter he went to the hermitage of Kaṇva.

Having seen the best of sages, peaceful and solely intent on meditation upon Śiva, he prostrated himself like a staff out of devotion, and standing by his side with palms joined in reverence. || 46 ||
He reported everything that had happened regarding himself to the sage;
having understood that sin, the sage spoke of the purification for that evil. (47)
Sent by the Sage, the king went to the city of Vārāṇasī;
having bathed and offered libations in the Jāhnavī, he beheld Śiva as Viśveśvara.
Then that sinless king, being liberated, went to his own city;
having given wealth to the Brahmins, he protected the kingdom. || 49 ||
From the renowned Urvaśī were born seven sons of great luster to Kroṣṭu, the son of Yadu; they were the progenitors of lineages endowed with excellent fame. (50)
Listen, O best of sages, to those who were indeed the principal ones and not others:
in the lineage of Koṣṭa, there were the famous Kratha, Vidarbha, and likewise Kośala. (51)
From him was born the one known as Sāttvata, and after him came Mahābhoja;
then Bhoja, Satyavāk, Satyaka, and from him Sātyaki.
Krathaka, Suṣeṇa, Subhoja, Naravāhana, Āhuka, Devaka, Śrīdeva, and Devasutrata. || 53 ||
Ugrasena, Kaṃsa, and the highly illustrious Vasudeva [were born];
and from Vasudeva upon Devakī, the daughter of Ugrasena, [Acyuta was born].
By the power of Bhṛgu’s curse, Viṣṇu was born as the lord of the thirty gods.
He who is known as Ananta and Śeṣa was born as Saṃkarṣaṇa from the beautiful wife of Vasudeva named Rohiṇī.
The sixteen thousand women who were the wives of Mādhava—|| 56 ||
Indeed, from them were born innumerable sons headed by Pradyumna;
and Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, is the eternal Supreme Soul.
Though he has accomplished all that was to be done, the master of yoga, the wielder of illusion, and the devourer of the universe himself—
therefore, there is none superior to Kṛṣṇa, the foremost of the devotees of Maheśvara.
Therefore, by worshipping him, Śambhu indeed becomes well-worshipped;
but by showing disrespect to Hari, the Lord becomes averse.
Therefore, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow should always be worshipped by those devoted to Mahādeva,
and especially so by his devotees, for the pleasure of the Lord of Girijā.
O twice-born ones, this lineage of Yadu has been recounted to you in brief;
it shall bring about the destruction of all sins for those who read or hear it.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Account of the Lineage of Puru," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 31 ||
I shall describe the Manvantaras; listen, O best of sages!
Six Manus have passed away, and indeed the seventh is currently prevailing.
Of these, Svāyambhuva was the first; after him, Svārociṣa is recorded;
then Uttama, Tāmasa, Raivata, and likewise Cākṣuṣa.
I have described the Svāyambhuva period at the beginning of the Kalpa;
in the Svārociṣa period, those gods are remembered by the name Tuṣitas.
I shall now describe the sages, O Lord of the Gods; their names are Vipaścit, Ūrjastambha, Prāṇa, Dānta, and Ṛṣabha.
Timira, and Śārvarīva—these seven are remembered as the ṛṣis;
O best of the twice-born, in the northern interval, however, the gods were the Sudhāmans.
The Pratardanās, Śivas, Santyas, and Vaśavartins—
these are declared to be their hosts, along with your twelve hosts.
The lord of gods named Sudānti, possessed of great strength and prowess;
as well as Rajas, Gotrabāhu, Savana, and Anagha. || 7 ||

Sutapā and Śukra—these seven are remembered as the sages (ṛṣis). During the interval of Tāmasa, the gods were Sudhī and Martya. Jyotirdharma, Pṛthu, Kalpa, Caitrāgni, and Savana [were the Manus]. || 8 ||
These seven sages are considered to be known as the Pīvaras; among them,
Devendra, served by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, was Śyāśvinī.
Having renounced the sovereignty of the gods and attained supreme detachment, and realizing that everything is impermanent, he then spoke to Bṛhaspati: || 10 ||
"O Blessed One, what shall I do with this kingdom, since its happiness is so trivial?
Tell me clearly, O Guru, by what means does one attain absolute liberation (kaivalya)? (11)
Bṛhaspati said:
There exists Mahādeva alone, and no other, who is the abode of infinite qualities, whose singular form is supreme bliss, and who bestows liberation upon men through meditation. (12)
"He removes the state of great delusion from those bound by the snare of ignorance;
the Śruti declares that the Lord of Umā is their liberator through mere remembrance. (13)
Seek quickly for refuge that Śambhu, the supreme Brahman, the light, the foundation, the imperishable and immutable, who bestows grace upon all.
Know that to be the reality of Śaṅkara, which is the supreme light among lights, bliss beyond darkness, and than which nothing is superior. 15.
Know him to be the Supreme Brahman, the Great Lord who is the soul of the universe;
O destroyer of the Asuras, know all things to have that as their essence.
For those who indeed consider themselves distinct from the Enemy of Tripura, they behold that God and do not return again and again [to worldly existence]. || 17 ||
O Lord of the Gods, those whose intellects have reached the certainty that Śambhu, the Supreme Self, the Great Lord, is superior to all—by them, the goal has been achieved. (18)
The gods, led by Hari and Brahmā, long for a vision of him; so too do the self-restrained yogins. Go for refuge to that Lord. 19.
Know him to be the wielder of the Pināka bow, into whom this world— from Mahat down to the specific elements— dissolves, and from whom it is born again.
Know him to be the Great Lord (Maheśvara), whose playful sport is this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings, and by whose absence its dissolution occurs.
He upon whose face Brahmā stands for the act of creating the world, Hari for its protection, and Rudra, the wielder of the trident, for its destruction—[that is she]. (22)
By even a mere fragment of whose grace mortals subject to death indeed become immortal; they worship the one whose banner is the noble king. 23.
Whether meditated upon for a moment or a muhūrta, or worshipped and remembered, he who swiftly bestows absolute liberation— worship that Maheśvara.
His very forms are three—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara. Seek refuge in that Lord through [the functions of] creation, protection, and dissolution. 25.
Seek refuge in that Rudra, within whom all beings reside, by whom this world is set in motion, and whom the Vedas call Brahman. 26.
Go for refuge to that Hara, the God who is worshipped with sacrifices by the exponents of the Vedas for the sake of liberation, and who bestows the fruits of their actions.
Know that which arises for those who have conquered their senses, mastered their breath, meditate, and whose karma is exhausted—that is the reality of Śaṅkara. || 28 ||
O Śakra, for those embodied beings such as humans who are bound by the rope of ignorance,
I see no deliverer other than Mahādeva.
Therefore, O Śakra, propitiate Śaṅkara through austerity; when he is pleased, he will grant you the supreme state of absolute liberation.
Having thus heard what was spoken by his preceptor, the lord of the gods then went to Badarikāśrama to propitiate the God.
Having gone there, he became one with matted hair, devoted to sacred ash, and with his senses conquered;
he bathed in the waters of the Mandākinī and consecrated the sacred ash with mantras.
Having fashioned the form with the *aniritya* and other mantras,
he worshipped the Lord of Gods with flowers and beautiful leaves.
Chanting the Śaiva vidyā, he remained solely intent on meditation upon Śiva;
in this manner, fourteen thousand years passed.
Then Śiva, the destroyer of Tripura, became pleased by the asceticism of the king of the gods; he said to Śakra, "O Śatakratu, choose a boon."
"O sinless one, I am pleased with this intense austerity of yours;
I shall grant you whatever you desire, even if it be difficult for you to attain. (36)
O Hari, when I am pleased, nothing at all is difficult to obtain.
In the two manuscripts designated as Vaṅga, there is no collection of words beginning with "īśitam" and ending with "na kiṃcid api durlabham.
Having thus heard the speech of Śambhu, he praised him with various hymns.
Having joined his palms in reverence and bowed down, he spoke to Maheśvara.
Indra said:
"O Blessed One, O Śiva, I have accomplished my purpose through the sight of you.
Enough with other boons, O Śambhu; let there be devotion to you in me. (39)

For an embodied being who is devoted solely to the supreme bliss of tasting the nectar of devotion to You, O Śambhu, how could there be any suffering? For he is one whose desires are already fulfilled. (40)
Until such time as devotion to the Lord of Gods arises in an embodied being, the unstable mind continues to wander among worldly objects. (41)
O Hara, the ocean of existence is crossed by embodied beings only so long as supreme devotion to your lotus feet is not attained. 42.
O Śaṅkara, a living being falls again and again into the pit of saṃsāra for as long as even a fragment of your compassion does not arise.
O Śiva, this poisonous tree of saṃsāra, which is terrifying on all sides, is cut down by the axe of devotion to you; it cannot be severed otherwise.
Having heard these words of Śakra and having looked upon him with compassion,
Śiva touched him with both his hands and bestowed upon him the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
The gods, headed by Virañci, are born due to the weight of their karma;
they perish at the time of dissolution and come into being again and again. (46)
Having gone to heaven, they have gone to hell, to the state of animals, and to humanhood;
again to the station of Virañci and so forth—such is the succession of the wheel.
Those who belong to the class of Śambhu’s Gaṇeśvaras do not return again to worldly existence;
having enjoyed all desired pleasures, they shall attain union (sāyujya) with Śambhu. || 48 ||
All these lords of the Gaṇas assume forms at will, act according to their own desire, and having enjoyed pleasures together with Śiva, they go to the state of Śiva. 49.
Having thus granted the boon of Gāṇapatya, which is so difficult to attain,
Śambhu vanished on the spot before the king of the gods, Śibi.
O twice-born ones, having obtained the boon of Gāṇapatya from the Blessed One, Śibi—
Then, by the command of that god, he went to his own city.
Devoted to the worship of Mahādeva and devoted to the stories of Mahādeva,
he shone in the station of Śaṅkara like another Nandīśvara.
O twice-born ones, this entire life-story of Śiva has been narrated to you;
it causes the destruction of all sins and bestows all perfections upon men. (55)
"O twice-born ones, those who recite this life-story of Śiva with faith obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; thus spoke the Sun. (56)

1475 || Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Deeds of the Lord of Gods Named Śibi," in the *Śrī Saura*, a secondary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 32 ||
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, in the interval of Raivata, Indra will be named Vibhu;
the gods are remembered as the Vaikuṇṭhas, and four hosts (gaṇas) are proclaimed. || 1 ||
Hiraṇyaroman, Viśvaśrī, Urdhvabāhu, as well as Aindrabāhu, Subāhu, and the great sage Parjanya. || 2 ||
These seven sages are declared to have been born in the lineage of Priyavrata;
O twice-born ones, Manojava became the lord of the gods (Surendra) during the Cākṣuṣa interval as well.
The groups of deities beginning with Bhāva are said to have been born from Āyu;
likewise Sumedhas, Virajas, Haviṣmat, Uttama, and Budha. || 4 ||
Aniyāmā and Sahiṣṇu—these seven are remembered as the Ṛṣis.
O son, the son of Vivasvat is remembered as Vaivasvata Manu. || 5 ||
Regarding that which exists there at present, O gods, I shall speak:
the hosts of Maruts, as well as the Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus are remembered [there]. (6)
Puraṃdara became the lord of the gods, the destroyer of the pride of the asuras;
and there were Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Atri, Jamadagni, and Gautama.
Viśvāmitra and Bharadvāja—these seven are considered the sages.
O twice-born ones, I have [described] the Manvantaras that have passed and the one currently present. (8)
I have already spoken; now I shall describe the process of reabsorption (pratisaṃcara); listen.
That which is this destruction of beings in the world is remembered as eternal and constant. (10)
That dissolution which occurs at the end of a kalpa is here called the occasional (naimittika);
it is when everything from the Great Principle (mahat) down to the specific elements (viśeṣa) goes to its destruction.
O twice-born ones, this is called the elemental dissolution (prākṛta-pratisarga) by the sages;
however, the absolute dissolution (ātyantika-pralaya) occurs only through knowledge.
And the Śruti declares that this knowledge of Maheśa is obtainable through devotion:
"When the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas has arrived and the destruction of all beings has come to pass... (13)
Then a severe drought occurs lasting for a hundred years;
all trees, shrubs, and creepers on the earth go to their destruction.
Then the Lord Gabhastimālī became Saptaratha;
at that time, the Sun drank the waters of the oceans with his rays.
Because of that, the bulls among sages become blazing rays;
these seven suns become filled with rays on all sides.
O best of the twice-born, by the heat of their rays, the earth is consumed along with its islands, mountains, and oceans.
Of the beings who were consumed by the fire of the sun's splendor and who had attained oneness with one another,
a single fire then came into being.
The Fire-god quickly consumes the entire universe with his flames;
having burnt the whole earth, he expands through the power of Rudra’s splendor. (19)
O best of the twice-born, having burned the heavens, it then fiercely consumes the netherworld (pātāla);
its flames rise up to a length of a hundred yojanas.
By his splendor, the fire of universal destruction itself, like the fire of time, having burned the four worlds along with the yakṣas, serpents, and rākṣasas; || 21 ||
This entire world appears like a mass of glowing iron;
from it, clouds arise on all sides along with flashes of lightning.
From Bhāskara were born the formidable Rāvaṇa and the preeminent sages, O Muni. (23)
Then they release rain in drops resembling elephants;
impelled by Brahmā, a hundred-year deluge occurs.
Then the fires at the end of the aeon are extinguished by floods of water, and the earth, together with its islands and mountains, is filled with waters. (25)
O best of the twice-born, the entire earth indeed dissolves into that terrible single ocean; therein dwells the God of gods, Prajāpati.
Entering into yogic sleep, he lies down meditating upon Maheśvara;
this, O best of sages, is declared to be the occasional dissolution (naimittika-pralaya).
Therefore, listen as I shall describe how the elemental dissolution (prākṛta-pralaya) occurs:
when two parārdhas have passed, the Lord Kālāgnirudra [manifests].
Having reduced the cosmic egg to ashes, he engaged in the *tāṇḍava* dance;
having drunk that supreme bliss, he gazed upon the daughter of the Mountain King.
She alone is that supreme power, eternal, daughter of Himavat, and auspicious;
Mahādeva is indeed one with her, for no distinction exists between them. (30)
At that time, Maheśvara alone remains there with his supreme Śakti, Pārvatī; there is no other whatsoever—so says the Śruti.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads; he is the Lord of a thousand forms.
The God has a thousand eyes and a thousand feet; he is Śiva.
The thousand-armed one, the soul of the universe, bearing a trident, with blazing eyes, his face formidable with fangs—Śiva is the embodiment of the Supreme Brahman. (33)
Having burnt away the entire universe beginning with Brahmā, he abides within his own splendor; the earth, joined with its own qualities, goes to dissolution into the waters. || 34 ||
Water dissolves into fire, and fire dissolves into air;
air dissolves into space, and space dissolves into the origin of the elements (bhūtādi).
All the sense organs go to dissolution in the Taijasa [ego], and the hosts of gods go to their destruction in the Vaikārika, O best of beings. (36)
O best of sages, the threefold ego (ahaṃkāra) dissolves into the Great Principle (mahat);
and the Great Principle, O eminent sages, dissolves into Viriñca.
The abode of that lotus-born Brahmā is in the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Thus, having withdrawn the elements and the principles (tattvas), the Blessed Lord Śiva—
That Blessed Lord remains alone; there is no second whatsoever.
O twice-born ones, the dissolution occurs by the will of the Lord of Pārvatī, and not otherwise.
The seers of reality say that the creation of Brahmā and the others occurs again and again;
his very powers are the three: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. (40)
The Śruti declares that the Trident-bearer is superior to all of them;
people know the one Great God alone in many ways. (41)
People who perceive through the lens of duality [worship] Brahmā, Viṣṇu (the wielder of the Śārṅga bow), Rudra, Vāyu, Indra, Ravi, Śaśin, Agni, Yama, Varuṇa, and Jana. (42)
Assuming various forms, the Lord Śaṅkara himself,
the auspicious Śiva who consists of all powers, bestows the fruit upon everyone.
Therefore, having renounced everything, one should worship the one Maheśvara,
who is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, free from qualities, and beyond darkness.
O twice-born ones, for others, liberation is attained gradually through such service;
however, by worshipping that Maheśvara, one is liberated in that very birth.
O wise ones, this dissolution has been described to you exactly as it was spoken by the Blessed One. What else do you wish to hear? 46.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Nitya, Naimittika, Prākṛta, and Ātyantika Dissolutions," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 33 ||
The sages said:
"The primary creation, the secondary creation, the genealogies, the periods of the Manvantaras, and the history of the dynasties—all this has been heard by us in its entirety. (1)
Now we wish to hear the life-story of the enemy of Tripura.
O Sūta, tell us of this wonder: how did the Blessed One formerly burn three cities with a single arrow as if in mere play?
O Lord of the World, having always constructed three cities in the world, we— || 11 ||
"O Lord, having obtained this boon from you, we shall wander through the three worlds;
then, after a thousand years, we shall meet one another. (12)
O best of gods, when these cities have become one, O Blessed One, he who would then slay them—[that one is worthy]. (13)
"O Lord, by this single arrow alone, death shall come upon us.
Having said to them, "So be it," Brahmā vanished from sight.
Then Maya constructed for them three cities in succession upon a wheel;
one was made of iron on the earth, while the one in the courtyard of the sky was made of silver.
O twice-born ones, in heaven there is a city of the asuras made of gold;
its width and length shall be one hundred yojanas each.
At that time, the divine city of Vidyunmālin was made of iron;
that of Tārakākṣa was silver, and that of Kamalākṣa was golden.
The delightful palace of Maya was spread across the three cities;
those three beautiful cities shone like another triple-world.
It was adorned on all sides by celestial chariots that resembled the sun.
It was crowded with elephants and horses, adorned with gate-towers and watchtowers,
and resplendent with Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and celestial women.
It was adorned on all sides by divine secret sanctuaries, by domestic *agnihotra* fires in every house, and by those perfected in the study of the Vedas.
O twice-born ones, all the wives of the Dānavas there were devoted to their husbands;
that place was graced by those Dānavas who were intent on the worship of Mahādeva.
O best of the twice-born, by the power of their asceticism, Śakra and the other gods were reduced to smallness. Having witnessed that sovereignty of the ancient ones,
those gods, scorched by their splendor, went to Viṣṇu and spoke as follows.
The gods said:
"O God of gods, Lord of the universe, bestower of fearlessness upon the three worlds!"
"You ought to protect us here from the fear of the Asuras of the three cities.
Having heard these words of the gods, the crusher of the Dānavas [spoke].
Govinda reflected in his mind, "What must be done?
How are those Daityas, who are devoted to Mahādeva, to be slain? (26)
Their sins are burnt away by the splendor of Hara; of this there is no doubt.
Even one who has destroyed the three worlds, if he is devoted solely to Mahādeva, [is purified]. || 27 ||
Without the grace of Śambhu, who in the three worlds could slay Kasta?
By a mere fragment of Śambhu’s favor, I have become renowned throughout the three worlds. (28)
Brahmā, the gods, the Daityas, the Siddhas, and likewise the Munis;
the Manavas, Rākṣasas, serpents, Gandharvas, and those who are the Pitṛs. (29)
The Mothers, Guhyakas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, and likewise humans—
none in the three worlds have failed to worship the Blessed Mahādeva.
Those fools who desire worldly success will become vessels of suffering;
therefore, having worshipped that Lord, the best of gods, with a formidable sacrifice— || 31 ||
Saying, "The Dānavas must certainly be slain," the Lord of Kamalā then went to the north of Mount Meru and [worshipped] Sadāśiva with a sacrifice.
Having gone swiftly to the three cities, he burned them and slew the great asuras.
"Having rendered all the Asuras completely destitute, you ought to return.
Then, having heard the words of Viṣṇu, the hosts of beings of great strength [prepared to depart].
Having bowed to Hari, ten million upon ten million of arrogant and terrifying beings set out for the three cities at his command. (36)
Having reached the three cities, they became deprived of their senses;
then those beings were defeated by the Daityas who abide on the path of truth.
Approaching once more, Śakra and the others spoke to the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa:
"O Blessed One, protect us! We have been defeated and are overwhelmed with fear. (38)
O you of excellent vows, having seen Śakra and the other gods, the imperishable Viṣṇu reflected:
"How shall the task of the gods be accomplished? (39)
There is no destruction through malevolent magic for these great-souled ones who are devoted to righteousness;
these Daityas are highly fortunate and dedicated to the vow of truth.
"The great asuras, who are devoted to the performance of Vedic and Smārta rites and intent on the worship of Mahādeva, must be slain only after first deluding them with Māyā. (41)
"Having resolved in his mind, 'I shall destroy the entire Tripura,' O lords of sages, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow created a master of illusion from his own body. (42)
Viṣṇu gave a very extensive treatise based on empirical observation,
in which the body alone is the self and there is no destiny in the life hereafter.
In the Saṃghāta hell, one indeed becomes conscious [of the suffering] as if from the power of liquor;
having stolen another's property, one experiences the consequences through that very act. (44)
O you of excellent vows, having instructed that scripture, Viṣṇu dispatched him toward Tripura; and he, the master of illusion, then departed.
Then, having entered the three cities, the Dānavas were deluded;
they abandoned their Vedic rites and their eternal devotion to Bhava.
At that time, even women who were wanton, having abandoned their devotion to a single husband, [were there];
and the sage Nārada also went there accompanied by his own disciples. (47)
O twice-born ones, by the command of the Wielder of the Discus, assuming illusory forms,
women who desired visible rewards and Daityas who desired visible rewards [were created].
Through the instruction of the high-souled Nārada,
they became mostly followers of heretical paths, abandoned by the path of the Vedas.
Then, having fallen away from the worship of Śiva, they became Dānavas;
thus the Lord Viṣṇu, the all-pervading one, assumed a form through his Māyā.
Having committed many acts of unrighteousness, O best of sages, they approached Mahādeva, the refuge of all embodied beings, for protection regarding Tripura. || 51 ||
Having prostrated like a staff and remaining composed while standing in the water, he praised the eternal Lord with an excellent hymn.
Salutations to you, the soul of all, to Śaṅkara, the remover of distress;
to Rudra, the blue-throated one, the fierce Rudra, and the wise one.
O crusher of enemies, you alone are always our refuge, and no other god;
you are the beginning, you are without beginning, you are the infinite and imperishable Lord.
He is primordial nature and the person, the direct witness, the destroyer, and the teacher of the world;
he is the protector and leader in this world, who is compassionate toward the twice-born and others.

The bestower of boons, consisting of speech, yet expressible as that which is spoken, and free from both the expressed and the expression—the Lord is to be meditated upon for the sake of liberation by yogis who are the foremost among those who know yoga. (56)
The wise declare that you, who abide eternally within the hollow of the heart-lotus of yogis, are the true nature of the Supreme Brahman;
they call you the Reality, a mass of splendor, higher than the highest.
"O twice-born one, they call him the Supreme Self (Paramātman) in this world. (58)
O Teacher of the World, everything seen, heard, and existing, as well as that which is being born, is said to be smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest. (59)
To you, the Great God, who has hands and feet on all sides, whose eyes, heads, and faces are everywhere, who is indefinable, omniscient, and free from all affliction— [I bow].
Viśvarūpa, Virūpākṣa, Sadāśiva, the unsurpassed one,
resembling ten million suns and like ten million moons.
He who resembles the fire at the end of an aeon, who is the Lord consisting of the twenty-six principles,
the initiator in this world, and the great-grandfather of Prakṛti.

The Vedas and those who know the essence of the Vedas proclaim You—the self-existent Lord, the bestower of boons, and the abode of all—as the very essence of the scriptures. O You of manifold forms, that which was created by You in this world in two ways has never been seen by us;
it consists of Daityas, Asuras, and Brahmins, as well as gods, demons, and all things mobile and immobile.
"Protect us, O Śambhu; there is no other refuge. Having destroyed the asuras in an instant, [save us], for all those Daityas have been deluded by your Māyā, O Supreme Lord. (65)
Just as waves and shoals of fish fight one another in the ocean,
so too do the gods and demons, rendered dull by their very dependence on that which is inert, all strive for victory therein.
Sūta said:
That man who, having risen at dawn and become pure, should recite or hear this meritorious hymn, shall obtain all his desires. (67)
Thus praised by the wielder of the discus with the recitation of the Rudra-mantra, Śambhu, the Great God, placing his hand upon Nandin, himself spoke these words: || 68 ||
Īśvara said: "O best of gods, I have learned of your purpose, as well as that of Viṣṇu and Māyāvala, and what has transpired regarding the Tripuras and the Asuras."
All those who have abandoned proper conduct and revile the Vedic dharma are Dānavas; because they were born from them, they are likewise to be slain by me.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva Soma, accompanied by Skanda, Nandin, and the lords of the Gaṇas, entered his divine abode.
Then the gods, headed by Brahmā, took their stand at the gate and offered hymns of praise;
thereupon Nandin, the leader of the Gaṇas, emerged with a trident in his hand.
Having seen him by the command of the God of gods, the hosts of deities praised with various hymns him who bestows desired objects.
At the command of the wielder of the thunderbolt, all the sky-dwellers showered rains of flowers upon the head of Nandin; at that time, Nandin became truly delighted.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Austerities of Vidyunmālin, Tārakākṣa, Kamalākṣa, and Others," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. ||34||
Sūta said:
Then Nandīśvara, with supreme joy, spoke to Brahmā and the others.
"You ought to prepare the chariot of Śambhu, together with its charioteer and its arrow."
Mounted upon his chariot, Mahādeva will destroy Tripura;
meanwhile, a chariot has been fashioned for the God of gods by Viśvakarman.
The chariot is supremely rich in splendor, auspicious, and composed of all the gods;
the sun and moon are known as its two wheels, and the digits of the moon are its spokes.
The twelve Ādityas were its subtle spokes, and the six seasons are remembered as its rim; O best of sages, the intermediate space became its hub.
Mount Mandara became its nest; I shall now describe the pole to you. Likewise, the mountain of sunrise and the mountain of sunset are said to be its base.
O eminent sages, Mount Meru is the filaments of the lotus, and the year is known as its stalk; the two solstices are said to be the two girdles of the two wheels.
O best of the twice-born, the Muhūrtas are known as the yokes of the chariot;
the Kāṣṭhās are to be understood as the poles, and the Kṣaṇas, O twice-born ones, as the axle-shaft.
The moments (nimeṣas) were said to be its yokes, and the units of time known as kalās and lavas were its shafts;
heaven was its fender, and both heaven and liberation were its two banners.

The two staffs are known as the renunciation of action and ritual sacrifice, which depend upon the staff; its joints are the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and its yoke-pins are the two [staffs], O twice-born ones—listen! (9)
O best of the twice-born, wealth and desire are called the shafts of the pole;
that which is called the Unmanifest is its intellect, and Viḍvala is its understanding.
Ego (ahaṃkāra) is its corner; the elements (bhūtas) are its supreme strength;
the ornaments are the senses; half [of the chariot] is the supreme gait.
The Vedas are said to be its horses, and the six auxiliary limbs (ṣaḍaṅgas) are its ornaments. 11.
The Dharmaśāstras, Mīmāṃsā, Purāṇa, and Nyāya as well. || 12 ||
The mantras, like bells when struck, are the inexhaustible arrows resting upon him;
the Rathantara and the other meters are the quarters that serve as the wheels of his chariot. (13)
The lords of rivers are remembered as his chariot blankets;
the auspicious rivers, beginning with the Gaṅgā, are adorned with all kinds of ornaments.
All [the women] bear female forms, hold chowries in their hands, and are auspicious; they are the seven horses, the stairs, and the divine Unborn One is the charioteer. 15.
The goad is the Praṇava, and likewise the lord of mountains is his bow;
the glorious lord of serpents is the bowstring, and Bhāratī is indeed remembered as the bell.
O twice-born ones, Viṣṇu became his arrow, Yama its shaft,
the sharpness of the arrow was the fire of time (Kālāgni), and thus was the chariot composed of gods.
Then, O lords of sages, while being praised by the hosts of sages, the Blessed One, Mahādeva, ascended his divine and unsurpassed chariot.
Having seen the god Vināyaka, who creates obstacles to one's own task, one should worship him with various auspicious foods, both solid and soft, and fruits. (19)
Having thus worshipped with *uṇḍeraka* cakes, flowers, and enchanting lamps, the Blessed One departed to burn the city.
The gods went before Śambhu; before them were the lords of the Gaṇas;
and before them was Nandin, who is saluted by all the worlds.
Then Śailādi, having ascended a celestial chariot that shone like ten million suns, set out with haste to strike down the Daityas, O bull among sages.
The gods set out from all sides, equipped with weapons and accompanied by their mounts;
likewise did the world-protectors, the Siddhas, and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
