The sages of purified souls and the Mothers, the mothers of the world,
went forth from all sides toward the God of gods with their palms joined in reverence.
The sky-dwellers and the Cāraṇas likewise showered rains of flowers;
Bhṛṅgī, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of crores of attendants, set out to destroy the three cities.
Śaṅkukarṇa and the mighty Gokarṇa departed, as did Kundadanta, Mahākāla, Ḍiṇḍī, Muṇḍī, and Gaṇeśvara. || 26 ||
Śatajihva, Sahasrākṣa, the mighty Vīrabhadra, he who is named Śiva, Viśikha, and likewise the great Pañcaśikha. (27)
Śatāsya, Aṣṭaṅka, Hasta, Piśacīśa, and Pinākadhṛk—
these and many other hosts of Gaṇas, numbering in the hundreds of thousands and tens of millions.
Surrounding it on all sides, O Lord, they prepared to destroy Tripura. || 28 ||
With his lotus feet bowed to by Vīraścin, Murāri, Vibhāvasu,
and others, he then indeed went with that Mother for the welfare of all the worlds to the Triple City (Tripura).
The wielder of the trident is capable of burning all this world, with its moving and unmoving beings, by his mere thought in an instant;
yet why did the wielder of the Pināka bow go there in person, accompanied by his attendants, to burn Tripura? (30)
"What is the use of a chariot, or of excellent arrows, or even of Śambhu’s attendants, for him who desires to incinerate Tripura?
What is this [display] on the part of one whose power to burn the three cities is unimpaired?"—so said the leaders of the gods, headed by Indra.
I believe that the Lord Pinākin has surely established all this for the sake of sport, in order to strike [us]; otherwise, what would be the purpose of such a grand display? (32)
Then the god Maheśvara, taking the bow in his hand and fixing an arrow to it,
swiftly focused his mind upon Tripura.
At that time, during the conjunction of Puṣya, all the Purāṇas attained oneness;
then, O Brahmins, a great and tumultuous uproar arose among the gods.
All the gods and sages praised the Supreme Lord;
the yakṣas, gandharvas, vāraṇas, siddhas, and kiṃnaras danced. (35)
Then Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, spoke to Mahādeva:
"O Blessed Lord, Consort of Pārvatī, the conjunction of Puṣya has now arrived. (36)

"O Lord of Gods, these ancient cities do not indeed attain a state of separation [from one another]. O Blessed One, it is fitting that you burn Tripura while they remain in this very state of union. (37)
O Lord of Gods, O Maheśvara, the gods and the Daityas are equal to you;
for the gods are righteous-souled, while the Asuras are likewise evil-souled. (38)
Therefore, O Lord worshipped by the universe, you ought to abandon your sport and burn Tripura for the sake of the welfare of the three worlds. (39)
Then the Lord of Gods glanced at the three cities with contempt; O Brahmins, they were reduced to ashes through the power of the Supreme Creator.
Then Upendra and the others, all standing upon his chariot with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the Blessed Lord, the Consort of Umā, while offering him praise.
"O Lord of Gods, O Master, although Tripura has been burnt by your glance,
the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes now wiped the bowstring while smiling."
He released the arrow with such force that Tripura was reduced to ashes.
O brahmins, those Daityas who were devoted to the Śāna [mantra], having destroyed their sins, all went to the world of Śiva by the grace of Śiva.
The gods headed by Virañci, the sages, the Siddhas, and the Kinnaras,
prostrating themselves like a staff, paid homage to Mahādeva.
Sūta said: Thus the Lord Śiva, the divine Viśveśvara, the husband of Pārvatī,
having granted the boon to Brahmā and the others, departed for Mount Mandara.
Then, O twice-born ones, the gods, being greatly delighted, returned to their own abodes;
free from enmity and with tranquil minds, they remained established through the grace of Śiva.
Thus, O tigers among sages, the burning of Tripura by the Blessed One has been briefly told; it is an unsurpassed and meritorious narrative. 48.
Whoever recites this narrative in the presence of Mahādeva, being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 49 ||
O best of sages, through faith, a man obtains prosperity, knowledge, fame, sons, and a wife; he shall also attain other desires. (50)

1645 || Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Account of Śivaratha Burning Tripura," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
The Sages said:
How did Upamanyu obtain the status of a leader of Gaṇas (*gāṇapatya*) from the Lord?
How was the Ocean of Milk obtained? You ought to explain this.
Sūta said:
That sage known as Upamanyu, the elder brother of Dhaumya,
who had obtained boons from Mahādeva and was like a second six-faced one (Kārttikeya), [spoke].
Once, while playing in the hermitage of his maternal uncle, that illustrious one,
Upamanyu, drank milk at his very house.
Returning again to his own hermitage, the boy said to his mother:
"Mother, come now; bring me that milk which is sweeter than that. (4)
This verse is not seen in the middle of the Kha manuscript;
therefore, his mother, having become sorrowful, embraced her son with reverence.
Then, having taken the seeds and ground them, that sweet-voiced woman [prepared the paste]. || 5 ||
She gave her son milk mixed with ghee along with conciliatory words;
O best of sages, having then drunk that milk given by his mother, he [proceeded].
"O mother, this milk was not given by you," he said these words;
seeing her son with eyes filled with tears, the mother became deeply distressed. (7)
Having wiped his eyes with both hands, he spoke this to his son:
"O son, for those dwelling in the forest, and especially for the poor..."
"That milk which you request is indeed always difficult for us to obtain;
and enjoyment is attained through the compassion of Śiva, O son, and not otherwise.
Sūta said:
O best of sages, having heard these words of his mother, even though he was but a child,
he spoke with humility to his auspicious and ascetic mother.
Upamanyu said:
"O Mother, abandon your grief quickly if the Lord Śiva exists;
I shall bring the Ocean of Milk from somewhere here into your presence at once."
Having spoken thus and bowed to his mother, the young sage,
impelled by his mother's command, departed to perform austerities.
O Brahmins, Upamanyu went to the Himalayan mountains and performed austerities for many hundreds of years, subsisting only on air.
Seeing the three worlds thus illuminated by the ascetic power of that Upamanyu,
the gods went to Viṣṇu and spoke as follows.
The gods said:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, Ancient One, Supreme Person!
You ought to protect us here from this fire that is consuming the three worlds. (15)
Having heard what was uttered by him, Viṣṇu then reflected upon it in his mind and went to Mount Mandara, the best of mountains, to see Śaṅkara.
Then, having bowed to Mahādeva and seeing him with palms joined in reverence, the blessed Viṣṇu spoke: "There is a certain boy on a mountain of the Himavat. (17)
This pair of verses is observed:
"With Śacī on his left, he went to the ascetic grove of that sage. [p. 132] 20.
Then, O observers of noble vows, Śambhu, assuming the form of Śakra, spoke with affection to the great sage Upamanyu, saying: "Choose a boon."
Having heard these words spoken by the wielder of the thunderbolt, he,
with his mind personally dedicated to Śivā, laughed and spoke.
O Śiva, I, whose spear is devotion, beg of you and not otherwise; O Śakra, enough with other boons that are as flickering as waves. (23)
For one who has not obtained grace, devotion toward Śaṅkara does not arise for even a moment, half a moment, a muhūrta, or even an instant.
O slayer of Vṛtra, even the state of being Brahman appears trivial compared to your feet;
therefore, my wish is that there may be only devotion to Virūpākṣa. (25)
O Śakra, if devotion to that Maheśvara is obtained even today, then even the state of Brahmā appears to me like straw; it could not be otherwise.
Having heard what was thus spoken by the sage, the Lord, the husband of Śacī, spoke to him as if in anger: "O sage, how is it that you do not know me?"
Be devoted to Me, offer salutations to Me, and be intent on My worship.
When I am pleased, what is there in this world that is difficult for you to obtain?
What is the use of that Lord of Pārvatī, who is beyond attributes, though he is a great soul?
"O tiger among sages, it is being done; therefore, choose a boon from me.
O twice-born ones, having heard these words of Śakra, Upamanyu, the foremost of the best of sages, became enraged and began to reflect.
1. Its conjunction is indivisible.
2. Ga Gha Ṅa. Cha.
A.
Of him,
the bearer of the form of Śakra.
Ah! What will become of this wicked-souled one, the lowest of Rākṣasas?
Having assumed the form of Śakra for the purpose of creating an obstacle to my ascetic penance. || 31 ||
Therefore, he must be slain because he reviles Śiva; for the sin arising from hearing his blasphemy is greater than that from neglecting him.
Having seen one who reviles Śiva, if one kills him with effort,
or even kills oneself, he attains the supreme goal.
Having thus pointed out the scripture, O lords of sages, Upamanyu spoke to the king of the gods, who was intent on slaying Śakra.
O Lord of Śacī, let that penance performed for the sake of milk be set aside for now;
I shall burn you, who are my own eternal body, with the fire of yoga. (35)
Having spoken thus, he respectfully took up a handful of grass with both hands;
then, having bound it with a cloth, he released it to burn Śakra.
Meditating upon the Lord Viśveśvara, the imperishable Supreme Self, he began to burn himself by means of the concentration on fire (vahnidhāraṇā).
When he had thus resolved, Śaṅkara, the wielder of the Pināka bow, who is blue-and-red in hue, approached and restrained him with a gentle concentration of mind.
Then, O Sage, Rudra, the Lord of the Universe, having recognized the firm devotion of the sage, [restrained] that most terrifying [form] which had been withdrawn there by Śailādi in another way.
He revealed himself, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns, with five faces and ten arms, and having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament. (40)
Seeing that all-pervading Lord, who was clothed in a leopard skin and possessed three or five eyes, the great sage Upamanyu felt his purpose was fulfilled.
He praised the Supreme Lord with various kinds of divine hymns;
pleased with him, the Blessed One granted him the Ocean of Milk.
O you of excellent vows, even for Brahmā and the other gods, the state of being a Gaṇapati is difficult to attain;
yet, O Sage, the God of Gods showed no regard for that [attainment] here.
He spoke again and again of devotion alone toward Virūpākṣa;
having thus granted him the boon, Mahādeva, together with Umā, [departed].
Being praised by the hosts of gods, he vanished right there.
Completely liberated from all evil, he goes to the world of Brahmā. || 46 ||
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Legend of Upamanyu," in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka within the *Śrīsaura*, an *Upapurāṇa* of the *Śrībrahmapurāṇa*. 36.
The sages said:
How was the Daitya Jālandhara slain by the wielder of the trident?
You ought to tell me now concerning the Sudarśana discus.
Sūta said:
There was one known as Jālandhara, who resembled the God of Death (Kṛtānta).
Born from the water-mandala, by him the gods were utterly defeated.
The world-protectors, the Sādhyas, the Vasus, the hosts of Maruts,
the Viśvedevas, the Ādityas, and the Rudras were likewise utterly defeated.
And the foremost of sages went to conquer Brahmā, the best of the gods, as well as Viṣṇu, the lord of the deities and destroyer of the Daityas, in battle.
A battle took place between him and Jālandhara, the lord of the gods;
having then utterly defeated Viṣṇu, he spoke thus to the Daityas: || 5 ||
"All the gods have been conquered, with the exception of the Three-eyed One;
today I wish to conquer that Blessed Maheśvara."
O best of the twice-born, having heard the words of Jālandhara, those sons of Diti [prepared for battle] together with Nandīśvara on the field of combat, maintaining an equal stance.
With their minds intent on fighting, they went toward that Lord, the God;
then the powerful Daitya Jālandhara, accompanied by the other Daityas, [proceeded].
Equipped with chariots and elephants, he proceeded to the presence of Śaṅkara;
and Śambhu beheld Jālandhara, who resembled a mountain of collyrium.
Laughing, he spoke to the Daitya who was arrogant due to the boon from Brahmā:
"Enough of fighting, O son of Diti; here, [be subdued] by my sharpened arrows."
"In an instant, with all your limbs severed, you shall become the prey of Death.
Having heard these words of the trident-bearing God of gods, Jālandhara—
Enraged, he said: "O Maheśa, why do you address the Lord, the three-eyed God of gods, with this string of words in vain? (12)
I shall strike you with this sharp-edged mace.
Jālandhara said: "O Śiva, why do you speak thus as if to remove even a mere line?"
Even Mount Meru and other such peaks remain; have they not been moved by me?
O Maheśvara, as for the line in the form of a wheel that was drawn by you— || 18 ||
Having extracted that [weapon], I shall then slay you along with Nandi and the others;
for in former times, when you were but a child, Brahmā was swiftly defeated by me.
By the playful power of Viṣṇu, the Blessed One was cast down a hundred yojanas;
Indra and the other guardians of the world were bound and kept in prison.
O Great Śiva, their women serve as slave-girls during the festival;
with their two arms, they have dammed the celestial river on the peak of the Himalayas for the sake of sport.
The world-elephants were cast into the ocean, as were Rāvaṇa and the others;
and when the submarine fire was blocked, it became as if a single vast sea.
Therefore, O Śambhu, you do not know how my prowess works;
today, having conquered even you, I shall send you to prison.
Having heard those words of the Dānava, Maheśvara instantly incinerated his army with a mere fraction of the fire from his eye.
Having effortlessly reduced a thousand *akṣauhiṇīs* to ashes, the Great Lord, the Destroyer of Cities, then spoke to Jalandhara.
The Lord said: "O Daitya, fulfill quickly that agreement which was previously made regarding the extraction of the writing; only then shall you be able to conquer me. (26)
Then, having heard the words of Śambhu, that bull among the Daityas, blinded by intoxication,
struck out with his two arms and strove with force to uproot the mountain peak.
O twice-born ones, that wheel known as Sudarśana was obtained with great hardship.
Or if he causes the twice-born to hear it with devotion, he goes to the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Jālandhara and Arari," in the glorious Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. 37.
Sūta said:
Among all four Vedas and in all the Purāṇas, there is no deity whatsoever equal to or superior to the illustrious Maheśa. || 1 ||
He under whose control Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva all abide, and from whom the origin of all the gods proceeds—he alone is said to be the object of meditation. (2)
There is no dharma higher than Śambhu; there is no purpose higher than Śaṅkara.
There is no happiness other than Śiva, and liberation indeed exists nowhere beyond Hara.
When men shall roll up space like a piece of leather, only then,
through not knowing Śiva, will there be an end to suffering.
Since he is the creator of Brahmā, the object of meditation for the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu),
and the source of Viṣṇu’s divinity and Indra’s power, there is indeed no other being superior to him.
The sages said: "O Sūta, destroyer of doubts, tell us the reason why some people, having abandoned Maheśāna, have become servants of Keśava."
At the time of death, they generally remember only the one whose banner is Garuḍa,
even though Śiva— the Lord Viṣṇu and husband of Śrī Pārvatī— is present.
The three chapters beginning with "In all four Vedas" and ending with "the cause for reviling Śiva" are not seen [in this manuscript].
In the manuscript designated as *kha*, something has been written on the outside at the point where the thirty-seventh chapter concludes.

For example—having transposed the concluding points of the preceding chapters, the Vaiṣṇavas have suppressed the latter part of three chapters dedicated to the narrative of Madhvācārya; this may be seen in other manuscript copies.
By the mere remembrance of Viṣṇu, the destruction of all sins occurs;
this is indeed the grace of Śambhu, and there is no need for deliberation on this matter. He who knows Śambhu in truth is Nārāyaṇa himself;
he who knows Nārāyaṇa is Śakra, the lord of the gods. (12)
He who knows Indra, the lord of gods, and Varuṇa, the guardian of the world and lord of waters— he,
an immortal in this world, knows all the guardians of the worlds in this manner.
He who knows the gods who are to be worshipped, being himself a seer and a knower of the Vedas, and he who knows the seers correctly—he alone is the best of Brahmins. (14)
He who knows that the Brahmin is composed of all the gods is a knower of the Veda;
he alone understands the secret of the Veda and is beloved by Hara.
Great fools, deluded by the māyā of Viṣṇu, do not know Śambhu as the cause of birth and so forth, nor Viṣṇu, who was born before Brahmā and the others.
There was a king named Pratardana, supremely righteous, the lord of the seven islands, the sole sovereign of the earth, and full of majesty;
he was a hero, pure-minded, an enjoyer of pleasures, a donor, and a protector of the meaning of the Vedas. 17.
He was the protector of all embankments, devoted to Brahman, and beloved by the Brāhmaṇas.
In his kingdom, the gods always received the most excellent oblations;
there was no heretic nor any Buddhist among the people in his realm. (19)
Once, having left the city, he went outside for the sake of sport;
then the king saw a mendicant and was struck with wonder.
He was asked: "Who are you? Where have you come from? What is the task you desire?
Where will you go? Tell us all that, and what is your caste? (21)
The mendicant said:
"O King, I am a merchant, a peaceful ascetic established in virtuous conduct;
other merchants are here, clinging to the hem of my garment."
The king said:
"What is dharma? What indeed is it there? By what is it known? Who speaks of it?"
The Kṣapaṇaka said:
"Non-violence is the supreme dharma; that which is self-restraint is the true reality.
It is understood by both the Buddhists and the Jains; its proponent is considered to be Jina. (24)

O King, I did not manifest myself out of fear of those twice-born Vaiṣṇavas, who were knowers of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, performers of sacrifices, and highly venerable devotees of Maheśvara.
Sūta said:
Thereupon the king, his mind distressed, fell into deep anxiety: "Fie upon my kingdom! Woe to my evil intellect; there dwells in my city one who stands outside the Vedic path."
"When I thus slay this wicked one, the subjects, being tranquil in soul, will say: 'This proud man has been killed by the king of evil intellect. (27)
If he were slain, what would happen? There are many such as him;
by placing the word "compassion" (dayā) at the forefront, dharma will prevail. || 28 ||
"Subjects who are outside the Veda cannot be governed by a king;
in that case, he would partake of their sin—so said the blessed Manu. (29)
Sūta said: Thereupon King Pratardana, having renounced his kingdom, performed penance,
meditating upon Sāvitrī in his mind with a constantly one-pointed focus.
Then, after some days, Brahmā became manifest;
pleased by his great austerity, he spoke these words: || 31 ||
Brahmā said:
"O son of noble vows, I have attained satisfaction; choose a boon.
Why are you distressed in your heart, and why has the kingdom been renounced by you?"
The King said:
"The Vedas are indeed the authority; they both declare and know exactly what is so.
There can be no doubt whatsoever regarding the scope of the authority of the Vedas. (33)
"Thus I beg a boon, O God; what need have I for any other boon?
I beg for a kingdom free of thorns, as the lord of the earth with its seven continents. (34)
Sūta said:
Having replied, "So be it," Brahmā vanished;
and Pratardana, the royal sage and lord of the earth, was deeply satisfied.
From that time forward, all righteousness was established in his kingdom; there were Brahmins who knew the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and who were firm in their vows. (36)

The performers of the Agnihotra sacrifice, the sacrificers, the ascetics, the celibate students, the various meritorious Śaivas, and the Vaiṣṇavas endowed with auspicious marks [all gathered there]. || 37 ||
In his highly meritorious kingdom, there was neither a heretic nor a rationalist;
all the ritual acts of those following the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life flourished at that time.
[139] Festivals for the devotees of Viṣṇu and the worship of Śiva take place in every house;
all honor the gods, and no man shows hostility toward anyone.
In every house there were commentaries on logic, Vedānta, and Mīmāṃsā; the kingdom resounded with the chanting of the Vedas, and sacrificial posts stood at every spot.
Just as virtuous husbands, honored by their elders, joyfully protect their faithful wives who are endowed with manifold enjoyments and are well-nourished, so too do they guard their own merit. (41)
Sūta said: When much time had passed in this manner, even those Daityas and Dānavas who were most sinful and performers of base deeds became Mlecchas and went to heaven.
But those whose lineage considers the Vedic path alone to be pure—all of them, having been released from hell, have indeed reached Amarāvatī. || 43 ||
Everywhere there are clusters of Tulasī plants; everywhere there is the worship of Hari;
and everywhere the Lord of Girijā is worshipped with Bilva leaves. (44)
How indeed do their ancestors dwell in hell? Having arrived in that kingdom, what would the servants of Yama do there? (45)
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, to that which was most wonderful:
when all those bound for heaven had departed and Yama was devoid of activity.
Then, having been honored by all the gods and Vasus in all the worlds,
that high-minded one, out of devotion to Dharma, went to the realm of Śakra.
Standing before all the gods with palms joined in reverence, Yama spoke: "Yama said:
Such is the eternal condition of the eighty-four hundred thousand classes of living beings. (48)
I now know that [soul] which has perished, if the Lord is authoritative:
whichever soul, being exceedingly sinful, was situated in whatever womb, such as that of an insect. (49)
Whether in hell or in Saṃyaminī, he was uplifted by his son;
established in the certainty of the Vedas, he performs the Śrāddha rites, the worship of the gods, and other duties.
Indra said:
"What distinction is there for us whose lives are lowly, when the sacred revelation (śruti) [declares otherwise]?"
"O gods, it is by his command that we act according to the truth. (51)
O priest, your wisdom appears brilliant to me;
previously, you have demonstrated the paths of the Cārvākas, the Buddhists, and others.
"O best of the twice-born, act in such a way that the Daityas and Dānavas, who have strayed from that path and been cast outside the Vedic way, are likewise [confounded]. (53)
"How can she be moved, my dear? For it is not possible to move her now that she is so pure."
"How am I capable of destroying one to whom a boon has been granted by Brahmā?
Indra and the others said: "When there is the birth of those Daityas and Dānavas who are difficult to behold... (56)
Then Śukra himself, out of compassion for them, will become diligent;
therefore, O tiger among Brahmins, why do you neglect us?
O venerable one, what is impossible for you? We have come to you for refuge;
all those wicked people of ours have been made devoted to the Vedas and ritual acts. (58)
O treasury of compassion, exert yourself to delude them—
the gods, the rākṣasas, and the evil-doing daityas. (59)
Sūta said:
While the gods were speaking thus, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati reflected upon a means for the protection of creation.
The Guru said:
"Let all you gods listen; I shall tell you a stratagem.
If there should be some god who is himself a deceitful Vaiṣṇava," (61)
His body marked with the conch and discus, adorned with tulasī wood,
bearing the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), and chanting the syllables of Hari’s name.
One who reviles the deities alone, without setting his mind upon the Lord;
one who hates Śiva, incites others to great sin, and slanders Śiva. (63)
If, through hypocrisy, an insult to Śiva should be committed within that kingdom, then all his ancestors shall go to a terrible hell. (64)
Then, among all the gods, not a single one spoke thus;
they said to one another, "This deed is not beautiful. (65)
And what outcaste could speak of Śiva as being equal to Viṣṇu, by whose grace Vaikuṇṭha attained such a station? (66)
Sūta said:
Then the Lord of Śacī, having summoned a Kiṃnara, spoke this to him:
"Go, O Kiṃnara; becoming a master of illusion, you must indeed go to the earth as a Vaiṣṇava."
But, moreover, Mahāviṣṇu alone is supreme, and Śiva is his servant.
Sūta said:
Urged by him with force, he went very slowly, terrified, assuming a hypocritical appearance so that people would say of him, "He is a saint. (71)
Having assumed all the insignia of a Vaiṣṇava, he wanders through that city;
he makes those former disciples his own and says, "Śaṅkara is not to be honored."
In some places he is not to be meditated upon, and in others he is not the primary one;
in some places he is this exalted soul, and in others he is a servant of Śrī Viṣṇu.
When such diverse understandings among men have been distinguished,
he then enters the royal palace surrounded by his disciples.
Even the circle of kings was moved [by him], yet nothing contrary was seen;
he was a devotee of Viṣṇu, profoundly peaceful, and one who had reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
All the worlds indeed offer him numerous gifts—horses, chariots, and wealth—and his sin, being concealed, is not seen. (76)
Sūta said: Once upon a time, on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī),
certain auspicious people, having observed a fast, went in the morning to worship the wielder of the discus (Cakrapāṇi).
Seated there with his disciples and women, protected by his own splendor,
he did not consider any brahmin as superior, even one who bore the mark of ashes upon his forehead.
In the meantime, King Śrī Pratardana arrived,
accompanied by many kinds of attendants who held kusha grass in their hands and were pure in their vows.
Some of them bore the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark,
while others recited the *Śivasūktas* and the hymns dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Surrounded by these various kinds of Brahmins, the king sat down and spoke words that were appropriate and composed of gentle syllables.
"O Lord, the divine attendant of Hari has arrived in person;
these harsh words of yours appear to my mind like a thunderbolt. [p. 142]
The pseudo-Vaiṣṇava said:
"Those who worship Dhūrjaṭi here with undivided minds—
[him] who dwells in the cremation ground, who is clothed in the directions, and who was born from the head of Brahmā— " (93)
How can one serve a serpent-eater who bears poison and wears matted locks?
Therefore, Viṣṇu—the beautiful Lord of Kamalā—should always be served.
The king said:
"What lowest of men can truly know the various forms of Rudra?
You appear like a Vaiṣṇava, yet you do not understand the meaning of the Vedas at all, O wretch! (95)
Sūta said:
Then the king, having reflected, thought, "I shall summon learned and most excellent Brāhmaṇas and determine the truth of this matter. || 96 || 1820 ||

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Śiva and Other Matters," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
[143] O Lord of the Three Worlds, what is this that is seen in you today?
A primordial person (puruṣa) devoid of even a mere form!
But here, this entire universe is nothing more than a snake made of rope, existing only within you.
Even though he has assumed the most worshipful form, the mountains fall and the ocean rises against the Lord of the Mountains.
Therefore, I do not consider this [body] here to be equal to a diamond. || 14 ||
Lakṣmī said:
You are the soul of all, the all-knowing, the creator, the speaker, the sustainer, the imperishable Lord;
you are the witness of all worlds—who indeed is superior to you? (15)
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
"O lady of excellent hips, all that you have said is indeed true regarding me;
for there is nothing whatsoever belonging to me that was not obtained from Śrī Maheśvara."
16 || "Alone, I create how many beings that are equal to me;
I know that reality, O Goddess, as do some others who are mine. 17 ||
A living being is not liberated from the sin of killing thousands of Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences as easily as by bowing to Śrī Śiva.
A person who has committed incest with the wife of a guru, one who constantly indulges in intoxicants, and a stealer of a Brahmin’s gold—such a person is never liberated. (19)
A killer of women, a killer of cows, a killer of kings, as well as a betrayer of trust, an ungrateful person, an atheist, and a greedy man— such a person is never liberated.
But one who merely perceives the commonality with Śrī Rudra shall not be liberated from bondage;
for nothing superior to Viriñci, Viṣṇu, and Śiva can arise.
Even if they were equal to Viṣṇu himself, living beings would never be liberated;
my master is Śrīkaṇṭha, and I am his servant forever.
Lakṣmī said: "O Lord Vaikuṇṭha, let us go to that place where Your Master resides;
on the beautiful Mount Kailāsa, we shall bow down to Sadāśiva. (23)
Sūta said:
Then, having mounted Garuḍa and gone to Mount Kailāsa,
they instantly gratified [Śiva] with various kinds of hymns of praise.
Then the gods, headed by Brahmā, and the Siddhas arrived there on the mountain; Rudra, seeking to witness the marvel, was surrounded by all of them.
Accompanied by Bhavānī, he went to that place where Pratardana was;
there Śaṅkara stood in the midst of all the celestial chariots of the gods.
The illustrious Maheśa said: "Tell me, how did all these immortals assemble?
What is the task, or what is unprecedented? And why is the king so overcome with anxiety?"
The gods said:
"Lord Pratardana, the king, obtained a boon through the power of destiny."
He is the proclaimer of the path of the Vedas and himself the originator of it. || 28 ||
O Lord, we employed deception for the sake of protecting the creation; furthermore, the gods caused you, the creator of all, to be insulted. (29)
Therefore, O Mahādeva, forgive this; this Kinnara has been set in motion by us, fashioned as a Vaiṣṇava devoted solely to censuring you.
Sūta said:
At that very time, however, the king came to learn of the news.
Taking up a sharp sword, he struck the kiṃnara out of anger.
The heads of those who sided with him were severed from their necks,
and many horses were subsequently slain.
No one can restrain that king whose mind is intent on merit;
the anger of that great-souled one was quelled by Mahādeva.
Then, when the clamor had subsided, Nandin, with great curiosity,
joined those various body parts back to the horse-headed form individually.
Having properly joined the heads with the bodies of horses, the wise one,
pure in speech, spoke these truthful words in the assembly of the gods.
The horse, by which face Śiva was once treated with contempt, now treats that very face with contempt;
and by the pride of bearing a ritual seal (mudrā), it treats his body with contempt.
Brahmā said: O King, I shall now tell you the truth regarding the future concerning the one who will rule the kingdom; listen to that with a concentrated mind. (37)
When the terrible Kali age has arrived and the surface of the earth is overrun by barbarians,
the lowest of men will fall away from all proper conduct.
At that time, in the middle of the Andhra country, there will be a certain unfortunate Brāhmaṇa from the south who is devoted to widowed Brāhmaṇa women.
From the transgression of that most wicked brahmin, a sinless son shall be born;
by fate, he will be a seeker of virtues and eager for Vedic study.
Having prostrated before the excellent teacher Padmapādaka, the proponent of Vedānta and the knower of the tradition of non-duality (advaita), he will make this request.
"What is the ritual, or where was it bestowed? Tell me the truth quickly, otherwise— " || 48 ||
"I shall reduce you to ashes, you who are devoid of brahmanical luster.
When this is said, he will tell everything according to the truth.
Then the teacher will pronounce a curse: "May the Siddhānta never flourish for you;
may you possess only dullness regarding the doctrine of supreme non-duality. (50)
"O Lord, tell me how your service might become fruitless for me," when he shall thus express much despondency. (51)
Later the Master will say: "Let your prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) be firm;
in the final conclusion (siddhānta), there is total blindness [for you]. My word is not otherwise. (52)
By means of that honey, he has scrutinized the prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣa) of the scriptures;
furthermore, he will endeavor to interpret the Vedānta otherwise.
O gods, to whatever extent the practice of Kali will prevail, to that same extent this deviant path of those who hate Śiva will flourish. (54)
But previously, from the Drāviḍa country, this [tradition] will gradually spread to Karṇāṭaka and Tiḷaṅga and extend along the banks of the Godāvarī. (55)
When the Kali age has reached its full extent, it will spread throughout Āryāvarta; base men will preach the false doctrine of Māyāvāda.
Merely by seeing them, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on;
for just as [the sun] becomes auspicious when entered by Rāhu, so too does the state of Svarbhānu [become auspicious].
Just as there were many who were green-colored, so too were these speakers of truth;
they were constantly intent on censuring yoga and were revilers of the agnihotra sacrifice. 58.
Those men who say that the Purāṇas are equal to the Vedānta go to hell merely by their trembling of the lips. || 59 ||
If, upon engaging in conversation with them, one's spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should decline,
it would be better to follow a Buddhist, a Jaina, or even the Kāpālika doctrine.
He clearly proclaims the invalidity of the Vedas; what indeed can be achieved by them?
Though he prides himself on the authority of the Vedas, he is not a follower of the Vedic path.
"An evil man, though himself powerless, speaks of the Supreme Lord as if he were not the Lord, merely by following the words of others.
Sūta said:
"When this had occurred, everyone then departed from there, each returning the way they had come."
The royal sage Pratardana, having made his kingdom free from all thorns, [attained liberation].
At the end of his body, he will attain supreme liberation characterized by non-duality;
thereafter, his disciples will become numerous.
Merely by means of the outward garb of renunciants, they pursue their own livelihood;
even while remaining hidden, they serve kings and are Kaulikas as well.

Some were addicted to approaching those who should not be approached and to eating what should not be eaten; others were devoted to drinking what should not be drunk, all of them distracted by various sensual enjoyments.
Though they are always mounted on vehicles and devoted to the service of kings,
they are intent on censuring non-duality, concealing their own weightiness with books.
In the Kali age, they will not understand the tenets of other philosophical systems according to their true nature; rather, with a mind intent on finding fault, they will merely recite them.
If the names of other deities are to be abandoned, then how is it that the most wicked recite the Veda, and how indeed do they propound logic? (68)
Furthermore, having repeatedly examined the authentic texts of the Mīmāṃsā treatises, those full of envy will seize upon the prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣa) of them all.
They will not speak of their own [lineage] because there is no means of valid knowledge [for it]; and those born of adultery will revile the Haṃsas and Paramahaṃsas.
As soon as they are born, the lowest of men will have certain individuals shaved and, merely by means of saffron-colored robes, will make them the masters of monasteries.
The office of a monastery superintendent, servitude, the accumulation of wealth, intercourse with female slaves, and envy—these are the five [faults] of those who profess the truth. (72)
Those who speak of ultimate reality say that the very nature of cyclic existence is itself the supreme truth;
those who speak solely of illusion maintain that the entire universe is a manifestation of māyā.
They do not know the pure reality, yet they speak of the universe as reality;
in this Kali age, alas, those who profess to speak of reality have become mere words.
O Brahmins, as the abundance of sins increases in the Kali age,
so too will there arise in the north those who are hypocritical Vaiṣṇavas.
Upon seeing one who speaks of Śiva in general, one who perceives Śiva in general, or one who associates with those who perceive Śiva in general, one should bathe along with one's clothes. (76)
In the Kali age, the most wicked Vaiṣṇavas will follow the path shown by Madhu;
thereafter, the Mlecchas and Śūdras will be excluded from the community.
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, listen to the majesty of the Lord of Pārvatī;
remain steadfastly intent upon always practicing devotion toward him. (78)

1898 || Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Entry of the Kali Age and Other Matters," in the *Śrī Saura*, a secondary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) within the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 39 ||
The sages said:
O Sūta, may you be blessed; tell us [of him] of whom Mādhava is a servant.
How can they speak of the equality between Śrī Maheśa and Viṣṇu? || 1 ||
Some speak of their equality, some of their opposite nature,
and indeed some declare the oneness of Keśava with the Lord.
O son of Sūta, tell us here in truth the boundaries of the established doctrine (siddhānta),
by which our doubt may be removed without contradiction.
Sūta said:
"Listen, all you sages, to this supreme conclusion established by the Vedas;
in all the Vedas, it is sung that there is no reality higher than Maheśa."
Furthermore, by the grace of Maheśa, for Vaikuṇṭha and the others as well,
This is the true conclusion of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas:
Indra, Upendra, and all others are indeed the servants of Maheśa alone.
He who knows the Lord, the beloved of Pārvatī, the Sovereign known through the Vedāntas— he is Vaikuṇṭha, the destroyer of the suffering of all embodied beings.
He who considers Vaikuṇṭha to be the true Lord is Purandara;
he who considers Indra to be the master of all is regarded as a sage.
One who obeys the command of the Sage attains the heavenly world;
yet, without knowing Śiva, the Lord, as non-dual, one is never liberated.
"When the terrible Kali Yuga has arrived, men will turn their backs on Śrī Śaṅkara;
this is the truth," so Dvaipāyana declared.
When Manmatha had been consumed by the fire of Rudra, his wife Rati lamented,
and even his friends were deeply distressed.
Spring and the other seasons arrived and said to her: "What is to be done regarding the cause of Śambhu, the lord of all the worlds, who has become a wretched beggar? (12)
Rati said:
"One should consider that this killer would become unworthy of honor in all the worlds;
therefore, an obstacle must be created by whatever means possible."
If his ill-repute were to be proclaimed and he did not waver at all, by that my suffering would find some slight relief, and not otherwise. (14)
Vasanta and the others said: "Candraśekhara is celebrated in the fourteen branches of knowledge;
and he is whom the sages of praised vows sing of in the Vedāntas. (15)
Brahmā, all the deities, as well as Indra, Upendra, and the others—
if anyone speaks of his inferiority, he is called a Cāṇḍāla by his actions.
If Viṣṇu or Brahmā is spoken of as being equal to him,
he is born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.
If even equality is not possible, what need is there to mention inferiority?
We desire freedom from our debt to our friend; this situation appears as a great crisis to us. (18)
Sūta said:
Then, having deliberated thus, they all, led by Mahāmoha,
performed a most terrible penance that struck fear into all the worlds.
At one time, the Blessed Brahmā, a treasury of compassion, appeared;
he was the fifth proponent of the doctrine of causality, and all were supported by Madhu.
Then Brahmā said to them, "Choose that which is desired by your minds."
"As is your word, so am I prepared to grant it.
Mōha and the others said:
"O Lord, our supreme friend, Kandarpa, has been destroyed! (22)
"O father, we shall endeavor to repay our debt to that Mahādeva by becoming revilers of the worship of Rudra. (23)
"So that Candraśekhara may not receive worship from us.
Brahmā said: "Now it shall not be so; however, this will come to pass after a long time."
"It has been declared by you that 'we shall exist,' and never otherwise;
for those worlds who are under your control, there is no worship of Dhūrjaṭi. (25)
This boon has been requested and granted; you may do as you wish.
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus to them, Brahmā then vanished on that very spot.
All of them, being distressed, deliberated together with Kali.
Kali said:
"It was not said by you just now that 'we shall come';
therefore, when my time arrives, everything will surely happen."
By what was said [in the words] "from us," they shall remain under our control;
they will become revilers, for no one considers him as other than Aramā.
Possessed by greed, delusion, and other such passions, and having encountered me in my terrible form,
they set aside the doctrine of causality and turned their backs on devotion to Śiva.
Sūta said: Then, when the Kali age had arrived, which was devoid of all righteousness and filled with cruel Mlecchas who brought about the destruction of Brahmins and cows—
In a place where the Vedic recitation and the *vaṣaṭ*-call have ceased, which is crowded with Jains, Buddhists, and others;
when a Brāhmaṇa has entered the path of the barbarians (*mleccha*), or when a Śūdra has killed a Brāhmaṇa—(32)
At that time, Vasantasena, the defiler of Karṇāṭa, Tiḷaṅga, and other lands, will be born from a Brahmin upon the widow’s field; he shall be known by the name Madhu. (33)
That most wicked Golaka, however, will worship the Lord who wears lotus-sandals and is devoted to the exposition of Vedanta as his disciple.
Having studied the entire scripture from that [teacher], he remained without performing the daily rites;
what was the *agnihotra*, what was the sacrifice—what cause would lead him to act in such a way? (35)
[151] Having heard those words, the guru, having ascertained that "this man cannot be a Brāhmaṇa," will speak to that wicked man once he has heard his speech.
The Guru said:
"Tell me truly, O defiler of the Vedas, what is your caste?
You are a hater of both ritual action and Brahman; your birth did not originate from a Brāhmaṇa. (37)
Madhu said:
"I was born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother; of this there is no doubt.
I speak the truth and not a falsehood; why then do you look upon me with suspicion, O Guru? (38)
The Guru said:
"O wretch, by whom was your mother given? Whose daughter is she, when, and how? To whom was she given, and by what rite? Tell me that without delay. (39)
Madhu said:
"O Lord, my mother was a widow; she became pregnant by a poor brahmin, and from that, this body was born. (40)
The Guru said:
"Since this wicked-souled one has studied the scripture from me through deceit, may this boundary of the established doctrine never flash before his mind. (41)
Madhu said:
"O illustrious one, your word shall not be otherwise; let my former position manifest firmly within my heart. (42)
The Guru said:
"Blindness regarding the established conclusion (siddhānta) and proficiency in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa)."
It shall indeed be so; however, let there be only one thing: that your disciples be virtuous.
Out of delusion they are devoid of established doctrine; out of greed they are servants of kings; out of anger they are harsh-speakers; and out of hypocrisy they appear beautiful through malice. (44)
By means of their doctrine of causality, they do not understand any of the scriptures;
they will soon go to the terrible hells for a long time. (45)
Sūta said:
Then, having received that curse, the evil-minded one named Madhu will compose a commentary on the Sūtras of Bādarāyaṇa.
Therefore, Madhvācārya was a great southerner by disposition in the Kali age;
his disciples and grand-disciples were neither in Āryāvarta nor in Utkala.
Its practice will not prevail in Gauḍa, nor on the banks of the Gaṅgā, nor on the banks of the Godāvarī,
nor in the midst of the Arbuda forest.
To whatever extent the wicked conduct of the Kali age shall prevail, to that same extent, O Great King, those who rely on logic will become rare in some places. (49)
Then, at a time of extreme depravity when it was oppressed by great barbarians,
a five-year-old renunciant, possessing a wicked intellect, having studied—
Accompanied by disciples and grand-disciples, he will propound the doctrine of causality. || 51 ||
The reality that "saṃsāra exists" is indeed true and cannot be sublated; therefore, one who speaks thus is a proponent of reality, while he who speaks otherwise is called a speaker of falsehood. (52)
"This phenomenal world is false and is held by us to be created by me";
thus these proponents of Māyā are, in reality, proponents of the ultimate truth (tattva). // 53 //
The Jaiminīya is indeed a true scripture that initiates the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa);
the Gautamīya, however, is a true scripture that establishes the Lord (Īśvara). || 54 ||
The doctrine of Kapila is the means for awakening the discrimination between the Spirit (puṃs) and Primordial Matter (prakṛti);
likewise, the Vaiśeṣika scripture is the proponent of the Lord (īśvara). The Yoga-śāstra of Patañjali and that Śaiva scripture are also held to be such [proponents of the Lord].
And that which reveals non-duality, the pinnacle of the Vedānta scriptures. || 56 ||
All the Vedas with their six auxiliary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, the Smṛtis, the Upapurāṇas, and likewise the auspicious Upasmṛtis [are contained therein]. || 57 ||
It is said that all the various sciences possess authority for their respective domains,
and they all proclaim that their intended purpose lies in the goals of human life; thus,
even when there appears to be some contradiction, in reality no contradiction exists.
They consider the illustrious Maheśāna alone to be the highest of all that is supreme.
Excluded from the path of the Vedas, those most wicked ones did not think at all [of him as such],
calling the teacher named Madhu the son of a widow.
O Brahmins, this great and wicked Cārvāka named Madhu will exist in the Kali age as a concealed propagator of insults against Śiva.
From delusion comes deviation from the established tenets; from anger, the rejection of the scriptures;
from greed, service to a king; and from hypocrisy, the deceiving of others. (62)

O Brahmins, in the Kali age, the act of sexual union with a courtesan will be practiced either for the sake of desire or as a matter of argument; this sixfold practice shall be proclaimed as the "speaking of truth."
Having established a five-year term and taking up a young boy in succession, those atheists will assume the office of *maṭha*-master out of greed for wealth. (64)
Those who are full of passion, addicted to sensual enjoyments, most sinful, and who engage in sexual intercourse with female slaves will protect only the lineage of the monastery.
[Verse 66] By name they were renunciants, yet at the holy ford they were mounted on vehicles along with their attendants;
they were mounted upon man-borne carriages, having cast aside the topknot and the sacred thread.
Fools who take his side, householders who revile Śiva,
are seized by a false pride in being Vaiṣṇavas and are destined for hell.
Vaiṣṇavas by mere dress, Brāhmaṇas by a mere sacred thread, debaters by mere anger, and scholars by their skill in dialectical argumentation. (68)
Some scholars will study the treatises for the sake of refutation, and they will conceal their own [views] by means of those belonging to others. (69)
Sūta said:
All of them, beginning with Mahāmoha, having consoled the beautiful Rati and seeking to dispel her sorrow, spoke in gentle words.
Delusion and the others said: "O Rati, do not grieve; I am Delusion, the friend of Kali;
Anger is the supreme kinsman of your husband, and Greed and Delusion are his brothers. (71)
When the Kali Yuga has reached its full extent, we— delusion, greed, and the rest—
shall dwell in the south, having descended as the one named Madhu.
Therefore, relying upon the doctrine of causality, we of crooked intellect shall do our utmost to prevent the worship of Śiva. (73)
Sūta said:
Having thus consoled Rati, they departed from here by the way they had come.
Thus has everything been related regarding the cause of the revilers of Śiva. (74)

1972 || Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Causes for the Equality of Maheśa and Viṣṇu," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 40 ||
The sages said: "O Sūta, you ought to tell us how Hari obtained that discus named Sudarśana from the blessed Mahādeva."
Sūta said:
A battle of wondrous appearance took place between the gods and the asuras.
Defeated by the Daityas, the gods sought refuge with Viṣṇu.
Having praised him with various hymns and prostrated, they stood before him;
all of them were terrified by fear, their limbs wounded and greatly distressed.
Seeing them, the Blessed One, Janārdana, the God of gods, said:
"O gods, for what purpose have you come? You should speak now."
Having heard the words of Hari, the gods, the best of deities, bowed down and said:
"We have all been utterly defeated by the Dānavas; we have come here to you for refuge."
"You alone are the refuge of the gods; you are the protector, O Supreme Person.
You ought to slay them quickly, O lotus-eyed one. (6)
For the sake of slaying Jālandhara, take up that discus which was obtained from Mahādeva by the wielder of the trident, and with it, destroy those of great strength.
Having heard those words of theirs, the lotus-eyed Blessed One said,
"O gods of excellent vows, I shall certainly do so."
Having gone to the Himavat mountain, he worshipped Śaṅkara;
having installed a liṅga there, he bathed it with auspicious waters scented with perfumes.
Having worshipped Maheśvara with the Rudra known as Tvaritā,
he then praised the Supreme Lord with the Thousand Names.
Having offered lotuses to the Bull-bannered Lord with each of his names,
he began to praise him with devotion using names beginning with "Bhava."
Viṣṇu said:
Bhava, Śiva, Hara, Rudra, Puṣkala, Mugdhalocana, Agragaṇya, Sadācāra, Sarva, Śambhu, and Maheśvara—[these are my names]. || 12 ||
The Lord, the Immovable One, the Ruler, the Thousand-eyed, the Thousand-footed;
the Most Excellent, the Giver of Boons, the Forest-Dweller, the Beneficent, the Supreme Sovereign. (13)

The bearer of the Gaṅgā, the wielder of the trident, whose sole motive is the welfare of others, the omniscient one, the progenitor of all gods, the mountain-bowed one, and the wearer of matted locks. (14)
Candrāpīḍa, Candramauli, Vedhā, Viśvāmareśvara, Vedāntasārasaṃdoha, Kapālī, and Nīlalohita. || 15 ||
He whose nourishment is meditation is indivisible; he is the lord of the Gaṇas and the husband of Gaurī.
He possesses eight forms and is the form of the universe; he is the triple aggregate of life's goals and the means to attain heaven.
He is attainable through knowledge, yet firmly ignorant; the God of gods, the three-eyed one;
Vāmadeva, the Great God, the skillful, the sovereign, and the steadfast. (17)
He is the one of universal form, the many-eyed, the lord of speech, and the one who dwells within the sacred mantras of revelation;
he is in harmony with every *praṇava*, marked by the bull-emblem, and has the king as his vehicle.
The Lord is the wielder of the Pināka bow, the bearer of the trident, possessed of variegated attire, and eternal;
he is composed of mind, a great yogi, steadfast, and Dhūrjaṭi, the sustainer of the cosmic egg.
The Death of Death, clad in animal skins, the fortunate one whose essence is the *praṇava*,
with serpents for his crest-jewel, possessing beautiful eyes, Durvāsas, the subduer of cities. || 20 ||
He whose weapon is sight, the preceptor of Skanda, the Supreme Lord, the ultimate refuge;
he who is without beginning, middle, or end, the Lord of the Mountain, the husband of Girijā.
He is the kinsman of Kubera, Śrīkaṇṭha, the most excellent one worshipped by the world, the gentle one,
the common one, Devaka, Daṇḍin, Nīlakaṇṭha, and Paraśvadhī.
Viśālākṣa, Mahāvyādha, Sureśa, Sūryatāpana, Dhāman, Kṣamākṣetra, Bhagavat, and Bhaganetrahā. || 23 ||
The fierce one, the lord of creatures, Tārkṣya, the lover of his devotees, the sweet-spoken, the giver, the compassionate, the skillful, the one with matted hair, and the subduer of desire. || 24 ||
100 || Śmaśānanilaya, Tiṣya, Maheśvara who dwells in the cremation ground, the creator of the world, the Lord of Beings, the Great Creator, and the Great Herb. || 25 ||
The supreme lord of cattle, the protector, attainable through knowledge, the ancient one;
he is right conduct, excellent conduct, the pure-souled one, Soma, the lover of Soma, and the wise one. || 26 ||

He who drinks the Soma, who drinks the nectar, the gentle one, the great leader, the one of great memory, the one whose enemy is unborn, the one worthy of being beheld, the one to be honored, and the bearer of the sacrificial oblation. || 27 ||
The creator of the world, the creator of the Vedas, the author of the Sūtras, the eternal one;
the great seer, the teacher Kapila, the light of the universe, the eye;
the wielder of the Pināka bow, the god of the earth, the maker of well-being, the giver of prosperity, the nectar.
The abode of the sustainer, the maker of the abode, all-pervading, and the range of all. || 29 ||

The creator of Brahmā, the creator of the universe, the source of creation, the Karṇikāra tree, the beloved, the poet, the one with branches, the one without branches, the one with cow-like branches, the auspicious one, and the unsurpassed physician. || 30 ||
He is the one whose water is like the Gaṅgā, the auspicious, the abundant, the immovable, and the firmly established;
he is the self-conqueror, the disciplined soul, and the charioteer who has the elements as his vehicle.
Accompanied by his retinue and the host of attendants, he is of excellent renown and has severed all doubt;
he is Kāmadeva, the one who brings about desire, whose body is covered in the dust raised from the earth.

He who delights in ashes, who sleeps upon ashes, who is the lover, the beloved, and the author of the sacred scriptures; he who has returned to his true nature, whose self is withdrawn from worldly existence, the mass of dharma—He is Sadāśiva.
He is difficult to find, difficult to traverse, and hard to overcome; he is skilled in all weapons. || 34 ||
He is the abode of internal yoga, the fine thread, the increaser of the thread;
he whose limbs are auspicious, who is the essence of yoga, the Lord of the world, and Janārdana.
He who effects purification by ashes, who possesses the splendor of Mount Meru, and whose form is pure. || 200 ||
Hiraṇyaretas, Ataraṇi, Marīci, and Māhimālaya; || 36 ||
The great lake, the great abyss, worshipped by hosts of perfected beings;
wearing a tiger skin, the serpent, the great elemental being, and the great treasure. || 37 ||
He whose self is nectar, whose body is nectar, the fivefold sacrifice, the wind;
he who abides in the twenty-five principles, the Pārijāta tree, both transcendent and immanent. (38)
Easily accessible, firm in his vows, heroic, and a unique treasury of guilelessness;
the preceptor of the castes and stages of life, a student of sacred knowledge, the conqueror of enemies, and the scorcher of foes. || 39 ||

The hermitage, the destroyer, the emaciated, the possessor of knowledge, the immovable, the moving, the embodiment of authority, the difficult to comprehend, the fair-winged one, and the one whose vehicle is the wind. (40)
The wielder of the bow, the science of archery, a mass of virtues, a mine of excellence;
infinite vision, bliss, the staff of punishment, the subduer, and self-restraint. || 41 ||
He is possessed of knowledge, of great body, the architect of all, and self-confident;
he is free from passion, self-disciplined, an ascetic, and the one who mounts living beings.
Disguised in the garb of a madman, he had conquered desire and conquered what is dear;
he was of auspicious nature, disciplined, and the lord of all the world’s creatures.
He is an ascetic, the liberator, the wise one, the primordial lord, and the imperishable;
he is the guardian of the world, the hidden self, the beginning of the kalpa, and the lotus-eyed one.
He who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, who is the self-restraint and the refuge of restraints;
he is Rahu, Surya, Shani, and Ketu; he is cessation and has the luster of coral.
The Supreme Brahman, accessible through devotion, the sinless one who offered his arrow at the deer,
he whose abode was made in the mountain cave, the soul of the wind, the Lord of the universe.
He is the immovable one regarding all actions, the creator, the auspicious one, and the bestower of auspiciousness;
he possesses great austerity and long austerity, and he is most firm, ancient, and eternal.
The section beginning with *amṛtātmā* and ending with *vidhiḥ* is not found among the sons designated as Ka, Kha, and Ga.
[Page 157] Day, year, serpent, measure, supreme austerity. (302)
The mantra that effects the year is the means of realization and the seer of all. || 48 ||
The Unborn, the Lord of All, the Perfected One, of great seed and great strength;
the Yogin, Yoga itself, Mahādeva, the Perfected One, the Origin of All, the Infallible. || 49 ||
Vasu, Vasumānas, Satya, the remover of all sins, Hara, the immortal, the eternal, the peaceful, the one with an arrow in hand, and the majestic one. || 50 ||
Bearing a water-pot, armed with a bow, master of the Vedāṅgas, knower of the Vedas, and a sage;
resplendent, the enjoyer of food, the eater, the leader of the world, and invincible. || 51 ||
Beyond the senses, the great illusionist, the abode of all, the crossroads;
the yogi of time, the great sound, the great enthusiasm, and the great power. || 52 ||

Possessing great intelligence and great heroism, he moves among living beings; he is the destroyer of cities, the wanderer of night, the sustainer of the departed spirits, possessed of great power and great splendor. || 53 ||
He is considered to have an indescribable form, glorious, and the attractor of all;
he is deeply learned, possessed of great power of illusion, self-controlled, and the source of fearlessness.
He who possesses vigor, splendor, and radiance; the dancer; the leader of all;
he who is eternally fond of the bell; whose nature is eternal light; the one who causes expansion. || 55 ||

The mantra is prosperous and possesses distinct syllables; it is a battle and a boat in the autumn. It is the beginning of the age, the bull of the age, profound, and the vehicle for purification. 56.
The beloved, the distinguished, the one desired by the learned, the Śarabha, the Sarabha, the bow;
the ocean, the foundation, victory, and the knower of the time of triumph. (57)
He is firmly established, the knower of the means of valid cognition, the golden-armored one,
the remover of distress, the host of gods, the Lord of Knowledge, and the refuge of the wise.
He is the child-form, the churner, the cutter, the impenetrable, and Guha;
he is the instrument, the cause, and the agent who releases one from all bonds. || 59 ||
403 || He is resolve, he is steadfastness, the giver of station, and the source of the world’s beginning;
he is the drum, the graceful, the universe, the self of existence, established within the Self. || 60 ||
The beloved of the king of kings, the radiant one, the crest-jewel of kings, the Lord;
the Lord of Heroes, Vīrabhadra, the master of the heroic posture, the Universal Sovereign. 61.
The crest-jewel of heroes, the seizer, intense bliss, the bearer of the river;
marked with the trident of the self-supporter, pervaded by light, and having Śivā as his refuge. || 62 ||
Vālakhilya, Mahācāra, Tigmāṃśu, Vāridhi, Khaga, Abhirāma, Suśaraṇya, Subrahmaṇya, and Sudhāpati. || 63 ||
He is rich in honey, the descendant of Kuśika, possessing cattle, the cessation [of suffering], the means for all;
he has an eye on his forehead, is the body of the universe, the essence, and the sustainer of the wheel of worldly existence.
Amoghadaṇḍa, Madhyastha, Hiraṇya, Brahmavarcasī, Parabrahmapada, Haṃsa, Śavara, Vyāghraka, and Anala. || 65 ||
Ruci, Vararuci, Vandyo, Vācaspati, Aharpati, Ravi, Virocana, Skanda, Śāstā, Vaivasvata, and Arjuna. || 66 ||
Liberation, the one of exalted fame, Śāntarāma, the conqueror of cities, the lord of Kailāsa, the enemy of Kāma, the progenitor, and the one whose eye is the sun. || 67 ||
He is the cessation [of suffering], free from fear, the architect of the universe, and unimpeded;
he is eternal, possessed of constant auspiciousness, and whose hearing and chanting are meritorious.

He whose fame is heard afar, the all-conquering, the one to be meditated upon, the destroyer of evil sounds; the deliverer, the remover of misdeeds, the invincible, the unbearable, and the dispeller of fear. || 69 ||

The beginningless one, the earth, the atmosphere, the goddess Lakṣmī, the wearer of a crown, the lord of the thirty gods, the protector of the universe, the destroyer of the universe, the great hero, and the one of radiant limbs. (70)
Janana is the origin of the birth of beings, and he is full of joy and endowed with wisdom.
Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Bhānu, Bhīma, and Bhīmaparākrama. || 71 ||
He is the sacred syllable Om, the one who walks the path of truth, the one of vast body, and the great bow;
he is the lord of birth, the Great God, who has reached the further shore of all the scriptures.
He is reality, the knower of reality, the one self, the manifestation, adorned with manifestations;
he is the seer, the knower of the Veda, Viṣṇu, who transcends birth, death, and old age.
He is the sacrifice, the lord of sacrifice, the sacrificer, the end of sacrifice, and he whose prowess is never in vain.
He is the great Indra, the difficult to sustain, the leader of armies, the limb of sacrifice, and the vehicle of sacrifice.
The origin of the five Brahmās, the source of stainless manifestation from all sides;
the self-born, without beginning or end, the sustainer of the six worlds, the wise seer.
Gāyatrīvallabha, Prāṃśu, Viśvāvāsa, Sadāśiva,
Śiśugirirata, Samrāṭ, Suṣeṇa, and Suraśatruhā. || 76 ||
Immeasurable, the destroyer of misfortune, the deliverer from death, free from all feverish affliction;
self-luminous, the light beyond all lights, immovable, the supreme Lord.
Tawny-hued, with a tawny beard, his body possessing the three Vedas as his eyes;
he is the trunk of knowledge, a possessor of great wisdom, the source of heroes, and the one who subdues calamities.
He is Bhaga, Vivasvat, Āditya, the teacher of yoga (yogācāra), and the lord of the day;
he is of noble fame, the diligent one, the one perfected in yoga, and the embodiment of both the existent and the non-existent. || 79 ||
He who wears a garland of stars, the lord of the celestial vault, whose self-abiding place has six supports;
he whose feet are pure, the enemy of sin, who dwells in the Maṇipūra, and whose movement is through the sky.
Seated upon the lotus of the heart, white-complexioned, all-knowing, Vṛṣākapi;
the gratified Lord of the House, Kṛṣṇa, the capable one who subdues misfortune. || 81 ||
He who destroys half of his enemies, who is invoked by many and praised by many;
whose arms are vast, who contains the Veda within him, who is the cow of dharma, and the source of wealth. 82.
The Sugata, who desires the welfare of the world, is a youth and the source of all that is wholesome. || 602 ||
Hiraṇyagarbha, the luminous Upendra, who dispels the darkness. || 83 ||
Aroga, Tapanādhyakṣa, Viśvāmitra, Dvijeśvara, Brahmajyotis, Subuddhātman, and Bṛhajjyotis Anuttama. || 84 ||
Mātāmaha, Mātariśvan, Manasvin, Nāgahāradhṛk, Pulastya, Pulaha, Agastya, Jātūkarṇya, and Parāśara. || 85 ||
He whose consciousness is free from obscuration, the one with wide-striding steps, the one praised in the Vedas;
he who has become the Self, the unceasing, Atri, the embodiment of knowledge, and the one of great fame.
The moon is the supreme crest-jewel of the world, whose prowess is truth;
he is like a great serpent, a great cosmic age, the wish-fulfilling tree, and the treasury of all arts.
He who adorns himself, the immovable one, the radiant, the one of supreme valor;
the swift, the lord of the seven, the impetuous, the leaper, and he whose charioteer is the peacock. 88.
Asaṃtuṣṭa, Atithi, Śukra, Pramāthin, Pāpaśāsana, Vasuśravas, Kavyavāha, Pratapta, and Viśvabhojana. || 89 ||

Victorious is he who subdues the enemy that is old age; he whose horse is red, the son of Tanūnapāt; he whose horses are speckled, whose source is the sky, who is of beautiful countenance, and the slayer of Tamiṣra. 90.
Nidāgha, Tapano, Megha, Pakṣa, Parapurañjaya, Sukhī, Nīla, Suniṣpanna, Surabhi, and Śiśirātmaka. || 91 ||
Vasanta, Mādhava, Grīṣma, Nabhasya, Bījavāhana;
Manas, Buddhi, Ahaṃkāra, Kṣetrajña, and Kṣetrapālaka. || 92 ||
Jamadagni is the ocean, the ripening fruit, and the creator of the universe;
he is to be known as the lower, the unsurpassed, the eldest, and the abode of supreme bliss. || 93 ||
The tree named Śaila, the burner, the enemy of the Dānavas, the subduer of foes;
Cāmuṇḍī, the progenitor, the beautiful one, the one free from thorns, the remover of the world's thorns. 94.

He who possesses the four Vedas, who is the four states of being, who moves through the four squares, who is the traditional scripture, who is the object of the traditional scriptures, whose deity is Artha, and who is the abode of Śiva. || 95 ||
Mahādeva is of adamantine form; he is all forms, both moving and unmoving;
he is the upholder of justice, justice itself, accessible through justice, and untainted.
The lord of gods has a thousand heads; he is the shatterer of all weapons.
He is shaven-headed, deformed, and misshapen; he carries a staff, is self-controlled, and is preeminent in virtues.
Piṅgalākṣa, Haryaśva, Nīlagrīva, Nirāmaya, Sahasrabāhu, Sarveśa, Śaraṇya, and Sarvalokadhṛk; || 98 ||
He is seated upon the lotus, the supreme light, free from all enmity, and the ultimate fruit;
he is the womb of the lotus, the great womb, the womb of the universe, and the one who is beyond all characteristics.
The god who partakes of the sacrifice, the bestower of boons, the lord of boons, and the one of great sound;
the divine teacher of gods and asuras, Śaṅkara, the source of the worlds. 100.
He consists of all the Vedas, is inconceivable, and is born from the truth of the deities;
he is the God of gods, the divine sage, and the bestower of boons upon gods and asuras. || 101 ||
The divine lord of gods and asuras, the great sovereign of gods and asuras, the bestower of boons upon gods and asuras, who is saluted by gods and asuras. || 102 ||
He is the great minister of the gods and asuras, the great refuge of the gods and asuras;
he consists of all the gods, is inconceivable, and is the self-born source of the gods.
He who is praised by the gods, the Lord without a superior, pervaded by the gods, the lion among deities, the maker of day;
the foremost of the wise, the most excellent, the highest of all the supreme gods. 104.
Delighting in meditation on Śiva, the illustrious one, the crested one, the lover of Śrīparvata;
holding a thunderbolt in his hand, the immovable, the knower of all things, the maker of night. 105.
The celibate student, the wanderer of the world, the practitioner of Dharma, the lord of wealth;
Nandi, the Lord of Joy, the humble one, the bearer of the naked vow, the pure one. || 106 ||
The overseer of the *liṅga*, the overseer of the gods, the overseer of dharma, and the bringer of the ages.
He is self-dependent, gone to heaven, heaven itself, creation, consisting of sound, and the resonance. || 107 ||
The overseer of seeds, the creator of seeds, the performer of dharma, the increaser of dharma; the deceptive, the deceptive one, the great deceptive one, the supreme lord of all beings. 108.
He whose abode is the cremation ground, the protector, the bridge of incomparable form,
the one who has transcended the world.
He who is affectionate toward his devotees. || 109 ||

The enemy of Andhaka, the hater of Madhu, the one who caused the falling of Viṣṇu’s neck, the one possessing the qualities of the two wings, the one whose end is water, and the breaker of Pūṣan’s teeth. (110)
Dhūrjaṭi, Khaṇḍaparaśu, Sakala, Niṣkala, Anagha, Ākāra, Sakalādhāra, Pāṇḍurāga, Mṛga, and Naṭa. (111)
Pūrṇa, Pūrayitṛ, Puṇya, Sukumāra, Sulocana, Sāmageya, Priya, Krūra, Puṇyakīrti, and Anāmaya. || 112 ||

He who is as swift as thought, the founder of a religious order, the one with matted hair, the lord of life, the bringer of the end of life, the infinite, he whose seed is wealth, and the bestower of wealth. || 113 ||
He is the one of good destiny, the one who is honored, the peaceful one, the dark-throated one, the bearer of the arts;
he is the proud one, the thinker, Mahākāla, the source of true prosperity, and the supreme refuge.
The teacher who revives the moon, the one established in the world, the great sovereign;
the kinsman of the world, the lord of the world, the grateful one, the one adorned by his own deeds. || 115 ||
He is without decay, imperishable, and tranquil; the best among all wielders of weapons;
consisting of splendor, possessing radiance, the illusion of the world, the foremost leader, and free from conflict.
Extremely amazed, with a serene soul, invincible and difficult to surpass, consisting of light and formless, he is the Lord of the World and the Master of the Waters. || 117 ||
The gourd-lute, the great Śoka, the Viśoka, the destroyer of sorrow;
the Lord of the three worlds, the soul of the three worlds, accomplishment, purity, and Adhokṣaja. || 118 ||

The lord of the people, whose characteristics were unmanifest, became manifest; he was both manifest and unmanifest, possessed of excellent conduct and supreme qualities, having gone beyond the state of Maya through his inexhaustible power.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Prajāpāla, Haṃsa, and Haṃsagati are considered his names;
he is Vedhā, Vidhātṛ, Sraṣṭṛ, Kartṛ, Hartṛ, and Caturmukha. || 120 ||
He who dwells on the peak of Kailāsa, who resides in the sun, whose movement is eternal;
he is the Golden Womb (Hiraṇyagarbha), the Sky, the Supreme Person (Puruṣa), the First-born, and the Father. 121.
The abode of beings, the lord of beings, the bestower of prosperity, the sovereign of the world;
he who is restrained, praised by the knowers of yoga, devoted to Brahman, and fond of Brahmins. 122.
Beloved by the gods, lord of the gods, knower of destiny, thinker of the divine;
having uneven eyes, large-eyed, giver of strength, increaser of joy. || 123 ||
Free from possessiveness, free from egoism, free from delusion, and free from affliction;
the destroyer of pride, the mirror, the proud one, and the transformer of all things. || 124 ||
He who has seven tongues, who possesses a thousand rays, who is gentle and naturally benevolent;
the lord of the past, future, and present, the source of all, and the destroyer of delusion. He is both the goal and the obstacle, the great treasury, and uniquely skilled in the bodies of others.
He is free from thorns, the creator of bliss, devoid of artifice, yet appearing through artifice.
He was possessed of courage, virtuous, truthful, a pillar of fame, and one who had mastered the traditional scriptures;
he was unshakable, a perceiver of virtues, not of a single fixed nature, and a performer of deeds for the world.
Śrīvallabha, Śivārambha, Śāntabhadra, Samañjasa, Bhūśaya, Bhūtikṛt, Bhūti, Vibhūti, and Bhūtivāhana. || 128 ||
He is bodiless yet abides in the body of the elements; he knows the times and possesses great fortune;
he is devoted to truth and great renunciation, and is intent upon the peace of desire. || 129 ||
Bestower of the means for the welfare of others, solitary, and an ocean of sacred revelation. || 1000 ||
Undaunted, perceiving virtues, stainless, and the destroyer of stains. || 130 ||
He who is naturally auspicious, the mediator, the slayer of enemies, and the destroyer of foes;
he who possesses a crest-lock, wears armor, wields a trident, bears matted locks, and is adorned with earrings. 131.
Wearing a girdle, clad in armor, bearing a sword, and adorned with garlands, he is the charioteer of cyclic existence;
he is deathless, the conqueror of all, a lion, a mass of splendor, and possessed of great majesty.
Innumerable, immeasurable in essence, valiant, skilled in action, the one to be known, the physician, the protector, the lord of sages who is the seventh and last. || 133 ||
He is unsurpassed, invincible, sweet, and pleasant to behold; he is the Lord of the gods, the refuge, the bliss, the All, and the goal of all that possesses sound. 134.
He is Time, the fortnight, the destroyer of skeletons, and he who has made Vāsuki his bracelet;
he is the great archer, the lord of the earth, the stainless one, and the one free from all fetters. || 135 ||
He is the one spread with jewels, the fortunate one, the bestower of perfection, the means for achieving perfection;
he is the revealed, the concealed, the artisan, the broad-chested one, and the mighty-armed one.
He who is the single light, free from fear, beloved by Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
he who is untainted, whose self is beyond phenomenal expansion, who is undisturbed, and the destroyer of all agitation.
He is to be praised, fond of hymns, the knower, whose form is the sky, and who is undisturbed;
he is the means to the state beyond suffering, a mass of knowledge, and uncreated.

He whose intellect is perfectly tranquil, who is not mean-spirited, who delights the heart, and who is eternally beautiful; he who is the object of meditation, the foremost leader, the Lord of the Earth, the embodiment of all perfections, and the Lord of the Night. || 139 ||

He is the ultimate guru, pure, affectionate toward those who have taken refuge in him, the essence, the knower of essences, the knower of the core, and the support for all sentient beings. 140 || 1091 ||
Having worshipped with supreme devotion, O twice-born ones, he praised the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain with this thousand names using white lotuses. (141)
O best of sages, for the sake of testing him, Śiva himself, out of devotion to Hari, concealed one lotus there among the lotuses.
When the flower had been taken away, Viṣṇu, wondering "What is this?", realized what had happened;
he then plucked out his own eye and worshipped Śaṅkara.
Then, having recognized Hari’s perfectly steadfast devotion,
Mahādeva manifested himself from the orb of the fiercely radiant sun.
Resembling ten million suns, three-eyed, with the moon as his crest-jewel,
the all-pervading Lord holds a trident, an axe, a mace, a discus, a spear, and a noose.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, and adorned with all ornaments—
having seen that Lord of the gods of gods, the Blessed One, whose eyes are like lotuses, [acted]. 146.
Again, they prostrated themselves like a staff at the feet of the wielder of the trident;
then, seeing Śambhu, the gods fled, overwhelmed by fear.
The realm of Brahmā trembled and the earth shook;
then, rising upwards in its fury, it consumed [the world] for a hundred yojanas.
O Brahmins, having seen that splendor of the Lord Śambhu, Śiva laughed and spoke to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who stood with his palms joined in reverence.
O Madhusūdana, I have now understood your divine purpose;
I shall grant you that wonderful, celestial discus, the Sudarśana.
O Daitya, O Viṣṇu, by my command, you must take up that which was created by me in the past for the benefit of all the gods, and assume it with its [divine] qualities. 151.
Having spoken thus, he gave him a discus with a brilliance equal to ten thousand suns;
Hari became renowned in the worlds as Puṇḍarīkākṣa. Then Śaṃdhu spoke again to that flawless Nārāyaṇa, requesting other boons as desired, O best of gods.
Having thus heard what was spoken by Śambhu, the Lord Janārdana,
with palms joined in reverence and filled with affection, spoke to the wielder of the broken axe (Khaṇḍaparaśu).
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Supreme Self, immutable Śiva!
"May my devotion to you be unwavering; this is my boon. (155)
The Lord said: "O Viṣṇu, O sinless one, firm devotion toward me shall arise within you;
by my grace, you shall become invincible in the three worlds. (156)
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, having thus granted the boon to the all-powerful Viṣṇu, Śambhu vanished; so the god Ravi spoke.
Whoever recites or even hears this divine thousand names uttered by Viṣṇu is liberated from all sins. (158)
One who recites this with total devotion certainly attains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices; or else, great knowledge shall arise. 159.
* Here, a certain interpolation is seen in both the Cachā and Saṃśita manuscripts.
It is as follows: "O Śambhu, let there be devotion toward you that is unwavering and undying;
O God of noble vows, I choose this boon and no other whatsoever."
Thus,
one who is beloved of Śiva shall attain great sovereignty.
In a mass of water that is otherwise difficult to cross, the water shall turn into dry land.
Great serpents act as necklaces, and the lion behaves like a pet deer;
therefore, the Blessed Lord Śiva should be praised with his thousand names.
It bestows all desires and, at the end of the body, the supreme goal. || 162 ||
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Attainment of Viṣṇu’s Discus," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 41 ||
The sages said: We have heard how Puruṣottama obtained the discus from Śambhu;
now we wish to hear the auspicious procedure for the worship of Śiva.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the procedure for the worship of Śiva in brief;
it is not possible to describe it in detail even in a hundred years.
Formerly, on the peak of Mount Meru, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
it was told by Nandin, the delighter of his lineage, to Sanatkumāra.
