Having approached Nandīśvara, the omniscient lord of the Maruts, as he sat comfortably, and having prostrated before him according to the prescribed rite like a staff, [he spoke].
Sanatkumāra asked about the sequence of the ritual for the worship of Śiva—
the bestower of boons upon all, the peaceful one, who is surrounded by tens of millions of Gaṇas.
Sanatkumāra said:
Salutations to you, O Gaṇeśa, who possess the splendor of ten thousand suns;
O you who are worshipped by the gods, tell me the procedure for the worship of Śiva.
Nandikeśvara said:
"O son of Brahmā, listen now to me as I describe the procedure for the worship of Śiva;
for you, O sage, are a devotee of Mahādeva, who is the soul of all."
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule and sipped water (ācamana) in the proper manner,
the wise man, having reached the place of worship, should then sit down.
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one should meditate thus upon Sadāśiva;
then, having performed the drying of the body, followed by its burning and immersion.
Having assumed the Śiva-body, one should perform the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa).
This mantra, which consists of the Sūtra, is the supreme essence of all the Vedas.
For the sake of its consecration, one should duly deposit the Brahma-mantras preceded by the *praṇava*; then, having deposited them, one should [anoint it] with sandalwood water.
O Lord of Sages, having thoroughly sprinkled the place of worship and the ritual materials,
their washing and consecration are prescribed by means of the *praṇava*.
One should place the *prokṣaṇī* vessel and likewise the *pādya* vessel,
as well as the *ācamanīya* vessel, having consecrated them according to the prescribed rule.
Having covered [the vessel] with that very water and sprinkled it, the one of dull intellect should pour water into those [vessels] and then cast in the ritual substances.
One should prepare the water for washing the feet with uśīra and sandalwood;
likewise, one should add camphor, nutmeg, and jātiphala, having ground them together with kaṅkola.
One should pour [the water] for the sipping rite with the *praṇava* in the proper sequence; one should offer sandalwood paste everywhere. Now listen regarding the *arghya* vessel.
Rice grains, flowers, tips of kuśa grass, as well as white mustard seeds, unbroken grains (akṣata), and likewise fried grain with clarified butter. || 17 ||
Then the wise one should cast kuśa grass, flowers, barley, rice, bahumūla, and tamālaka into the prokṣaṇī vessel while reciting the Praṇava.
O best of the twice-born, having taken the vessel for sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇī) with the *bhavagāyatrī* and the *gāyatrī* mantra, he should sprinkle the two door-keepers.
At my side [he saw] the four-armed one, possessing a splendor equal to ten thousand suns,
with the face of a monkey, three eyes, and beautifully adorned with a garland of flowers.
One should worship Nandīśa, who is enriched by the splendor of all ornaments;
and on the right, Mahākāla, who is of terrible form and inspiring fear.
With a face made terrifying by fangs and resembling a mass of the fire of cosmic destruction,
he then entered the inner chamber of Śambhu with a perfectly concentrated mind.
O Sage, one should offer five handfuls of flowers with the five Brahma-mantras;
then, the wise person should devoutly worship Mahādeva with perfumes and flowers.
One should then begin the purification of the linga, including Skanda and Vināyaka, according to the rules, using gentle mantras preceded by the syllable Om and ending with "namas. (24)
Thereafter, one should arrange the seat upon the lotus of the petals of sovereignty; then,
one should place the mandala of fire upon the pericarp.
Having placed the solar and lunar [deities], one should indeed place Dharma and the others in the intermediate directions.
Then, in the directions starting from Adharma, [the wise one] should worship the three qualities at the edge of Soma, then the three principles (tattvas), and thereafter Śambhu. || 27 ||
One should cause the deity to rest according to the prescribed rite with water mixed with fragrances;
then, one should offer the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) which have been prepared according to the rules with the recitation of mantras.
O Sage, at the very beginning there, one should bathe [the deity] with water mixed with milk, using the *praṇava* mantra,
as well as with clarified butter, honey, curd, and sugarcane juice.
One should perform the purification of the water many times according to the rules with mantras;
then, having covered [the image] with a white cloth, one should bathe the Moon-crested Lord.
With *kuśa* grass, *apāmārga*, camphor, *jātī*, and *campaka* flowers;
with white *karavīra*, as well as *mallikā*, *kamala*, and *utpala* lotuses. || 31 ||
O son of Brahmā, having filled that water with auspicious flowers, sandalwood paste, and other such items, one should then install the mantras beginning with Sadyojāta therein.
Then, with a golden pitcher, and likewise with one of silver, or with a conch, or with a beautiful and auspicious earthen one. || 33 ||
One should bathe [the deity] with water containing kusa grass and flowers, preceded by the recitation of mantras:
namely, the Pavamāna, the Rudra, and the Vāmīyaka hymns.
Or again, by the Rudra named Tvaritā, or by the Nīlarudra, or likewise by the Atharvaśiras Rudra. || 35 ||
O Sage, [one should worship] with the meritorious Rathantara, or with the Śrīsūkta,
or with the Puruṣasūkta, and with the Jyeṣṭhasāman of Viṣṇu.
One should bathe the Lord of the gods with the five Brahma-mantras, or with the Sūtra-mantra, or with the Praṇava, for the attainment of the fruit of all sacrifices.
A garment, two sacred threads, as well as water for sipping, a beautiful and auspicious crown, and likewise ornaments; || 38 ||
One should offer mouth-perfume and all food offerings with the *praṇava*.
Then [one should meditate upon] the God who resembles crystal, partless and imperishable. (39)
The medicine for those afflicted by the disease of existence is devoid of beginning, middle, and end.
That which is known as the Śivaliṅga is established as the Śivaliṅga;
one should worship the top of the liṅga with the Praṇava mantra alone.
Having praised Mahādeva with hymns, having prostrated and performed circumambulation, and having again offered flowers and scattered them about; || 43 ||
Having prostrated at the feet of the God of gods, one should take leave;
thus, O son of Brahmā, the worship of Śiva has been described in brief.
Whatever is secret in all the Vedas, just as it was heard by Bhayā from Śambhu.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, that worship of Śiva which the blessed and learned Sanatkumāra heard from the blessed Nandīśvara has been recounted by me.
Whoever, being self-restrained and full of devotion, recites this sequence of the ritual for the worship of Śiva,
shall be liberated from all sins and honored in the world of Brahmā.

2181 || Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Worship of Śiva," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 42 ||
Sūta said:
There is another vow that removes sin and bestows virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation;
it is the vow named Umāmaheśvara, renowned throughout the three worlds.
O best of the twice-born, this most excellent [rite] should be performed on these lunar days: the full moon, the new moon, and likewise on the fourteenth day.
Practicing celibacy, eating sacrificial food, speaking the truth, and being well-restrained,
one should at the end of the year fashion an image out of gold or silver.
O twice-born ones, having gratified [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should worship according to the prescribed rite,
adorning [him] with garments, flowers, and various auspicious foods.
One should arrange the splendor with banners, canopies, and celestial ornaments;
one should worship the preceptor with devotion using garments, ornaments, and decorations.
He goes to the abode of Maheśvara, having gone to which he does not grieve. || 11 ||
There, having enjoyed the pleasures of Maheśvara for three hundred kalpas,
at the end of that time he enjoys the pleasures of Vaiṣṇava in the presence of Viṣṇu.
Subsequently, endowed with enjoyments, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
falling from the world of Brahmā, he attains the worlds of Prajāpati.
Falling from that world, he who is thereafter honored by all the worlds reaches the realm of Soma and enjoys pleasures according to his desires. || 14 ||
Having enjoyed great pleasures there in the unsurpassed worlds of Soma, Deva, Indra, Gandharva, and Yakṣa, at the end of that time, [he dwells] on the summit of Mount Meru.
At the end of that, having attained the worlds of the world-protectors, he rejoices;
thereafter, by the remainder of his karma, he becomes a single being upon the earth.
The vow named Umāmaheśvara, which bestows all happiness, was formerly proclaimed by Śaṅkara for the sake of Pārvatī and Ṣaṇmukha. (17)
Agastya received it from the six-faced one (Kārttikeya), and from him my guru obtained it;
I, in turn, have received this supreme [teaching] from Dvaipāyana, the best of sages.
O best of sages, listen now to another vow called Śūlavrata:
for one year, a person who is well-restrained should remain without food on the new moon day.
Having fashioned a trident out of flour, one should offer it at the end of the year to Śiva,
along with a silver lotus having a pericarp made of gold.
But with devotion, one should place it on the head; everything else is as before.
Released from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, one goes to the supreme goal. (21)
Having attained the worlds previously described, at their conclusion, that lord of the earth,
firm in his vows, [shall remain] for one year on the full moon and new moon days.
At the end of the year, one should offer an image rich with all kinds of perfumes;
by this vow, O twice-born ones, one indeed obtains the same fruit as before. (23)
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days,
one who has conquered the senses,
even if endowed with all worldly enjoyments, is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 24 ||
Forgiveness, truthfulness, compassion, charity, purity, restraint of the senses, worship of Śiva, fire-offerings, contentment, and likewise non-stealing; || 25 ||
This common dharma is traditionally taught as being tenfold across all vows. || 26 ||
O best of sages, listen to this "Remover of Sins" which is distinct [from others],
as it was formerly proclaimed by Śambhu, the god of gods, to the six-faced one (Kārttikeya).
Having prostrated according to the rules with devotion before the God of gods seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, the son of Girijā questioned him.
Skanda said:
"By what means, O Blessed One, would incomparable good fortune arise?
How does a man thrive in happiness, possessing sons, grandsons, wealth, and sovereignty? (29)
Therefore, O Mahādeva, grant me that supreme vow among all vows, by the performance of which, O Lord of Gods, a man attains sovereignty. (30)
Even a woman born of a servant's family becomes lotus-like;
a prince shall conquer his enemies just as Garuḍa conquers serpents.

A Brāhmaṇa, having attained the splendor of Brahman (brahmavarcasa), shall become preeminent among all; even one who has strayed from the duties of his caste and stage of life attains perfection through him. || 32 ||
Īśvara said:
Listen, my child, I shall proclaim the most excellent of vows. There exists the vow of Gaṇapati known as Dūrvā, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
The Blessed One practiced [austerities] upon his chest along with Pārvatī, Padmā, Sarasvatī, Mahendra, Viṣṇu, and Dhanada. || 34 ||
And by other gods, dūtas, gandharvas, and likewise by kinnaras, having fashioned him, O Lord of Obstacles, seated upon a golden pedestal-throne; [p. 171] 37.
Likewise,
having established the dūrvā grass situated upon that support, one should place it there.
In a water-pot or a copper vessel. || 38 ||
One should worship [the deity] encircled within a *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala with red [offerings] and with five lotus petals.
My other beloved Hari-priyā (2) [is adorned] with other fragrant flowers and fragrant leaf-stalks (patrikā). || 40 ||
Then one should prepare an offering of fruits and sweetmeats;
O Lord of the Universe, I worship you with these offerings according to the prescribed ritual. 41.
Having spoken thus, one should indeed worship the Son of the Mountain-Dweller with faith:
"Come, come, O God Heramba, King of Obstacles, Elephant-faced One!"
Having sat upon the seat, O God, be the bestower of all desires.
Thus ends the mantra for invocation and seating:
"O son of Umā, salutations to you, the eternal one who pervades the universe!
Cut asunder the entire flood of obstacles; I offer you water for the feet. (43)
Thus ends the mantra for the arghya and pādya offerings.
"To the Lord Gaṇeśvara, the son of Umā, the Creator—I now present this worship; accept it, O Blessed One, salutations! (44)
Thus is the mantra for incense.
Salutation to Vināyaka, the heroic, the giver of boons, the elephant-faced one;
salutation to the divine son of Umā, the preceptor of Kumāra. || 45 ||
To the pot-bellied hero, who removes all obstacles. || 46 ||

Thus ends the mantra for the flowers: "O you who were born from the body of Umā, for the sake of slaying the Dānavas and for the grace of the worlds—may that God, the consumer of the universe, protect us. (47)
Thus is the incense mantra. "To you, the supreme light, for the sake of illumination and the bestowing of all perfections—to you, the Great God, the Self, I offer this lamp; obeisance! (48)
Thus ends the mantra for the lamp.

This verse does not exist in the manuscript designated as Ghaṅaja; furthermore, in the manuscripts designated as Ṅaja, this meaning of the verse is absent. With the exception of the manuscript designated as Saṃśita, the entire collection of words beginning with "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*) and ending with "certainly" (*nūnam*) is missing from all extant manuscripts.
*gaṇānāṃ tvā gaṇapatiṃ havāmahe* (We invoke you, the Lord of hosts, among the hosts).
O Brahmaṇaspati, poet among poets, most renowned, sovereign lord of the sacred hymns, hearing us with your protections, sit upon your seat. 49.
Thus ends the mantra for the offering: "O Lord of the Gaṇas, Chief of the Gaṇas, Son of Gaurī, Elephant-faced One! By your grace, O Lord of Splendor, may my vow reach completion. (50)

Thus ends the mantra of supplication. Having thus worshipped Vighneśa with extensive offerings according to one's means, one should present the presiding Lord of the Gaṇas, along with his ritual implements, to the preceptor.
"O Blessed One, O Brahmin, accept Gaṇarāja along with this sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
By your word, let this vow today reach completion, O observer of noble vows. (52)
This is the mantra for the gift.
Thus, he who performs the concluding rite after practicing this for five years obtains his desired objects and, at the end of the body, attains the state of Śaṅkara.
Alternatively, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight, one who has restrained the senses should likewise perform the three vows; thus he shall attain all success.
O Six-faced One, he who performs this supreme vow without the concluding rite (udyāpana) must perform a morning bath with white sesame seeds.
Having fashioned an image of Gaṇapati out of gold or even silver, the wise man,
having bathed it well with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), should worship it with dūrvā grass.
And with devotion, O Śikhidhvaja, using these ten mantras accompanied by *dūrvā* grass—
thus has this auspicious rite, which bestows all accomplishments, been described, my son.
The vow of Gaṇapati involves dūrvā grass; what else do you wish to hear? || 57 ||

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Umā-Maheśvara and Dūrvā-Gaṇapati Vratas," in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka within the *Śrī Saura*, an Upapurāṇa of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*. || 43 ||
The sages said: "O Lord, you ought to tell us here what fruit a mortal obtains by constructing a temple of Śiva using materials ranging from clay up to precious gems."
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, to the power of the Supreme Lord;
it is said that by constructing a temple of Śiva, infinite fruit is obtained.
O best of Brahmins, whoever constructs even a temple to Śiva made of clay with every effort for the sake of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation; || 3 ||
And whoever should construct a temple for the Supreme Lord known as Kailāsa,
Whether it be the mountain named Meru, or the one named Mandara, or even the snowy mountain (Himalaya).
The best of the twice-born [saw] Mount Nipadri, Mount Nīla, and the one named Mahendra,
with celestial chariots that fulfilled all desires and resembled mountain peaks.
Having gone to the divine state of Śiva, he rejoices for a long time like Śiva himself,
enjoying his desired pleasures until the great dissolution (mahāpralaya).
Having abandoned the objects of the senses with his teeth [firm], he shall attain union with Śiva;
even if it be fallen, broken, worn out, or likewise cracked.
One who, as before, should have a pavilion (maṇḍapa), a temple (prāsāda), or likewise a gate-tower (gopura) constructed with very beautiful white plaster (sudhā). || 8 ||
A person who performs work in the temple of Śiva, whether for the sake of their livelihood or otherwise, obtains merit exceeding that of the patron; of this there is no doubt.

He who goes [to Rudra’s abode], even once, for the sake of accomplishing his own enjoyment in the temple of Rudra, goes to the heavenly world along with his kinsmen; of this there is no doubt. || 10 ||
Having obtained happiness, he performs his duty and rejoices;
yet when that mortal becomes incapable of building a temple for the Lord, [he too must act]. (11)
Or even by means of sweeping and other such acts, one may obtain all desires;
for he who performs the sweeping with a soft and fine broom [attains them]. (12)
The fruit of a thousand *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts is obtained in a single month by one who,
having established a fire before Śiva, worships Śaṅkara.
He who offers his own body as an oblation goes to the auspicious state of Śiva;
having become abstinent from food in a sacred field of Śiva, he should renounce his life-breaths.
Through the grace of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), he attains union with Śiva;
then, having cut off his own feet, he shall dwell in the sacred field of Śiva with hands [as his means]. 15.
At the end of the body, one attains union with Śiva; there is no doubt about this.
Whatever fruit is obtained from a horse sacrifice, that very same fruit comes from the sight of this sacred field.
From entering [the temple] more than a hundred times, the merit is doubled by beholding the Liṅga;
worship is a hundredfold greater than that, and bathing in the water is even more so. (17)
Having sprinkled it with water according to the fourfold ritual procedure, the knower of mantras [should proceed].
Having adorned it with canopies and other beautiful umbrellas,
as well as with water-bubbles, half-moons, and golden leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.
With white, blooming lotuses and likewise with red and blue water-lilies,
the best of the twice-born [were honored] by means of a variegated celestial chariot adorned with strings of pearls.
With white clay vessels, very smooth full jars,
and with garlands of fruits and sprouts like victory banners, he was radiant.
Having drawn an excellent lotus joined with fifty mountains, along with fifty rows of lamps and various kinds of incense; || 27 ||
Having fashioned a lotus according to the prescribed rite, measuring one cubit in size, either with powders of that same color or with white powders; || 28 ||
One should thus place Lord Bhava, the Lord of Gods, within the pericarp of the lotus;
one should then assign the Rudras to the petals in sequence, starting from the east.

O you of excellent vows, having thus worshipped the best of gods with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order, using mantras for all the castes beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.
There, one should feed fifty Brahmins according to the prescribed rules,
and [bestow upon them] a rosary, a sacred thread, two earrings, and a water-pot.
*The verse concerning the meaning of the words *baṅga*, *sājñata*, and *pustaka* is not present;
furthermore, in the manuscripts designated as *baṅga*, *ca*, *cha*, and *ja*, the portion beginning with "sitaiḥ" and ending with the word "aṃśu" is absent.* [p.
And having given a seat, as well as a staff, a turban, and even a garment to those best of the twice-born for Śambhu, the God of gods; || 32 ||
Having thus offered the great caru oblation and likewise a pair of black cattle, and finally having presented a mandala of that same color to the God of gods; || 33 ||
The wise one should offer the substances required for the sacrifice to Śiva,
while reciting the syllable *oṃ* for each letter in successive order.
I shall now describe in brief the fruit that a mortal obtains by thus devoutly painting this supreme mandala of colors:
having studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs according to rule and in the proper manner.
Having performed sacrifices in due order according to the rules, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, || 36 ||
Then, having performed the Viśvajit sacrifice and fathered sons like myself,
he went to the forest-dwelling stage of life (vānaprastha) together with his wife and his sacred fires.
Having performed all the penances such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and having renounced everything, O twice-born ones,
and having studied the Brahma-vidyā, they attained knowledge through diligent effort.
Having illuminated the object of knowledge through wisdom, the knower of yoga attains the fruit;
one obtains that same fruit from the mere sight of the mandala of castes. 39.

O best of the twice-born, having drawn and smeared a dwelling or hermitage with whatever materials available, [one should place it] either to the north, to the south, or even behind [the sacred fire].
Or, having decorated the four corners on all sides with colored powders,
one should scatter fragrant flowers, incense, and the four kinds of lamps.
Thus he should pray to Īśāna; he goes to the world of Śiva. || 42 ||
Having enjoyed great pleasures there for hundreds of millions of kalpas,
that man shall fill the temple of Śiva with the auspicious fragrances of his own body.
Having attained the state of a Gandharva in due course and being highly honored by the Gandharvas,
he gradually returns to this world and becomes a powerful king. 44.
These waters, originating from the ocean, become pure when filtered through a cloth;
O tigers among sages, they are especially so when free of foam and when taken from a river.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, all Vedic rites must always be performed with pure water for the sake of complete success. (46)
Since non-violence is the supreme dharma for all living beings,
one should therefore perform [all actions] with every effort using water filtered through a cloth.
The vehicle of fearlessness is meritorious and the most excellent of all gifts;
therefore, violence must be avoided everywhere and at all times. (48)
When they, devoted to the welfare of all beings through mind, action, and speech,
have shown the path, they go to the world of Śiva.
Whatever sin is produced for men by destroying the entire three worlds,
one incurs that same sin by killing even a single person in the temple of Śiva.
The best of the twice-born should always perform the killing of flowers for the sake of Śiva;
likewise, the king should perform the killing of animals for the sake of sacrifice and the punishment of the wicked. (51)
No women whatsoever should be killed, especially those born of the lineage of Atri;
the sin resulting from the slaughter of an Ātreyī would be equal to the murder of a Brahmin.
O best of Brahmins, no women whatsoever should be killed by any of the twice-born, even if they are devoted to sinful deeds, according to all the codes of dharma. (53)

Therefore, one who is endowed with non-violence and other virtues, who is peaceful and dear to the people of Śiva, and who has firmly established devotion in Śiva, is liberated in that very birth. (54)
Abandoning everything else, the wise should practice devotion toward Viśveśvara, the three-eyed one, the all-pervading, and the omnipresent. 55.
Just as the minds of men are always attached to sons, wealth, and the like, if they were likewise [attached] even once to Virūpākṣa, how far would the state of Śaṅkara be? (56)
In whatever manner they worship Śambhu, Mahādeva bestows upon them a corresponding fruit; devotion is never without its result.
If that lowest of twice-born men, blinded by delusion, worships the Lord while still impure from food remnants,
that man enjoys abundant pleasures in the world of the Piśācas.
One who is full of wrath attains the station of the Rākṣasas; one who subsists on smoke attains the state of the Yakṣas.

Indeed, one habituated to singing attains the state of the Gandharvas, and likewise one habituated to dancing. One who is habituated to fame attains the state of Indra, and one who subsists on water attains the state of the Moon.
One should worship the Lord continuously for one year with the Gāyatrī mantra.
Having attained the Prājāpatya [state], one becomes a creator of the universe oneself;
and by means of the Praṇava alone, one attains the Brāhma and likewise the Vaiṣṇava [states]. (61)
How could joy not arise in us to hear the nectar of auspicious discourse? || 2 ||
Sūta said: In ancient times, all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, desiring to behold Maheśvara, went to Mount Mandara, the mountain most dear to Śambhu.
Having offered praise with palms joined in reverence, the gods stood before Hara;
then, seeing them, the Supreme Lord Mahādeva acted with effortless ease.
The knowledge of Brahmā and the other celestial dwellers had been stolen away;
they beheld that very God, the Self, standing before them.
Out of ignorance, they questioned him once, saying, "Who are you?";
the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, replied, "I am indeed the ancient one."
O best of gods, I existed at the very beginning, I exist now, and I shall exist in this world;
there is no one else whatsoever besides me.
O best of gods, there is nothing else whatsoever that exists apart from me;
I alone am both the eternal and the non-eternal; I am Brahmā, I am the Lord of Brahmā.
I am the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions, as well as primordial nature (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa).
I consist of the three worlds, the Anuṣṭubh meter, and the Paṅkti meter— the very essence of the triple Vedic meters.
I am the Truth, peaceful in every respect; I am the Guru, as venerable as the three sacrificial fires;
I am the Earth, I am the vehicle of Hara, I am the Sky, and I am the Lord of the worlds.
I am the best of all principles; I am the most excellent lord of the waters.
I am the waters, O Blessed Lord, I am the Ruler; I am the splendor, and I am also the sacrificial altar.
This meaning of the verse exists in the two books edited by X [p.
"I am the Ṛgveda, I am the Yajurveda, and I am the Sāmaveda, the self-born."
I am the Atharvan mantra and likewise the best of the Aṅgirases.
I am the Itihāsas and Purāṇas; I am the ritual manual (kalpa) and indeed I am creative imagination (kalpanā).
I am the imperishable (akṣara) and the perishable (kṣara); I am patience (kṣānti), peace (śānti), and the sky-goer (khaga).
I am the secret in all the Vedas; I am the forest-dweller and I am also the unborn.
I am the Puṣkara, the purifier, and that which is beyond the center. 14.
I am outside and likewise within; I am the immutable one before all.
I am light and I am darkness; I am Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Intellect, ego, the subtle elements, and the senses—all these are indeed myself; he who knows this is the best of gods.
He alone is the all-knowing, the All, the Self of all, and the all-seeing.

O best of gods, I satisfy the earth with cows, all the Brahmins with the status of Brahminhood, and the sacrificial offerings with oblations; likewise, I satisfy Truth with Truth and Dharma with Dharma by means of my own splendor. (17–18)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there;
they no longer beheld the god Rudra, the supreme cause.
The gods, along with Nārāyaṇa, as well as the gods headed by Indra and the sages, meditate upon that Supreme Self, Rudra, the auspicious Śaṅkara.
Then, with their arms raised upward, the gods spoke to him who brings about the true state of things.
The gods said: "This Blessed One is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara. (21)
Skanda, Agni, as well as Candra, the fourteen worlds, all living beings, as well as Sūrya, the eight Somas, and likewise the planets; || 22 ||
He is Prāṇa, Kāla, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Amṛta; He is the Supreme Lord.
He is the past, the present, the future, and the eternal Maheśvara. (23)
Salutations again and again to Him, the Truth, the entire universe, the whole world;
likewise, Om at the beginning, and similarly Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ in the middle. || 24 ||
Formerly you were the universal form, and you are always at the head of the world;
you are the Lord of the Gods, the twofold reality of above and below.
You are peace, as well as nourishment and contentment; you are the unoffered and the offered,
the universe and that which is beyond the universe, the giver, the eater, and the Lord.
O God, O Śaṅkara, you are indeed the eternal Truth, both the higher and the lower, the constant ultimate refuge even for the wicked.
We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal; we have reached the light, we have found the gods.
What can hostility now do to us? And what, O Immortal One, can the malice of a mortal do? 28.
This world is to be known as imperishable, subtle, and undecaying; it is the progeny of Prajāpati, pure, gentle, ungraspable, and foremost.
By his own splendor, he effortlessly swallows the fire with his fiery power, the wind with his windy power, and the moon with his lunar power.
Salutation to Him, the withdrawer, the great devourer, the wielder of the trident;
all deities reside in the heart, and the vital breaths are established in the heart. (31)
In the heart you are the womb; there are three measures, but he is beyond them.
His head is to the north, and likewise his foot is to the south.
He who is the living being beyond [the physical] is the eternal form, manifest;
he who is the syllable Om is indeed the God, the Manu, who stands pervading all.
He is infinite, subtle, white, and indeed like lightning;
he is the Supreme Brahman, he is Īśāna, and he alone is Rudra.
"You are Maheśvara himself, Mahādeva, without a doubt;
because he thus raises [the sound] upwards, he is celebrated as Oṃkāra. (35)
Because he leads forth the vital breaths (prāṇa), he is therefore designated as Praṇava;
because he pervades everything, he is the eternal Sarvavyāpin (the All-pervading One). || 36 ||
Neither Brahmā nor the blessed Lord Hari has perceived its beginning or end, as have others; therefore, Rudra is the infinite and supreme cause. (37)
Because he delivers one from saṃsāra, he is called the Deliverer (Tāra);
having become subtle, he always presides over bodies. (38)
Therefore, the Lord Nīlalohita is always known as subtle;
he is both blue and red because of his connection with Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
This verse does not appear in the two manuscripts designated as *baṅa*.
180] Therefore, because it is greater than the great, it is celebrated as the Supreme Brahman. || 41 ||
Then the Lord, the non-dual, the fourth, the auspicious Śiva, [spoke] to Īśa:
"To this Lord of the world, the one who beholds heaven, the tawny-colored Sovereign. (42)
O Indra, he who is the Lord of all that stands and moves at all times, and who is the Lord of all branches of knowledge—that is what is called Īśāna. (43)
Whatever the Blessed One beholds, He causes others to behold otherwise;
Mahādeva, through yoga, Himself imparts the knowledge of the Self.
And because he is called the Blessed One, Maheśvara is the God of gods;
Maheśvara seizes all the worlds in due order.
This Lord of Gods emits [the world] and also causes it to abide by his mere play.
For this God indeed pervades all directions; he was born first, and he is within the womb.
He alone has been born, he is yet to be born; facing every direction, he stands with faces on all sides. 46.
This foremost [reality] should be diligently worshipped by the virtuous, from which words turn back, unable to reach it along with the mind. (47)
The very non-grasping of that [object] which speech here speaks with effort—both the lower and the higher—is itself what is called "pārāyaṇa. (48)
Thus they speak of the omniscient Śaṃkara, who is blue-and-red (nīlalohita):
"He is all this; salutation to him, the tawny Puruṣa, Śiva. (49)
He alone is that great Rudra;
he is the universe, the past, and the future—the world born in many ways from you, existing here and now.
The Lord has golden arms; the Sovereign is also golden;
he is the husband of Ambikā, the Ruler, whose seed is gold, and who has the bull as his banner.
Umāpati, Virūpākṣa, Viśvabhuj, and Viśvavāhana—
he who appointed the eternal Brahmā as the son of Aṅgiras.
He bestowed upon him that knowledge which illuminates the Self—
the single Puruṣa, Rudra, invoked by many and praised by many.
In the center of the heart, which is the size of the tip of a hair, is the adorable Viśvadeva in the form of fire.
Those wise ones who perceive him as abiding within themselves attain eternal peace, and no others. (54)
Greater than the great and subtler than the subtle, that immutable Self,
the Great Lord, is seated in the cave of this living being.
The entire world and all beings, as well as the lotus of the universe itself, reside within the heart;
it is a cavern situated within the expanse of the sky, standing above the end of the universe.
There too, one should meditate upon the pure sky as the syllable Om, the Supreme Lord,
the size of a hair-tip, situated in the center, immortal, and the ultimate cause.
Truth is Brahman, Mahādeva, the Puruṣa who is dark and tawny, the one with sublimated vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), the Lord, the three-eyed, the unborn and eternal. || 58 ||
He who presides over the womb is indeed the Lord by virtue of being the source;
he is the ancient Īśāna, the fivefold Self within the body. (59)

They say that even within the vital breath (prāṇa) lies the mark of the inner mind—that wherein there is anger, as well as craving and forbearance. Having severed craving, which is the root of the multitude of causes, worship only the Lord Hara. They say he is higher than the highest, more stable than the most stable;
he is the progenitor of Brahmā, of Viṣṇu, and of the two fires, the eternal Sadāśiva.
Having meditated, one should enter the fire together with the sacrificial ladle while uttering the words individually;
having restrained the five elements according to the sequence of the rules for the qualities of the measures.
There are five measures, four, three, and then two;
finally, there is one measure and the measureless, which abide at the twelve ends.
Having become established in stability and having become immortal, one should practice that Pāśupata vow.
We shall practice this Pāśupata vow in brief.
Having established the fire according to the rules with [mantras] originating from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas...
Having fasted, being pure and bathed, he himself shall wear white garments.
Wearing a white sacrificial thread and adorned with white garlands and unguents, the wise man, free from passion, should offer oblations; he shall become free from passion.
The five vital airs for the sake of purification, speech, mind, and conduct;
likewise the ear, tongue, nose, mind, and intellect. (67)
The calves, the anus, and likewise the penis, are always obstructed. (68)
Skin, flesh, blood, fat, and likewise bones;
sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell. (69)
O Caitra, may the elements—the earth and the others—be purified within my body; likewise, by the will of Śiva, may my inner vital breath, mind, and consciousness be purified. (70)
Having offered oblations with sacrificial fuel (samidh) to Varuṇa in due order,
and having withdrawn the Rudra-fire, he should carefully take up the ashes.
With the mantra beginning with "Agni," the wise one should wipe his limbs and touch them;
this is the divine Pāśupata vow that effects liberation from bonds. 72.
This has been declared for virtuous Brāhmaṇas and likewise for Kṣatriyas, as well as for worthy Vaiśyas and especially for ascetics (yatins). || 73 ||
Liberation has indeed been seen through this method even for those living in the stage of forest-dwellers, for virtuous householders, and for those practicing celibacy. (74)
Having properly grasped the *agnihotra* with the mantra beginning with "Agni," that Pāśupata Brahmin should also wipe his limbs and touch them.
A learned twice-born man covered in ashes is truly liberated from the sins arising from great transgressions; he is not defiled by them, of this there is no doubt. (76)
One who is devoted to vigor is considered vigorous; one devoted to the sacred ash is esteemed as possessing the power of ash.
A Brahmin who is devoted to bathing with ash, who sleeps upon ash, and has conquered his senses [attains the highest state]. || 77 ||
"Being liberated from all sins, one shall attain union with Śiva.
Having spoken thus and having praised the Lord, the blessed Brahmā, the sovereign master, [departed]. || 78 ||
Then the Lotus-Seated One himself, covered in ashes, ceased his entire [manifestation];
thereafter, the Lord, the Master of Creatures (Paśupati), acted for the sake of gracing them.
Having gone there, the Lord established his presence together with Umā.
Then the foremost of the gods praised Rudra, who was thus present before them.
With the Rudrādhyāya, the bull-bannered Lord of gods, the God of gods and husband of Umā,
looked upon the gods with compassion.
"I am pleased," said the Lord of Gods, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, after granting the boon;
O sages, one obtains everything through faith in the presence of Śiva. (84)
O best of sages, at the end of the body, one attains the state of Gaṇapati.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Pāśupata Vow of Rudra, the Soul of All," in the glorious Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 45 ||
Sūta said:
O best of sages, listen as I shall proclaim the majesty of Śiva,
which has been celebrated in many ways by numerous eminent sages through various scriptures.
They say he is of the nature of both being and non-being, and he abides as both the existent and the non-existent;
some sages and wise men behold him as Śiva. || 2 ||
By the second [category], namely the modification of the state of being, "existent" (sat) is expressed;
that which is devoid of the unmanifest (avyakta) would be the unmanifest non-existent (asat). || 3 ||
Both of them are of the nature of Śiva; nothing exists apart from Śiva.
And because he is the lord of those two, Śiva is called the Lord of Being and Non-being.
Some sages who contemplate the principles say that Maheśvara is Śiva, who consists of both the perishable and the imperishable, and likewise transcends the perishable and the imperishable.
The unmanifest has been called the syllable-less (akṣara), while the manifest is declared to be the syllable (akṣara);
in your form as Śaṅkara alone, the supreme is said to be manifold.
Beyond those two is Śiva, the peaceful one, who is beyond the perishable and the imperishable;
he is called Mahādeva Maheśvara by the wise according to the ultimate truth.
Some teachers declare that Śiva, the supreme cause, is the collective whole (samaṣṭi), the individual parts (vyaṣṭi), and the cause of both.
The lords of sages say that the unmanifest is the totality (samaṣṭi) and the manifest is the individuality (vyaṣṭi);
these two forms of Śambhu have been described, and there is no other reality whatsoever.
Indeed, Śiva, the Supreme Lord, is called by those learned in the Yoga scriptures the cause of both of them— the collective and the individual cause.
Śiva is described by some as having the nature of both the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). [p.

The wise have declared that the twenty-four principles are designated by the term "field" (kṣetra), while the Supreme Lord, the enjoyer, is designated by the term "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña). The sages have said that there is nothing whatsoever other than Śiva.
Some praise Mahādeva, the lord of sages, in this way.
One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas according to the correct sacred revelation [understands]:
"By prāṇa one breathes out, and by apāna one breathes in. (14)
O twice-born ones, it breathes out by means of the vyāna, and likewise it breathes up by means of the udāna;
it breathes equally by means of the samāna, and it thinks by means of the mind.
When he, endowed with the instruments of equanimity, exists while investigating through the intellect that this [Self] is indeed the Supreme Maheśvara, then— || 16 ||
The eternal Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) is called "the Awakened" by the wise when, endowed with the internal organs, he moves about according to his own will. (17)
Indeed, the Self is called "asleep" when it is itself free from suffering, neither joined with the external organs nor likewise with the internal organs. (18)
Completely liberated from all substrates and devoid of both merit and demerit, he indeed always rests in his own true nature; this state is sung of as "deep sleep" (suṣupti). || 19 ||
This Śaṅkara wanders between the state of the individual soul (svānta) and the state of the awakened one (buddhānta),
coming and going like a fish in the bed of a river.
Just as a hawk or a garuḍa, exhausted, rests in a mountain cave with its wings folded, so too does this inner self (pratyagātman). || 21 ||
The speech pertaining to the waking and dreaming states is stilled within them again and again;
then, having attained supreme clarity (*saṃprasāda*), one becomes composed of supreme bliss (*parānandamaya*).
This entire worldly transaction of the Supreme Self occurs solely through ignorance;
for if the qualities and their attributes were truly present, how could He be devoid of them during deep sleep? (23)
O best of the twice-born, when ignorance exists as the causal condition, people understand that even the Self wanders as the intellect wanders. (24)
For the self is eternal and omnipresent; by virtue of its proximity to the intellect, the self is said to be exactly as the intellect may be. (25)
Some say that Śaṅkara is the embodiment of both knowledge and ignorance;
yet the unsurpassed form of Śiva is the lord of both error and knowledge.
He attained this through his mind; so say some who are knowers of the scriptures.
Regarding objects of manifold forms, consciousness is called delusion;
the cognition in the form of a self is celebrated as intellect (buddhi) and knowledge (vidyā).
Reality devoid of conceptual construction is designated as "supreme.

Śiva is described by some as being of the nature of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower; he is the sustainer of all worlds and the supreme Lord who ordains them. The wise declare that the twenty-three principles are denoted by the term "the manifest" (vyakti).

They speak of primordial nature (prakṛti) by the word "the manifest" (vyakta), and likewise they describe the person (puruṣa), who experiences the qualities (guṇas), by the word "the knower" (jña). || 31 ||
In that regard, that form which belongs to Śaṅkara is neither unmanifest nor distinct from Śaṅkara;
it is the cause even of the three qualities and is beyond all primordial nature (prakṛti). || 32 ||
That very same Blessed Lord Śiva is fourfold and threefold;
he alone is the self of all beings and the source of the existence of all beings. (33)
The all-pervading God abides, yet He is not seen everywhere;
He is the Yogi among yogis and the cause of all causes. (34)
He who is the Rudra even among the Rudras and the deity even among the deities—the Great Lord whom even the gods beginning with Brahmā do not know. (35)
Knowing which, neither rebirth nor even death exists again. || 36 ||
When calamities arise for embodied beings that bring about the loss of life, at that time there is no other means of deliverance than Śiva, the sole kinsman of the world. (37)
He always dwells within all excellent beings among all embodied creatures;
therefore, Maheśvara, though devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), is called the "bearer of bodies" (dehabhṛt). || 38 ||
Much time has passed here; let one birth be spent there.
Let this liberation first be investigated through a single birth.
"By devotion to the Lord Śambhu," thus spoke the god Ravi;
"by remembering Śambhu even once, the accumulations of afflictions perish. (40)
He attains liberation; the attainment of heaven is considered an obstacle for him.
Therefore, having obtained this human birth, which is so difficult to find and as flickering as a flash of lightning— || 41 ||
This verse does not appear in the manuscripts of the *Kāmasaṃjñinī*.
One should always worship Śiva with devotion for the sake of attaining the Self.
In this world, which is asleep in the slumber of delusion and crowded with hundreds of bonds that fetter living beings.
Those men who have gone for refuge to Śiva have accomplished their purpose;
they are indifferent toward sons, wives, houses, fields, wealth, grain, and land.
Having obtained this, O fool, do not become arrogant; for Ramā is transitory by nature.
Abandon anger, lust, greed, delusion, and likewise pride. (44)
O people, worship Īśāna, the bestower of desired fruits, as long as death has not arrived and as long as old age has not come. (45)
One should worship the Lord only so long as there is no impairment of the senses; those who do not worship the Lord of Gods are deluded by the intoxication of sense-objects.
For they grieve like forest elephants stuck in the mud after they have died;
time brings imminent ruin, and prosperity is the very seat of calamities. (47)
Meetings end in partings, and everything that has arisen is heavy with sorrow;
those who, knowing this, worship Maheśvara in his form as the Linga—|| 48 ||
They obtain vast and inexhaustible desires both in this world and in the next;
therefore, O lords of gods, propitiate the Omniscient One who faces all directions. (49)
By that very means, you shall swiftly attain union with Him; of this there is no doubt.
Even one who is burdened with great sins should worship Bhava with devotion. (50)
He too goes to the supreme abode, accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage;
[the merit of] thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices [is attained].
Those who go there after fashioning a linga and where children play do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of worshipping Maheśa.
Whether made of sand or even of clay, they indeed become kings;
yet they must endure suffering that is internal, celestial, and caused by other beings.
Having understood this regarding the gods and others, one who seeks liberation should worship Śiva—
from the shoreless and limitless, terrible ocean of saṃsāra,
which has the great net of delusion, the crocodiles of desire and anger, and the waves of pleasure. (54)
The wise one, a knower of Vedānta and a yogi, free from the sense of "mine" and devoid of egoism;
self-controlled, well-restrained in meditation, free from hope, and devoid of longing.
He is free from all attachments, beyond the pairs of opposites, and undisturbed.
Renouncing the fruits of all actions, appearing like one who is dull-witted, blind, or deaf,
he is friendly toward all living beings, remaining impartial toward friends and enemies alike.
In this way, liberation would not be so difficult to attain as it is for such a yogi;
everyone on earth and in the netherworld would be liberated from the qualities born of primordial nature.
Knowing thus that liberation, which has many means of accomplishment, is indeed very difficult to attain,
worship Mahādeva through the application of ritual action, or otherwise.
Ritual action, worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and the chanting of the names of Śambhu—these are declared to be the yogas of action; through these, Maheśvara is to be worshipped.
Whatever desire one may contemplate with a mind fixed upon Śiva after having worshipped him, one attains that very thing; so Sāvitrī said in the past.
Chanting its name, delighting in its ritual action, with his mind absorbed therein—
O Brahmins, the man who is free from desire attains that state.
He who always worships Aśaṅka shall be like Rudra upon the earth,
destroying the sins of all mortals through both sight and touch.

2449. Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Śiva," in the *Śrī Saura*, a secondary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) within the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. 46.
The sages said: "O Sūta, you who are skilled in speech, tell us what that highly fortunate Sāvitrī, devoted to her husband and of excellent complexion, has said."
Sūta said:
Having seen her in heaven, radiant and adorned with every virtue, Arundhatī—the most excellent among women and possessed of a pure smile—questioned her. (2)
There are hundreds of gods belonging to the Sun (Sāvitra) who dwell in heaven;
likewise, there are these wives of the gods, as well as the Siddhas and the wives of the Siddhas.
Neither they, nor others, possess such fragrance, nor beauty, nor physical form,
nor splendor as you do together with your husband.
O woman of excellent complexion, the ornaments produced by the thought-power of the celestial damsels do not shine as they do for you and for your husband.
The splendor of the celestial palaces of the inhabitants of heaven, such as Śakra and others, does not exist;
yet the splendor of your own palace possesses the radiance of ten thousand rising suns.
Those people who, relying on them, worship Maheśvara correctly. || 15 ||
To them, the Lord of All grants liberation, which is exceedingly difficult to attain.
Sūta said:
Then, having been addressed thus by Sāvitrī, those lords of sages, with delighted minds, prostrated before Brahmā and Śiva and spoke as follows. (17)
Arundhatī said:
She is worthy of worship, she is worthy of salutation; she is virtuous, she is devoted to her husband—she who always honors Sāvitrī and the Lord of Himavat. || 18 ||
By propitiating him, Diti obtained sons headed by Śakra;
from him were born the Daityas Diti and Vinatā, who gave birth to Garuḍa and Aruṇa.
In ancient times, Śacī herself worshipped the Lord of Umā;
who then would not worship that Īśa, the granter of desired objects? || 20 ||
Then, having thus welcomed her who shared half the body of Vasiṣṭha, he said:
"This alone is the entire knowledge, which is the worship of the Great Lord. [p. 189] 36.
Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, consumed, or presented as a bali-oblation and worship to Śiva shall, without a doubt, yield exclusively and ultimate fruit. (37)
For even after millions of births, human birth in the land of action is only occasionally attained by men, as it yields the fruits of heaven and liberation. (38)
Having obtained such a rare opportunity as this, those who do not worship Śiva here—
where indeed does discrimination reside in the hands of those fools?
For he, when propitiated, bestows upon men the fruits of both this world and the next.
The Blessed One, the Earth, bestows [these]; who would not honor him in return? || 40 ||
O best of Brahmins, whatever one desires, having propitiated Maheśvara,
one obtains that without doubt, just as Vaiśravaṇa did in the past.
Whether seen, worshipped, meditated upon, touched, or even praised, he who grants liberation to human beings—who, then, would not worship Śiva? (42)
O best of sages, even a dog-cooker (outcaste) who is a devotee of Śiva is superior to a twice-born;
however, a twice-born who is devoid of devotion to Śiva is the lowest of dog-cookers. (43)
Whatever action a man performs in a temple of Śiva—
whether out of greed, attachment, or negligence— he shall become the sole sovereign of the earth.
The sages said: How did Vaiśravaṇa formerly propitiate Maheśvara?
Therefore, O Sūta, you ought to tell how that state of being Kubera was attained.
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, to that which was spoken regarding the seventh interval—
the narrative indicating the majesty of Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
In Avantī, there was a certain twice-born man renowned as Somaśarman, who was always devoted to the affairs of sons, fields, wife, and so forth. (47)
Then, having abandoned his household life, deluded by greed for wealth,
he wandered over the entire earth with its villages and towns.
When he had departed from that house, his large-eyed wife,
constantly deluded by the god of love, became one who moved entirely according to her own will.
Once, by the power of fate, she had a son born from a Śūdra;
he was evil-minded, extremely secretive, and was known by the name Duḥsaha.
This alone is the supreme duty; this is the highest austerity.
This alone is the complete knowledge and the worship of the Great Lord.
Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, chanted, or presented as a bali-oblation and worship unto Śiva, that shall result in absolute and ultimate fruit; of this there is no doubt. (37)
For even through millions of births, human birth on the land of action is only occasionally attained by men, as it yields the fruits of heaven and liberation. (38)
Having obtained such a rare opportunity as this, those who do not worship Śiva here—where indeed does discernment reside in the hands of those fools? (39)
For what man would not worship that Blessed One, who, when propitiated, bestows the fruits of this world and the next? (40)
O best of Brahmins, whatever one desires, having propitiated Maheśvara,
he attains it without doubt, just as Vaiśravaṇa did in ancient times.

Whether seen, worshipped, meditated upon, touched, or even praised, he who grants liberation to human beings—whom do people seek other than Śiva? (42) O best of sages, even a dog-eater (*śvapaca*) who is a devotee of Śiva is superior to a twice-born (*dvija*);
however, a twice-born who is devoid of devotion to Śiva is lower than a dog-eater. (43)
Whatever action a man may perform at the abode of Śiva for Śiva—
whether out of greed, attachment, or negligence— he shall become the sole ruler of the earth.
The sages said: How did Vaiśravaṇa formerly propitiate Maheśvara?
Therefore, O Sūta, you ought to tell how that state of being Kubera was obtained.
Sūta said: Listen, all you sages, to that which was spoken regarding the seventh interval.
This is the narrative indicating the majesty of Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
In Avantī, there was a certain twice-born man renowned as Somaśarman, who was constantly engaged in the affairs of sons, fields, wife, and so forth. (47)
Then, having abandoned his household life, deluded by greed for wealth,
he wandered over the entire earth with its villages, cities, and towns.
When he had departed from that house, his large-eyed wife, who was constantly infatuated by the god of love, began to act according to her own will. (49)
Once, by the power of destiny, she had a son born from a Śūdra;
he was a wicked soul, extremely secretive, and known by the name Duḥsaha.
Then, after a long time, he became overwhelmed by calamities;
abandoned by all his kinsmen, he stood upon a path beset by adversaries. (51)
Then, afflicted by distress, he entered the abode of Kapiccha at night with his requisites. || 52 ||
When the lamp had almost gone out and was on the verge of being extinguished,
he indeed gave it his final wick for the purpose of searching for wealth.
There, a man stood tall like a great elephant, performing worship to the gods;
shouting loudly, "Who is this? Who is this?", he held an iron club as his weapon. (54)
And he, though terrified and fleeing out of fear for his life, being of deluded intellect and deeply distressed, did not know his own birth or even his past actions.
Slain by the city guards, he died at the end of his time and was thereafter born as a king in the region of Gāndhāra, famous by the name Sudurmukha.
Devoted to song and instrumental music, arrogant, and intensely fond of the company of courtesans, he was a fool who caused distress to the people and was excluded from all religious duties. || 57 ||

However, being ignorant of mantras, he constantly worships with flowers, animals, food offerings, perfumes, and so forth, a *liṅga* that has come down through the succession of his royal lineage. (58)
Recalling his former deeds performed in the temples of Śiva,
he indeed gave many lamps, brilliantly blazing with ghee and oil.
Once, while devoted to hunting,
that valiant king died, slain in battle by his former enemies on the auspicious bank of the Airāvatī.
O son, by the power of his worship of Śiva, with all his sins utterly destroyed, he became the powerful lord of all the Yakṣas, Viśravas.
Then that righteous-souled Kubera, well-versed in the Vedas and the scriptures,
duly worshipped Īśāna on the bank of the Tvaritā river.
With this hymn, he praised with devotion Him who grants all desires.
Kubera said:

"I bow to the unborn, ancient God, who is honored by Upendra, Brahmā, and the king of the immortals; whose eyes are equal to the moon, the sun, and fire; who bears the insignia of a lord of men; and who is the cause of both dissolution and creation. (63)

The sole Lord of all, the unique kinsman of the thirty gods, attainable through meditation, the abode of the world, the support of all speech, possessed of infinite power, an ocean of knowledge, and a mine of the quality of steadfastness. (64)
7. "Then, from that, the helmeted one [is born].
I bow to the Lord, who holds the Pināka bow, the noose, the goad, and the trident in his hands; who has matted hair and resembles a thousand clouds;
who wears the Kālakūṭa poison as a garment; and who is the protector of the forest. 65.
[He saw] Kapālin, Mālikā, and other gods; the most excellent one, Bhīma, who wears the Gaṅgā on his head; and the ruler together with Satī, as well as the one with the excellent head.
The virtuous proclaim that single light to be the twin-syllabled, devoid of qualities, and immeasurable;
it is far-reaching, worthy of worship by those who know the Vedas, the essence of all, situated within the heart, and supremely pure.
I bow to the storehouse of splendor, who wears the young moon upon his crest, whose fierce fangs flash,
who is the fuel for Time, the granter of desires, seated upon the throne of Dharma, and established in his primordial nature.
He who is beyond the senses, the healer of all, the conqueror of enemies, transcending the three qualities, unborn, and effortless;
who is composed of mind and composed of the Vedas, the *haṃsa*, the Lord of Prajāpati, Indra invoked by many.

I perpetually bow again and again to Him, whose form is the single sound of the Unstruck (anāhata), whom the lords of ascetics, the knowers of Yoga, meditate upon for the sake of severing the long-standing bonds of saṃsāra.
He who has neither form nor power, neither non-existence nor intrinsic nature—he is the Supreme.
He is known as Viṣṇu, Pitāmaha, and others; I bow to that inconceivable Vāmadeva.
Having propitiated Śiva in his fierce form, the venerable Agastya rescued the ocean;
likewise, Dilīpa obtained the entire earth. I take refuge in that source of the universe. (72)

While the hosts of gods in heaven, headed by Brahmā and Indra, worship Him and enjoy various desires, I praise Śarva here, I bow to Him, I conquer [myself] for Him; I revere the one worthy of reverence and take refuge in Him. 73.

Having praised the Lord in this manner, he ceased; at that very moment, the God, the granter of boons and dispeller of darkness, whose splendor was equal to a thousand suns, bestowed three boons upon Vaiśravaṇa.
Having then appointed the illustrious Guhyaka king as his sovereign over them, the three-eyed Lord,
whose word is never in vain, departed for Kailāsa, his lotus feet worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and the other gods.
In the fourth [birth], he attained friendship with the guardians of the quarters, the status of the lord of wealth, and sovereignty over the inhabitants of heaven;
thus, possessing matchless power and a fame that surpassed even Indra's, he became truly happy.
Likewise, the lord of the demons and the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, having worshipped him whose beautiful crown is the moon—
the maker of night— and being himself a maker of night yet unvanquished in his senses, attained liberation once the defects of his passion for battle had subsided.
Many paths to heaven have been prescribed; they are difficult to accomplish and beset by many obstacles.
But this straight path—remembrance of the Enemy of Tripura—is easy and yields great fruit in the mere twinkling of an eye. (78)

O mortals, this very marvel has been witnessed here; even the gods and asuras alike sing songs of praise for this divine majesty: "Blessed indeed are those who dwell in the region of the land of Bhārata!"
Through their state as gods, men repeatedly become [beings] who constitute the path to the abode of heaven and liberation.

Having renounced their actions—without intending their fruits—to Rudra, who is the form of the Supreme Self, those stainless ones reach the end of their karma and cross over; they proceed [to liberation]. (81)
Know that this bondage of the body exists for the sake of performing auspicious deeds;
indeed, they were born in the stainless lineage of the Bharatas within the region of Prācya-khaṇḍa, being steadfast in the dharma of Śiva.
Even those devotees here who, through a hymn of praise,
[worship] the sole Lord of love;
They go to that world of darkness, though they possess great power proclaimed by Purandara. || 83 ||
Sūta said:
Thus was Vaiśravaṇa born by the grace of Mahādeva;
all of this has been told in its entirety, O best of sages. (84)
Whoever should read or even hear this is liberated from all sins;
such a person shall dwell in the world of Brahmā for a kalpa—thus spoke the divine Sun.

Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Dialogue between Arundhatī and Sāvitrī," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 47 ||
Sūta said:
I shall speak again of the majesty of the trident-bearing God of gods;
it instantly destroys even many sins for those who read or hear it.
Yogis who have conquered the six enemies— the senses— and are free from egoism,
worship Śiva, whose nature is the Self, through the yoga of knowledge.
Those virtuous ones who have been purified by the waters of sacred fords, by charity, sacrifice, austerity, and vows,
worship Maheśāna through the yoga of action.
Greedily addicted and ignorant, they do not worship the Lord of the Universe; like fools who are neither subject to old age nor death, these worms of hell remain [in their state]. || 4 ||
By the power of destiny, some supreme men are born here on earth who are devoted to the dharma of Śiva, peaceful, and always intent upon the scriptures of Śiva.
Neither its form nor its configuration can ever be described by any living beings, nor can it be seen by those of unrefined self.
Let my words be taken to heart, or let your soul be directed toward what is auspicious;
when the house is already ablaze, it is impossible to dig a well.
Therefore, let the worship of that [Bhava] be performed, which utterly eradicates and severs [suffering].
Know that mind to be the knower of action which operates within Śaṅkara;
she is Vāṇī, the imperishable consort who delights in the infallible Śambhu, the Lord of Speech.
Those two ears are truly heard by which the auspicious stories of Him are listened to;
those two feet of men are fruitful which go toward the temple of Śiva. 11.
Those two eyes are truly auspicious by which Śiva is beheld;
those two hands are considered fruitful which perform His worship. (12)
That very action which is performed with Śiva as its object becomes fruitful;
this is the supreme fortune for men, and this is the devotion desired by them.
Devotion to the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, which brings about the highest good and leads to liberation, is such that enemies do not harm him, nor do demons devour him. (14)

The lords of the serpents do not bite a man who is devoted to Rudra. Having completely renounced the objects of the senses—which, though appearing sweet when ripened, are actually as delightful as poison—one should thus worship Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world. 15.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, compassion, and benevolence toward all beings—for him who always possesses these qualities, O Bhārata, Śaṅkara is pleased. (16)
Śaṃkara is pleased with one who, having seen the worshipped Liṅga, rejoices with devotion, or who performs the triple symphony of song, dance, and instrumental music.
Śaṃkara is pleased with him whose devotion to Maheśvara consists of the desire for action through speech, mind, and body—even if he is afflicted by calamity. (18)

Just as all the footprints of living beings are contained within the footprint of an elephant, so too, O Lords of Sages, all phenomena are contained within the auspicious Dharma; there is nothing surprising in this. (19)
O best of the twice-born, they say that there are other dharmas here which have small foundations, yield small fruits, and are characterized by haste;
however, the virtuous declare the Śivadharma alone to have a great foundation and to consist of many auspicious forms. (20)
This verse does not appear in the manuscripts designated as Ghaṅa.
195] May the Blessed Lord Bhava, the cause of the world, be gratified. 23.
Having given ten mountains and the sixteen great gifts,
and having given ten cows, one shall attain [the fruit] upon seeing the Liṅga.
That king who is not a devotee of Śiva but is devoted to other gods is like one who,
having abandoned his own young wife, takes pleasure in others.
For even those who perform some act in the abode of Śiva under a pretext do not go to hell, even if they are sinful men. (26)
Those who perform sweeping and other such tasks, as well as those who beautify the roads, will certainly become protectors of the earth, equal to the gods. || 27 ||
In this regard, O best of the twice-born, listen to an ancient account;
having heard it, living beings for the most part do not fall into delusion. (28)
In the interval between Svāyaṃbhūva Manu, there was a most righteous king, renowned as Naravarma, in the region of Pañcāla. || 29 ||
He was skilled in divine mantras, endowed with energy and purity, possessed of majesty, proficient in the sixfold policy, of great courage, and one who spoke with a smile preceding his words. (30)
Among his thousands of wives, she of most beautiful form was renowned as Sudevī, the chief queen of the ten [brothers]. (31)
Endowed with all virtues, of excellent complexion like Śacī, she was beloved by her husband, virtuous, and possessed a radiance equal to the light of the moon. (32)
Every day, he performs the beautification of the entrance and the beautification of the path at the auspicious temple of Śiva by sweeping the ground and other such acts. (33)
This verse does not appear in the manuscripts designated as Ghaḍa. [p. 196] Gālava questioned that slender-limbed woman as she stood in private: || 34 ||
"Speak, O highly fortunate one! For what reason are you constantly engaged in sweeping in the temple of Hara, turning away from all other duties? (35)
Thus addressed by that sage at that time,
the large-eyed lady, full of humility, smiled and spoke to Galava, the lord of sages.
I have no other supreme devotion as I do toward acts such as sweeping;
I shall tell you of a deed performed by me in the past.
Formerly, I was a female vulture, a bird that traveled through the sky;
once, while wandering about, I went to Mount Kiṣkindha.
It is like another Hemakūṭa mountain, crowded with perfected Vidyādharas;
it is a wondrous forest, free from affliction, where the Sky-Liṅga (Khaliṅga) resides.
Merely by the sight of whom wise men go to heaven—having worshipped that very Lord with flowers, incense, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings. (40)
For at that very moment, someone had placed an offering (naivedya) beside it;
having circumambulated the linga, he came there to take it. || 41 ||
"O illustrious one, I was afflicted by hunger and made an effort toward the food offering; while I was taking it, O Brahmin, I gradually wiped away the dust with my two wings. (42)
Then, by the turn of fate, that which was done before the god was accomplished in an instant;
at that moment, the worshipper of that god arrived there.
After some time, I died and was reborn in the house of Vasu;
I was given by him as the first wife to Nṛvarman.
By virtue of that power, she became the most excellent among ten thousand queens;
she was honored by the king, beloved by him, and endowed with sons and grandsons.
Having thus performed the sweeping of dust in the house of Īśvara unintentionally,
I was born as the daughter of Vasu, the king, and likewise possessed the memory of my former birth.
"Having performed the sweeping out of desire, I shall not be yours.
Thus addressed by the queen, he was delighted and then spoke to her.
Having propitiated the Lord of the Gods, the destroyer of Tripura and the bestower of all things, what wonder is there that you have attained this state, O abode of virtues? 48.
Whether out of ignorance or even out of fear, one must indeed perceive Maheśvara here in this world. (50)

Who would not take refuge in that Lord, by the mere remembrance of whom even various hells are severed, by remembering whom one attains the state of the gods, and through worshiping whom one reaches nirvāṇa? (51)
The fruit for embodied beings arises from faith over time;
however, Śaṅkara fulfills all the desires of those who petition him with immediate results.
Even those men who constantly remember Maheśvara with deceit,
they too, upon casting off the body, go to the stainless world of Śiva.
Those people by whom firm devotion has not been established toward this Śambhu, the teacher of the moving and the unmoving, and of immeasurable splendor, have clearly been cheated.
Even if a prostration to the Wielder of the Trident is performed by anyone out of negligence,
the knot of worldly existence does not arise for them again, even at the end of a kalpa.
So long do embodied beings wander in saṃsāra, devoted to grief and delusion, as long as they do not worship Virūpākṣa. 56.
Those men who, even just once, recite the Śiva Purāṇa and other such works from the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, or those who listen to them with devotion; || 57 ||
"The fruit that results from vows, fasts, gifts, and bathing at sacred fords—that shall belong to them; of this there is no doubt," so said the Supreme Lord.
Those whose greed for sense objects has perished, who are free from longing, whose minds are serene, and who are intent on the worship of Śiva,
go to the supreme, eternal, and untainted state of Śambhu, which the wise proclaim.

His lineage is purified, his ancestors are uplifted, and by him the earth and the twice-born are sanctified—he in whose heart Śaṅkara, the eternal, beginningless, and infinite-formed, always resides. (60)

Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Sudenī," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 48 ||
The sages said:
O Romaharṣaṇa, we wish to hear the greatness of Pārvatī—
how she slew the Daityas, headed by Raktāsura.
Sūta said:
Having prostrated before the Great Goddess, who forms half the body of Śaṅkara, [he spoke].
She who is praised by the Lord of Mahendrāṇī and who bestows grace upon her devotees.
[Page 198] Between the two manuscripts designated as Gha and Ṅa, the entire series of words beginning from "thirty-three" and ending with "the Mahābalas" is absent.
In the manuscript designated as *x jhasaṃśita*, the collection of words beginning with "Vidyunmālī" and ending with "eva cetu" is not present.
[p. 199] Having abandoned the two sacrifices and the fasts shown by the celestial sages...
O celestial women, enjoy manifest pleasures as you desire! || 16 ||
Thus, by the words of the lord of the Daityas, the performance of sacrifices was then destroyed;
the Vedas were no longer studied, and the deities were no longer worshipped.
Festivals did not take place; everything was then possessed by demons. Consequently, the world became devoid of dharma, as if overrun by barbarians.
From the destruction of Dharma, the power of the Lord of the Gods diminished;
perceiving Śakra to be weakened in strength, the Dānavas rushed toward him. (19)
Thus deeply overwhelmed by the asuras, the king of the gods abandoned his kingdom and,
having approached Bṛhaspati, spoke these words.
Permitted by Raktāsura, thousands of millions of Daityas were harassing everywhere for the sake of my destruction; of this there is no doubt. (21)
I am unable to remain here, nor can I depart, being pursued by them;
I desire to fight in every way—whatever is destined to happen, let that happen.
Whether one is perishing or even fighting,
life lasts only so long as Fate does not wipe away the letters written upon his forehead.
O Brahmin, pray for my victory; I shall fight with my enemies.
It is better to blaze brightly for a moment than to smolder for a long time.
