With joyful minds and devotion, they worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rites with various offerings, bowing down before her whose lotus-feet are praised by Gandharvas, Siddhas, and gods.
They attain the fruits of the greatness of Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svaḥ. || 61 ||
Those of pure intellect who sing of the Daughter of the Mountain, behold her, meditate upon her, or remember Śivā—
the Goddess Gaurī Umā, the sole deity of the universe— [attain liberation].
[I salute] the Goddess, whose diverse body consists of the entire universe and its origins, who has the sun, fire, and moon as her eyes, and whose face is Time.
Alas, those alone are truly blessed who worship in their hearts her who possesses a multitude of long arms extending in the eight directions and who smiles with a gentle disposition. 63.
By the foremost of the Ikṣvākus, Puru, Pṛthu, Rāghava, Dhundhumāra, Māndhātṛ, Haihaya, Yayāti, Ajamīḍha, and others,
who were longing for health, progeny, sovereignty, victory, and happiness.
The Blessed Bhavānī was fully honored by the men.

O noble descendant of Bhṛgu, worship the Goddess who is the mistress of yoga, Vedavatī, Bhavānī, Brāhmī, Kumārī, and Subhagā Vāṇī; worship Nārāyaṇī, Haimavatī, Anantā, and the primordial source of the universe.

Fame, learning, happiness, venerable longevity, prosperity, nourishment, and the destruction of misfortune—all these come to those living beings who possess devotion to Him; for them, meditative absorptions accompanied by yoga lead to liberation.
Even one who is lowly, dull-witted, born of humble lineage, timid, deceitful, fickle, or lacking in effort—
if such a person here exerts themselves for the sake of worshipping the lotus feet of Gaurī, [they shall attain success].
Indeed, he is beheld even by the gods with reverence.
Even that which has been performed or left unperformed meets with obstruction, despite the methods acquired through karma and despite exertion; yet,
by bowing down to the dust of the lotus feet of the Noble One, one becomes free from passion.
O child, as long as it is not held upon the head by people. || 68 ||
Knowledge, austerity, noble birth, various arts,
heroism, intelligence, humility, and cleverness—
these virtues are most auspicious for those who possess them.
Devoid of Gaurī’s grace, they become like blades of grass. || 69 ||
Until then, the elixir is not perfected, nor are the alchemical preparations, nor the mantras that yield great results, nor the radiant spells;
and practitioners on earth, as well as the wicks of their lamps, continue to suffer.
O sage, as long as Bhavānī, the giver of boons, is not satisfied.
Those who are devoted to the worship of cows and Brahmins, intent on their own duty, averse to liquor and meat, pure, and followers of Śiva;
Mṛḍānī is always pleased with those who love the truth and are devoted to the welfare of all living beings, O wise one.

One should always meditate with body, mind, and speech upon Her who is the source of all elements, the supreme beyond the objects and senses, whose nature is the inner organ and the Self, who is eternally imperishable, and the bestower of all goals. (72)
There is one unborn female, red, white, and black in color, who produces many offspring of beautiful form;
indeed, one unborn male lies by her, enjoying her, while another unborn male abandons her once she has been enjoyed. (73)
O Bhārgava, this power of yours, the Mother of the Three Worlds, has been proclaimed as a secret of the Vedas;
if you desire to hear it, then speak forth, for what is there that cannot be told among the wise? (74)
Those mortals who either hear or read this narrative endowed with hymns to Bhavānī,
having enjoyed inexhaustible sensual pleasures here, attain the supreme abode of Śambhu.
Sūta said: O twice-born ones, having heard this auspicious account of Bhavānī as it was thus narrated by the sages, the illustrious Purandara was filled with supreme devotion.
Then Pārvatī propitiated the Supreme Goddess and obtained various boons, including a kingdom free from all obstacles. || 77 ||
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Narration of Pārvatī’s Power," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 50 ||
The sages said: "O Sūta, disciple of Vyāsa, O high-minded one, you ought to tell us the determination of the lunar days (tithis) as well as the rules for expiation."
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, to the supreme determination of the lunar days (tithis);
for when the lunar days are not determined, no ritual act reaches fulfillment.
One should perform Vedic rites— whether they be Śrauta, Smārta, vows, gifts, or any other Vedic action—
only when the lunar days have been definitively determined, and not otherwise.
Generally, those desiring the fruit [of their actions] should fast on the final part of the lunar day;
for the great seers have declared that the root [of the rite], performed for the sake of pleasing the ancestors, is the ancestral (pitrīya) [portion]. || 4 ||
If that [lunar day] upon which the sun sets lasts for three muhūrtas, it is considered complete for all religious duties; such is the case with a tri-tithi.
In the case of decline, the eastern [altar] should be prepared; likewise, in the case of increase, the northern one should be made.
The eighth day of the dark fortnight and the fourteenth day (bhūtā) should be observed as the face-to-face lunar days (saṃmukhī).
The wise know that there are two white and two black beginnings of the yugas;
on the white ones, the rite should be performed in the forenoon, and on the black ones, in the afternoon.
The sixth lunar day pierced by the Nāga (the fifth), the seventh pierced by Śiva (the sixth),
and the eleventh pierced by the tenth must never be observed as a fast under any circumstances.
Having thus ascertained the lunar day more precisely by means of the sun and the moon,
the observer of vows should always fast on the eleventh, the third, and the sixth.
The eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) joined with the tenth (Daśamī) destroys the fruit of the prescribed rite;
likewise, breaking the fast on the thirteenth (Trayodaśī) violates the vow of the twelfth (Dvādaśī).
However, if not even a single moment of the entire twelfth day can be obtained for the breaking of the fast, [one may proceed otherwise].
At that time, the lunar day (tithi) of Ekādaśī was overlapped by the tenth day (Daśamī). || 13 ||
Whether it be in the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, there are two Ekādaśīs;
the ascetic should observe the latter, while the householder should always observe the former.

One who does not observe the New Moon (Darśa), the Full Moon (Paurṇamāsa), and the seventh lunar day (Saptamī) as the day of the ancestors (Pitṛvāsara) when they are overlapped by the previous tithi, falls into hell. || 15 ||
Sinīvālī should be chosen by the twice-born who maintain the sacred fires for the performance of the śrāddha rite;
likewise, Kuhū should be chosen by women, as well as by Śūdras and others who do not maintain the sacred fires. (16)

For men, on occasions such as the breaking of a fast (pāraṇa) or death, the lunar day (tithi) is considered to be that which exists at the specific moment [of the event]. However, for rites performed at night, that which extends through the evening (pradoṣa) should always be accepted.
The lunar mansion under which the sun sets should be observed for the fast, or that one which is joined with the moon at the onset of night, O radiant one. (18)
The sixteen nāḍīs prior to and the sixteen nāḍīs following the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti) constitute the auspicious time for bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and other rites. 19.
This verse does not exist in the manuscript designated as Ghasaṃjñita.
217] Merit acquired from bathing and giving gifts at midday is nearly equal to that of a transition [of the sun].
During the night transit of the sun, or on the day of the equinox or solstice.
One should perform recitation and other rites for as long as the solar or lunar eclipse lasts;
one should neither sleep nor eat during that time, but should eat after bathing once both have been released.
When the sun and the moon have been eclipsed and have reached their end,
having seen this, one should bathe on the following day and eat while maintaining silence.
Even during birth-impurity or death-impurity, a woman should not abandon her fast,
because it has been ordained by the Vedas and proclaimed by those who speak according to the Veda.
Therefore, whether in cases of negligence, suffering, birth-impurity, or even misfortune, a wise man should perform his vow after bathing; otherwise, he incurs the loss of his vow.
Rites such as the worship of the gods must always be performed by those who have received initiation;
for there is no impurity arising from death (śāva) among them, nor any birth-impurity (sūtaka), since they are [identical with] the Self.
O Śivā, for one who performs the worship of the gods, or for one who maintains the sacred fire,
as well as for celibate students and ascetics, there is no ritual impurity (sūtaka) affecting their bodies.

Any lunar day (tithi) that is designated by the word "great" (mahat) or accompanied by an epithet should be known as equal to the new moon day (amāvāsyā) for the performance of rites involving giving, study, and other rituals.
Indeed, during the dark fortnight, the paths are designated as "prior" and "middle";
there are three [sets] of four and eight [days], occurring in sequence starting from the seventh [tithi].

The fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Mādhava, the thirteenth day of the month of Nabhasya, the third day of the bright fortnight of Mādhava, and the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika. (29)
These are declared to be the beginnings of the Yugas, all of which bestow inexhaustible merit;
they likewise occur during the solar transits into Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius.
O great sages, at the end of the Yugas, beginning with the Kṛta Yuga,
on the thirteenth day of the fortnight of Śrāddha, when the moon is in the Maghā constellation and the sun is in the Hasta constellation.
Whenever that occurs, the "elephant-shadow" (gajacchāyā) is attained through meritorious deeds during the Śrāddha rite.
The six Aṣṭamīs marked by the pairs of the bow (5), the woman (3), and the navel (9) are known as the "mouths of the sixty-eight" (ṣaḍaśītimukhāḥ). || 32 ||
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Aśvayuja, the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, the third day of the month of Caitra, and likewise that of Bhādrapada. (33)
Likewise, there are twelve auspicious transits of the Sun;
on these lunar nodes (parvan), one should give gifts such as cows, mountains, and so forth.
They bestow gifts upon the foremost of the twice-born and attain an imperishable state. || 37 ||
A self-controlled man should offer even water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors;
by him a Śrāddha is considered performed for a thousand years—this is a secret which the ancestors declare. (38)

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Determination of Lunar Days and Other Matters," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 51 ||
Sūta said:
O best of sages, listen as I shall proclaim the expiation for all castes,
just as the Sun-god has declared their purification.
It is said that evil is of two kinds: manifest and indeed secret;
the manifest is countered by the manifest, and likewise the other by the secret.
They were knowers of the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras, masters of the principles of the Dharma-shastras,
liberated from desire and anger, tranquil in soul, and having conquered their senses.
They are equal toward both enemy and friend, free from violence and greed,
numbering twenty-one, or seven, five, or three.
The Śruti declares that whatever those who have been enumerated say shall be the Dharma:
"A slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, a drinker of intoxicants, a thief, and likewise one who violates the teacher’s bed. (5)
These are the perpetrators of great sins (mahāpātakin), as is he who would associate with them; indeed,
he who dwells for a year with these outcasts (patita) through constant use of their vehicles,
beds, and seats, knowing their status, becomes an outcast himself.
A slayer of a Brahmin shall dwell in the forest for twelve years with self-restraint.
Constantly subsisting on almsfood and bearing the skull of a corpse as his banner,
he should wander for alms once a day, proclaiming his transgression to men.
Upon the completion of twelve years, however, he removes the sin of killing a Brahmin;
or else, he may enter blazing fire or even throw himself from a precipice.
Or one should even practice fasting, or give up one's life for the sake of a Brahmin.
Or one may give up one's life for the sake of the guru; this expiates the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Or, having gone to Vārāṇasī, one may cast off one's vital breaths there in due course of time.
Completely liberated from all sins, he goes to the supreme state of Śiva.
But the drinker of liquor shall then drink heated liquor that is the color of fire.
He becomes pure once he is cleansed by fire; or else, O King, he should drink milk,
cow urine, or even ghee, and thus the twice-born man is released from that sin.
And for the sake of pacifying that sin, he should also perform the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa; likewise,
O twice-born ones, one who has stolen gold should approach the king.
Proclaiming his own deed, he should say, "You ought to kill me here.
Then the king, having seized a pestle, should himself strike him down with great force.
O twice-born ones, by such killing, he is released from that grievous sin through various means;
however, one who has violated the Guru’s bed shall embrace a red-hot iron woman.
O twice-born ones, through contact with whomever one becomes associated,
one should perform the vow for each of them in order to remove that respective sin.

"Having bathed in the final purificatory ablution (avabhṛtha) of the horse-sacrifice, all twice-born men who have committed sins shall be purified at that very moment"; thus indeed did the Sun himself declare.
Having had sexual intercourse with a mother’s sister, a maternal aunt, a father’s sister, or a sister’s daughter, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances.
Or he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for the removal of that sin;
likewise, having approached his brother’s wife or his sister’s daughter, he should do so for the removal of the sin.
Indeed, four or five *cāndrāyaṇa* penances have been prescribed for one who has approached the daughter of his maternal uncle, as well as the wife of a friend. (21)
Having fasted for a day and night, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance;
likewise, upon approaching a woman in her courses, one becomes pure after three nights.
Gha Ṅaḥ — [The letter Gha and the nasalized Ṅa.]
This verse does not exist in the meaning of the *śloka*;
that is, this verse is not present in the manuscript designated as Ḍa.
And upon approaching a prostitute, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance. || 24 ||

No other expiation for these [sins] has been seen by the supreme seers in the scriptures; through a year's practice, it is recorded that one undergoes the penance prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed.
If, in that case, no atonement for the procreation of offspring is prescribed when a Śūdra woman has been married by a Brāhmaṇa,
then there is no sin in approaching her, nor likewise in the procreation of offspring.
And for approaching a widow, one should perform the Sāṃtapana vow. || 27 ||
By [doing so] for a year, he indeed becomes equal to one who has violated the teacher’s bed.
Having approached a female actor, a female dyer, a female basket-weaver, or a female leather-worker, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having killed a consecrated Kṣatriya, one should observe the vow prescribed for Brahman-murder.
Upon killing one who has not been initiated, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for six years.
But having intentionally killed a Vaiśya, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for three years.
Having killed a Brahmin woman, a Brahmin shall observe a vow for eight years;
for killing a Kṣatriya woman, for six years; and for a Vaiśya woman, for three years.
One becomes purified by a *caitrasena* [fast]; the same applies even to the killing of a Śūdra woman.
Having killed a prostitute through negligence, some small gift is appropriate here.
A monkey, a mongoose, a crow, a boar, and likewise a mouse;
or else a cat, a frog, a dog, a cock, or a donkey. (33)
Having killed a horse, one should perform the *pādakṛcchra* penance;
for killing an elephant, the *kṛcchra* is prescribed; for killing a cow, the *taptakṛcchra* and the *pārāka* are prescribed.
The wise have observed that no purification whatsoever exists for the intentional killing of a cow, nor for the theft of food, whether chewed or swallowed, as well as vehicles, beds, and seats. (35)
For flowers, roots, and fruits, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is the purifier;
likewise for grass, wood, trees, dried food, and molasses. (36)
For stealing garments, skins, or meat, there shall be a fast of three nights;
as also for stealing a parrot, a crane, an owl, or a pigeon.
And the blue jay, the porpoise, the baloka, and likewise the barka. || 38 ||
Having eaten these, a twice-born man should fast for twelve days;
having eaten nālikā and taṇḍulīya, he should perform a kṛcchra penance. (39)
Having intentionally eaten the fruit of the *udumbara* tree, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance;
having eaten *alābu* or *kiṃśuka*, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance. (40)
If one drinks those milks which are unfit to be drunk, this vow must be observed:
by subsisting for one month on cow's urine and cow dung, one is purified.
By drinking *asurā* liquor, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow;
for the intentional consumption of semen, feces, or urine, one should properly perform the *prājāpatya* penance.
Upon eating the flesh of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
A Brāhmaṇa, having consumed the leavings of another Brāhmaṇa, should perform the Kṛcchra penance;
for consuming the leavings of a Kṣatriya, he should perform the Taptakṛcchra, and for a Vaiśya, the Atikṛcchra.
A twice-born man, having eaten the leavings of a Śūdra, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
having drunk water from a vessel that held liquor, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow. || 45 ||
If one should feed someone without knowing that they are a perpetrator of a mortal sin, a seller of the Vedas, a woman in her menses, or a Cāṇḍālī; 46.
Having fasted for three nights, he is purified by the five products of the cow;
likewise, a twice-born man who, having been anointed with oil, should void urine or feces [is purified in the same way].
Purification shall occur after one day and night for the acts of shaving the beard and engaging in sexual intercourse,
as well as for riding upon a donkey-cart or a palanquin.
He who enters [the fire] becomes purified within three nights;
however, among all sins, the greatest sin is the reviling of the deities. (49)
He who, out of delusion, performs [such an act] shall perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances; he who even once utters a reproach against Śiva, the Supreme Lord.
No purification performed by sages is seen in the Purāṇas;
yet, if the Guru should perform purification out of compassion for the Supreme Lord, [it is permissible]. (51)
He who hears disparagement of his guru must perform three *cāndrāyaṇa* penances;
and the fool who sits upon the same seat as his guru [must likewise do so].
There is no atonement for that; indeed, it is a most grievous sin.
Some also desire an expiation for what was done through ignorance;
one should perform the Sāṃtapana penance as well as four Cāndrāyaṇas. (54)
This procedure for purification has been declared for the sake of a Guru's desire to accept [a disciple];
however, by failing to give one who has been verbally betrothed, it becomes equal to the murder of a Brahmin.
There is no atonement for him, even by giving hundreds of villages;
for the theft of Śiva’s property, even in the slightest degree, is a sin equal to that against a guru.
Likewise, reviling Śambhu as well as one’s guru, and similarly reviling the devotees of Śiva and the disparagement of knowledge; || 57 ||
O twice-born ones, there was likewise censure of Girijā, Viṣṇu, Skanda, and the elephant-faced one, as well as of the yogins and even of the revilers themselves.
All these sins are indeed equal to the killing of a Brahmin;
therefore, one should not revile them by deed, thought, or word. (59)
"If one desires an eternal state," so said the divine Sun;
"for repentance is indeed the cause for every expiation. (60)
For it is certain that sin does not depart when devoid of that [repentance];
once the expiation has been performed, one subsequently engages in that very same sin. (61)
What has been done would become as if undone; that sin remains as it was before—whether the sins be gross or various subtle ones. (62)
Meditation upon Śiva for even a moment quickly destroys them;
I shall now declare an expiation for the purpose of removing all sins.
Composed in mind, immersed in water, meditating on Śiva with a serene intellect,
one is liberated from sins by reciting "Hara" eight times.
On that meritorious fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should worship the Lord of Gods, the God of Gods, the Consort of Umā.
He who, having recited the Atharvaśiras, removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin—
on that very ninth day, he should worship the Lord Umāpati.
Having gone for refuge to Śaṃkara, one is liberated from all sins. || 72 ||

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Rules for Expiation," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 52 ||
The sages said:
We have heard in its entirety the great knowledge pertaining to Maheśvara,
as well as the rules for the castes and stages of life, and the means of expiation without exception.
Now we wish to hear about the marriage of the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, listen to that which the Lord formerly spoke when questioned by the son of Mārtaṇḍa, after he had been praised with an excellent hymn.
Manu said:
"O Blessed One, exactly as it was asked, so has it been spoken by you.
All of that has been heard, O Father, and it has been firmly established in my heart. (3)
"You know the majesty of the Blessed Lord, the husband of Pārvatī;
there is no one other than you who knows it—so says the Śruti. (4)
Since you are another form of the Lord, being yourself the Supreme Lord,
you alone know the majesty of the Great Ruler.
I go for refuge to you alone— Rudra, the giver of boons, Śiva, the supreme cause, the scorching one, the thousand-eyed, the golden-hued.
The Sun who creates light, the radiant one, the imperishable light of lights;
the Lord of Ambikā, Maheśāna, the luminous maker of day.
[He who has] golden arms, matted hair, is named Oṃkāra, and is possessed of great wisdom.
Sūta said:
Having thus heard the words of Manu, Divākara spoke as follows.
Therefore, I shall explain it; listen, O you who are like bulls among sages.
That goddess Dakṣatā Satī, who was worshipped by the three worlds, having abandoned her body born of Dakṣa, became the daughter of the Mountain. (16)
She is renowned by the name Kālī, the Great Goddess whose form is the universe;
she is the embodiment of universal consciousness and the awakener of universal consciousness.
Presided over by that Kālī, Himavat, the best of mountains, became a holy place, O twice-born ones, bestowing liberation upon all embodied beings. || 18 ||
It is the abode of the Siddhas, the Munis, the Gandharvas, the celestial dwellers, and the Kinnaras; it bestows merit upon men through mere remembrance. (19)
Desiring Śiva as her husband, Kālī went to that best of mountain peaks to perform austerities with the permission of her parents. (20)
Then, in the meantime, there was born in the lineage of the Daityas a heroic Tāraka, a thorn to the worlds, who was like death itself to the dwellers of heaven.
Having propitiated Brahmā through austerity, he obtained a boon from him;
by that exceedingly powerful Tāraka, the gods were put to flight.
Those who forcibly abducted the wives of the gods—Śakra and the others of renowned prowess—were themselves thoroughly scorched by the fire of grief. (23)
Together with Śakra, they went for refuge to Brahmā, the lord of the thirty-three gods.
Then the Lotus-born One spoke to those who had arrived.
Brahmā said:
"O gods, you have indeed come into my presence while performing the Kura penance."
— "O gods, speak that all; I shall clearly tell you the means. (25)
The gods said: "Terrified by the fear of Tāraka, O Lord, we have come to you for refuge;
since we have fear of death, O God, it behooves you to protect us from him. (26)
"O best of gods, we do not obtain even a moment's peace;
for thirty thousand years,
there was then a most terrible battle between Hari and Araka, day and night, without respite."
Nevertheless, he was not conquered by that god of gods, the wielder of the discus.
Knowing that he was invulnerable, the mighty one abandoned the great ocean and departed;
with his mind then bewildered, he went quickly to Śārṅga. (29)
O Lord, we, being thus terrified, have indeed come to you for refuge.
We have come; therefore, O Lotus-born One, be our giver of happiness and protect us from that [danger].
Brahmā said: Listen all you immortals to my words, which shall bring you great happiness.
A certain person named Erisairaka performed supreme austerity. (31)
Seeing the world of mobile and immobile beings being consumed by the ascetic power of that Daitya,
I went into the presence of Tāraka in order to grant him a boon.
"Choose a boon, my child," I said to that great asura.
Then the king of the Daityas, having saluted me with palms joined in reverence, spoke to me. (33)
The boy said:
"O Lotus-born One, I am incapable of being slain by all the gods, including Viṣṇu and the others. O Lord, grant me such a boon that I may become so. (34)
"O best of gods, having granted him that boon saying 'So be it,' I asked another thing for your benefit: 'Tell me, why are you to be slain?
Tāraka said:
The gods, having drunk the seed of this Kapardin Nīlalohita, the Lord of the lords of gods, became embryos together with Viṣṇu. || 36 ||
"From those born thereafter, there will be death, or perhaps nothing else desired.
Having said, "So be it," I then [ascended] to the summit of Mount Meru.
[There is no verse for the one holding the designated book.
226] "O gods, I do not see that savior who will slay him. (39)
O twice-born ones, having heard the words of Brahmā, the thousand-eyed lord of Śacī reflected in his mind, "How will this come to pass? (40)
Together with the Guru and the deities, that king of the gods spoke once more:
"O gods, let a means be devised for the birth of a son for Hara himself."
Having spoken thus, the gods, headed by Śakra, together with Brahmā,
went to the northern peak of Meru where Mādhava resides.
The immeasurable-souled one remained hidden, oppressed by fear of Tāraka;
seeing the gods including Brahmā, Mādhava spoke joyfully: || 43 ||
Mādhava said:
"O gods, what means has been devised here for the sake of slaying Tāraka? If there is one, let it be told, so that our well-being may be restored."
Sūta said: Having thus heard the words of Viṣṇu, Brahmā and the other foremost gods related to Viṣṇu exactly what had been told to them by Brahmā.
Reflecting, "What should be done now? the king of the gods mentally recalled Kāma, who is unconquerable by both asuras and gods.
Knowing what Śakra was thinking, Kāma, the lord of Rati himself,
who bears the flower-bow, approached the husband of Śacī and spoke.
Koma said:
"O best of the gods, O Lord, what task must be performed by me?
For who would seek your station through such intense austerity? (48)
