[One should not strike] a Brahmin who is thus lamenting, or one who is insane, or one who is trusting, or one who has fallen, or one who is fleeing, or one who is addicted to passion, or one who is unarmed. (56)
The inhabitants of the world saw one who was naked, miserable, and likewise aged, covered with nails and hair, with disheveled hair, intoxicated, and asleep. (57)
Those fools who will surely destroy [this] shall remain unable to rise from the ocean of hell,
like an elephant stuck in a pit.
Therefore, go for refuge to where Guha, the son of Śambhu, resides;
I do not venture to slay a child in this world of moving and unmoving beings.
When Śakra had spoken thus, O Bhūka, all beings, mobile and immobile, became deeply distressed and spoke again these words that kindled their wrath: (60)
* This verse does not exist in the manuscript designated ṄacaChasaṃjñin.
269] The elements said:
O Śakra, just as the embryo of Diti was destroyed by you through violence,
where did your policy go then during that cruel act of causing an abortion?
Thinking "it is impossible," O giver of honor, you have become prudent;
for, O Lord, it is only a prudent man who acts toward an impossible task. (62)
And what man indeed would be a hero who would fight a child in battle, even against a hundred Śakras with the falling of millions of thunderbolts? (63)
"Even a single hair-tip cannot be cast down.
Thus was Purandara addressed by those hosts of spirits.
Just as a fire blazes when consecrated by streams of clarified butter, so he,
inflamed by the fire of his wrath, spoke these words to them.
Raising the vajra with his hand, the slayer of Vṛtra, whose weapon is the thunderbolt, [acted].
Indra said:
"Just as in the past the embryo of Diti was destroyed by me after entering her body, so now it is being slain along with all moving and unmoving beings."
Then, having gone there, I shall slay him as a moth is consumed by fire;
who could withstand me in battle when I have taken the thunderbolt in my hand? (68)
Having spoken thus, O brahmins, Śakra, impelled by the fire of his wrath, then commanded the Sādhyas, the gods, and the suns.
I shall go to Śaradhāna seeking the slaughter of the boy, mounted upon a great elephant with four tusks, possessing the luster of a swan, a jasmine flower, or the moon. (70)
"Bring before me my beloved lord of elephants—one as deep as the ocean, with long trunks and a voice like a thundercloud. (71)
Drenched with the blood of Daityas and Dānavas, it was terrifying;
then, by his command, he was quickly provided by the gods with all their weapons.
Having been presented to Śakra, Purandara ascended it along with the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Vasus, and the hosts of Maruts.
Accompanied by the Ādityas and the Aśvins, he set out for the slaying of Skanda,
ascending the vault of the sky while being praised by all beings, both moving and stationary.
While apsarases were dancing, kinnaras were playing musical instruments,
and gandharvas, skilled in song and singing beautifully, were singing his praises.
Shaken by the immortals, celebrated with divine songs by the celestial *kiṃnarīs*,
and incessantly gazed upon with longing eyes by the beautiful goddesses of heaven, he was drunk in by them. (78)
Being honored by hosts of sages and siddhas, Vajradhara, wearing a crown and filled with joy,
then proceeded with speed toward Kumāra, just as Hari or Indra [proceeds] against the sons of Danu.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Dialogue between the Supreme Lord and the Gods," in the *Śrī Saura*, a secondary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) within the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 62 ||
Sūta said:
Having thus gone to where the son of Pārvatī was seated, the thousand-eyed lord of Śacī beheld him, who possessed a brilliance like ten thousand suns.
Having seen it in the form of a heap of Malaya fire, he spoke to Nārada.
Indra said: "O divine sage, what is this that shines, a hundred times higher than Meru, pervading the world with its splendor and causing terror to all beings? (2)
Having thus heard the words of Śakra, the Blessed One, the son of Padmabhū,
then spoke to the Lord of Śacī, who was mounted upon the elephant Airāvata.
Nārada said:
"O Lord, O Śatakratu, this is surely the power of that very embryo which was deposited by you along with the immortals."
This is neither a mass of suns nor a collection of mountains;
it has been colored by the child as he was being brought forth, together with the gods.
Below, for sixteen thousand yojanas,
its height is recorded as eighty-four [thousand] and its width as thirty-two [thousand].
This entire mountain Meru has become golden;
likewise, after a thousand years had passed, its splendor attained the state of Skanda.
O God, by the fourth [day] he will have form, and then by the fifth he will possess limbs;
by the sixth, O Vaipra, he will be able to conquer the three worlds with his two feet.
Or again, he will protect you along with your companion on the seventh day—
the prince, the boon-granting god who increases the joy of Pārvatī.
Equipped with various weapons and adorned with various ornaments.
Thus he spoke concerning the son of Umā, who was being attended by his mothers and hosts of attendants, as he approached the sacrificial offering of the enemy of Jambha.
The enemy of Vṛtra released his thunderbolt, terrifying with its rising sparks;
but the son of Pārvatī, regarding that thunderbolt as mere straw, pierced him with a single arrow, and he fell down unconscious.
Then, taking up another arrow that resembled a blazing fire, he—
The six-faced Guha cut off the umbrella, the banner, and the flags of Hari;
with another sharp weapon, he indeed pierced the hand of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Just as Śambhu struck Ruru in battle with an arrow equal to the sun,
so too did he take up another shaft and strike Śatakratu.
Moreover, with another sharp arrow, equal to fire, he effortlessly severed the crown of Hari.
Guha quickly pierced Yama with five arrows, Nirṛti with ten, and Varuṇa with fifteen shafts.
Having struck Vāyudeva with twenty arrows and Ravi with fifteen,
he then struck King Soma with thirty more in the battle.
He quickly struck Śakra with five hundred life-taking arrows,
and the other gods with three or five arrows each.
Uttering a roar like a hero, Śambhu’s son indeed pursued Śakra,
along with the Vasus, the Ādityas, and the mighty Maruts.
Surrounded by Śaikhakas and Karālās like a king of śarabhas surrounded by lions,
the beloved of Lord Śaṅkara then beheld those who had arrived.
Like a lion toward small deer, he pursued the gods;
then the thousand-eyed Indra struck Skanda again with his thunderbolt.
But when he was struck, from him there arose beings of beautiful form:
the gods, the Vedas, the worlds, and Agni and Divākara.
Then the divine minister Vṛhaspati, possessed of great wisdom, spoke thus: 24.
"Enough of this battle with the son of Mahādeva, O Lord of Gods!
I shall instruct you in what is for your benefit; listen to it, O Thousand-eyed One.
If you wish to enjoy happiness, do as I say."
Having established an alliance with him, the kingdom will be free from thorns.
"Consume him, making yourself steady, and utterly destroy the Dānavas;
for not even the slightest pain is produced in him by the blow of your thunderbolt. (27)
O Śakra, how can he be carried away by hundreds like you? || 28 ||
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, having heard those words of the preceptor of the gods, Śakra then sought refuge in that very Kumāra, the son of Pārvatī.
Indra said:
"Be gracious to me who have come to you for refuge; I bear your feet upon my head with devotion.
O son of Śarva, become the lord of the gods; O you who are like Śambhu, accept my kingdom. (30)
O lotus-eyed one, here is my salutation with joined palms upon my head; abandon your fierce anger.
For the wrath of the virtuous always comes to an end when directed toward those who bow before them; this is well-established in the minds of the noble.
Then, O lords of sages, having heard the words of Indra, the six-faced Lord, overcome with compassion, spoke to Śakra.
Skanda said:
"What shall I do with a kingdom? Enough of common enjoyments! By the grace of my parents, there is nothing that is not already mine."
O Lord of Śacī, O Purandara, by virtue of my friendship, you alone should rule this kingdom here free from all thorns; [subdue] all enemies for me.
Having heard these words of Skanda, the Lord of Śacī spoke again:
"O Blessed One, no other among the gods is known to be as powerful. (35)
Therefore, O son of a lord, you yourself must rule the kingdom here! What is a mere child, and what is a battle? What is policy, and what is prowess? (66)

O Lord, where is such incomparable knowledge? Where is such intelligence and such gentleness? Where is such illusory power (māyā)? Where is such courtesy? Where is such tranquility and such graciousness? 37.
[273] For you are indeed [praised] by bards and minstrels with their own forms and their own qualities. || 38 ||
He was being praised by Vidyādharas and Yakṣas possessing various millions of virtues, as well as by the immortals, Siddhas, and hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
"O God, O delighter of your lineage, I shall become your general; remain supreme over all and enjoy the three worlds, O Six-faced One! (40)
"You are all-pervading and present in all beings, just like the god Maheśvara.
Having heard these words of Śakra, the son of Ambikā spoke again.
Skanda said:
"Fear not, O Śakra; do not be afraid. Rule your kingdom free from all thorns."
You are Indra, you are the king of the gods; you alone are the Lord of the universe.
"Those Dānavas who have not yet risen up,
by whom you were utterly defeated— remembered by you, I shall slay them. (43)
Enough with these words from Vahni, O Śakra; what is the use of speaking again and again?
In truth, O destroyer of asuras, I shall be your friend.
Then, looking at the son of Mahādeva who was free from desire, he said: "Alas, even you do not wish for the status of Indra; therefore, Guha, become the commander of the army."
"Let it be so," Kārttikeya said to the Lord of Śacī. Then, by the command of Parameṣṭhin, he was honored by all the gods.
Then Guha was consecrated according to the prescribed rite into the command of the army;
meanwhile, the command of the army had been given by Hara to Kumāra.
Then the Nāraka demon quickly approached the prince;
seeing him arrived, the son of Pārvatī then effortlessly and swiftly consumed that great Daitya, just as fire burns cotton.
Having consumed the terrible Tāraka like a moth in a flame,
Skanda, with a joyful heart, then sat upon his mother’s lap.
The blessed Mahādeva also, having dismissed Brahmā and the others along with Viṣṇu,
vanished in an instant together with his attendants.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Dialogue between Nārada and Indra," in the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka within the *Śrīsaura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrībrahmapurāṇa*. || 63 ||
The sages said:
O Sūta, you have narrated the marriage of the Supreme Lord.
The birth of Kārttikeya and his heroic exploits.
Do you know the greatness of the Blessed One, the enemy of Tripura? || 3 ||
Since the Blessed Lord Bādarāyaṇa was properly propitiated by you,
through his grace you have obtained that supreme knowledge of the Lord,
which is difficult to attain even for sages and great-souled ones among all the scriptures. (4–5)
Sūta said: O best of the twice-born, listen to that which was previously spoken by Brahmā with a delighted mind to the high-souled Nārada.
Brahmā, the treasury of splendors, was seated in bliss in the world of truth (Satyaloka),
attended by ṛṣis, munis, siddhas, and the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs.
Seeing him being sung of by the Gandharvas and praised by the hosts of Maruts, Nārada bowed down according to the prescribed rites and spoke to the one who delights in [the Lord]. || 8 ||
Nārada said:
O God of gods, Lord of the world, four-faced one, best of the gods! [Tell me] the majesty of the yoga of devotion toward the trident-bearing God of gods. (9)
Brahmā said:
Having bowed down to Śaṅkara—the peaceful, immeasurable, and healthy one;
the supreme light, without beginning or end, devoid of qualities, and beyond darkness—10.
I shall proclaim the yoga of devotion; listen, O Nārada of noble vows, to the greatness of the yoga of devotion as it was heard by me from Śambhu. (11)
Devotion to the Blessed Lord Śambhu is indeed difficult for embodied beings to attain;
yet, if it is somehow obtained, there is nothing at all that remains difficult for them to achieve.
O Nārada, it is through devotion alone that one attains sovereignty, the status of Indra, and even my own state; indeed, one surely attains the state of Viṣṇu and liberation as well. (13)
Devotion to Bhava reduces to ashes the accumulated heap of both auspicious and inauspicious karmas, just as fire does to fuel. 14.
Even if one were a barbarian, provided he is endowed with devotion to Bhava, there is no knower of the Vedas nor a performer of sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma who is equal to him. (15)
Even if a man constantly commits terrible sins, he is never stained by those evils if he is a devotee of Śiva. (16)
Those high-souled ones who are devotees of Śiva are liberated, there is no doubt;
even those of evil deeds, O Sage, through the grace of the Wielder of the Trident.
O Nārada, whoever worships the Blessed Lord, the consort of Umā, even once, obtains a fruit that is superior even to the horse sacrifice.

Knowing that life is as flickering as a drop of water on a lotus leaf, one should therefore set one's mind upon the welfare of the self, [fearing] the hells that follow death and are difficult to endure. (19)

O tiger among sages, one who directs their mind toward Śiva is liberated from this most terrifying cycle of worldly existence; yet, such a mind directed toward Śarva is exceedingly difficult to attain.
O Sage, for those embodied beings who are fearful and situated within the mouths of the serpents of existence, you are their deliverer; such is the sacred revelation regarding Mahādeva. (21)
If there is devotion to Śiva, why would anyone have fear? By the grace of the Supreme Lord, one certainly crosses the ocean of worldly existence.
For those seeking heaven, those desiring liberation, and even those longing for the state of Brahman, devotion alone to Virūpākṣa is the path; there is no other, according to the Śruti.
O Nārada, devotion alone should always be cultivated by the wise toward the Lord of the Universe, the wielder of the Pināka bow, who is devoid of beginning, middle, and end.
O sage, renouncing everything else, become a devotee of Hari;
through the grace of that Śambhu, you will quickly be liberated. (25)
By even a mere fragment of whose grace I attained the state of Brahmā, and Viṣṇu likewise attained the state of Viṣṇu—who would not serve that Śiva? (26)
"Gifts given to Śiva, oblations offered to Śiva, bathing for Śiva, and recitation for Śiva—their fruits are inexhaustible; so said the Blessed Lord Śiva. (27)
Whatever fruit is obtained by those dwelling at Kurukṣetra and likewise at Naimiṣa,
as well as at Prayāga, Prabhāsa, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean— [that fruit is attained here]. 28–29.
At Rudrakoṭi and Gayā, at Śāligrāma and Amareśvara, at Puṣkara and Bhārabhūteśa, and at Gokarṇa and Maṇḍaleśvara; || 29 ||
The fruit of that may be attained through devotion to the worship of Bharga in a single day;
there is no merit greater than the worship of the Liṅga in the three worlds. (30)
When the Liṅga is worshipped, the entire universe becomes worshipped; of this there is no doubt.
Those whose souls are deluded by Māyā do not know Maheśvara.
O Nārada, it is indeed through the grace of the Blessed One that they know this:
whoever, upon seeing Śiva worshipped, bows down with a spirit of devotion. (32)
The fruit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice is certainly attained by those who, moreover, possess peaceful minds, are devotees of Śiva, and have conquered their senses. (33)
O Nārada, even they do not behold the face of Mortal (Yama); nor do they see the holy pilgrimage sites and sacred abodes that exist upon the earth.
O Nārada, all those [deities] indeed dwell within the Śivaliṅga;
therefore, the Liṅga should always be worshipped constantly with a spirit of devotion. (35)
He who, having abandoned the worship of the Liṅga, worships other deities, has not bathed in any of the sacred fords; indeed, he is inferior to all.
Just as a foolish person, having abandoned a jewel, looks instead for glass,
so too [does he act] on the fourteenth day, the eighth, and likewise on the full moon day.
On the new moon day, or on the thirteenth day, one should worship the Moon-crested Lord;
he has bathed in all sacred fords and is initiated into all sacrifices.
O Sage, at the end of the body, one who is constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva attains the world of Śiva, which is difficult to reach, and is freed from the consequences of great sins.
One would not be stained by the faults committed [by others], just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water;
this occurs simply from seeing devotees of Śiva or even from conversing with them but once. (40)
O Nārada, whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even one born of the lowest caste, he obtains the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice. (41)
A devotee of Śiva is always worthy of worship, even if he has fallen into any state whatsoever;
one should not examine his conduct, nor his lineage, nor likewise his religious observances.
O Nārada, one who has his forehead marked with the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) is indeed worthy of worship;
yet he who, through action, mind, or speech, reviles devotees [is not]. (43)
O Sage, there is no escape from hell for that deluded soul;
with the exception of the devotees of Śiva, Yama is the punisher of all. (44)
For one who has taken refuge in Śiva, there is no sacred thread, no staff, and no earrings.
Wearing saffron robes is not the cause at all; rather, devotion alone is the cause here, even if those devoted to Paśupati are engaged in sinful deeds. (46)
O Nārada, even they do not behold the mouth of Yama—those who possess peaceful minds, are devotees of Śiva, and have conquered their senses. (47)
O Nārada, having attained the human condition, those who are devotees of Śiva— whether dead or living— are to be known as lords of the Gaṇas.
For one who has this [devotion], there is no fear even from Yama, let alone from a king;
O Nārada, listen as I relate a wonder that occurred in the past.
O Sage, there was indeed a king in Ujjayinī named Satyadhvaja;
he was righteous, firm in his resolve, and devoted to the protection of his subjects.
Having enjoyed the entire earth, he then went to heaven in the course of time;
he was the son of that great-souled one known as Vasuśruta, who was devoted to his sons.
Devoted to the worship of Mahākāla, fixed upon it, and dedicated to it,
he did not rule his subjects according to dharma, having been cast out from the duties of a king. (2)
Having utterly abandoned the wicked, that king indeed slays the virtuous;
there is no welfare for the subjects, for he is an adversary everywhere.
And when that thousand-year reign of Vasuśruta had passed, the Mlecchas, having seen the sacrifices of the sacrificers, destroyed them.
Then the time of death arrived, most terrifying for embodied beings; perceiving him to be a great sinner, the servants of Yama approached him. (55)
Thinking, "He is a devotee of Śiva," the three-eyed ones bearing tridents arrived;
a celestial chariot that fulfills all desires was brought by the messengers of Śiva.
Then all the messengers of Yama, the servants of Death, who were exceedingly cruel and held nooses, staffs, and swords in their hands, prepared to seize that king. (57)
Then the lords of the Gaṇas, seeing those servants of Yama, became enraged;
they [attacked] with tridents, mallets, clubs, and likewise with musalas.
Having severely beaten the messengers who carry out Yama’s commands,
he was led to the divine city of Śiva, from which return is difficult to obtain.
The servants said:
"Listen, O Dharma, to what happened between the Lord and the lords of his hosts: having struck all the enemies with arrows, the wicked Vasuśruta was led away."
He did not worship the gods with sacrifices, nor the brahmins, nor even his guests;
he did not protect his subjects through righteousness—how then did he go to the city of Śiva? (61)
"You understand the true nature of dharma; you are the one who wields the rod of justice.
Therefore, speak, O Bharata, for we are your obedient followers. (62)
O Nārada, having heard their words in this manner, the King of Dharma, the son of the Sun, spoke these profound words to his servant Kiṃkara.
Yama said:
"I am indeed the ruler of all beings—of gods, asuras, humans, and even all living creatures—with the sole exception of the devotee of Śiva; of this there is no doubt."
Who indeed can truly comprehend the greatness of the devotees of Śiva?
The Lord Mahādeva alone is their ruler, and no other.

Great-souled devotees of Śiva who are always intent on the worship of Śarva—you must diligently avoid them, even if they are devoid of the conduct prescribed for their stage of life (āśrama). || 66 ||
Even the conduct prescribed for the castes and stages of life has been abandoned by him;
if one is a devotee of Śaṅkara, he is not to be disciplined, for he is indeed worthy of worship. (67)
You must avoid devotees of Śiva with great effort;
even if they are engaged in sinful deeds, no sin exists for them.
I am afraid of the devotees of Śiva, just as deer are of a lion;
previously, I was slain by the Lord during the carrying away of Śvetarā.
From that time forward, I have been indifferent; we are not servants to his devotees.
If that King Vasuśruta does not protect his subjects, [we shall not help him]. (70)
Nevertheless, since he is a devotee of Śaṅkara through his mind, speech, body, and actions, how can sin ever touch him, for that Lord is ever-gracious? (71)
He who beholds the god Mahākāla, the three-eyed one,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the supreme state of Śiva.
"O servants, you must all pay homage to that Lord Mahākāla, the God who is worshipped by Śiva. (73)
Having given even a single *raktikā* to Śivā, or even more, it would be beneficial. || 16 ||
Therefore, one should worship Śiva even with leaves, fruits, flowers, or water;
that is declared to yield infinite fruit, for devotion alone is the cause in this matter. (17)
One should perform an anointing of the Liṅga with divine and delightful fragrances;
such a person is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred divine crores of years. || 18 ||
The merit from anointing oneself with fragrant sandalwood paste is double that [of other perfumes];
the merit from agallochum (cīgara) should be known as eight times greater than that of sandalwood. || 19 ||
A gift specifically to a dark-complexioned guru is held to yield double the fruit;
therefore, the merit of a gift of saffron is ordained to be a hundred times greater than that.
By smearing the liṅga with sandalwood paste, agallochum, saffron, nābhi, rocana, and saffron, one shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
Having fanned a linga well-smeared with fragrances with a palm-leaf fan,
one is honored in the world of Śiva for ten thousand years.
One should give a peacock-feather fan that is exceedingly beautiful;
such a person is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred divine crores of years. (23)
In place of the verse beginning with *mātṛhā*, a slightly different version of the verse’s meaning is found in the manuscripts designated as K, Kha, Ga, and Jha.
It is as follows: "One should worship the Moon-crested Lord with unbroken *bilva* leaves.
Having given even as much as a single *raktikā* to Śivā, or even more, [it shall be effective]. || 16 ||
Therefore, one should worship Śiva with leaves, fruits, flowers, or even water; that which follows is said to be the fruit, for devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
One should perform an anointing of the Liṅga with divine and delightful fragrances;
such a person is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred divine crores of years. || 18 ||
The merit from anointing oneself with fragrant unguents is doubled by the use of sandalwood;
the merit from agaru is known to be eight times greater than that of sandalwood.
The fruit is especially desired to be double when [the gift] is made with black agallochum;
from that, the merit of saffron is ordained to be a hundredfold.
Having smeared this liṅga with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, nābhi, rocana, and saffron, one shall attain the state of Gaṇapati.
Having fanned the well-anointed liṅga with a palm-leaf fan,
one is honored in the world of Śiva for ten thousand years.
One should give a peacock-feather fan that is exceedingly beautiful;
such a person is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred divine crores of years. || 23 ||

In place of the verse beginning with *mātṛhā*, in the manuscripts designated as Ka, Kha, Ga, and Jha, a slightly different meaning of the verse is observed. For example: "One should worship the Moon-crested Lord with unbroken bilva leaves.
Having given even a single *raktikā* to Śivā, or perhaps more, [the merit is attained]. || 16 ||
Therefore, one should worship Śiva even with leaves, fruits, flowers, or water;
that is declared to yield infinite fruit, for devotion alone is the cause in this matter. (17)
One should perform an anointing of the Liṅga with divine and delightful fragrances;
such a person is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred million divine years.
The merit from anointing oneself with fragrant sandalwood paste is double that [of other perfumes];
the merit from agallochum (cīgara) is known to be eight times greater than that of sandalwood. || 19 ||
The fruit is especially desired to be double when [the gift] is made with black agallochum;
from that, the merit of saffron is ordained to be a hundredfold.
Having smeared the liṅga with these— sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, nābhi, rocanā, and saffron— one shall attain the state of Gaṇapati.
Having fanned the Liṅga with a palm-leaf fan after it has been well-anointed with perfumes,
one is honored in the world of Śiva for ten thousand years.
One should give a peacock-feather fan; it is exceedingly auspicious and beautiful.
For a hundred divine crores of years, one is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 23 ||
In place of the verse beginning with "mātṛhā" (*mātṛhetyādi*), in the manuscripts designated as Ka, Kha, Ga, and Jha, a slightly different version of the meaning of the verse is observed.
It is as follows: "One should worship the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) with unbroken bilva leaves.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who gives a chowrie adorned with jewels and gems, or one with a handle made of gold, silver, and so forth, to Śiva. (24)
Surrounded by divine women with chowries held in their hands, he ascends an excellent celestial chariot and, accompanied by the Gaṇas, goes to the auspicious state of Śiva.
With flowers or leaves produced in the forest or on the mountains— those that are not stale, free from holes, not dyed red, and devoid of insects— (26).
Or one may worship Śiva even with flowers grown from one's own garden;
through the excellence of the species of flower, the merit shall be correspondingly greater.
By giving ten measures of gold to one who is rich in the virtues of austerity and conduct and who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, one indeed obtains that same fruit. (28)
If worship is performed for the god Śambhu with Arka flowers, the Karavīra flower is praised as superior to thousands of Arka flowers. (29)
A single bilva leaf is superior to a thousand karavīra flowers;
a single śamī leaf is superior to a thousand bilva leaves. || 30 ||
A single flower of the Śamī tree is superior to thousands of Arka flowers;
a single flower of Kuśa grass is superior to thousands of Śamī flowers. || 31 ||
A lotus flower is superior to thousands of kuśa flowers;
a bakula flower is superior to thousands of lotus flowers. || 32 ||
Just as a single *dhattūraka* flower is superior to thousands of *bakapuṣpa* flowers,
so too a *bṛhatpuṣpa* is superior to thousands of *dhattūraka* flowers.
The *droṇa* flower is superior to thousands of *bṛhatpuṣpa* flowers;
the *apāmārga* is indeed superior to thousands of *droṇa* flowers. || 34 ||
A beautiful blue lotus is superior to thousands of apāmārga plants;
he who offers a garland made of a thousand blue lotuses [attains great merit]. (35)
Listen to the fruit of the merit of one who worships Śiva according to the rules with devotion:
for thousands of crores of kalpas and hundreds of crores of kalpas. (36)
The illustrious one, possessing prowess equal to Śiva, shall dwell in the city of Śiva.
The *jātī*, the *vijayā*, and the *pāṭalā* are to be known as being equal to the *karavīra*. (37)
The white mandāraka flower and the white lotus are equal to that;
the nāga, campaka, and puṃnāga flowers are recorded as being equal to the dhattūraka.
One should carefully avoid the randhuka, the ketaki flower, the kunda, the yūthī, the madantikā, the śirīṣa, and the arjuna flower.
Golden kadamba flowers should be offered to Śaṅkara at night;
all other flowers [should be offered] by day, and mallikā jasmine flowers may be offered both by day and by night.
The *jāti* flower remains fragrant for a watch (three hours), while the *karavīra* remains so day and night;
however, flowers that are infested with hair or insects, or those that are withered and stale, [are not to be offered]. 41.
O Nārada, one should discard flowers that have fallen on their own as well as those that are damaged; nor should one worship with buds the image of anyone whatsoever.
One should not worship the God with *kalika* flowers, except for *campaka* and water-born flowers;
there is no fault of using stale flowers in the case of water-born lotuses, *utpala*, and *campaka*.
If flowers are not available, one should offer even leaves;
if fruits are not available, one may offer even grasses, shrubs, or medicinal herbs.
In the absence of medicinal herbs, however, he becomes worshipped through devotion;
one who worships Śiva even once with unbroken bilva leaves [attains the same]. 45.
Freed from all sins, that man who worships the Liṅga even once with Dhattūraka flowers is glorified in the world of Rudra. || 46 ||
Having obtained the fruit of ten million cowries, he is glorified in the world of Śiva—
he who, with devotion, worships the liṅga even once with bṛhatī flowers.
Having obtained the fruit of giving ten thousand cows, one shall go to Śiva;
[one should worship with] jasmine, blue lotuses, and flowers such as the nāga, puṃnāga, and campaka. (48)
Aśoka, śveta-mandāra, karṇikāra, vakula, karavīra, arka, mandāra, śatapuṣpā, and keśara. (49)
Whosoever worships Śiva with these flowers—kuśa grass, apāmārga, kumuda, kadamba, and kuraṇṭaka—as they may be available; || 50 ||
Listen with a one-pointed mind to the fruit that he attains:
[he travels] in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and resemble ten million suns. (51)
With flower garlands being scattered about, with the sounds of singing and musical instruments, with the sweet voices of women, and likewise with those moving about at will; || 52 ||
Whoever should create [an image] radiant with various flowers on the auspicious festival days (parva-kāla). || 54 ||
Surrounded by a thousand attendants, he traveled in the Puṣpaka celestial chariot,
endowed with the pleasures of divine women, good fortune, play, and delight.
He attains inexhaustible worlds, his teaching unassailable;
in all the worlds beginning with Śiva, he goes wherever he desires.
Through the application of devotion in worship and other such acts, the single fruit of all these rites is to be known as equal; however, the specific result varies according to one's wealth.
If one plucks flowers oneself and worships Śiva with them,
Maheśvara, the God of gods, accepts those offerings directly.
One should indeed offer incense made of black agallochum mixed with camphor to Śiva continuously for half a month; hear now the fruit of his merit. (59)
Having enjoyed pleasures in the city of Śiva for thousands of millions and hundreds of millions of kalpas, he shall at the end of that time become a lord of the earth.
Śaṅkara directly accepts guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter;
by offering incense for half a month, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
He who burns guggulu resin with clarified butter on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight goes to the supreme abode where the god who wields the Pināka bow resides.
By offering a bilva fruit mixed with clarified butter, one attains the supreme goal;
incense perfumed with these [substances] is six thousand times superior [in merit].
He who, having placed honey within a vessel of two mirrors joined together, offers it to Śarva with the mantra of the arghya,
shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
One should prepare well-prepared food with a prastha measure of śāli rice;
having offered that caru-oblation to Śiva, especially on the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī).
For as many grains of rice as there are in that food offering,
for that many thousands of years one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
● The portion of space [p.
By offering balls of sugar, pieces of sugar-candy, clarified butter, and various edible foods,
and by giving those cooked with clarified butter, the merit becomes a hundredfold.
By the offering of a ghee lamp to Śiva,
one obtains a divine celestial chariot extending for a hundred yojanas, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Whoever should prepare a beautiful garland of lamps with ghee during the month of Kārttika,
especially on the fourteenth day or the new moon day (or whichever is appropriate), || 59 ||
Resembling ten thousand suns, illuminating the quarters with his splendor,
that mass of radiance, stationed in his celestial chariot, shines eternally like the sun.
One should carry the lamp on the head, especially throughout the entire night;
or else, O Nārada, one may hold it with both hands upon the forehead or on the head.
In celestial palaces resembling ten thousand suns and fulfilling all desires,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for a hundred times ten thousand divine kalpas.
Having offered a perfectly stainless mirror before Śiva,
he became as pure as the rays of the moon, illustrious, fortunate, and capable of assuming any form at will.
Having performed a circumambulation with devotion around the temple of Śiva, a man is honored in the world of Śiva for ten thousand times ten thousand kalpas.
O Nārada, one obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices by means of constructing wells, groves, and water-stations for travelers, as well as through works dedicated to the temple of Śiva.
Beings, whether stationary or moving, are utilized in acts such as digging and uprooting, whether intentionally or unintentionally. (76)
They attain Śiva, there is no doubt, by the grace of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
The sacred field of Śiva (Śivakṣetra) of the Supreme Lord extends for one krośa in every direction;
for embodied beings who die there, it is the cause of attaining union with Śiva (śivasāyujya).
This measurement of the sacred field is prescribed for a liṅga installed by human beings. || 78 ||
In Svāyambhuvakṣetra it shall be one yojana, and in Ārtha it is half of that;
even one of sinful conduct who meets his death there, O Nārada, [attains liberation].
* Here, it appears that "by night" (*śarvarātryā*) is required for the meter.
286] He too goes to the abode of Śiva, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform bathing and other rites there. || 80 ||
Therefore, one should construct a dwelling near a sacred field of Śiva;
[and] that water which stands before one, situated near a Śiva-liṅga— || 81 ||
This place is known by the name Śivagaṅgā; one may cross over [suffering] by bathing and other rites there.
Furthermore, whoever constructs a large reservoir or even a well at the hermitage of Śiva [shall attain merit].
Together with twenty-one generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva. || 82 ||

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Power of the Five-Syllabled Mantra," in the *Śrī Saura*, a subsidiary Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. 65.
Brahmā said:
Whether it be a flower or even a leaf, if it is offered at Śrī Liṅga, that is declared to yield infinite fruit; it becomes the cause for liberation. || 1 ||
O Lord Śiva, when you are pleased, what object indeed is difficult for men to obtain?
Therefore, one should perform [all actions] with every effort for the sake of pleasing Śiva. || 2 ||
As much as Śiva is capable of bestowing, so much is he able to grant;
therefore, a person should perform all that for the sake of pleasing Śiva, even if it does not lead to personal happiness. || 3 ||
For men who perform deeds for the sake of pleasing Śiva, supernatural powers and accomplishments are not far off; O Lord of Men, when he is pleased, what indeed could be difficult to attain? (4)
Those best of men who always worship Viśveśvara with love shall enjoy happiness here for a long time and, indeed, attain liberation at the end.
Those men on earth who worship the illustrious Śambhunātha with devotion become worthy of veneration by the world of men;
they possess houses filled with gold and, at the end of their bodies' existence, they attain the realm of Śiva.
Whether one be a Brahmin, a drinker of spirits, a thief, or one who has violated the teacher’s bed—
whoever remembers Śiva at the time of death shall attain union with Śiva.
One who devoutly wears on one's head the floral remains (nirmālya) of the Lord of Pārvatī obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
This verse does not exist anywhere.

The half-verse beginning with *ḍacha-saṃjñinaḥ* and ending with *tasmād iti* does not exist. Furthermore, the five verses beginning with *tuṣṭe śiva* and ending with *śivaloka-bhājaḥ* do not exist in the manuscripts designated as *ga*, *ja*, and *jha*.
His sins are destroyed; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. || 10 ||
Out of delusion, one should not wear the remains of an offering (nirmālya) from Śambhu, nor should one eat it;
one should not even touch it with the foot, nor step over it, O Nārada. (11)
By stepping over the floral offerings (nirmālya) of Śambhu, one is born as a Cāṇḍāla.
Pṛthūdaka is a great sacred ford (tīrtha), as are the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā. || 12 ||
O Sage, the Narmadā, the Sarayū, the Kṣiprā, and likewise the river Godāvarī are always present here at the bathing-place of Śambhu.
The bathing water of Śambhu should be used, for it contains all sacred pilgrimage sites;
by wearing it, one is liberated from the multitude of sins at that very moment.
In a self-manifested (svāyaṃbhū) liṅga, one made of stone (bāṇa), one born of jewels, one fashioned from metal,
or a liṅga consecrated by a perfected being (siddha), Caṇḍa is not authorized.
Devotees should diligently wear the water from his feet and his flower garlands;
even sins born of mind, speech, and body do not touch them.
Nārada said:
"O Father, what is called a *liṅga*, and by whom is it presided over?
O Blessed One, tell me all this, for this is indeed a most excellent wonder. (17)
Brahmā said:
"The unmanifest is joined with this linga, which is bliss beyond darkness;
because of that effort of Mahādeva, Śaṅkara is the possessor of the linga."
In ancient times, when the world was a single, terrible ocean and all moving and stationary beings had perished,
that which is of the nature of Śiva manifested for the purpose of awakening me, Viṣṇu.
From that time forward, Viṣṇu and I, with supreme devotion and joy,
have worshipped the peaceful one who bears the form of the Liṅga and whose emblem is the bull.
Nārada said:
O Lotus-born One, you ought to tell me for the sake of your enlightenment how the Liṅga—which is blissful, undecaying, and eternal—came into being in the past. (21)
"Who are you, and for what reason do you lie here? Arise quickly, O evil-minded one! 23.
"Engage in battle with me; I alone am the Lord of the Universe.
Or else, seek refuge in me, the God who bestows fearlessness upon the three worlds. (24)
Having heard these words of mine, the immeasurable-souled Madhusūdana smiled and said to me: "Why do you vainly indulge in pride? (25)
I am the creator of all the worlds; I am their protector, of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, at the end, I am the destroyer; there is no one else equal to me.
When this dispute had thus arisen between me and the divine wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
there then appeared that Liṅga which takes away the pride of both of us.
Resembling ten million fires of cosmic destruction, filled with garlands of flames, it is devoid of beginning, middle, or end, and is free from decay or increase. || 28 ||
Within that liṅga resides Mahādeva, the eternal self-luminous one;
he is the Puruṣa with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
The Lord who is half-woman, the infinite mass of splendor, is difficult to approach;
let the question of seniority between you two rest for now, for I shall say something. (30)
"If Mādhava sees the root of this linga of mine, he will surely become the eldest," so it was spoken by the God. (31)
"If the lotus-born one beholds the crown of this Linga,
then he shall become the eldest," so it was spoken by the God.
O son, having thus accepted what was spoken by Śambhu, O Nārada, I went to see the top of that very liṅga.
O divine sage, as those two deluded souls proceeded for a thousand years, a vast amount of time surely passed for them, their minds filled with wonder.
Without having seen the root of Hari, that god returned once more;
O Sage, at that time I too returned just as Hari had done.
Having gone to him alone for refuge and having praised him with various hymns,
Mahādeva, becoming pleased, spoke these words.
The Lord said: "O Mādhava, by my grace, become superior to all;
you alone shall be the foremost among my devotees, for you indeed are worthy of worship and honor."
"O Hara, worship me in the *liṅga*, for I indeed assume the form of the *liṅga*. From this point forward, there is no doubt that all other dwellers of heaven [shall do likewise]. (38)
Through the worship of the Liṅga, I swiftly destroy ignorance;
for those devoted to the adoration of the Liṅga, there is no fear born of saṃsāra. (39)
Having thus granted me a boon, Maheśvara said to me:
"O Viraja, I shall grant you [another]; accept this most excellent boon. (40)
O Grandfather, be honored by the world of moving and unmoving beings;
O Creator, receive the four Vedas with your four mouths.
Having thus granted the boon to us both, the God of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow,
the Lord of the Universe and self-luminous light, vanished in an instant.
From that time forward, Viṣṇu and the other gods, the Daityas and Dānavas, Gandharvas, sages, Siddhas, Yakṣas, Nāgas, and Kinnaras [all honored him]. || 43 ||
O Sage, having worshipped the supreme Liṅga, they attained the highest perfection;
there is no other means of ultimate welfare in these three worlds than the worship of the Liṅga.
Having understood this, O celestial sage, you yourself should be devoted to the worship of the Liṅga in sacred fields, at holy fords, and in forests and groves. (45)
Those divine marks established by the gods and asuras, O Nārada, should indeed be beheld by the wise with faith alone. (46)
In this way, they too become partakers of liberation through the grace of Śambhu.
Nārada said:
"O Brahmin, tell me of those divine places in which Śiva is present, and describe their majesty in its entirety."
Brahmā said:
"O Nārada, I shall tell you here of the majesty of the divine liṅgas and of the sacred fords; listen, O destroyer of sins, to that which destroys evil."
That supreme form of Śiva, through devotion to Śiva, is the Lord of the worlds—
Nārāyaṇa himself directly manifest, as well as I and other deities. (50)
It truly dwells in the ocean; thus it is remembered as the King of Tīrthas.
Jambūdvīpa is of great merit, and within it lies the salt-water sea.
Sin committed during a day and night perishes by the mere sight [of it];
having touched it, the ocean surely destroys the sin of three nights.
Sin committed during seven nights is destroyed by mere sprinkling;
that produced during a fortnight by drinking [the water], and that of two fortnights by bathing. 53.
He who constantly bathes in the salt ocean during the seasons, on the eighth day, on festival days, and throughout the rainy season before the sun has risen; || 54 ||
Having fasted for one night at the time of the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), the fruit of giving a tawny cow to a learned Vedic scholar is certain for him.
Having bathed on the day of Vyatīpāta, on the Chidrā days, during the solstices, and at the equinoxes, one obtains the fruit of having given a hundred pieces of gold.
And at the beginning of a Yuga, a man who bathes according to the rules in the salt ocean indeed obtains the same fruit as that which comes from giving a thousand cows at Kurukṣetra. || 57 ||
A mortal certainly obtains that fruit of the gift of land, as well as whatever other gifts are renowned in the worlds by the wise. (58)
One obtains the fruit of those [meritorious deeds] during the eclipses of the moon and the sun;
O Nārada, such a person becomes purified, as if liberated from the submarine fire (vaḍavānala).
Therefore, there is no sacred ford (tīrtha) superior to this upon the surface of the earth;
[namely] the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, Revā, Candrabhāgā, and Vedikā.
Where these rivers meet, one should perform a bath in the great ocean;
whatever terrible sins there may be, such as the killing of a learned Brahmin (bhrūṇahatyā) and others—[all these are destroyed].
They perish in an instant by the power of that union;
and the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices is certainly attained. (62)
On the shore of the ocean is a supreme, unassailable Liṅga of splendor,
where in ancient times, O child, seventy million sages attained perfection.
From that time forth, O Nārada, I am known by the name Saptakoṭīśvara;
I am the god Nārāyaṇa, the eternal Moon, and the Sun.
The Maruts, the Munis, the Siddhas, those who move through the sky, and those who move upon the earth—
having worshipped the supreme Liṅga, Śiva Saptakoṭīśvara.
O Nārada, they attained supreme perfection in that liṅga.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of the Worship of Śiva and Other Matters," in the *Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa* of the *Śrī Brahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka.
Brahmā said:
Those men who behold Mahākāla in Ujjayinī shall attain the supreme world, having gone to which one does not grieve. (1)
That is called the divine linga of Mahākāla;
by touching that linga, [the devotees] went to Śiva with their very bodies.
Having understood that, I placed there a stone in the form of a cock at Mahākāla; from that, he became Kukkuṭeśvara.
In that very same beautiful city, there is one known as Śūleśvara;
by the mere sight of him, one obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice. || 4 ||
To the east of Śūleśvara is the supreme Liṅga, Oṃkāra.
There, with a restrained mind and concentrated focus, one should perform the ritual bath.
On the second day, on the third day, or even on the tenth, O Nārada.
If, within a fortnight, a month, or six months, one beholds Śaṅkara in a dream,
one attains sublime knowledge that is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
He who, having bathed in the pool with a concentrated mind, beholds the Oṃkāra-liṅga,
attains the fruit of a thousand initiations and goes to the supreme goal.
There, Śiva was propitiated by the sage Agastya through austerity,
and the Blessed One manifested himself under the name Agastyeśvara.
By the sight of that [place], one is freed from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
right there is the holy ford named Śaktibheda, frequented by sages.
Having bathed there, the person who beholds the Blessed One is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Skanda. || 11 ||
There are tens of millions of sacred fords (tīrthas) all around Ujjayinī;
the entire majesty of them was spoken by Skanda in the Skanda Purāṇa.
O celestial sage, at Kurukṣetra there is Maheśvara named Sthāṇu;
it was there that I performed penance and attained supreme Brahmanhood.
O twice-born one, the Vālakhilyas and others attained supreme perfection there;
formerly, Pulaha resided there in the abode of Sthāṇu like a gnat.
Having died, he enjoyed various divine pleasures according to his desires;
at the end of that, by the power of Sthāṇu’s delusion, he was born as my son.
Where the Great Lord named Sthāṇu, who embodies all the gods, resides;
a person who worships him even once shall attain the state of Śiva.
O best of sages, Prayāga is renowned as the king of sacred fords (tīrtharāja);
there, the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is world-famous.
Having bathed there and gone to heaven, and having enjoyed pleasures according to his desire,
he dwells where Maheśvara, the supreme benefactor of all, resides.
By visiting it, the best of men attains inexhaustible light;
this other supreme and secret sacred site is known as Gayātīrtha.
O Śambhu, wherever the feet of the Blessed One are firmly established,
there the ancestors attain imperishable satisfaction through the offering of funeral rice-balls (piṇḍa).
If a man, having bathed in the Mahānadī, should touch the foot of Rudra,
he attains the world of Śiva and rejoices together with his ancestors. || 21 ||
Mahākāla is a great sacred ford (tīrtha), beloved of the Destroyer of Time;
there too, the God of Gods placed his foot upon the earth.
Having bathed there, the wise man who beholds with devotion the foot of the Lord of Pārvatī shall attain the state of Śiva. (23)
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Narration of the Greatness of Mahākāla," in the Śrī Saura Upapurāṇa of the Śrī Brahmapurāṇa, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 67 ||
Generally, those desiring the fruit of the gods should fast at a sacred ford (tīrtha) until the end of the day;
for the great seers have declared that the root of the ancestral rite (pitrya) is for the sake of pleasing the ancestors. || 1 ||
If that [lunar day] upon which the sun sets lasts for three muhūrtas,
they consider that lunar day to be complete for all religious duties.

The eighth, eleventh, sixth, third, and fourteenth lunar days should be observed when joined with the following day; the others [the fifth, seventh, ninth, and twelfth] are joined with the preceding day. (3)
Likewise, Vṛhattapā, Rambhā, Sāvitrī, Vaṭapaitṛkī,
and Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, along with Bhūtā, should be observed on the lunar day that is present at the time of the rite.
In the case of a self-manifested (svāyaṃbhū) liṅga, one made of stone, one made of jewels, one fashioned from mercury,
or a liṅga consecrated by a perfected being (siddha), Caṇḍa has no authority.
The Vāṇaliṅga, Svayambhū, and likewise Candrakānti—
by consuming the food offering (naivedya) of Śambhu, one gains merit equal to that of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Vṛṣa, Caṇḍa, Nṛpa, Caitra, Somasūtra, Punarvasu; Caṇḍa, Somasūtra, again Caṇḍa, and again Punarvasu. (7)
Alkali, fermented gruel, a bronze vessel, lentils,
chickpeas, and sesame oil— these six are said to destroy the potency of mantras.
Having placed it on the left side and grasped it with the left hand,
and holding it in the right hand, one should offer a handful of water into the oil.
*Kakha gajha saṃśita puṣru*: there is no conclusion of a chapter here;
rather, the portion beginning with "For what reason, O Blessed One," and so forth—which was included in this manuscript as the sixty-ninth chapter—is actually a continuation of this very [chapter].
The syllable *gu* signifies darkness, while the syllable *ru* signifies obstruction;
because it obstructs darkness, the word *guru* is so designated. (10)
One who abandons the guru meets death; one who abandons the mantra encounters poverty. By abandoning both the guru and the mantra, even a perfected one (siddha) shall go to hell.
One [grain] should be offered toward the sun at midday;
at both twilights, one should throw water three times for the destruction of the Asuras.

One should not make two brothers officiate together, nor should one make a father and son do so; one should not make one who maintains no sacred fire officiate, nor should one make the husband of a pregnant woman officiate.
"One is considered to be without the sacred fire as long as one does not obtain a wife;
one possesses the fire when joined with a wife—thus Manu has declared."
A prostration with only one hand, or even a single circumambulation,
as well as service performed at the wrong time instead of the proper time, causes the merit of a year to perish.
In an assembly hall, in a sacrificial shed, in a temple, or in the presence of a guru;
And each individual salutation destroys previously accumulated merit. || 16 ||
Cow’s milk, cow’s ghee, mung beans, sesame seeds, and barley—these are known as the non-alkaline group; others are considered the alkaline group.
Flies, mosquitoes, prostitutes, beggars, mice, astrologers, and village headmen—these seven are consumers of others' food. (18)

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Determination of Lunar Days and Other Matters," in the *Śrīsaura*, a minor Purāṇa (*Upapurāṇa*) belonging to the *Śrībrahmapurāṇa*, within the dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka. || 68 ||
Nārada said: By what cause is the Blessed One Maheśvara the Time of time?
O Blessed One, O Lotus-born, I wish to hear; tell it to me.
Brahmā said: Formerly there was an excellent sage known by the name Śveta;
he would resort to the waters of sacred fords (tīrtha) as well as observe the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama).
The peaceful leader of the Māheśvaras, devoted to the worship of Mahādeva— Kāla, terrifying with staff in hand, has come to take him away.
Having seen Kāla, that best of Brahmins, his senses agitated by fear,
touched that linga with both hands while meditating upon Maheśvara.
O Sage, Kāla spoke laughingly to Śveta, the best of sages:
"Out of fear of me, everyone practices celibacy and austerities."
Those devoted to their own duties praise the giving of gifts at sacred fords.
Out of fear of me, the gods perform sacrifices and various kinds of rituals;
therefore, arise, for you have fallen under my power as one bound by my noose.
"O bull among sages, today I do not see even a donor [of such a gift];
thus have I heard your words, O Nārada, regarding Time. (8)
Then, terrified, he spoke to Yama, the wielder of the noose who appeared formidable: "How can you deign to lead me away from here, when I am devoted to the worship of the Lord? (9)
"Tell me, why should those devoted to the worship of Śiva have fear of you?
Being addressed thus, Yama, out of anger, seized the eminent sage by his neck and began to throttle him.
While he was quickly meditating upon Maheśvara with very firm bonds,
then the god Mahādeva, the sustainer of the three worlds, manifested himself.
Upon seeing the Lord of the gods, the sage was then filled with joy;
Śaṅkara then said, "Release my devotee Kāla."
"My devotee is indeed independent; how can he be led away by you?
The son of the Sun has transgressed that which was spoken by the God of gods. (13)
